Sports.title: Gary Lineker claims Premier League transfer could cost Arsenal Champions League
Sports.content:
Gary Lineker claims Premier League transfer could cost Arsenal Champions League

Arsenal are looking to take the final step in the Champions League but Gary Lineker reckons Barcelona, off the back of edging Rodri, could outdo them in Europe

View 2 Images Gary Lineker still fears Arsenal could come up short in the Champions League (Image: Getty)

Gary Lineker fears Arsenal's lack of a superstar could ultimately cost them in the Champions League and expects the arrival of Rodri makes Barcelona a genuine challenger.

‌



The Gunners will play in Europe as the Premier League champions and have reached the quarter-finals, semi-finals and then final in successive seasons. Mikel Arteta now wants his side to take the final step after last season's heartbreaking loss to PSG on penalties.

‌



Arsenal began their Champions League campaign with a win in Napoli, but Lineker fears the north Londoners still lack the out and out superstar who can help lead them to a first ever European Cup.

‌



Instead he feels as if Barcelona, who already had Lamine Yamal in their ranks, could prove the biggest challengers to Arsenal. They've just added Rodri from Manchester City for £65million and the midfielder has shown himself to have a winning mentality and be one of the world's best performers.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



Lineker said on The Rest is Football podcast: "Arsenal will be one of the favourites but I don’t think overall they’ve got quite the superstars that some of the other big guns in Europe have. I do think Barcelona might be quite tasty and take some beating this season now they’ve got Rodri in there as well in that crucial position."

Rodri heads to Barcelona off the back of a trophy-laden period at City, who continued to thwart Arsenal up until last season. The Spaniard has also just been named the best player at the World Cup, where he lifted the trophy.

The Gunners' pursuit of a world class forward was well documented. They eyed up Vinicius Jnr before he decided to extend his stay at Real Madrid, and then they were heavily linked with Julian Alvarez. Micah Richards believes the Atletico Madrid star would've been the final piece of the jigsaw.

‌



View 2 Images Rodri's move to Barcelona makes them an even more formidable outfit (Image: Omar Arnau/Quality Sport Images/Getty Images)

"I’ve got no doubts about them in the Premier League but I’m not sure about Arsenal in the Champions League," he said. "If you go back to last season they were actually favourites early doors because of how good they are defensively. I think for them to be real force in Europe, Julian Alvarez would have been perfect.

"I just feel at times that for Arsenal to take their game to the next level, they would be almost complete if they had that superstar striker. Julian Alvarez would have been perfect for that position."

Sports.title: Who are Sabah? Champions League minnows led by ex-Man Utd youth coach who won quiz show
Sports.content:
Sabah FK didn’t even exist as a football club 10 years ago. But tonight they will make their Champions League debut against Manchester United.

The Azerbaijan Premier League champions have already faced a long journey just to make it into the league phase. That’s nothing compared to the story of manager Valdas Dambrauskas, who turned a Who Wants to Be a Millionaire prize into a managerial career, which also saw him work with United.

Sabah, who were established in 2017, won their first-ever league title last season. They have come through four rounds of qualifying, beginning with a victory over Welsh champions TNS.

Finnish side KuPS and AGF of Denmark were also put to the sword before the Azeri side won a dramatic play-off against Israeli title holders Hapoel Be’er Sheva. They left it very late, though, scoring in the fourth minute of added time to force extra-time before clinching a 6-4 aggregate victory.

‌



FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Man Utd's 2027 transfer plan already in tatters as priority target agrees deal READ MORE :

Man Utd REJECTED chance to sign Kylian Mbappe after Ryan Giggs scouting mission READ MORE :

Their Lithuanian boss Dambrauskas cut his managerial teeth in England after winning £725 on ‘Millionaire’ in 2002 - equivalent to six months' wages in his homeland at the time - and putting it towards his studies at London Metropolitan University. He studied sports science and coaching on the Holloway Road, a short walk from Arsenal's Emirates Stadium, where he will return with his team in January.

"From the day I arrived, it was all about the dream to become a football coach," he told Flashscore in August. "It went in stages. First to learn the language. Then to 

View 3 Images Sabah boss Valdas Dambrauskas coached in England at the start of his career (Image: Getty Images)

‌



"I went to every possible course or conference to improve myself. Then I started to dream and plan how to get a job in professional football. I knew in England it would be impossible, but I would get a chance in my home country."

Early in his career, Dambrauskas took on youth coaching roles with a number of English clubs, including a spell at United’s soccer schools. The 49-year-old then won titles in Lithuania and Bulgaria before leading Sabah to a domestic double in his first season.

He credits a spell working with Brentford for helping set him on the path for success. “I understood that to be a professional football coach in England and move up, to be a head coach or manager, was impossible," he said

“With my Lithuanian passport, with the country’s name that nobody can pronounce, with my surname that nobody can pronounce and, on top of that, I was never a professional player. But I knew that my experience from Brentford, as well as my coaching badges, could give me a chance somewhere else."

‌



View 3 Images Joy-Lance Mickels top-scored for Sabah last season (Image: Getty Images)

Watch Man United vs Sabah on TNT Sports This article contains affiliate links, we will receive a commission on any sales we generate from it. Learn more from £25.99 TNT Sports Get TNT Sports here Product Description Manchester United host Sabah FK in their opening Champions League fixture on September 10 . Fans can watch the game live on TNT Sports via HBO Max or Prime Video's TNT Sports channel.

His team’s success owes a lot to Joy-Lance Mickels, the German-born Rwanda forward who bagged 23 goals last season. The 32-year-old is in his second spell at the club, having returned after a year with Al-Faisaly in Saudi Arabia.

Other stars of last season’s title run include Aaron Malouda, son of former Chelsea and France winger Florent, who left for Basel after scoring nine times last term. However, United’s opponents have needed to be creative when it comes to their summer recruitment.

‌



Among their new additions this term are South African defender Aden McCarthy, signed from Kaizer Chiefs, and former Sheffield United winger Christian Nwachukwu. They have also added Younes Lachaab on loan from Lille, with the 21-year-old having already turned out for his parent club in the Champions League.

Dambrauskas’ team scored 75 goals in 33 league games last term, and his attacking philosophy has been refreshing. He has pointed to Arsene Wenger and Marcelo Bielsa as inspirations, as well as former United interim boss Ralf Rangnick.

“If one word can describe my way, it would be domination,” he said after his team booked their place in the Champions League. “I am not afraid to take risks. The best result for me would be 4-3 with four different players scoring and four different players giving an assist.”

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino on Tottenham return: 'I'd have managed Spurs in the Championship'
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino says he would have taken the Tottenham job - even if they were in the Championship.

United States boss Pochettino confirmed he did get an approach to go back to Spurs last season when the club was stuck in a relegation scrap. But Pochettino insisted he was fully committed to leading the US into the World Cup and has subsequently signed a contract until 2030 because he enjoys the role so much.

When asked if he would have taken the Spurs job in the Championship, said: “Yes, of course. Tottenham? Yes, of course. It’s the only club that always I am open to help. Whatever division. Another club, no. But Tottenham, yes.”

Former Spurs boss Pochettino, who had five years at Tottenham and is still adored by the club’s fans, has said previously that one day he would like to go back.

‌



But Pochettino says the timing has never been right - and that was the case when he got the call after Thomas Frank had been sacked. “Yeah but in this moment they called everyone, they called all the coaches! Free and not free!”

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

Tottenham had a brief and disastrous spell with Igor Tudor in charge and now Roberto De Zerbi has been charged with reviving the club’s fortunes. But Pochettino, having initially admitted he would like to return to club management, has become further entrenched with his job as US boss and he fell deeper in love with the role during the World Cup.

Pochettino, together with his staff including trusted assistant Jesus Perez, helped joint hosts US top their Group and reach the last 16 before they lost to Belgium. The Ex-Spurs boss says he decided to stay with the US because of the support from the federation and also from the fans during the tournament.

‌



Pochettino said: “One thing that changed our mind: the people. The human beings in the federation. Because before the start of the World Cup we met the whole board, the federation board in New York, before starting working with the players in Atlanta.

“And they offered us to do four more years. I said 'yeah but if we lose all the games in the World Cup…’ But they said: ‘No, we trust in you, we trust in your job, we trust in your vision, in the way that you behave. You stayed here when it was possible to move somewhere else.’

View 2 Images Pochettino remains a popular figure at Tottenham (Image: Darko Vojinovic/AP/REX/Shutterstock)

“When we finished the World Cup, our vision was completely different because we created something. The fans were amazing. The people were so excited. The players changed their mindset. After one week, the federation called and we said: ‘we are ready for it.’”

‌



His passion is obvious for the job. He still has affection for Tottenham and even sympathy for former chairman Daniel Levy after he was ousted. “I think he feels like [I did] when I was sacked! Now he knows the feeling,” said Pochettino. “I am sorry for him.”

Pochettino even admitted that he might consider the England job one day in the future. Yes, even as an Argentinian. Especially after the bad blood following the World Cup semi final.

He said: “One thing I don’t want because the USA guys will kill me, if the headline is: ’Mauricio will consider English job.’ No, it is like I am considering it now. One day if I am free.

“For me it is because we are very similar in the way we feel the passion of football. I think we are very similar. I love the countryside, I love the farms and here it is amazing. I think you respect all the things that I also grow up with in my country.

‌



“It is true it can be controversial because an Argentinian guy is thinking to maybe one day defend the flag of England and we were involved in a war…"

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino sticks boot in on Mike Dean over 'stupid' antics after backlash
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino sticks boot in on Mike Dean over 'stupid' antics after backlash

Mauricio Pochettino says Mike Dean made a mistake in making a joke at "sensitive time" following the recent backlash over comments made by the ex-Premier League ref

View 2 Images Tottenham boss Mauricio Pochettino had to be held back (Image: GETTY )

Mauricio Pochettino says Mike Dean has a habit of saying “stupid” things - and is being “controversial” to stay in the spotlight.

‌



Former Premier League referee Dean caused outrage last week when he said on a podcast that he would play his own games during matches to see how long he could go without blowing the whistle or leaving the centre circle.

‌



Former Tottenham boss Pochettino was involved in one high-profile bust-up with Dean when the referee turned TV pundit made a comment which enraged the Spurs coaching staff as they left the pitch following a defeat at Burnley in February 2019.

‌



Pochettino admits the latest Dean controversy has not surprised him given his history with the official who is now a regular on Sky Sports. The United States boss said: “What he said was a stupid thing. But our code is we never talk about what happened on the pitch. It's like what happened in Las Vegas - stays in Las Vegas.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

“But in that moment we were under pressure. The perception was ‘Tottenham need to win something.’ It's true that we were a little bit under pressure.

‌



“We were disappointed in that game. One stupid thing, it makes you react so quick. It's not that we cannot deal with it.

“But it was like in my position, I would never do that. How do you say? Make a joke? I'm not going to be the funny guy to do some joke if you are under pressure in your job.

“He was controversial. His character now - he's showing how he was. People maybe like him, people maybe do not. Maybe now he's playing a little bit with the personality, and to try to be funny, and to create some controversial things.

‌



“He's putting some salt, pepper, like a chili, some condiments (on a steak). He needs to understand that ‘OK, let’s not put gasoline on to the fire.’

“It was always funny to be with him. We had a good relationship. It was only this action, that situation, that was tough because we were in a very sensitive moment.”

View 2 Images Pochettino is back Harry Kane for the Ballon d'Or

‌



Meanwhile, Pochettino says this should be “Harry Kane’s time” to win the Ballon D'Or. He is backing the England captain to be crowned the best player in the world, with Kane is the bookies’ favourite to get the award next month after being nominated along with the likes of Kylian Mbappe, Rodri and Lionel Messi.

Pochettino claims Kane’s 73 goal haul last season means he is the most deserving candidate in this year’s voting. And he says Luka Modric, Fabio Cannavaro and Karim Benzema all deserved it as the crowning glory in their career and Kane should get the same respect even if Bayern and England did not get past the semi final in the Champions League and World Cup respectively.

United States boss Pochettino said: “My wish… I hope yes. I think he deserves it as the reward for his career and for all what he has done in football.

‌



“I don’t know if he is going to be punished for the World Cup or the Champions League because he played in the semi final and the semi final. Maybe he will be punished, I don’t know.

“But, for me, it’s Harry Kane’s time. It’s not clear today who is the No1 in the world who should win. In the past, it was more clear. I think he deserves it. He deserves it in his career like Modric or Cannavaro. Benzema. I think if I pick one then it’s Harry Kane.”

Sports.title: Liverpool news: £130million transfer opportunity as top replacement option emerges
Sports.content:
Liverpool news: £130million transfer opportunity as top replacement option emerges

Liverpool could already have their eye on another marquee signing

View 3 Images Andoni Iraola has already witnessed a key departure at Anfield (Image: Getty Images)

Liverpool could look to pounce on a transfer opportunity next summer after missing out on key targets last month. The Reds forked out almost £200million on the signings of Jeremy Jacquet, Victor Munoz and Bradley Barcola in Andoni Iraola's first transfer market as Reds boss.

‌



The summer marked a new era for the Premier League giants, but could also be looked at as a missed opportunity. Liverpool attempted to recruit Yankuba Minteh and Ismaila Sarr last month as potential replacements for Mohamed Salah and were knocked back by Brighton and Crystal Palace in their efforts.

‌



However, their failure to acquire the wingers could lead the Reds to chase a target that could cost £130m. Meanwhile, a leading option to replace a key departure from Anfield has emerged.

‌



FOLLOW OUR LIVERPOOL FB PAGE! Latest Reds news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Rayan opportunity

Liverpool may boast an impressive forward line, but they do so without having signed an out-and-out right-winger this past summer. The Reds signed Victor Munoz and Bradley Barcola to bolster their attacking options, but failed to bring in a like-for-like replacement for Mohamed Salah, after deals for Minteh and Sarr fell through in the final days of the window.

Trent Alexander-Arnold and Curtis Jones destroyed by foreign media after Liverpool reunion READ MORE :

Jamie Carragher leaves Micah Richards in stitches with bankruptcy joke on live TV READ MORE :

The long-term successor to the Egyptian icon could come in the form of Bournemouth star Rayan. The Brazil international will have a £130m release clause able to be triggered from next summer, the Athletic report.

‌



The 20-year-old was brought to the Premier League in January under Iraola and impressed heavily with five goals scored and two assists provided in 15 games. The Cherries are expected to decline any approach for the winger before the release clause becomes active.

View 3 Images Rayan could be on the move next year (Image: Getty)

Sporting director replacement option

The exit of Richard Hughes from Liverpool was announced last week, with the former sporting director opting to leave Anfield a year before his contract was set to expire. The departure of the Scotsman leaves a sizeable gap in the Reds' footballing operations.

‌



FSG technical director, Julian Ward, who previously was the club's sporting director in 2022 after the departure of Michael Edwards, has been named as a strong contender to succeed Hughes.

View 3 Images Julian Ward is currently FSG's technical director (Image: Liverpool FC via Getty Images)

According to The Athletic, Ward is among the leading names to take over the role, with current assistant sporting director David Woodfine and director of football development Pedro Marques also being named as possible internal options. However, Ornstein refused to rule out a possible external hire.

Sports.title: Garcia reveals why he snubbed face-off with Benn
Sports.content:
Ryan Garcia offered no apologies for missing Tuesday's face-off with Conor Benn, adding it was "funny" to see the British fighter pretending to square off against his dad, Nigel.

Garcia is set to embark on the first defence of his WBC welterweight title against Benn at the T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas on Saturday night.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Benn hit out at Garcia for 'bottling it' after American failed to show up for face-off in Las Vegas (Credit: @Zuffa Boxing)

Earlier in the week, the pair were due to meet at the Mandalay Bay Hotel for a media event, but the American fighter did not show up, with Benn subsequently claiming his opponent had "bottled it".

During a press conference on Wednesday, Garcia said: "I wasn't there because I didn't want to be.

"Look, we have a face-off at the press conference [Thursday], then at the weigh-ins [Friday] and then a final face-off literally in the ring when the refs give you instructions.

"I've been doing this for so long. I've had fight weeks in Vegas before. I've never had to do a face-off on [Tuesday]. So I have a routine to do, and it's just something I didn't want to do.''

"It was funny seeing him [Benn] staring at himself."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Benn is relishing his status as the underdog ahead of his fight against Garcia

Benn, meanwhile, believes Garcia's absence let the fans down.

"Ultimately it's disrespectful to the public because they deserve it,'' he said on Wednesday.

"The public deserves us giving you guys the best. This is what we do. This is what we're here for.''

Benn: Weight cut dragged me through the pits of hell

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Benn said he had been 'dragged through the pits of hell' in trying to make weight for the fight

Benn comes into this fight as the underdog after stepping up to middleweight to fight Chris Eubank Jr. He lost his first fight against his rival in April 2025, before avenging that loss later that November. He comes into this weekend's bout after beating Regis Prograis at a 150lbs catchweight in April.

Should Benn make the weight at Friday's weigh-in, this will be the first time that he has fought at the welterweight limit in over four years, with his last fight at under 147lbs coming against Chris van Heerden in April 2022.

The 29-year-old hit back at those who have doubted his ability to make the weight, but added he felt like he had been "dragged through the pits of hell and had a fight with satan" during his preparations.

"A lot of people said I couldn't make the weight, watch me do it," Benn said, adding he went through 15 weeks of dieting before the fight.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player The pair have exchanged a war of words in the build-up to Saturday's world title fight

"I've done it, and that's it."

Benn added that this would be his last fight at 147lbs and is hoping to move up in weight after this to 160 or 168lbs.

Garcia said he didn't want to hear any excuses from Benn after the fight regarding his weight cut.

"All we can do is go by past experience," Garcia said. "He cut back down to 150lbs to fight Regis Prograis. We have seen how he bloated up. Now he has an extra three pounds to go. I don't want to hear any excuses. He doesn't have a rehydration clause.

"I don't want to be hearing any crybaby s*** from him. He's trying to set up a narrative, because when he gets his a** whopped, he'll say: 'I was drained'. I'm about to beat his a**, it doesn't matter how much he weighs."

Sports.title: Park Hill and May Hill clashes feature as Leger meeting begins at Doncaster
Sports.content:
Doncaster's St Leger meeting gets under way on Thursday, all live on Sky Sports Racing, with a pair of classy Group Two contests taking centre stage.

3.00 Doncaster - Consent and Danielle headline strong field

A top-class field has assembled for the Group Two Betfred Park Hill Fillies' Stakes where Consent and Danielle feature among nine runners.

Danielle, fourth in this contest last year, ended the campaign with an emphatic nine-length win in Listed company here in November. A winner of the Bronte Cup on her return this season, she disappointed at Goodwood and will be hoping to bounce back under William Buick.

Consent finished a neck second in this race last season before landing Group One honours in the Prix de Royallieu. She has struggled to match those highs since and connections reach for the cheekpieces.

Andrew Balding's Prizeland took the Galtres Stakes at York with plenty to spare and rates an each-way player, while Waardah will enjoy any easing of the ground. She finished ahead of the top pair at Goodwood and must be feared if able to repeat the feat in a first-time hood.

Fairy Glen was only beaten half a length in the Prix Vicomtesse Vigier in May and would have claims if fit enough on her return.

Image: Danielle returns to Doncaster on Thursday

3.35 Doncaster - Unbeaten Musical Times heads up in grade

Unbeaten Musical Times heads up in grade for this Group Two Betfred May Hill Stakes.

The Charlie Appleby-trained filly arrives having impressed on both starts to date and tops the betting under William Buick. Having outpointed the reopposing Scommessa Sicura on her debut at Newmarket, she oozes quality when landing the odds at Yarmouth and deserves a crack at this better contest.

Scommessa Sicura has finished in the top two on her five starts to date and produced a career-best when second a Salisbury last month.

Joseph O'Brien saddles Ballyskeagh who ran a huge race to finish runner-up in a Group Three at Curragh over the mile and that gives her solid place claims, while Speckles was fifth that day and may improve again.

1.50 Doncaster - Night In Vegas spearheads big field

All eyes will be on Night In Vegas as he bids to plunge another huge pot in this Weatherbys £300,000 2-Y-O Stakes.

Eve Johnson Houghton's colt sets the standard having finished fifth in the Coventry at Royal Ascot before landing the £200,000 Tattersalls Somerville Auction Stakes on his last start. That entitles him to be a short-priced favourite, and he is weighted to go close.

Plenty have chances including George Boughey's Shadwell colt Mithaaly. He stepped up on his first two starts to win comfortably at Windsor and should be monitored in the market.

Zigazig Ah took the Weatherbys Super Sprint at Newbury back in July before failing to fire at Goodwood. She chased home Night In Vegas at Newmarket and looks capable of better.

Joseph O'Brien's experienced Seven Nation Army completes the shortlist.

Image: The St Leger is the headline race on Saturday at Doncaster

Elsewhere on Thursday…

The Sky Sports Racing cameras also head to Lingfield and Worcester. Marquessofanglesey has hit the crossbar a few times now and may make that experience finally count at Lingield (3.15) under Rob Hornby.

Over at Worcester, Harry Cobden gets aboard former Cheltenham Festival runner-up Crebilly, taking on hat-trick seeker Youdecide and Snipe for the Skelton team (2.10).

There is British interest at ParisLongchamp in the Group Three Prix Gladiateur as Midak represents Ian Williams, taking on former Group One winner Double Major.

Sports.title: Zverev's US Open rocky road turns into smooth sailing to the semi-finals
Sports.content:
Alexander Zverev ‌took another big step towards a second Grand Slam ‌title by beating Dutchman Botic van de ​Zandschulp 6-2 7-5 6-1 to reach the US Open semi-finals.

The 29-year-old French Open champion and Wimbledon runner-up got off to a slow start in his campaign at Flushing ​Meadows but has steadily found his range.

Zverev played five-set matches in each of the first two matches, but he has won his last three in straight sets and is the only man to reach all four Grand Slam semi-finals this year.

Into his 13th major semi-final, Zverev will face Karen Khachanov in the last four for a spot in Sunday's final.

"I ‌think you saw in the first two rounds, I really didn't play well," said Zverev, who has spent 16 hours and 40 minutes on court, the most by any man en route to the semi-finals at the US Open since 1991.

"In other tournaments I would be out in the first round, but here I can fight back and play best of ​five sets, play four-and-a-half hours. I've started playing ⁠better throughout the tournament and I'm ⁠definitely happy to be in the semi-finals here."

The German was far from steady on serve early ‌on at Arthur Ashe Stadium, coughing up five double faults in an erratic start, but Dutchman Van de Zandschulp leaked forehand errors to ‌allow the top seed to break in the fifth game and then take the first set.

Van de Zandschulp regrouped in the second set and came close to levelling the contest, but Zverev absorbed ⁠the pressure and reeled off three games in a ​row towards the end as the momentum ​swung firmly in the German's favour.

Zverev, the 2020 runner-up, fired ​an overhead smash to break early in the third ⁠set and cruised home from there to reach his third semi-final in New York.

Sports.title: Poch: I hope to return to Premier League in future
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino has always been good company - warm, engaging and likeable. Having had a few weeks to reset away from the spotlight, there were enthusiastic hugs all round for the Sky Sports News team as we all swapped summer stories. His, though, has been rather busier than ours.

The former Tottenham boss guided the USA team to the last 16 of the World Cup, where the host nation's dreams of victory came to a crashing halt against Belgium, but that barely tells the story of an extraordinary few weeks for the Argentine.

There was Donald Trump - there was always going to be - and the changing-room team talk. There was Trump, FIFA and Folarin Balogun's suspension of his suspension, and along the way, Pochettino became something of a fashion icon.

Then a few weeks later, another significant headline - Pochettino had, a little surprisingly perhaps, signed for four more years with the USA.

Where to start? I smile before jesting, and Pochettino just laughs and says he's ready. His reflections on the World Cup seem like as good a place to get going.

Image: Pochettino had to cope with the Folarin Balogun suspension saga at the World Cup

For Pochettino, the biggest takeaway is how much he and his coaching staff, including his long-term lieutenant Jesus Perez, have learned.

"We are much better coaches now," he insists. It is revealing because the World Cup has reinforced his appetite to keep learning and evolving. He talks about the importance of the smallest details, the difficulty of getting every decision right and the challenge of translating his ideas to a group of players who spend far less time together than a club side. He adds, "Everything needs to be perfect."

There were times during the tournament when life must have felt a little wild, I suggest. There's managing at the World Cup, then there's managing at a home World Cup for a nation whose President rather enjoys the spotlight. Unsurprisingly, Pochettino chooses his words carefully, focusing on the support and backing Trump gave the side.

At the time, he was asked about his role in getting the Balogun suspension suspended, and he admitted the "politics and manipulation" did overshadow the game against Belgium. Pochettino understood the anger around the situation, but his role was much simpler - "If you pay attention to the noise, you become crazy." FIFA allowed Balogun to play and he says, "When the letter arrived the day before the game confirming Balogun was available, the decision was straightforward."

Balogun has been in the headlines again over the past few weeks after his proposed move from Monaco to Everton collapsed late on Deadline Day. Pochettino has not spoken to him yet. He has deliberately given him some space because he knows it would have been a difficult situation. He would, he says, have liked to see Balogun playing in the Premier League. Instead, he remains at Monaco, and Pochettino hopes he can get himself into a good place.

'I hope to return to Premier League in future'

Image: Mauricio Pochettino has been in charge of the USA since September 2024

There was of course the fashion too. Pochettino has always taken his style seriously, but I am not sure even he could have imagined the impact his touchline navy ensemble would have had. It created its own headlines - not least because Wayne Rooney went out and bought it. "I saw him. He looked good on him, like a top coach," he laughs.

It really was a summer that had it all.

Then, as the footballing world moved on from the World Cup, the rumours linking Pochettino to a number of clubs looking for a manager began. But that speculation was short-lived with the news that he was staying with the USA.

If Pochettino sees out his contract until 2030, six years away from club football feels a long time. Is that his Premier League story over? He disagrees, and for him his desire is not only to be back in English football, but to compete for honours.

"I have the ambition," he says. "My dream now is to be in the USA for four years, but after that, why not? We are still young, and I think coming back is always my goal; to win the Premier League, to be in the Premier League and to build a project with the possibility of winning."

"I love the football here. I think to have the chance again is one of my wishes and I hope that happens."

Did Poch come close to Spurs return?

Image: Pochettino led co-hosts US to the last 16 of the 2026 World Cup

That unfinished business takes me back to an interview I did with Pochettino 18 months or so ago - he spoke about wanting to one day return to Spurs. At the time, Tottenham were struggling under Ange Postecoglou. Since then, Postecoglou has gone, and Thomas Frank and Igor Tudor have arrived and departed as the club got perilously close to the drop.

So did that call to rescue the club ever come? Pochettino says of a return: "Always I say, one day, why not?"

So was it ever a possibility this time? Pochettino says: "People talk and maybe we receive some approach, but it never was close." Not this time then.

What about some of those other jobs - at one point AC Milan looked like a possible destination.

"We were not open during the World Cup to talk with different clubs that were interested," he says.

But were there clubs interested? "Yes, always," he says as if that is the norm. "Yes, always have different, you know, options," he teases.

I try again - did any of them come close to taking your attention? "We never gave the opportunity to be close. We always closed the door before it got close."

Poch assesses old clubs Spurs and Chelsea

Image: Pochettino (left) and assistant Jesus Perez were in attendance at Craven Cottage on Saturday to watch Fulham lose to Crystal Palace

So what of where his old club Tottenham are right now, because I joke it is never dull at Spurs.

"They are investing like other clubs", and Pochettino sees the logic after a couple of difficult seasons. Tottenham have changed their approach and are spending big on players who already know the Premier League. I think back to how close Pochettino was to delivering Spurs glory in the league and Europe and how little he spent by comparison - what would he have given to have had £300m to spend? There's a mischievous smile, and he pretends he couldn't possibly understand what £300m is.

So does he think this new strategy will work? "You never know," he replies. "We need time to see if that works or not.

"Like in all the games, when you make a decision like a coach that can work well or not. I think it's a different strategy and a different way to operate. I always wish the best for Tottenham because it's in my heart."

There's also been a big shift in direction at his former side Chelsea. The head coach role he held two years ago has now been changed to manager, while there has been a significant change in transfer policy with the club buying Premier League-ready players rather than projects under Xabi Alonso.

Pochettino is reluctant to make direct comparisons, but he sees similarities in the ambition of both clubs, and concedes "buying players like this you can expect to fight, to be a contender for the Premier League."

Chelsea's defeat to Arsenal has already provided an early reality check, but Pochettino is urging patience with Alonso.

"Of course they are disappointed after the defeat against Arsenal, but I think we need to give time to Xabi's first season after three games in the Premier League," he says.

"I think we need to give time, and of course for Tottenham the same."

For Pochettino, Arsenal are very much in pole position.

"Mikel [Arteta] is the best coach in the Premier League today," he says. "Knowing what he needs to do, it's going to be tough to beat them."

Sports.title: Top four in the world set for US Open semi-finals showdown
Sports.content:
Two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka will bid to move one step closer to a third straight US Open title when she faces familiar foe ‌Jessica Pegula, while Elena Rybakina will take on home favourite Coco Gauff in the semi-finals on Thursday from midnight - live on Sky Sports Tennis.

For the first time since Wimbledon in ​2009, all four top seeds at a Grand Slam have reached the semi-finals, with Sabalenka, Rybakina and Gauff all former major champions and third seed Pegula seeking a maiden Grand Slam title.

Sabalenka has reached the semi-finals here for a sixth consecutive year and is now two wins away from becoming the first woman ‌since Serena Williams from 2012 to 2014 to win three straight titles in New York.

The top seed had not dropped a set before surviving her toughest test of the tournament ​on Tuesday, edging Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova.

The Belarusian will face a familiar opponent in third seed Pegula, with their rivalry returning to Flushing Meadows for a third straight year after Sabalenka denied the American the title in 2024 and then beat her ​again in last year's semi-finals.

Does Pegula have the edge?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the clash between Jessica Pegula and Emma Navarro

Sabalenka leads their head-to-head 9-4 but Pegula has won two of their last three ⁠encounters, including a victory in the Berlin Open semi-finals earlier this year ⁠in which she took the deciding set 6-0.

"I think it's fun to look at the rivalry we've had. She's got to me here the last couple of years," Pegula said.

"I have been able to beat ‌her a few times, maybe on a smaller stage, so I think that's going to be kind of a hurdle for me to get over."

Sabalenka will head into the semi-final after surrendering top spot in the world rankings, which Rybakina secured with her quarter-final victory over Olympic champion Qinwen Zheng.

The Australian Open winner will become the 30th woman to top the WTA rankings and the first from Kazakhstan to reach world No 1 when the new rankings are released after the ⁠tournament.

Sabalenka, who had held the top spot since October 2024, said she would gladly trade it for ​another US Open title.

"I'll be more than happy," she said. "Yes, three-peat. Sounds great."

Did you know?

The top four seeds have reached the women's singles semi-finals at a Grand Slam event for the first time since Wimbledon in 2009, and for just the second time in the Open Era at the US Open after 1975



New world No 1 up against the fan-favourite

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the clash between Coco Gauff and Mirra Andreeva.

Rybakina's reward for reaching the semi-finals for the first time in New York is a meeting with fan-favourite ​Gauff, who produced a stunning comeback to beat fifth seed and fellow French Open winner Mirra Andreeva.

The 2023 ⁠US Open champion was on the brink of defeat in the second set before saving two match points and turning the match around.

Gauff's victory put her into the semi-finals at a second straight Slam after her run to the last four at Wimbledon, and she will have the home crowd behind ⁠her as she bids to clinch a second US Open title.

"Elena is playing some great tennis," said Gauff. "Congrats to her for being the new world No 1 or will be the new World No 1. I think that's incredible.

"We played each other in Toronto. That didn't go my way, so I think I just have to learn from that match.

"I know I'm going to have some aces hit on me and some winners hit on me, but I'm going to keep fighting and give it my all."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Gauff and Andreeva produced an epic 39-shot rally, with the American coming out on top

A third Slam title or revenge for Gauff?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the quarter-final between Elena Rybakina and Qinwen Zheng

Rybakina will bid ​for a third Grand Slam title, while Gauff will have revenge on her mind after the Kazakh beat her in ​three sets in last month's Canadian Open semi-finals.

On playing Gauff, Rybakina said: "I will expect that a lot of people are going to support her.

"I just need to stay aggressive. I think from where I was coming to this tournament, being injured and not practicing, I think we came pretty far. Now we just last push and important to still enjoy. Hopefully it's going to go my way."

The pair are tied 1-1 in their previous meetings and will face off for a place in Saturday's final.

Sports.title: Arteta explains new role for transformed Odegaard
Sports.content:
Martin Odegaard is a player transformed at the start of this season - and Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta puts his captain's impressive form down to fitness and new positioning.

Odegaard was the match-winner again for Arsenal on Wednesday, thumping in the only goal of the game in the Champions League victory at Napoli.

That hit followed his clinching strike against Chelsea in the Premier League on Sunday and takes his total to four goals in five appearances this season across all competitions.

Odegaard only scored once for Arsenal during an injury-hit 2025/26 campaign but now his stats are up across a range of other attacking metrics, too.

Image: Martin Odegaard is having a much bigger impact in the final third this season

"First of all he needs to be available and last year he missed so many games through injuries," said Arteta when asked in his post-match press conference about Odegaard's improvement.

"The quality's always been there. It's never been a question," added Declan Rice, speaking to Sky Sports. "Last year, to have two shoulder injuries like he did, then a MCL injury he did, it's never easy.

"But then you see him at the World Cup and how he's started this year. That's the Martin we know and we love, he's our captain. We need to keep giving him the ball and letting things happen."

Arteta also highlighted how fresh combinations with team-mates are playing a part.

"He's got that edge and different relationships around him as well and that helps," said the Gunners boss.

"He can start to go by different heights in the team, especially in the attacking phase, and when we get him into those positions he's a really dangerous player."

That is demonstrated by Odegaard's touches in the opposition box going up from 2.5 per 90 minutes last season to 4.3 per 90 minutes so far this term.

Image: Martin Odegaard produced a starring performance against Napoli

Arteta put Odegaard's freedom to advance into more threatening positions down to the skills of his team-mates in open play, which the Arsenal head coach suggested had been missing previously.

"We have a lot of players that can take the ball there and progress the ball much better than we did in the past," Arteta explained.

"When that happens, [Odegaard] needs to take different heights and angles and positions in order to disorganise the opponent and he's done that really well."

Image: Martin Odegaard's pass map against Napoli shows the areas he operated in

Christos Tzolis is likely to be one of those players Arteta is referencing. The summer signing has four assists to his name already, with three of those coming for Odegaard goals, including the winner in Naples.

But the Arsenal attack down both flanks and through the middle looked extremely dangerous at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona.

Arsenal had 26 shots in total - their most on record (since 2003/04) in the competition. An expected goals total of 4.05 showed they should have got far more for their efforts.

Odegaard, though, did step up and deliver the key moment.

"That's what we need," said Arteta. "The players with the mindset to decide a game and play with personality. To keep taking chances and risks.

"He's getting into those positions much more in recent games and now you feel he has the emotional state that he knows the ball can go in, and he scored an incredible goal tonight."

Odegaard playing with freedom and flair

Analysis by Sky Sports' Nick Wright:

Odegaard is a player in form. That much was clear from early in the game against Napoli. He oozed class and confidence, demanding the ball then finding the gaps in Napoli's defence and threading passes forward. Everything went through him.

His goal, brilliantly taken from the edge of the box after a 29-pass build-up, proved crucial. He now has four in five games this season, a stunning turnaround having only managed one in 36 last term. Odegaard, uninhibited by injuries, looks a different player.

Image: Martin Odegaard celebrates scoring against Napoli

Showing his team-mates how to finish was only one part of his performance. He also ended the game having had more touches, made more passes and created more chances than anyone else on the pitch. Napoli couldn't really get near him.

The scooped pass to release Ben White for the golden chance somehow spurned by Piero Hincapie was one of many examples of his ingenuity against the massed ranks of Napoli players but there were plenty of others. He played with freedom and flair.

"Martin is contributing goals," added Arteta after the game. "That is obviously impacting results which is what we want from our attacking players, to be decisive, and certainly he was that today."

Arsenal continue to feel the benefits.

Sports.title: Chelsea’s 2016-17 Premier League title should be given to Spurs, says Pochettino
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino says Chelsea should be stripped of their 2016-17 Premier League title for financial rule breaches and the honour retrospectively awarded to Tottenham, who he led to second place that season.

Chelsea were fined £10m by the Football Association in July and given a suspended two-window transfer ban for multiple violations of the rules during the Roman Abramovich era. They were also fined £10.75m by the Premier League in March.

The club were found to have used unlicensed agents and sought to obscure the nature of their transfer business between 2009 and 2022. The deals that took Eden Hazard, Willian, David Luiz and Nemanja Matic to Stamford Bridge were among those found to have transgressed. Those players were central to Chelsea’s 2016-17 triumph under Antonio Conte.

The club’s BlueCo ownership self-reported the breaches when it took over from Abramovich in 2022 in the hope of mitigating the punishment, and the club avoided a points deduction. Pochettino, who went on to manage Chelsea in 2023-24 and is in charge of the US, believes the authorities did not go nearly far enough. His Spurs team finished seven points behind Conte’s Chelsea.

“We should win one Premier League, we should have been awarded it,” Pochettino said as part of a wide-ranging interview. “If that [Chelsea’s rule-break] was true, then we deserve to be champions that year, for sure. They were punished, they admitted it? So that’s it. The title should be for the team that was second.

“We can say that they scored goals, they won games. OK. But it’s completely fair to say that we didn’t compete before the start of the season with the same card. Maybe with the same rules, we could’ve signed some players that would have made the team better or scored more goals.”

Between 2009 and 2022, Chelsea won three league titles, two Champions Leagues, two Europa Leagues, four FA Cups and one League Cup. It was put to Pochettino that Hazard had made a particular difference in the 2016-17 title race; the winger scored 16 goals in the competition.

“Maybe yes,” Pochettino replied. “I have no doubt and I’m not scared to say the truth. The Chelsea fans will be upset with me. But if we were at Tottenham and broke the rules, I’d admit the same: ‘We don’t deserve the title because we broke the rules.’

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“It’s impossible if only some clubs play with offside and another plays with no offside. Or one plays with VAR and another plays with no VAR. For everyone it needs to be the same rules. And then you have the capacity to create the best team.

“I don’t say that Chelsea didn’t play well, that Conte was not great. I don’t say that. I don’t want the message to be twisted. But if you broke the rules then ciao – you need to give it to another team. I don’t know why that didn’t happen. What is being promoted and incentivised is to break the rules. If you don’t punish in the way that you need to punish, I say: ‘Yeah … I lost my job [at Spurs] because we didn’t win a title.’”

Sports.title: ‘That’s how it started’: Dambrauskas’ journey from Who Wants to Be a Millionaire to Champions League
Sports.content:
Valdas Dambrauskas can reel off the questions and answers without a moment’s pause. Who won the first Academy Award for best actor in 1929? It was Emil Jannings, even if someone else might have been tempted to go with Charlie Chaplin. Which country publishes the highest number of daily newspapers? India was the clear winner. Can you name the nation that produces the most electricity per capita in the world? His family, watching back home, clasped heads in hands but he was right: back then, in 2002, the answer was his native Lithuania.

It was enough to win Dambrauskas about £725 in his appearance on Six Zeros – A Million, the Lithuanian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? “At that time it was quite big money,” he says. “I could have bought a flat in my home town; it was a very difficult period there and they were almost free. But my plan was to go to England and follow my dream to become a coach, and that’s how it started.”

More than two and a half decades later the story continues at Old Trafford where Dambrauskas will manage the Azerbaijani champions, Sabah, in their Champions League debut on Thursday night. The club’s journey is some tale in itself given Sabah, who came through a dramatic playoff with Hapoel Be’er Sheva, did not exist until 2017. But the path taken by their head coach, a 25-year-old office worker with only a modest football background when his general knowledge skills were put on display, is virtually unparalleled in the modern game.

The money he won helped Dambrauskas and his girlfriend, now wife, to move to north London and establish themselves in an alien environment. “I would have done it anyway – the show came in the middle of our planning,” he says of the move, which became an ambition after a work visit to Norway in 2000.

In Scandinavia he had grasped the extent of the Premier League’s incipient popularity. “I realised this was where real football is. There was no pathway to coaching in Lithuania if you hadn’t been a player; it was impossible. But if I could take a course in England, maybe I could get a chance to step on the ladder at home.”

Dambrauskas spent eight years in London. “The start was very, very difficult. I wasn’t speaking decent English, had no contacts, we didn’t know anyone, we lived in different places, did all kinds of jobs.” He worked in a Muswell Hill pub, delivered newspapers in the area, held down jobs in a nursery school, as a gardener, in sales, and as a self-employed handyman, often simultaneously. The hours were relentless but so was the young man’s focus.

Dambrauskas during his appearance on Lithuania’s version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? Photograph: x

It was a life of an immigrant couple straining every sinew to make their way. Their first child was born in 2004; by then Dambrauskas, who had studied philosophy and social sciences in Lithuania, had enrolled on a sports science and coaching course at London Metropolitan University. From his classroom on the 10th floor he could see the Emirates Stadium sprouting up during that spell of Arsenal invincibility.

The Access to Sports Project, based in Finsbury Park, is a stone’s throw from Arsenal but galaxies away in another sense. It is where Dambrauskas landed his first coaching role, giving sessions to children on Saturday mornings and during school holidays. His next step is all the more remarkable for what has passed since. A round of interviews with Manchester United Soccer Schools brought the chance to work with youngsters around the country, and sometimes on residential trips abroad, under the banner of the then serial title winners. Despite the name it was a far cry from even academy football, but the injection of confidence was transformative.

“It was John Shiels, CEO of the Manchester United Foundation, who gave me the chance. I don’t know what he saw in me – I came in with very broken English and couldn’t express myself as I can now – but he really supported me. At the end of the year he wrote me an appraisal of what I’d done. He said that I was good and could do much more. It was a massive, massive boost for me.”

Through a friend at university, Dambrauskas became involved with the community sports organisation London Tigers. “He told me they always needed coaches.” Eventually he took charge of their semi-professional team, which played in the Spartan South Midlands League. “That was where it really started, coaching at some kind of level.” It meant managing in the FA Vase and the early rounds of the FA Cup.

Dambrauskas also undertook part-time roles at Fulham and Brentford before working as a sports activator for Central YMCA on Tottenham Court Road. He would later take a broader role as sports development manager at London Tigers and took his coaching badges at the London Football Association. “It was a time with no holidays, no days off. I’m a big reader, I read all the time and studied constantly. Sometimes I would finish my university work on the bus. I took every kind of education I could and went to every possible course for every meeting.

“Over the years I had countless interviews for coaching roles, for jobs at centres of excellency in London and outside, so many CVs and applications, but I understood early on that it’s very difficult in England to get on the ladder and that to coach at professional level there was probably impossible. If there is a story where someone is starting in the community scheme and going all the way to become a head coach, I am still to find it.”

View image in fullscreen Dambrauskas geeing up his players during his spell in charge of Hajduk Split, which ended in 2022. Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty Images

By late 2010 he felt ready to pursue what had originally been the end goal: a role in Lithuania. He had started working with their under-17s and agreed to join Ekranas, national champions at the time, as assistant manager. “I had the London Tigers job, 15 hours a week at Brentford and some other things here and there. We had a good life and people thought I was crazy going back home and earning about a fifth of what I was getting in England. But the biggest risk in life is not to take risks.

“I’m forever grateful to my wife for being behind me. We always faced questions: twenty- or thirtysomething guy always studying, trying to work in football, spending all his money on books and courses rather than buying an apartment or something for the family. But I’m very happy with how it turned out and nobody questions those decisions now.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

A kaleidoscopic career bloomed. By December 2014 he had become head coach at Zalgiris Vilnius, the biggest club in Lithuania, winning two more league titles and various cups in a move that felt unthinkable during a humble upbringing in the tiny northern town Pakruojis. “My childhood was not a gift. My dad died when I was 11, and if he knew that I had the job at Zalgiris and that we won so many trophies he would be the happiest person in the world.”

Dambrauskas was not content to stop there. “You are basically nobody and suddenly you get this job. Then you have to prove yourself to everybody again and again and again. So you reached this step on the ladder but what’s next? How do you go to the next level?”

After three years he joined the upwardly mobile Latvian club RFS but harboured concerns about the prospects of leaving the small Baltic football bubble. In the event he need not have worried. Since 2020 he has managed in Croatia with Gorica and Hajduk Split – the latter are “like a tattoo you can’t ever take out, it leaves a mark on you” – in Bulgaria with Ludogorets, in Greece with OFI Crete, in Cyprus with Omonia and with the Hungarian club Diosgyor, who he describes as having “one of the biggest hidden football potentials in Europe”.

Itinerant career paths such as that are, especially in eastern and southern Europe, nothing new. But Sabah had been courting Dambrauskas for two years before he took over in 2025. Once the stars had aligned, he worked a miracle. In 2024-25, Sabah had finished 41 points behind the biggest club in Azerbaijan, Qarabag. Last season Sabah beat them to the title by nine points, earning their crack at the Champions League qualifiers. “I’m really grateful to Qarabag. Every game against them is like taking a master’s degree.”

View image in fullscreen Dambrauskas embraces a Sabah fan after presiding over a 4-1 aggregate victory against The New Saints in Champions League qualifying. Photograph: Jan Kruger/Getty Images

He waxes lyrical about the stability and facilities available at well-backed Sabah, who were cheered on with fervour befitting a national team when they thrillingly overcame an injury-time deficit against Be’er Sheva. Their success has come with a multinational squad that plays bold, front-foot football in the style he preaches. “But if you don’t understand the human being in front of you, it’s very difficult to pass him your ideas and build trust,” he says.

“What is important in east Africa can be completely different from what someone needs in west Africa or anywhere across Europe. You need to be able to understand different cultures, different traditions, different ways of speaking or behaving. Without that it’s impossible to do anything, and I believe this is where my strength lies.”

It is a glorious piece of circularity that Dambrauskas and Sabah will be watched from the stands on Thursday by a number of his old colleagues from Manchester United Soccer Schools. He beams at the thought; none of this could have seemed remotely attainable during their time on the grass together. “But I had this belief. I had this confidence all the time that I could do it.”

He is equally delighted that the draw has also brought a January visit to Arsenal, that huge presence in his eyeline during those years studying on Holloway Road. He is 49 and would surely lever himself among Europe’s most sought-after coaching properties if he can take Sabah further. “We’re going to respect everyone but not be afraid of anyone. There’s a very nice song by the Lithuanian band Colours of Bubbles called Truth or Dare. Very soon we’re going to find out the truth about ourselves and what we can do. It will be very beneficial for us because I don’t want this club to be a one-day wonder.” As final answers go, it may be his most significant yet.

Sports.title: Alexis Mac Allister makes his point as Liverpool fight back to defeat Atlético
Sports.content:
It was the time and place for Alexis Mac Allister to do his talking on the pitch and the disgruntled Liverpool midfielder delivered on cue. “Very sad” over Liverpool’s refusal to offer him a new contract, while Dominik Szoboszlai and Ryan Gravenberch were getting theirs, Mac Allister made Anfield very happy with a match-winning display against Atlético Madrid.

The Argentina international, one of five World Cup finalists involved in an absorbing, delicately-poised contest, vented his frustrations in the best possible and most professional way – from behind an immaculate 20-yard strike into Jan Oblak’s goal rather than a microphone. Mac Allister believes he is playing for a new deal this season and promised to give “100% to my last day” at the pre-match press conference. He was true to his word to extend Atlético’s winless sequence against English opposition in the Champions League league phase to 11 matches.

For Andoni Iraola, it was the perfect start to life as a Champions League coach after an imperfect start to the game. Diego Simeone’s switch to a 3-5-2 formation caught Liverpool cold and it was only when they regrouped in the aftermath of Marcos Llorente’s latest Anfield goal, and again during the half-time interval, that their performance level improved. Mac Allister’s timely moment, Alexander Isak’s relentless industry, Florian Wirtz’s creativity and another performance of drive and intelligence from Szoboszlai ensured the Liverpool head coach had plenty to savour.

“I have to blame myself a bit for the start of the game,” Iraola said. “Atlético surprised us with the way they approached the game. They haven’t used that system too much this season and it’s difficult if you are not ready for it, but we adjusted and played better. In the second half we were the best team. We came back for the third time [this season] and that showed the players are pushing and they have character.”

It was a night of firsts. Iraola coached a Champions League game for the first time in his career – he did take charge of 12 Europa League matches with AEK Larnaca in 2018-19 – Bradley Barcola made his first Liverpool start following a £123m move from Paris Saint-Germain and Julián Álvarez was in Atlético’s starting lineup for the first time this season since his failed attempt to join Barcelona. All appeared to have been forgiven – for now at least – as his name was cheered by the small pocket of Atlético fans when the teams were announced before kick-off and he repaid them by creating the opening goal.

View image in fullscreen Dominik Szoboszlai scores Liverpool’s equaliser late in the first half. Photograph: Dave Thompson/AP

Llorente was the scourge of Anfield yet again when Álvarez threaded a pass behind the home defence and the right wing-back raced clear on goal. The man who named his dog Anfield after scoring twice to eliminate Jürgen Klopp’s team from the competition in 2020, in the game played while Madrid was in lockdown from the Covid pandemic, lofted a confident finish beyond Alisson. It was Llorente’s fifth goal at Anfield, half of his entire total of Champions League goals. He had been kept onside by Milos Kerkez, who endured a poor night with his positioning and distribution before atoning with a key role in Liverpool’s equaliser.

Álvarez almost doubled the visitors’ lead when granted far too much time and space to take aim from almost 30 yards. Alisson, at full stretch, intervened with a superb finger-tip save. Anfield was growing restless at Liverpool’s carelessness on the ball and Atlético’s comfort on it. But the threat and control from the hosts increased.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Wirtz drew a fine save from Oblak at the end of a flowing move involving Barcola and Isak. Liverpool then drew level thanks to tenacity from Kerkez, a lovely touch from Ronald Araújo and Szoboszlai’s instinctive finish. The left-back won possession with a clean, crunching challenge on Lee Kang-in before finding Barcola. The France international was denied a goal on his full debut by Oblak’s low save but Wirtz kept the pressure on and Szoboszlai, having been halted on the edge of the area, got a second bite from Araújo’s clever flick. The midfielder’s first time shot sailed into the far corner.

Barcola should have put Liverpool ahead when played through on goal by Wirtz early in the second half. The winger had time to measure the finish but pulled it wide of Oblak’s right-hand post. He would later depart with cramp. Liverpool were ahead one minute later when the lively Rio Ngumoha beat Llorente and his cross fell to Mac Allister via a deflection off Isak. Mac Allister told Szoboszlai to leave the ball and drilled home an unstoppable left-footed drive from 20 yards. Atlético remained dangerous and the introduction of Ademola Lookman added an extra dimension to the visitors’ attack but Liverpool defended impressively to secure a deserved victory.

Sports.title: Ødegaard ‘edge’ delights Arteta as Arsenal secure narrow win at Napoli
Sports.content:
After their record-breaking feats last year in the Champions League, Arsenal are at it again. But having been delayed along with hundreds of travelling supporters by travel chaos on Tuesday, Mikel Arteta’s side had to bide their time against Napoli until Martin Ødegaard continued his rich vein of goalscoring with the crucial strike 15 minutes from full time.

Perhaps it was the fact that, at Uefa’s insistence, they were forced to wear red shorts for the first time since a Premier League game against Watford in 2022 that Arsenal were not quite at their flowing best here and missed a hatful of chances.

Yet they were deserved winners in the end and the substitute Noni Madueke should have made the ­victory more comprehensive late on.

Having come so close to breaking their duck in this competition last year after becoming the first team to win all eight of their league stage matches, Arsenal look capable of going one better this time if Ødegaard can keep up this sparkling form.

He now has four goals in his last five games after scoring once in all competitions last year and it was the Norway captain whose name was being chanted by the fans who were kept behind more than an hour after the final whistle.

“That’s what we need – players with that mindset to decide the game and to play with that personality,” said Arteta. “He’s getting into those positions much more in recent games and I feel he has this emotional state that he knows that the ball can go in. He’s got that edge and he’s now got different relationships around him [in the team] as well. That helps.”

Arteta has bad memories of this stadium after being sent off in a 2-0 defeat during the Champions League group stage in 2013. But Arsenal’s most recent match here ended in victory as they qualified for the Europa League semi-finals under Unai Emery in 2019. Both clubs have been crowned domestic champions since then, with Napoli ending their 33-year wait in 2023 then doing it again two years later. Yet Champions League success has continued to elude them after finishing 30th in the league phase last season.

View image in fullscreen Mikel Arteta talks with Kevin De Bruyne, the former Manchester City midfielder, after the match. Photograph: Ciro De Luca/Reuters

That was in stark contrast to Arsenal, who were unbeaten over 14 matches before falling at the final hurdle. It was telling that Arteta kept faith with four of his back five that started against Chelsea on Sunday, with Piero Hincapié replacing Riccardo Calafiori at left-back but failing to match the Italian’s finishing ability with one glaring miss. Mikel Merino, Eberechi Eze and Viktor Gyökeres also made their first starts of the season but largely disappointed, with the Sweden striker making way for Kai Havertz just before Ødegaard’s winner.

Those Arsenal supporters that did make it to southern Italy had no problem making themselves heard throughout, with plenty of empty seats in the home sections despite Max Allegri’s attempts to rally Napoli’s fans beforehand. The game quickly settled into a pattern as the visitors set up camp in Napoli’s half and the hosts attempted to hit them on the break. Kevin De Bruyne – no stranger to facing Arsenal after a decade in the sky blue of Manchester City – forced David Raya into a rare mistake after a typically driving run through the midfield but the ball was scrambled away to safety.

That came just after a spectacular overhead kick from Bukayo Saka at the other end had been saved by Alex Meret. Merino should have scored when he was set up by Eze’s clever header across the face of goal before Ben White drilled a shot straight into Meret’s grateful gloves.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Matteo Politano managed to test Raya again as Napoli continued to find gaps in Arsenal’s normally watertight defence. Saka blazed over after a brilliant through ball from Ødegaard on the stroke of half-time, with replays confirming the assistant had been wrong to raise his flag.

View image in fullscreen Martin Ødegaard scores the only goal of the match at Stadio Diego Armando Maradona. Photograph: Image Photo Agency/Getty Images

Meret did not return for the second half and was replaced by Vanja Milinkovic-Savic, once on Manchester United’s books. The Serbia goalkeeper was a mere spectator for a flowing Arsenal move featuring a sumptuous scooped pass into the area that ended with Hincapié missing the target after being picked out at the far post by Ben White’s header. Suddenly Napoli found themselves suffocated by a blanket of red. Allegri, who knows what it feels like to have lost in a Champions League final after suffering that fate twice in three years at Juventus, responded by switching to a back five and trying to hang on.

Arsenal’s pressure eventually told when another substitute, Christos Tzolis, exchanged passes with White and teed up Ødegaard, whose shot flew in off the post despite Milinkovic-Savic just getting his fingertips to the ball. Havertz had a goal disallowed for offside in injury time, but the mission was already complete.

Sports.title: Champions League roundup: Raphinha shines as Barcelona thrash Feyenoord
Sports.content:
Raphinha let his goals do the talking after being omitted from the Ballon d’Or shortlist, striking twice as Barcelona eased to a 5-1 win over Feyenoord in the Champions League.

The Brazilian was a surprise omission from this week’s 30-strong list of candidates for the prestigious award but brushed any disappointment aside to continue his early season hot streak at a rain-soaked Camp Nou. The forward finished brilliantly in the third minute and added a second just before the hour mark to down the Eredivisie side and take his tally to eight goals in six outings at the start of the campaign.

The summer signing Karim Adeyemi produced a stunning finish, Lamine Yamal stroked a free-kick through a gap in the Dutch wall and recent arrival Gabriel Jesus opened his account for the club just two minutes after stepping off the bench.

There was little to celebrate for Giovanni van Bronckhorst on his Barça return but Sem Steijn gave the visiting fans something to enjoy when he poked in at far post late on.

“The most important thing is we are playing like a team, like one unit,” the Barcelona head coach, Hansi Flick, said. “We controlled the game, we are dominant and this is fantastic to see. This is our style and how we want to play.”

Ferran Torres scored a hat-trick and Ousmane Dembélé also starred as Paris Saint-Germain began their quest to win a third successive Champions League title by thrashing Slovan Bratislava 6-1 at the Parc des Princes.

View image in fullscreen Paris Saint-Germain’s Ferran Torres celebrates scoring their fifth goal with Ousmane Dembélé. Photograph: Benoît Tessier/Reuters

Last year’s Ballon d’Or winner Dembélé had scored twice by the midway point of the first half in the French capital, and then set up Spain’s World Cup final hero Torres to make it 3-0 by the interval.

Torres, a close-season signing from Barcelona, added two more just after the restart to complete his hat-trick before the hour mark, with Suleiman Camara pulling one back for the Slovakian champions and Fabián Ruiz then sealing PSG’s win.

Elsewhere, Stuttgart’s Ermedin Demirovic struck a 12-minute first-half hat-trick to ⁠earn ⁠a ​3-1 victory over Viking Stavanger.

He opened the ​scoring after 20 minutes with a touch at the near post, but Viking, making their first appearance in the league phase of the Champions League, were level two minutes later when Zlatko Tripic finished a ⁠swift counter-attack with his left foot.
