Sports.title: ‘That is criminal’ – Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer have hilarious argument after Man-of-the-Match prize awarded
Sports.content:
‘That is criminal’ – Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer have hilarious argument after Man-of-the-Match prize awarded

Morgan Rogers couldn't believe that he didn't get awarded Man of the Match after Chelsea's 6-3 win over Leeds United in the Carabao Cup.

The Blues were trailing 1-0 at half time in their delayed game before Xabi Alonso introduced Rogers, Cole Palmer and Pedro Neto at half time to totally flip the game.



5 In the end, it turned into a great night for Chelsea Credit: Getty

Palmer scored twice and Rogers grabbed FOUR assists, but it was the former who claimed the Man of the Match award.

This led to a pretty hilarious argument live on Sky Sports between the pair.

It started with Rogers, who said: "Mate, I got four assists! Nah, nah, I can't believe that. That is mental. He scored a penalty. That is mental."



Palmer then said: "I started the comeback. But I'll say you should have had it."

To which Rogers responded: "Don't mention me. I am just a bystander. That is criminal."



Rogers robbed

There is no question that both players had a huge impact on the game even if it wasn't immediate.

That is because Leeds doubled their lead early in the second half through Brenden Aaronson.



They had opened the scoring through Tarik Muharemovic's towering header and were good value for it.

But Dan James' foul on Pep Chavarria in the Leeds box changed everything.

5 Rogers was left absolutely stunned that he didn't pick up Man of the Match Credit: Sky Sports

5 The duo's banter and off-field relationship appears to be helping on the pitch as well



Palmer stepped up to score a penalty, and he bagged the equaliser soon after.

Reece James hurled a throw-in into the box that Rogers flicked into Palmer's path.

The England international wrapped his left boot around it and sent it into the far corner.

It was soon 3-2 with Rogers grabbing his second assist after Palmer had played a pass to him.



The pass wasn't quite perfect, so the former Aston Villa man lunged at the ball.

He won the 50/50 and sent it through for Neto, who struck a lovely first-time strike off the inside of the far post.

The hat-trick of assists came for Rogers as he dribbled down the right and played a low ball into the box.

5 Palmer began the Chelsea fightback, scoring two of their six goals Credit: Getty



Danny Welbeck controlled, turned and fired it home via a slight deflection.

There is definitely the argument to suggest the fourth assist for Rogers might not actually be his.

He drilled a low cross in that deflected to Valentin Barco, who lashed home from close range.

But even if it doesn't go down as his, he still definitely got a hat-trick of assists.



Alonso's thoughts

It has been an exciting start to life for Alonso at Chelsea with his side scoring and conceding plenty of goals.

And he admitted after the game that he got his team selection wrong with nine changes from the defeat to Arsenal.

5 Alonso's men have been the great entertainers this season, scoring 16 goals in five matches in all competitions so far Credit: Getty

He said: "Yeah, there was so many changes. There was a risk.

"Things weren't going the way we planned, so we had to change (at half-time). I take responsibility with the first half.



"They knew they weren't starting and they were ready to make an impact. I'm happy with the result and the reaction."

But he is pleased to see Palmer and Rogers linking up so nicely, adding: "For sure, it's so important. To have a great chemistry between them. They enjoy assisting together. It's important for the team."

Sports.title: Richarlison 'wants to RIP UP his Tottenham contract' with unhappy star looking to force return to Brazil after being relegated to under-21 squad
Sports.content:
Richarlison wants Tottenham to terminate his contract so that he is free to move to Brazilian club Vasco, according to reports.

The 29-year-old wantaway, who was Tottenham's top scorer with 11 goals last season, failed to secure a transfer before deadline day and is now training alone in exile after being omitted from Roberto De Zerbi's official 25-man Premier League squad and relegated to the under-21s.

Richarlison had hoped to return to Everton as part of a deadline-day swap deal involving Iliman Ndiaye, but the move ultimately collapsed - paving the way for the Toffees winger to join Manchester City for £65million instead.

According to Brazilian outlet Globo, Richarlison is furious with Tottenham's decision not to register him for the Premier League and wants the north London club to rip up his contract so that he can join Vasco as a free agent.

The report claims Richarlison's lawyers are set to file a request in court to terminate his deal, which is due to expire at the end of the season.

Richarlison’s case is similar to that of fellow Brazilian Renan Lodi, who claimed in court last year that he was prevented from practising his profession after being left out of Al-Hilal's Saudi Pro League squad. He was subsequently able to sign for Atletico Mineiro after securing the unilateral termination of his contract.

Richarlison reportedly wants Spurs to terminate his contract so that he is free to move to Vasco

The Brazilian has not been named in Roberto De Zerbi's official 25-man Premier League squad

It is also reported that Richarlison wishes to play for the Rio de Janeiro outfit until December 2026 before considering his options.

Last week, De Zerbi told Richarlison his Tottenham exile is a problem entirely of his own making, revealing the Brazilian rejected contract talks at the start of the summer.

Spurs went on to sign Manchester City duo Omar Marmoush and Savinho to bolster De Zerbi's attacking ranks this summer after the club narrowly avoided relegation last campaign.

'You don't know one important thing,' said De Zerbi before Tottenham's 0-0 draw with Nottingham Forest on Saturday. 'At the beginning of pre-season I spoke to Richarlison and asked him if he wanted to extend his contract because I was happy to keep him with us, and he didn't want to.

'So, Richarlison is a good player, yes. He was important last season, yes very important. He's a good guy, yes. But in the end, I have to stop myself putting pressure on the players if the players show me they want to leave.

'So, I'm sorry for him but we have to go to another page and work with Dominic Solanke and Omar Marmoush.'

Sports.title: How an Azerbaijani football team from a town smaller than SKEGNESS are plotting to stun Manchester United in the Champions League tonight - led by manager who appeared on Who Wants To Be A Millionaire!
Sports.content:
Manchester United make their return to the UEFA Champions League after two years away against a side that was not even formed by the time Marcus Rashford made his debut for the Red Devils back in 2016.

Michael Carrick's side are preparing for the visit of Azerbaijani minnows FK Sabah, this week celebrating their ninth birthday, on Thursday night as overwhelming favourites, with major bookmakers pricing them at around 1/10 on to win.

But upsetting the odds is what Sabah have done for years now, from ending Qarabag's dominance in the Azerbaijani Premier League, qualifying for the UEFA Champions League for the first time ever, while staying committed to the 'Moneyball' philosophy of recruitment.

The gulf between the two is absolutely enormous. Sabah's squad is valued at around £14.5million, while Manchester United's is north of £775m. One Carlos Baleba is almost five times as expensive as Sabah's entire first team squad.

Manchester United are three times winners of this competition while for everyone at Sabah, it will be the first time hearing the Champions League anthem as a competitor under the Old Trafford lights on Thursday night.

Daily Mail Sport takes a closer look at Manchester United's lesser-known upcoming opponent…

FK Sabah have qualified for the group phase of the Champions League for the very first time

Players are still in shock but now they are determined to show they belong on the big stage

WHAT'S THE BACKSTORY?

Sabah are based in Masazir, a city 20 miles away from the capital city of Baku. To put Masazir into context, it's 19,000 population, give or take, makes it smaller than Skegness.

They go by two nicknames, 'The Owls', which is the most common, while others have referred to them as 'The Students' given they have only been in operation since September 2017.

Starting from scratch for the 2017-18 season - when United youngster Harry Amass, who could be involved on Thursday night, was still in primary school - they entered into the second division of Azerbaijani football.

Sabah would finish fifth but earned themselves a default promotion as the four teams ahead of them that season - Khazar Baku, Qaradağ Lökbatan, Shuvalan and MOIK Baku - all failed to obtain a suitable licence to play in the top flight.

Sabah had what they needed, were promoted and haven't looked back since, winning the double last season by winning their first Azerbaijani Premier League title to go well with Azerbaijan Cup, thus ending Qarabag's monopoly on success in their homeland.

It also meant that by going on to reach this stage, Sabah are in the history books as the youngest club to ever reach the league phase or group stage of the UEFA Champions League. History makers.

HOW DID THEY REACH THE GROUP PHASE?

In dramatic circumstances, if we're being honest.

Sabah's inexperience, and at times naivety, meant they went into every qualifying game as the unseeded underdog.

They finished with 10-men in their first round clash against Welsh champions The New Saints, beating them 2-0 at home, before having a man sent off, and 2-1 in the reverse leg in Wales.

A 3-0 aggregate win over Finland's KuPS followed in round two, while a 2-1 first leg defeat to Denmark's AGF Aarhus in round three had Sabah staring elimination in the face. They responded with an emphatic 4-0 win on home soil.

Then came the real drama in the play-off round when they faced Hapoel Beer-Sheva of Israel.

Sabah lost the first leg 2-1 and found themselves down 4-3 on aggregate with seconds remaining, only for substitute Tellur Mutallimov to score in the 94th minute to send the game to extra-time.

Two more goals would follow, sealing progress, while the Israeli side went down to nine men by the time all was said and done. Sabah had done it. More history.

Navigating four qualifying rounds is notoriously difficult and has only been achieved by six teams prior to Sabah's success.

Kazakhstan's Kairat (2025-26), Slovan Bratislava of Slovakia (2024-25), Moldova's Sheriff (2021-22), Swedish side Malmö (2021-22), Hungarian giants Ferencvaros (2020-21) and Serbian side Red Star Belgrade (2018-19 and 2019-20) have previously managed it.

They have had to take the long road, qualifying through four rounds as underdogs in every tie

It all culminated in an historic night against Hapoel Beer-Sheva where they won it in extra-time

Players were mobbed in front of their supporters having been seconds from elimination

WHAT ABOUT THE MANAGER?

When it comes to manager Valdas Dambrauskas the stories are endless.

One that is worth revisiting is his time living in England and working for Manchester United's Soccer Schools.

But to get there, and to place him in England, it's important to tell the tale of how Dambrauskas used the winnings from an appearance on the Lithuanian version of 'Who Wants to Be a Millionaire' to get there.

Dambrauskas, 49, was not much of a player and had retired by the age of 23 having never played higher than the third tier in Lithuania.

Wanting to be a coach but without the means to do so, he went on to 'Who Wants To Be A Millionaire' and left with 4,000 litas - around £2,500. With that money he moved to London to embark on the start of his coaching journey, working odd jobs on the side including newspaper delivery and childminding to supplement his income.

The rising star coach enrolled to study Sports Science and Coaching at London Metropolitan University and cut his teeth in coaching as a volunteer around London.

Dambrauskas was willing to coach anyone and the Access to Sports Project, which helps provide dedicated coaching to deprived kids in Finsbury Park, opened a door, before other volunteering gigs popped up with Kingsbury London Tigers, a community set-up with a wide range of aged teams, all while still studying.

The Lithuanian started off in the younger age groups before accelerating through to managing the first team in the Spartan South Midlands League (ninth division), the FA Cup and the FA Vase.

By now his name was gaining traction on the lower-level coaching circuit and after becoming the first Lithuanian to clinch the UEFA coaching licence under the tutelage of the London Football Association, Manchester United opened the door.

It was 2004 when Manchester United, through their Foundation, brought Dambrauskas in to help with their Soccer Schools. He now found himself inside a professional operation, even if not as a first team coach.

Manager Valdas Dambrauskas has had to take an unorthodox route to reach the very top

Dambrauskas moved to England with winnings from Lithuania's 'Who Wants To Be A Millionaire'

'That was the best thing that could happen in my life,' Dambrauskas told BBC Sport.

'I went through three or four interviews. I will be forever grateful to [Foundation chief executive] John Shiels, the way he gave me this chance, because I didn't have experience.

'I'd never been in a place with so many great personalities as I got in the Manchester United Soccer Schools.'

Moves to west London pair, Fulham and Brentford, the latter saw him needing to take night buses across London to make the sessions, would follow, before moves abroad followed.

He won the domestic quadruple with FK Žalgiris back in Lithuania, won the Bulgarian league with Ludogorets and clinched domestic cups in Latvia with RFS and Croatia with Hajduk Split before joining FK Sabah in 2025.

But it was in England, where he returns this week, that he really shaped himself as a coach.

'I lived in England when the battle between Manchester United and Arsenal was the biggest rivalry. Alex Ferguson and Arsene Wenger,' Dambrauskas added this week.

'Now I'm going to come back as a coach in the Champions League and hear that anthem. It's really amazing.'

WHAT'S HIS STYLE OF PLAY?

Sabah line up in a similar 4-2-3-1 set-up that Michael Carrick favours and so while the value of the players on display may be different, the formations should look close to the same.

Dambrauskas likes a fluid attack and allows players to drift across the front-line, while a lot of onus is placed on full-backs creating overloads in wide areas. All things that Carrick has shown a desire to do, too.

Since becoming a dominant force in their homeland, Sabah have become a possession-dominant side.

But in the Champions League they are acutely aware that they will spend long spells without the ball and so to see them in qualifying has been to see a team that looks well drilled and a nightmare to mark on set pieces.

The physicality and height of the side Dambrauskas has built means that set-pieces are a major part of their arsenal and given United looked vulnerable from them against Hull City, it will be no surprise to see this area of the game targeted by Sabah.

Sabah have burst onto the scene and in less than a decade have gatecrashed Europe's premier club competition, due in no small part to the work of Dambrauskas.

'His influence goes beyond tactics,' Sabah president Magsud Adigozalov told Azerbaijani outlet Report last week.

'He has instilled a mindset and winning mentality in the team.

'Even in the most difficult moments, the team never abandons its game or fighting spirit, which is the result of the coach's work.'

Attacker Joy Lance Mikels is one of the key dangermen that is out to punish Manchester United

SO, WHO ARE THE PLAYERS TO WATCH?

Sabah promise an element of surprise to most given they have spent most of their early years of existence in relative obscurity from the European masses.

That being said, their ability in transition means they can and will be a threat to United if Carrick's side slack off.

Here are a two players United must keep a close eye on…

Joy Lance Mickels (Winger)

Probably the man Sabah are pinning their hopes on if they are to shock the world with a win at Old Trafford.

Rwandan attacker Mickels is an incredibly direct forward who finished last season as the club’s top goalscorer.

He was nurtured in Germany, spending eight years at Borussia Monchengladbach’s academy, before eventually winding up at Sabah in 2021.

Now in his second spell, Mickels looks a more accomplished player but had he not held his nerve he may not have ever got to this point.

‘After two weeks I actually wanted to call everything off. At that point I was still living in a hotel, didn't have a flat in Baku and hardly anyone spoke English,’ Mickels told Transfermarkt back in 2023.

Now he’s thriving and heading for Old Trafford. No doubt glad he didn’t pack his bags all those years ago!

Tymoteusz Puchacz (Left Back)

Married to an influencer, experienced Polish full-back Puchacz is used to making noise on and off the pitch.

The 27-year-old, who joined Sabah after a loan spell at Plymouth Argyle, brings bags of experience after being part of two European Championships squads for Poland.

Having played for Lech Poznań, Union Berlin and Trabzonspor, Puchacz should not be overwhelmed by what is ahead at Old Trafford and that is invaluable to Sabah.

Moreover, he is an attack-minded full-back that will want to put pressure on Diogo Dalot. He has also added a set-piece threat to his game given he is one of Sabah's main takers.

Little known fact about the former Argyle man, he was crowned the victor when appearing in Poland's version of hit TV show 'Traitors', in this case known as 'Saboteur'.

Polish footballer and influencer Tymoteusz Puchacz takes set-pieces and is one to watch

WHAT'S THE OWNERSHIP SITUATION?

Rather than be propped up by one single rich owner, Sabah is made up of a number of high profile figures from Azerbaijan's business and public administration.

Sabah's founder, Yagub Huseynov, sits on the supervisory board, while the club is run day-to-day by president Adigozalov.

With a limited history and a national giant to overthrow in Qarabag, the ownership group found themselves inspired by the Moneybag philosophy, popularised by the Oakland Athletics' general manager Billy Beane in Major League Baseball back in 2022.

'We could not compete financially with many established European clubs, so we had to find our own competitive advantages,' Adigozalov said in an interview with Euronews.

'We were inspired by the Moneyball philosophy, which demonstrated that intelligent use of data and recruitment can help a club compete far beyond what its financial size might suggest.'

Sports.title: Manchester United join forces with other top-flight clubs to pressure Premier League into confirming Christmas fixtures schedule following fan backlash
Sports.content:
The Premier League will announce the scheduling of its Christmas fixtures today – following pressure from clubs to make an earlier call.

Manchester United were among those who asked the competition and broadcasters to bring the announcement forwards to allow fans more time to plan and minimise disruption.

And it would appear they have been successful, with the timings due to be made public more than a month earlier than they were last season.

All fixtures are originally listed at 3pm on Saturday, but are subject to being changed after broadcasters have decided which games to televise.

United officials met with senior counterparts at the Premier League and broadcasters to urge that match-going fans should be looked after and ask for earlier decisions on December scheduling to make it easier for those who attend to plan their journeys.

The Football Supporters Association is also understood to have been involved in talks with those involved.

Pressure from clubs and fan backlash has lead the Premier League into confirming their Festive fixture schedule

Last season, the top flight said it would announce fixtures for the festive period on October 15. However, when Daily Mail Sport revealed only one match would take place on Boxing Day on October 27, thanks to calendar pressures driven by UEFA competition expansions, an announcement remained elusive.

The story was confirmed when the fixture schedulings were eventually announced on October 31 with United’s home fixture with Newcastle United the only one to take place on December 26, with an 8pm kick-off.

Boxing Day this year falls on a Saturday and it is expected that a number of top flight matches will take place.

An announcement on fixture timings is expected this afternoon, according to well-placed sources.

Sports.title: 'The arrogance of the linesman is mental... he's looking at me as if I've just volleyed his cat!': Angry Charlton boss Nathan Jones fumes at official after disallowed goal in 0-0 QPR draw
Sports.content:
'The arrogance of the linesman is mental... he's looking at me as if I've just volleyed his cat!': Angry Charlton boss Nathan Jones fumes at official after disallowed goal in 0-0 QPR draw

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Outspoken Charlton manager Nathan Jones didn't hold back in his criticism of a linesman after seeing his side draw 0-0 with Queens Park Rangers.

In a tight London derby, Charlton thought they had taken the lead when Tyreece Campbell scored in the 39th minute after being put through by Oliver Skipp. However, linesman Bhupinder Gill adjudged the Jamaica international to be offside in a tight call.

And reflecting on that incident in his post-match interview, Jones was scathing of Gill - labelling him as arrogant during his rant, claiming his protestations were met with utter disdain.

'They were giving offsides willy-nilly, we had one offside which wasn't,' the Addicks boss fumed to Sky Sports.

'The goal is a great goal from a great counter-attack, it's onside and it [the decision] has cost us three points once again.

'I think the arrogance of the linesman is mental because he's looking at me as if I've just volleyed his cat. He's looking at me as if I have done something and going "nah".

Charlton manager Nathan Jones was left livid at a linesman during their 0-0 draw with QPR

Tyreece Campbell had a goal disallowed for a tight offside call in the first half on Wednesday

'He's made the biggest error of the night and he's cost us the game and that is the Championship because the Championship is brutal.'

The result sees Charlton move up to fifth in the Championship table after being thumped 4-0 at Jones' old club Stoke City at the weekend, with the visitors also being reduced to 10 men.

That defeat also saw Jones critical of the officials - with the Welshman left 'bitterly disappointed' with Robert Madley for some of the referee's decisions, including the award of a 15th minute penalty which he believed gave Stoke a lifeline back into the contest.

'I've gone in and seen him [the referee]. I'm bitterly disappointed with my own team's performance, but I'm as bitterly disappointed with another performance as well,' the 53-year-old said on Saturday.

'There were so many things that went against us but straight after the penalty we went under for 20 minutes - and my teams don't normally do that.

'But we've done it twice here. That's the thing that hurts me and hurts my teams, us going under like that.

'I think they [Stoke] need me to come here because they get better results when I get back.

'We had a great start and wanted to silence the crowd, but we gave away an absolute gift [for the opening goal]. That can't happen.

'But after the penalty, fair play to Stoke, they never looked back. After that gift of the penalty they were far better.

'I'm definitely going to get it [a hostile reception] when I come back here, but I expected that. I had it when I was manager, so I'm definitely going to get it as an opposing manager.'

Sports.title: The five worst cricket teams to tour England in the last five decades - where do Pakistan's 2026 side rank after series from hell?
Sports.content:
Pakistan’s tour to the UK has lurched from one crisis to the next, with horrific on-field performances matched by barely believable events off it.

Babar Azam’s team appear appear to be careering to a 3-0 whitewash after barely laying a glove on an England side that came into this series devoid of confidence themselves, following a winless 18 months in multi-match series and seeking new direction under the new captaincy of Joe Root after the retirement of Ben Stokes.

But how does this set of performances and results compare to the very worst by touring teams here over the past 50 years?

Here Daily Mail Sport ranks the top five worst...

5th: Pakistan, 1978

Series result: England win 2-0

Thrashed in the two 55-over matches preceding the three-match series, a team led by Wasim Bari were regularly sliced and diced by an emerging Ian Botham.

At Lord’s, Botham became the only cricketer in history to score a Test hundred and take an eight-wicket haul in the same match.

Pakistan had two of the three leading scorers in the series in Sadiq Mohammad and Mohsin Khan, but a distinct lack of depth to their travelling party diluted any competitive edge they might have boasted.

The Pakistanis produced an average score of 169, losing the first two Tests by an innings. The highest average among their other top-six players was in the teens. Without Imran Khan, the bowling lacked venom.

Ian Botham (right) was at his explosive best against Pakistan in 1978, dismantling a side captained by Wasim Bari (left)

4th: India, 2011

Series result: England win 4-0

The presence of icons like Sachin Tendulkar, Rahul Dravid and Mahendra Singh Dhoni made the chasm between India’s team of 15 years ago and England all the more galling for their passionate fanbase.

Dravid struck three hundreds across the four matches, but all ended in defeat - two by an innings and the other two by margins of 196 and 319 runs.

The bowling offered nothing once Zaheer Khan limped out early, contributing to Dhoni whipping off his pads off to bowl at Lord’s, and Zaheer’s fellow left armer RP Singh being lured from a beach holiday in Florida.

All told they accounted for just 47 of the 80 available England wickets. During two months here, they also lost the one-off Twenty20 international and left winless, following a 3-0 scoreline in the one-dayers.

The great Sachin Tendulkar (pictured) was one of a number of star names in India's team in 2011 - but it didn't stop them getting hammered by England

3rd: Australia, 1985

Series result: England win 3-1

It was the same series result as four years previously, only this 3-1 England win lacked the high quality drama of its Botham-fronted predecessor.

The Australians under Allan Border were in a huge state of flux, although they did not have to contend with the selection restrictions placed upon their 1975 counterparts due to World Series Cricket.

Bob Holland and Murray Bennett were chosen to bowl spin while 20-year-old newbie Craig McDermott was in a seam-bowling cartel including an over-the-hill Jeff Thomson, who turned 35 in the mauling at Edgbaston in the fifth Test of six.

Australia had been level at 1-1 thanks to the heroics of Border, their one world-class talent, at Lord’s, but from the third Test onwards it felt like holding back the dam.

England were hardly a vintage outfit themselves during the 1980s, but innings wins for David Gower’s men in the fifth and sixth matches emphasised what a summer of home dominance it had been.

Allan Border is bowled by Richard Ellison (top right) during the fifth Test of the 1985 Ashes. His side lost comfortably to an England team that were hardly a vintage outfit themselves

2nd: Bangladesh, 2005

Series result: England win 2-0

Michael Vaughan’s England flexed their muscles for the historic Ashes victory later that summer by toying with a team that had only been playing Test cricket for five years.

Conceding runs at 5.13 runs per over and unable to bat for more than 40 overs until the final innings of the two-match series, it was a privilege of which they didn’t look worthy.

England bowled woefully by their own admission at Lord’s, yet were abetted by some questionable shot selections from the Bangladeshis. Such was the gulf in quality between the teams, in fact, that Vaughan declared at lunch on day two at Chester-le-Street, just three wickets down.

Both Tests concluded on their third mornings. The only solace for the tourists came in Cardiff with a triangular tournament win for the ages against Australia.

Steve Harmison celebrates dismissing Bangladesh's Nafis Iqbal in the first Test as Lord's

1st: Pakistan, 2026

Series result: England winning 2-0 midway through third Test

From the removal of Test coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and the unprecedented sacking of seven players two-thirds of the way into the series, to the resignation of Misbah-ul-Haq as a selector and an investigation into conduct within the squad, there hasn’t been a dull moment.

Amid the chaos came a tongue in cheek observation that the call-ups of Mohammad Imran Randhawa, 29, and Mohammad Imran Jr, 25, had come about because they didn’t know which one to pick.

The latter had only made eight first-class appearances in five years as a professional cricketer, making him in customary Pakistani cricket logic, the obvious favourite.

Babar Azam’s team appear appear to be careering to a 3-0 whitewash after barely laying a glove on an England side that came into this series devoid of confidence

The bowling has thus far bared more teeth in Birmingham, via the inclusion of the slingy Razaullah, but the batsmen are on course to pack an ignominious record with them when they depart.

Since the World Wars, no team has finished a Test campaign here without having reached 200 at least once – Pakistan have so far made 171, 135, 110, 194 and 133.

Only one opportunity for remedy remains.

Sports.title: Rodri apologises after leaked video showed Barcelona star brutally ridiculing Spanish rivals Valencia
Sports.content:
Barcelona midfielder Rodri has offered an apology to Valencia's players and fans after disparaging remarks he made about the team's lack of quality were leaked.

Rodri, who left Manchester City to join the Catalans this summer after steering Spain to World Cup glory, was caught by television cameras ridiculing Valencia after he was substituted during Barcelona's 5-0 thrashing of the LaLiga outfit last Sunday.

Using enhanced audio and lip-reading technology, Spanish network Movistar deciphered Rodri describing Valencia as 'really poor' after Barcelona team-mate Pau Cubarsi asked for his opinion on the team.

Before carrying out his post-match media duties following Barcelona's 5-1 Champions League victory over Feyenoord on Wednesday, Rodri issued a public apology to Valencia and revealed he phoned up club captain Jose Gaya to make amends.

The Spaniard said: 'In life when you make a mistake, you have to come out and ask for an apology. I'd like to apologise to those who felt offended, to Valencia fans, players, anyone who felt offended by my words. I had a phone call with my friend and team-mate Jose and asked for forgiveness, I apologised to the whole squad.

'I'd also like to make clear that it was an expression of surprise. Anybody who sees the video can see that. At no time did I want to bully or take out of context any bad moment of any team - not at all.

Rodri's disparaging comments about Valencia were picked up by television cameras last week

The Barcelona midfielder has offered an apology to the club after ridiculing them on the bench

🚨🗣️ Rodri à Cubarsí depuis le banc : « Très faibles. Ils sont vraiment très faibles, ceux-là, hein ? Très faibles, mec. Ils n’ont même pas dépassé le milieu de terrain en deuxième période. » pic.twitter.com/5s9z20yQsM — Blaugranation (@Blaugranation_) September 7, 2026

'We all want - or in my case I want - Valencia to get back to the place where it should be, which is being one of the best clubs in this league. Simply, wanted to say that. I'd also like to say it was a private conversation, and I think from there we should all learn a bit more that sometimes things are taken a bit out of context, but at no time did I mean any disrespect and I reiterate my apologies to Valencia Club de Futbol.'

Rodri, who came off against Valencia in the 62nd minute with Barcelona already 3-0 ahead, was captured by cameras saying: 'They're poor. They're really poor, eh? Man, they haven't even got over the midfield line in the second half.'

The 2024 Ballon d'Or winner started his career at Villarreal, Valencia's archrivals, before moving to Atletico Madrid in 2018.

A year later he signed for Manchester City, where he won four Premier League titles, two FA Cups, three League Cups and a Champions League trophy.

Barcelona have enjoyed an excellent start to the season since Rodri's £65.4million switch to the Nou Camp this summer, winning all four of their LaLiga matches so far to sit top of the table ahead of Sunday’s trip to Levante.

Sports.title: Chelsea should be STRIPPED of their last Premier League title - with Tottenham crowned instead, says Mauricio Pochettino... as he reveals Spurs DID contact him earlier this year and he WOULD have gone back even if they'd been relegated
Sports.content:
Ten years ago, Mauricio Pochettino was embarking upon a season in which his Tottenham team scored 86 goals and collected 86 points, and he is convinced they should be crowned as champions.

Chelsea won the Premier League in 2017 but have since admitted breaking the rules by making secret payments exceeding £47million to unregistered agents and third parties to secure transfers.

Pochettino has no doubt the Blues should be stripped of that title. He also believes it should rightfully go to Spurs in the same way an Olympic silver medallist would receive gold if the gold medallist were disqualified.

'We should win one title, one Premier League,' insists USA boss Pochettino. 'We should have been awarded it. They were punished. They admitted it. The title should be for the team that was second.

'We deserve to be champions that year. We didn't compete with the same rules. It's impossible if some clubs play with offside and others don't or one plays with VAR and another plays without VAR. For everyone the same rules and then the same capacity to create the best team.'

Chelsea were fined this year by the Premier League for the illegal payments covering a period from 2011-18 and including the deal to sign Eden Hazard who excelled in the 2016-17 season when they beat Spurs to the title under Antonio Conte.

Chelsea won the Premier League in 2017 - but Mauricio Pochettino wants it taken off them

Pochettino has seen Chelsea punished over secret payments to unregistered agents

They escaped sporting sanctions because the offences were self-reported and they helped the investigation.

'Maybe with the same rules we could've signed some players that would have made the team better or scored more goals,' says Pochettino. 'It's not me complaining, it's the truth.

'I have no doubt and I'm not scared to say the truth. The Chelsea fans will be upset with me but if Tottenham broke the rules, I'd say we don't deserve the title.

'I don't say they didn't play well or that Conte wasn't great. I don't want this message twisted. But if you broke the rules, then "ciao", you need to give it to another team.'

Pochettino has managed both clubs. His single season at Chelsea will not live long in the memory but his five years at Spurs is the club's finest era in recent history albeit without lifting a trophy.

Playing fluent, attacking football and with Harry Kane banging in the goals, they were Premier League and Champions League runners-up and all on a budget restricted by investment in a new stadium and training ground.

Chelsea's John Terry and owner Roman Abramovich hold up the club's last league title

Tottenham finished second in the Premier League - on 86 points - behind winners Chelsea

From January 2018 to July 2019, Spurs did not make a signing. The cumulative spend from the first five of his six summer transfer windows did not break £300m.

So, does he envy Roberto De Zerbi's summer spree of 10 signings at a cost close to £400m?

'I am happy,' says Pochettino, back home in London before this month's international break. 'Tottenham is still my club, and I want the best for them.

'If they have the possibility to spend on proven players in the Premier League it's good for the club. After the relegation battle it's important to improve and not to suffer.'

This free-spending strategy is led by a new generation of the Lewis family who own Spurs, patriarch Joe's daughter Vivienne Lewis and her son-in-law Nick Beucher along with chief executive Vinai Venkatesham and sporting director Johan Lange.

Just over a year has passed since Daniel Levy was ousted as Spurs chairman. And, although there were times when their relationship was tense, Levy and Pochettino grew close and remain in contact.

'He feels like I did when I was sacked,' says Pochettino. 'Now he knows the feeling. Yes, I keep in touch with him. I never made the situation personal.

'It's like you receive the letter and you are sacked, pick up your things and you can never come back. Maybe 200, 300 people that were your family, you cannot say goodbye, cannot send a text, cannot do nothing.

'That was really, really tough for me. I was talking with him about that. Of course, I'm not happy that now he feels the same because I am not a person with bad feelings.

Pochettino is in regular contact with Daniel Levy - who now also finds himself out at Spurs

'It's difficult because for him. For 25 years he was building his house, his club, and what happened after, for sure, was tough for him, for his family and of course I am so sorry for him and for everyone.'

Pochettino confirms he was contacted by Spurs earlier this year, as they lurched in midseason panic from Thomas Frank to Igor Tudor and came perilously close to relegation.

'Yes, but in this moment they called everyone, all the coaches, those free and not free,' he jokes, but he is serious when he adds. 'If I was free, of course, I come. But I wasn't free. I was preparing the World Cup.'

Pochettino was committed to leading the USA into the World Cup as hosts, but his initial two-year contract was expiring after the tournament and there was no decision made on his next move.

Ever since leaving in 2019, he has always been open about his desire to return one day to Spurs and would not have been deterred had they been relegated to the Championship.

'It's the only club that always I am open to help, whatever division,' he says. 'Another club, no. But Tottenham, yes.'

When Tudor's interim tenure quickly turned sour, Spurs secured De Zerbi on a long-term deal and the notion of a romantic reunion in N17 evaporated again for Pochettino.

'The timings were never the best,' he says. 'When I was free, I never received a contact and then when I was working, I received a contact, but I cannot make the decision to come back. A little bit unlucky. Maybe one day the stars will align and it can happen.'

At the World Cup, his USA team made a flying start, firing the imagination of a nation where football is far from top of the bill, only to lose to Belgium in the last 16 amid a row raging about Folarin Balogun's escape from suspension and claims of interference by the president, Donald Trump.

Tottenham hired Roberto De Zerbi - but Pochettino says he did speak to them about the job

Pochettino rejects the Balogun affair as an excuse, only that his team did not perform to their best when it mattered most. And explains how bonds forged with the US football federation around the World Cup and the public reaction to those early successes convinced him to sign a new four-year deal.

'Before the World Cup we met the board in New York and they offered us four more years,' explains the 54-year-old Argentine. 'I said, 'Yeah but if we lose all the games…' and they said, 'No, no, no we trust in you and your vision and the way you behave'.'

The US federation was aware there would be clubs trying to tempt Pochettino, but he promised to entertain no offers and make no negotiations, focus on the World Cup and then reconvene.

When that time came, he was ready to sign until 2030, another World Cup cycle and has upcoming friendlies against Peru, Chile, Mexico and Canada.

He is part of a band of elite former Premier League coaches including Thomas Tuchel, Jurgan Klopp and Carlo Ancelotti, now plying their trade in international football.

'It's more pure,' admits Pochettino when asked about the allure. 'It's intense with limited time, but you enjoy a lot one week with the players.

'The players are not toxic, they come because they want to enjoy, they want to play, they don't have time to become upset or disappointed because they don't play. It's all very motivated and the moment they start to become upset they go home to their clubs.'

Meanwhile his son Maurizio, 25, is playing career at Inter Escaldes, Andorra's first club to reach the league phase of UEFA competition in the Conference League.

And his affection for Spurs will not fade. Nor his affection for English football despite the fierce rivalry with Argentina rekindled by a World Cup semi-final. He will not reject the idea he might one day managing England when his work at the USA is complete.

'With our experience maybe yes,' says Pochettino. 'I believe in diplomatic things.' As if to prove it, he offers his unequivocal backing for England captain Kane to win the Ballon D'Or.

'It's Harry Kane's time. It's not clear today who is number one in the world and should win. In the past, it was more clear. He deserves it in his career and if I am to pick one then it's Harry Kane.'

Sports.title: Alexis Mac Allister learns his lesson after public revelation over his Liverpool future - more of these destructive winners and there will be a new contract in front of him, writes IAN LADYMAN
Sports.content:
Alexis Mac Allister is a World Cup champion and Premier League winner but even the most experienced footballers occasionally learn lessons. The Liverpool midfielder this week learnt that maybe it’s best to earn new contracts by winning matches rather than lighting up press conferences. Mac Allister’s decision to preface this game by moaning about the lack of a new contract offer was either clumsy or sinister in its timing. Only he knows his motive but what is certain is his manager Andoni Iraola – only three meaningful games into his Anfield tenure – could have done without it. But here, out on the grass where it really mattered, Mac Allister rescued an important European game against a high calibre opponent with a 20-yard shot so pure and powerful and destructive that it may as well have been accompanied by the crashing of cymbals and the banging of drums. Much more of that and there will indeed be a piece of paper in front of the Argentinean with his name on it and maybe a 27-year-old footballer of great experience will reflect on that over time. Liverpool needed the goal, too. Unconvincing early on against Diego Simeone’s streetwise side, Liverpool had fallen behind to a Marcos Llorente goal after 17 minutes. Liverpool came from behind to beat Atletico Madrid 2-1 in their Champions League opener Alexis Mac Allister scored the winner, a day after he cast doubt over his Liverpool future Andoni Iraola picked up a victory in his first game as a manger in the Champions League And though Dominik Szoboszlai had equalised just before half-time, the game was very much in the balance before Mac Allister delivered so sweetly at the Kop End. This had felt like the biggest test of Liverpool’s early season beforehand and that was how it turned out. Atletico have not started the Spanish league season particularly impressively but they were familiar in much of what they did here. When Llorente gave them the lead in the 17th minute, it was his fifth goal against Liverpool – exactly half his total Champions League tally – and that pretty much summed things up at that stage. Atletico were sharp and hungry and as irritatingly sly as ever. It felt at times as though they were rolling out a blueprint with which to thwart Liverpool that had been well drilled through the years. Patience is certainly a virtue when a team plays a Simeone side. They will give you nothing and try and take plenty, especially when the referee isn’t looking. For a while they were too comfortable here and it took Szoboszlai’s goal just before half-time to settle Iraola’s team down a little. After that, doubtless to Iraola’s relief, it was a different game. The new Liverpool manager - in charge of his first Champions League game – had handed £125m Bradley Barcola his first start and asked young Rio Ngumoha to play on the other side after Cody Gakpo reported with a minor injury. Liverpool could have scored within 15 seconds. Szoboszlai robbed an opponent straight from the kick-off and played Alexander Isak in down the right only for the Swede to pull his right foot shot across goal and wide. It was a really good chance but didn’t immediately serve to preface more of the same. Instead it was Atletico who carried the first half threat, looking to penetrate Liverpool’s dreadfully square back four whenever they broke through the centre of the field. Iraola had stuck with the same full-backs who had started last Friday’s win at Ipswich. Both were to feature in Liverpool’s equaliser but left-back Milos Kerkez was all over the place for the first half an hour. He often is. Kerkez, once a Bournemouth player for Iraola, seems to do everything at 100 miles an hour and as such hardly ever looks in control. Either going forward or in retreat, the Hungarian injects chaos in this Liverpool team and at some point he is going to have to learn. Here, he was a yard behind his defensive team-mates as Julian Alvarez played Llorente through towards the Kop for the Spaniard to lift the ball over Alisson Becker and into the goal with ease. Atletico were worth their lead at this point and Liverpool’s immediate response was unconvincing. They were slow and clunky with the ball and – with their best defensive midfielder Ryan Gravenberch inexplicably left on the bench yet again - as open as a barn door when they were without it. Marcos Llorente had put Atletico 1-0 ahead to continue his superb record against Liverpool Dominik Szoboszlai equalised before half-time, and Mac Allister's had a decisive intervention Bradley Barcola made his European bow for the Reds on what was his first start for the club Alisson saved well from Alvarez when Atletico caught the Liverpool defence square again in the 27th minute and only in the ten minutes before half-time did the home team start to deliver any kind of momentum and threat. Atletico goalkeeper Jan Oblak saved well from Florian Wirtz after Isak’s superb far post pass before Kerkez showed great heart to win the ball in midfield and set in motion the move that led to the equaliser. His pass across the penalty area allowed Barcola to shoot and when the ball ran loose off the goalkeeper, right-back Ronald Araujo had advanced to flick it cleverly to Szoboszlai who side footed it gently into the corner. Simeone’s team came again as Alex Baena volleyed wide but at the start of the second half it was Liverpool who found a rhythm. Barcola should have scored his first Liverpool goal – shooting wide after Wirtz played him clear – but soon after Mac Allister slammed in his redemption goal from 20 yards after Ngumoha’s run across the byline preceded a hurried clearance from a Spanish defence feeling the squeeze for the first time. The adrenaline rush of a deficit being turned into a lead in the space of ten minutes was significant and almost tangible. It didn’t herald further Liverpool dominance, though. Indeed it was Alvarez who spurned the next chance of the game, side footing at Alisson when he should have done better from 14 yards. By now Barcola had gone off with what Liverpool will hope was only cramp. With fifteen minutes left, it was Atletico who were once again pushing. In vain, as it turned out. This felt big for Liverpool and their manager. And maybe for Alexis Mac Allister too.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan

Semi-final: Italy vs Northern Ireland

Semi-final: Wales vs Bosnia and Herzegovina

Final: Wales/Bosnia and Herzegovina vs Italy/Northern Ireland - Tuesday, 7.45pm kick-off

Play-off Path B:
