World.title: Liberia: SpoonTV CEO Cuts a Deal, Trades Prison for Testimony
World.content:
Monrovia — SpoonTV CEO Stanton Witherspoon has secured his release after prosecutors credited him with providing substantial assistance in the investigation and prosecution of a multimillion-dollar scheme involving the sale of fraudulent nursing diplomas and transcripts.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

Witherspoon, who pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud, was originally sentenced in November 2023 to 41 months in prison and three years of supervised release.

But on September 9, 2026, U.S. District Judge Rodney Smith granted a government motion under Rule 35(b) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, reducing Witherspoon’s sentence to time served and eliminating the supervised-release requirement. The remaining counts against him—Counts 2 through 6 and Count 8—were dismissed.

The $5.17 Million Scheme

According to prosecutors, Witherspoon was a 50% owner of Siena Education Center LLC and Siena College of Health II LLC, as well as founder and president of Nursing Education Resource Center LLC (NERC).

Prosecutors said Witherspoon worked with Rene Bernadel, Alfred Sellu and Cimoyne Alves through NERC to recruit and train aspiring nurses.

He later worked with Eunide Sanon and Siena to provide fraudulent nursing-school diplomas and transcripts. The documents were used by students to obtain fraudulent certification as registered nurses or licensed practical nurses.

Witherspoon was held responsible for approximately $5.17 million in losses.

His total offense level was calculated at 26, with a criminal history category of I, resulting in a federal sentencing guideline range of 63 to 78 months. He ultimately received a 41-month sentence in 2023.

Testimony Against Co-Conspirators

The government’s decision to seek a reduction in Witherspoon’s sentence was tied directly to his cooperation with federal investigators and prosecutors.

Before entering his guilty plea, Witherspoon was interviewed by agents from the FBI and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General about individuals involved in nursing-school fraud schemes.

Prosecutors said his cooperation subsequently contributed to cases against several defendants.

Among those was Carleen Noreus, who operated a separate fraudulent nursing program known as Carleen Health Institute. Witherspoon testified against Noreus at trial, and she later pleaded guilty to wire fraud and money-laundering conspiracy charges. She is awaiting sentencing.

Other defendants who pleaded guilty to wire fraud conspiracy charges included Cimoyne Alves, Lemuel Pierre and Cleophat Tanis.

Witherspoon also provided an affidavit identifying nursing students who had received fraudulent degrees and transcripts. That information was forwarded to the National Council of State Boards of Nursing, allowing state licensing boards to take remedial action.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Florida, together with HHS-OIG and FBI investigators, supported the reduction, citing the scope and usefulness of Witherspoon’s cooperation.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Christopher J. Clark filed the Rule 35(b) motion on behalf of the government.

From Conviction to Freedom

The court’s decision means Witherspoon has now completed his federal prison sentence and will not be required to serve the previously imposed three years of supervised release.

His release has generated considerable reaction in Liberia, where Witherspoon is a prominent media personality and the head of the Spoon Network.

Witherspoon was a vocal supporter of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai and the Unity Party Alliance during the 2023 Presidential and Legislative Elections.

He used the Spoon Network to campaign for Boakai, then a former vice president and opposition candidate, and helped to organize political events involving the Boakai campaign in the United States.

The media entrepreneur was subsequently credited by supporters with playing a role in mobilizing Liberians abroad and helping the Unity Party candidate defeat then-President George Weah.

Despite his support for Boakai, however, Witherspoon has since used his media platform to criticize aspects of the administration, regularly highlighting what he describes as policy failures and missteps by officials of the government he once strongly supported.

‘Now That We Are Free, We Will Talk’

Following the court’s decision, Witherspoon appeared on his Spoon Network and thanked his wife, relatives, pastor, staff and Liberians who supported him during his legal ordeal.

He also sought to separate his release from Liberia’s political divisions.

“God didn’t do this for me. God did it because He is God,” Witherspoon said.

“This is not about the Unity Party, not about CDC, not about who is in government. We will continue to talk; we are not going anywhere. Now that we are free, we will talk.”

He thanked Liberians, politicians and private citizens who had contacted him, prayed for him and wished him well.

The news of his release has produced mixed reactions, with supporters celebrating the decision while others have questioned the court’s action in reducing his sentence.

Spoon Network Celebrates

Tetee C. Karneh, CEO of the Spoon Network, also appeared briefly on Spoon Talk following the ruling and thanked the network’s staff and Witherspoon’s wife for standing by him throughout the legal proceedings.

Karneh, who previously served as General Manager of Spoon FM before being elevated to CEO as Witherspoon focused on his legal case, attributed his release to divine intervention.

She also thanked the Liberian people for their support and expressed appreciation to the U.S. court system.

Snowe Welcomes Release

Bomi County Senator Edwin Melvin Snowe also welcomed Witherspoon’s release in a statement posted on Facebook.

“My dear friend, Stanton, through it all, you looked unto the hills from whence cometh your help. You kept the faith, you trusted God, and today, your prayers have been answered,” Snowe wrote.

He described Witherspoon as “a free man” and said he shared in the relief and gratitude surrounding the end of the difficult chapter.

“May this experience strengthen your faith even more and remind you that no matter how difficult the journey becomes, God remains faithful,” Snowe added.

For Witherspoon, the federal court ruling closes one chapter of his legal battle—but his active role in Liberia’s highly charged media and political landscape could open another, particularly after his declaration that “now that we are free, we will talk.”

World.title: Liberia: Boakai Puts Banks, Borrowers and Government on Notice As NPLs Hit 19%, Demands Urgent Fix
World.content:
Monrovia — President Joseph Boakai has called for urgent and coordinated action to resolve Liberia’s persistent non-performing loan (NPL) problem, warning that the crisis is restricting access to credit and threatening the country’s broader economic growth.

Jaheim T. [email protected]

Speaking Wednesday, September 9, at the opening of the National Conference on the Resolution of Non-Performing Loans at the Ministerial Complex in Monrovia, President Boakai said the issue must no longer be treated as merely a technical banking concern, but as a national development challenge.

The three-day conference, convened by the Central Bank of Liberia, is being held under the theme, “Resolving Non-Performing Loans to Unlock Access to Finance for Private Sector Growth and Job Creation.”

The gathering brings together government officials, commercial banks, regulators, the judiciary, the Legislature, private sector representatives and development partners to examine the causes of distressed loans and develop measures to improve credit recovery and expand access to financing.

President Boakai said the consequences of unpaid loans extend far beyond bank balance sheets.

“This issue, in my view, is really about people,” the President said, pointing to farmers seeking financing to expand production, young entrepreneurs looking for capital, businesses hoping to expand and create jobs, and depositors whose funds must be protected.

He warned that when loans remain unpaid, money that should circulate through the economy becomes trapped, forcing banks to become more cautious and making credit harder and more expensive for legitimate borrowers.

“That is why the theme of this conference … is both timely and important,” Boakai said. “This is not simply a banking problem. It is a national development challenge.”

Liberia’s NPL Burden

CBL Executive Governor Henry F. Saamoi provided a stark picture of the problem, revealing that Liberia’s banking sector recorded a non-performing loan ratio of 19.1 percent at the end of 2024, nearly twice the prudential benchmark.

Although the ratio declined to 12.9 percent in 2025, Saamoi cautioned that the improvement was driven largely by loan restructurings and write-offs rather than sustainable recoveries.

The figures, he said, underscore the need for structural reforms aimed at strengthening repayment performance, credit discipline and debt recovery.

“Liberia’s elevated level of non-performing loans demands decisive action,” Saamoi said.

He compared Liberia’s situation with other countries, noting that Ghana recorded an NPL ratio of 21.8 percent in 2024, while Nigeria recorded 8.1 percent, Guinea 6.7 percent and The Gambia 4.6 percent.

According to Saamoi, international experience shows that systemic NPL problems cannot be resolved through isolated action by regulators or banks.

“Governments must play their part. Regulators must play their part. Banks must play their part. The judiciary must play its part. Borrowers must play their part and development partners must play their part,” he said.

Boakai Demands Accountability

President Boakai stressed that resolving the existing stock of bad loans must be accompanied by measures to prevent new ones.

He called for stronger credit reporting systems, improved land administration and collateral registration, better use of technology, expansion of responsible digital financial services and reforms to Liberia’s insolvency framework.

He also placed responsibility on both lenders and borrowers.

“Banks must lend responsibly and conduct proper assessments of those to whom they lend,” Boakai said. “Borrowers must also understand that loans are obligations that must be repaid.”

He further emphasized the importance of enforceable contracts and collateral, as well as an effective judiciary capable of resolving disputes fairly and efficiently.

“Contracts must mean something. Collateral must mean something,” he said.

But the President reserved some of his strongest remarks for what he described as Liberia’s tendency to produce recommendations without sufficient follow-through.

“The success of this conference will not be measured by the speeches we make or the recommendations we write. It will be measured by what we do after we leave this room,” Boakai said.

“Liberia has had many conferences. We have produced many good reports and recommendations. What our people need now is implementation.”

He urged participants to leave the conference with clear commitments, assigned responsibilities, realistic timelines and a mechanism for monitoring implementation.

Finance Minister Links Government Arrears to Bad Loans

Finance and Development Planning Minister Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan broadened the discussion, arguing that government’s own payment practices can contribute to the accumulation of non-performing loans within the banking sector.

Ngafuan explained that when government fails to pay contractors, suppliers and service providers on time, those businesses may struggle to service loans they previously obtained from commercial banks.

“What begins as a government arrear can eventually end up as a non-performing loan on the balance sheet of a commercial bank,” Ngafuan said.

He said the Boakai administration is therefore seeking to restore government’s credibility as an economic actor by honoring legitimate financial obligations.

“When this government contracts with you, government must pay you,” Ngafuan declared.

He acknowledged that the administration inherited significant legacy obligations but said the government is addressing them within available fiscal space while seeking to avoid creating new arrears.

Ngafuan said the current national budget provides nearly US$235 million for debt service, including more than US$90 million for commercial debt.

He also cited approximately US$25 million budgeted for debt service to the World Bank, arguing that government must demonstrate the same repayment culture it expects from citizens and businesses.

“We cannot call upon citizens and businesses to honor their obligations to banks while government fails to honor its obligations to those banks,” he said.

From Bad Loans to Productive Capital

For the CBL governor, the ultimate objective is not merely to reduce the NPL ratio but to free up capital for productive economic activity.

Saamoi said the conference is expected to produce three key outputs: a conference communique, an NPL resolution policy roadmap and a reform action plan.

The roadmap is expected to identify practical reforms in credit risk management, debt recovery, collateral enforcement and credit discipline, while also assessing the regulatory, legal and judicial systems governing loan recovery.

Ngafuan said resolving distressed assets should ultimately redirect capital toward agriculture, manufacturing, construction, trade, technology, housing and other productive sectors.

He argued that government alone cannot employ every Liberian and that sustainable job creation requires a stronger private sector capable of investing, innovating and expanding.

President Boakai similarly linked the NPL crisis to his administration’s ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development, which seeks to expand employment, empower women and young people, strengthen agriculture and food security, improve infrastructure and grow Liberian businesses.

The President said those ambitions cannot be achieved without a financial system capable of providing affordable and reliable financing.

A Test of Implementation

The conference comes at a time when Liberia’s financial sector continues to face the twin challenge of improving loan recovery while expanding access to credit for businesses and households.

For Boakai, the challenge now is to move beyond diagnosis.

“We know the problem. We have brought the right institutions together. Now we must move from discussion to action,” he said.

Saamoi echoed that position, describing the conference as an opportunity to establish a new chapter in Liberia’s financial sector—one marked by stronger banks, healthier balance sheets, greater financial inclusion, expanded access to credit, increased investment and more jobs.

“The ultimate measure of success of this conference will not simply be a lower NPL ratio,” Saamoi said. “Success will be reflected in greater access to credit, better repayment terms and performance, stronger businesses, expanded investment, increased employment opportunities and improved livelihoods for our people.”

For the Boakai administration, the resolution of bad loans has therefore become part of a broader economic question: how to unlock capital trapped in distressed assets and put it back to work in an economy where farmers, businesses, entrepreneurs and young Liberians are demanding greater access to finance.

World.title: Liberia: McGill Rejects Costa’s Drug Cartel Allegation, Demands Evidence
World.content:
Senator Says Claims Linking Him to Alleged Narcotics Network Are “False, Malicious and Unsupported”

Monrovia — Senator Nathaniel F. McGill has strongly rejected allegations by political commentator Henry Pedro Costa seeking to link him to an alleged drug cartel, describing the claims as false, malicious and unsupported by credible evidence.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

The allegation comes amid heightened public scrutiny of Liberia’s ongoing investigation and prosecution of individuals accused of involvement in the country’s recent high-profile narcotics cases, with competing claims and counterclaims increasingly playing out in the media and political space.

In a recent podcast, Costa allegedly claimed that Gerald Smith told investigators that Senator McGill was linked to a drug cartel. The allegation has not been independently substantiated by FrontPage Africa.

Responding through an official statement, the Office of Senator McGill categorically denied any connection between the senator and drug trafficking or an alleged narcotics organization.

“The Office categorically rejects these allegations as false, misleading, malicious, and entirely unsupported by credible evidence,” the statement said.

The senator’s office maintained that McGill has never associated himself with a drug cartel, drug-trafficking operation or illegal drug business.

It cautioned against presenting allegations based on insinuation, speculation or unverified claims as established facts before the Liberian public.

Denies Financial Link to Gerald Smith

A central aspect of the statement was the office’s denial that McGill ever received money from Gerald Smith or anyone associated with him in connection with alleged drug-related activities.

“The Office further states unequivocally that Senator McGill has never received money from Mr. Gerald Smith or from anyone associated with him in connection with any alleged drug-related activity,” the statement said.

According to the senator’s office, McGill’s relationship with Smith was strictly professional and arose from their respective government positions.

At the time referenced, Smith served as Deputy Director of the National Security Agency, while McGill served as Minister of State.

Their interactions, the office said, occurred within the normal course of official government responsibilities.

‘Produce the Evidence’

McGill’s office challenged anyone making allegations against the senator to take the claims beyond public commentary and submit whatever evidence exists to Liberia’s investigative and judicial authorities.

“If any individual possesses evidence establishing otherwise, the appropriate course is to present that evidence to the relevant investigative and judicial authorities,” the statement said.

The office emphasized that allegations and repeated references to unverified claims should not be confused with evidence.

It argued that accusations involving serious crimes such as narcotics trafficking should be handled through credible evidence and established legal processes rather than political rhetoric.

The statement also referenced what McGill’s office described as previous attempts by political actors associated with the Unity Party to connect the senator to the reported US$317 million cocaine seizure.

The office maintained that no credible evidence has been publicly established linking McGill to the narcotics seizure.

Drug Investigation Becomes Political Battleground

The latest dispute adds another layer to an increasingly contentious national debate over Liberia’s drug investigations.

The government’s prosecution of suspects in connection with major cocaine seizures has generated intense political controversy, with opposition figures, political commentators and government officials trading accusations over who may have known about, facilitated or benefited from the alleged narcotics operations.

McGill’s office warned that reducing serious narcotics allegations to political accusations could undermine public confidence in legitimate investigations.

“The Office considers it inappropriate for serious matters involving alleged narcotics trafficking to be reduced to political accusations without substantiating evidence,” the statement said.

It argued that unsupported allegations could distract from the need for transparent and evidence-based accountability.

The office therefore called on those making allegations to produce the evidence underlying their claims and, where appropriate, submit that evidence to competent authorities for independent investigation.

McGill Says He Is Ready to Respond

Despite rejecting the allegations, McGill’s office said the senator remains willing to respond to legitimate questions and credible evidence.

“Allegations of criminal conduct must not be presented as established facts in the absence of verifiable evidence,” the office said.

It maintained that the appropriate test for the allegations is evidence, not political assertion.

The statement concluded with a direct challenge to those advancing the claims: if evidence exists, it should be submitted to the authorities; if no evidence exists, the allegations should not be used as political propaganda or as a basis for publicly characterizing the senator as involved in criminal conduct.

The statement was issued by the Office of Senator Nathaniel F. McGill, Republic of Liberia.

World.title: Liberia: Bishop Brown Cautions Opposition Leaders Amid Ongoing Collaboration Talks
World.content:
Monrovia — Former Liberia Council of Churches President, Bishop Kortu Brown, has urged opposition politicians to approach Liberia’s political challenges with greater responsibility, cautioning them against allowing the pursuit of political power to overshadow the national interest.

By Obediah Johnson, [email protected]

Brown, who is Founder and General Overseer of the New Water in the Desert Apostolic Pentecostal Church, said Liberia’s political class has a responsibility to create an environment where disagreements can be managed through dialogue rather than confrontation.

His appeal comes at a time when political actors from opposition parties and members of the governing establishment have increasingly engaged in discussions aimed at addressing national issues and exploring areas of common interest.

While welcoming recent roundtable engagements involving opposition leaders and lawmakers associated with the ruling Unity Party, Brown said such meetings would only be meaningful if they produced discussions centered on the welfare of ordinary Liberians.

He made the remarks during a thanksgiving service at his church in Brewerville, outside Monrovia.

For Brown, Liberia’s political future should not be reduced to the question of who will control the Executive Mansion after the 2029 elections.

He argued that political leaders should be more concerned about the decisions they make today and how those decisions affect the country’s stability and future generations.

Brown acknowledged that politicians naturally seek state power, but maintained that the outcome of elections ultimately cannot be determined solely by political calculations.

“Liberians have seen everything. We’ve seen war and peace, CDC and UP,” he said, emphasizing that Liberia’s political history should encourage leaders to act with greater responsibility.

He called on opposition politicians to become a constructive force capable of criticizing government while also contributing ideas toward solving the country’s problems.

Brown said opposition leaders should not view political engagement solely through the lens of gaining power, but should also consider their responsibility to maintain peace and national cohesion.

His message was particularly directed at political leaders preparing for the next electoral cycle. He urged them to engage one another, communicate with government officials and seek common ground on issues affecting Liberians.

Brown believes political disagreements are inevitable, but warned that the manner in which those disagreements are handled can either strengthen or weaken the country.

He therefore encouraged opposition leaders to maintain dialogue among themselves and with those currently exercising state authority. “God is in control of this country,” Brown said, stressing his belief that Liberia’s political destiny cannot be determined entirely by human calculations.

He urged opposition leaders to make peace and demonstrate political maturity as they prepare for the 2029 elections.

The religious leader also cautioned Liberians against allowing historical grievances to dictate contemporary relationships.

He warned against attempts to punish or seek revenge against members of the present generation because of wrongdoing committed by their ancestors.

According to Brown, Liberia’s history contains numerous examples of conflicts that began with disputes involving families and communities and later developed into wider divisions.

His appeal was therefore not limited to political parties. He called on Liberians generally to resist the temptation to inherit conflicts and grievances from previous generations.

Brown’s remarks also reflected on Liberia’s turbulent political history.

His reference to “war and peace” and successive political administrations underscored the dramatic changes the country has experienced over the years.

For him, those experiences should provide sufficient lessons for the current generation to avoid repeating the mistakes that contributed to division and instability.

He maintained that Liberia still has people capable of contributing positively to national development if given the opportunity. “But Liberia still got some good people that can be used to produce more good people,” he said.

The statement appeared to be a call for greater confidence in Liberians themselves and for the country’s political and social institutions to encourage citizens who can contribute constructively to national life.

Brown also commented on the legal situation involving former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor, whose temporary release on medical grounds has attracted considerable political attention.

He commended the court for granting Taylor compassionate relief and placing her under house arrest in connection with the ongoing cocaine case.

The former vice president’s detention had become a politically sensitive issue, particularly among supporters of the opposition National Patriotic Party and other political actors who had raised concerns about her health and treatment.

Brown argued that Taylor’s release had helped ease political tensions surrounding the case. He said the development should provide an opportunity for Liberians to redirect their attention toward issues affecting their daily lives rather than allowing political disagreements to escalate.

His comments came against the backdrop of wider concerns over political polarization and the increasingly heated exchanges among supporters of rival political camps.

Brown also challenged Liberians to reconsider what he described as a culture of constant complaint. Rather than spending their energy blaming government, relatives or other people for their difficulties, he encouraged citizens to make productive use of whatever opportunities and resources are available to them.

His appeal extended beyond politics to personal responsibility. Brown suggested that national progress requires citizens to recognize their own capacity to improve their circumstances while simultaneously holding public officials accountable.

The distinction, he implied, is between constructive criticism and a culture in which citizens remain focused entirely on what others have failed to do.

With Liberia’s next presidential and general elections still ahead, Brown’s intervention places renewed emphasis on the conduct of political actors before the campaign period intensifies. His message is that the competition for political power should not come at the expense of national peace.

He wants opposition parties to remain engaged, but responsible; critical, but constructive; and ambitious, but mindful of the consequences of political confrontation.

The 2029 elections will inevitably produce competing interests and competing visions for Liberia. But Brown believes the country should not have to pay the price for those differences. His broader appeal is for political leaders to learn from Liberia’s history rather than reproduce it.

For Brown, the most important political calculation is not simply who wins an election, but whether Liberia remains peaceful, united and capable of giving its citizens a better future.

World.title: Liberia: NPA Security Director Charles Roberts Under Fire for Calling MDR Lawmaker ‘Monkey’
World.content:
MONROVIA — Charles Roberts, Security Director at the National Port Authority and a vocal supporter of the ruling Unity Party, Wednesday described Nimba County lawmaker Kortor Sehwongbay Kwagrue as a “monkey” in a Facebook post.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

The statement, which has since been deleted from Roberts’ official Facebook page following public criticism, came after Representative Kwagrue challenged officials of the Unity Party-led government over what he described as growing arrogance, inaccessibility and “meanness” toward ordinary Liberians.

The confrontation has drawn attention not only because of the language used by a government official, but also because Kwagrue is a member of the Movement for Democracy and Reconstruction (MDR), an affiliate of the Unity Party.

At a time when the Joseph Boakai administration is seeking to consolidate its political base and deliver on its development agenda, the public exchange has raised questions about how members of the governing alliance respond to criticism from within their own political ranks.

Rep. Kwagrue’s remarks were essentially a warning to the Unity Party leadership that political power can be lost when government officials become disconnected from the citizens who helped put them into office.

The Nimba County lawmaker urged the ruling party to examine what he described as mistakes similar to those that contributed to the defeat of the former Coalition for Democratic Change (CDC) administration. He argued that the CDC’s experience should serve as a political lesson for the Unity Party, particularly at a time when some government officials are allegedly becoming increasingly distant from grassroots supporters.

Rep. Kwagrue’s message was not that President Boakai had failed in every respect. In fact, the lawmaker expressly described Boakai as a “developmental president” and acknowledged that his administration was making progress. His concern was that the President’s achievements could be overshadowed by the conduct of people around him.

According to Rep. Kwagrue, a president’s political legacy cannot be protected simply by constructing roads, implementing development projects or signing government contracts. He maintained that political leaders must also maintain direct relationships with the people and ensure that their officials remain accessible.

“The reason people in Liberia will die for Joseph Boakai with sincerity is because he made a personal impact on them,” Rep. Kwagrue said, arguing that many government officials have become so removed from ordinary citizens that the people they are supposed to serve do not even know where to find them.

The lawmaker questioned how citizens could tell ministers the truth about conditions in their communities if those officials were inaccessible. He, therefore, called on the Unity Party to reconnect with grassroots politicians and supporters who worked to bring the party to power during the 2023 elections.

Rep. Kwagrue warned that political organizations cannot expect loyalty from citizens who feel abandoned after elections. “You need to go back to the same grassroots politicians you were begging in 2023 to come together,” he said. “Call them now, before it is too late, and accelerate the work for the people.”

The lawmaker’s argument extended beyond party organization to the economic conditions confronting ordinary Liberians. He maintained that hunger, unemployment and economic hardship can become political issues when citizens believe that government officials are benefiting from public resources while the population continues to struggle.

“A hungry man is an angry man,” Kwagrue said, warning that government officials who isolate themselves within inner circles could eventually face the consequences at the ballot box. The Nimba lawmaker also challenged the notion that development alone guarantees political support.

He argued that voters could recognize government achievements and still remove the politicians responsible for them if they did not feel a personal connection with those leaders. “You can do all the development, but if you don’t make personal impact on the voters, they will see the development and still vote you out,” he said.

It was this broader criticism of government officials that preceded Roberts’ intervention. Instead of responding directly to Rep. Kwagrue’s arguments about government performance, Roberts focused his response on the lawmaker himself.

In the Facebook post that was later deleted, Roberts referred to Rep. Kwagrue as “this monkey” and questioned why the lawmaker and others associated with the Unity Party would criticize members of the governing establishment. “This Monkey and all who Unity Party helped to bring to town had the audacity to come put mouth on UP people,” Roberts wrote.

Roberts also challenged Rep. Kwagrue to demonstrate whether he had distributed his legislative salary to his constituents in Nimba County, apparently in response to the lawmaker’s concerns about government officials helping ordinary citizens.

He questioned whether Kwagrue believed government officials should work and then distribute their salaries to citizens. Roberts further indicated that he did not intend to engage extensively with the lawmaker, ending his post with the statement, “SECURITY Man can’t talk plenty.”

But the controversy that followed demonstrated that Roberts’ decision to enter the debate had generated a dispute much larger than the original disagreement. The “monkey” reference quickly became the dominant issue, with critics arguing that the language was unacceptable, particularly coming from someone occupying a government position.

Rather than weakening Rep. Kwagrue’s criticism, the response appeared to shift public attention toward Roberts’ conduct. The question became less about whether Kwagrue was right or wrong in his assessment of government officials and more about whether a government official should respond to political criticism by insulting an elected representative.

The reaction was not limited to opposition figures. Several people identifying themselves with or expressing support for the Unity Party publicly condemned Roberts, creating an unusual situation in which supporters of the governing political establishment were themselves criticizing one of its vocal defenders.

Peter Dahn rejected Roberts’ suggestion that the Unity Party had simply handed Kwagrue his political position. Dahn argued that Kwagrue’s election was ultimately determined by voters in District #5, Nimba County, who placed their trust in him.

“Let’s make one thing clear: Unity Party did not single-handedly put the lawmaker in office,” Dahn said. “It was the overwhelming support, trust, and confidence of the people of District 5, Nimba County, combined with Hon. Kortor’s commitment to his people, that brought him to power.”

James Kollie also defended the substance of Rep. Kwagrue’s intervention, portraying the lawmaker’s criticism as a warning about the long-term political consequences of ignoring unemployed and struggling supporters.

“He’s speaking for you and those that do not have jobs,” Kollie said. “He’s more concerned about the next election not this short-term glory, Brother!” Kollie urged political actors to reach out to party supporters who were still searching for employment and opportunities. He argued that party members should be answering one another’s calls and creating opportunities for supporters rather than becoming disconnected after gaining political power.

“He’s speaking for tomorrow,” Kollie added. Abdullah Lumeh, who also identified himself as a Unity Party partisan, was even more direct in his criticism of Roberts.

“As a Unity Party Partisan, I strongly condemn this statement coming from Charles, referring to a National leader as a Monkey, this is very wrong!” Lumeh wrote.

Jimmy Bugbay similarly argued that Roberts could have disagreed with Kwagrue without attacking him personally. Bugbay maintained that criticism of government officials does not automatically justify an aggressive or insulting response.

“No. Expressing that some officials are mean or treating people poorly doesn’t require Charles Roberts to respond by being rude or arrogant,” Bugbay wrote. “He could acknowledge the criticism, disagree respectfully, or explain the officials’ position without insulting anyone. Likewise, criticizing someone’s behavior doesn’t automatically justify responding with hostility.”

The public reactions have placed Roberts’ deleted post at the center of a wider discussion about political conduct and social-media behavior among government officials. The controversy has also revived concerns about the increasingly confrontational nature of Liberia’s political discourse, where disagreements over public policy and government performance can quickly become personal disputes.

World.title: Liberia: China Urges 109 Foreign Journalists Participating in the CIPCC Program to Help Connect China with the World
World.content:
BEIJING, China — The Government of the People’s Republic of China has urged 109 journalists from 101 countries participating in the second session of the China International Press Communication Center (CIPCC) 2026 program to help strengthen understanding between China and the rest of the world through objective and firsthand reporting.

By J.H. Webster Clayeh, [email protected]

The call was made Tuesday, September 8, 2026, during the opening ceremony of the international media exchange program held at the Renmin University of China in Beijing.

The CIPCC is a major international media exchange and journalism program organized under the China Public Diplomacy Association (CPDA).

Established in 2014, the program brings journalists from developing countries and the Global South to China for firsthand reporting, professional exchanges and cultural experiences.

Speaking at the opening ceremony, China’s Assistant Minister of Foreign Affairs, Hong Lei, said the CIPCC was established to provide a bridge for media professionals from Global South countries to come closer to and better understand China.

“I hope through your participation in the program, you will become “bosom” friends of China and help better connect China with the world,” Mr. Hong said.

The Chinese Assistant Foreign Minister also urged the journalists to develop what he described as an intimate understanding of China’s history and dynamism and to present the world with what he called a true, multidimensional and panoramic picture of China through objective coverage and diverse perspectives.

“I hope you will delve deep into the vivid practices of Global South countries advancing modernization together, and bring them to a wider audience, so that the world will hear the voice of South-South cooperation, and the story of our win-win cooperation will become the prevailing narrative of our times,” he said.

Mr. Hong added: “I hope you will transcend the barriers between different cultures and civilizations and strengthen the bond of mutual respect and mutual learning, so that dialogue between civilizations will continue forever.”

Replacing Stereotypes with On-the-Ground Observations

Also speaking at the ceremony, Tong Xiaoling, Vice President of the China Public Diplomacy Association, called on participating journalists to use their objective lenses to help reshape narratives about China.

She said the world is undergoing profound changes amid what she described as “intertwined” global challenges, making cross-border media exchanges increasingly important.

“Against this complex backdrop, candid exchanges among cross-border media practitioners are all the more essential. Stereotypes ought to be replaced by on-the-ground observations, and global narratives ought to be enriched by diverse perspectives, so as to inject public opinion

momentum into mutual trust, enhanced understanding and deeper cooperation among nations,” Madam Tong said.

She added: “News media serve as bridge across national borders and bonds connecting peoples. Transcending geographical divides, they enable societies to see one another’s true realities. Grounded in facts, they mitigate misperceptions and prejudices and create viable pathways for dialogue among civilizations.”

According to the CPDA Vice President, over the past 12 years, the China International Press Communication Center has worked to establish a platform for media professionals worldwide to perceive and engage with China.

She said the program has advanced China-foreign press exchanges and public diplomacy while expanding its outreach from selected regions to countries across the globe.

“Successive generations of overseas journalists have traveled across China. With pens and cameras, they have toured the country, witnessed its development and experienced its culture. Through professional perspectives, authentic writings and vivid footages, they have chronicled the development transformations, people-centered vitality and cultural heritage of China in the new era.”

More Than 700 Journalists Trained Since 2014

This year marks 12 years since the inception of the China International Press Communication Center, with Renmin University of China hosting participating journalists in its dormitory facilities during the program.

Professor Zhang Donggang, Secretary of the Communist Party of China Renmin University of China Committee, said the CIPCC program is China’s largest and most comprehensive professional development

program for foreign journalists and one of the programs with the greatest influence.

“For more than a decade, successive groups of foreign journalists have engaged directly with Chinese society and observed China’s development, while bringing to China the -experience, cultures and concerns of their own countries and regions,” he said.

Professor Zhang added: “Since 2014, Renmin University of China has played a major role in hosting the program and has trained more than 700 media professionals from over 100 countries and regions. In doing so, it has created an important platform for journalists from China and around the world to deepen understanding, expand exchanges, strengthen cooperation and build mutual trust.”

World.title: Revised legislation to enforce disaster risk reduction
World.content:
Northern Province Acting Permanent Secretary Beauty Undi-Phiri says the amended Disaster Risk Management Act Number 02 of 2026 and the 2024 Disaster Risk Management policy will effectively enforce disaster risk reduction.

Ms Undi-Phiri says that the revised documents are key in fostering a paradigm shift by moving from a reactive approach to a proactive approach in disaster risk management.

She said this in a speech read on her behalf by Northern Province Planning Unit Assistant Director Christopher Bwalya during the Provincial Dissemination of the amended disaster risk management act number 02 and the 2024 disaster risk management policy meeting in Kasama District.

And Principal Planner in the Office of the Vice President Lukonga Luwabelwa said the amended act is key as it seeks to integrate risk management and climate change adaptation.

Mr Luwabelwa stated that the documents will improve coordination at national and local levels through operationalisation of structures at all stages.

World.title: World Vision donates K4 million medical supplies to Kabompo
World.content:
World Vision Zambia has handed over medical supplies and consumables valued at over K4 million to Kabompo District Health Office in North-Western Province.

World Vision Zambia National Director Marc Nosbach says the donation is aimed at strengthening the health system and improving service delivery in the district.

In a speech read on his behalf by World Vision Kabompo District Area Development Programme Manager Joseph Kayafa during the handover of medical supplies and consumables to the District Health Office, Mr Nosbach said the donation represents World Vision Zambia’s commitment to strengthening health systems, improving service delivery, and ensuring people in the district have access to quality health care services.

“The transfer of these commodities represents our shared commitment to strengthening the health system, improving service delivery and ensuring that the people of Kabompo have access to quality health care services when they need them most,” he said.

“World Vision Zambia is honoured to hand over medical supplies valued at US$254,599.98, equivalent to K4,582,799.64. These supplies include critical medical consumables for the laboratory, theatre, radiography department, medical wards, and other essential service points within the district health system,” the National Director said.

Mr Nosbach also reaffirmed World Vision Zambia’s commitment to supporting government efforts in improving the livelihoods of communities in Kabompo District.

“World Vision Zambia remains a dependable and valued development partner. Our partnership with Kabompo District extends beyond today’s handover; we remain committed to supporting government priorities and contributing to improved health, nutrition, education, child protection, livelihoods, and community resilience,” he said.

District Commissioner Hubert Chinyanga has thanked World Vision Zambia for supplementing the government’s efforts in service delivery in the health sector.

“We want to thank World Vision Zambia for this gesture. By doing so, you are supplementing the government’s efforts in health care service delivery. These items received today will enable health workers in these facilities to provide quality health care services to our people in the district,” he said.

The District Commissioner also called for prudent utilisation of medical supplies in health facilities across the district.

World.title: Newly sworn in Mpulungu civic leaders urged to transform district
World.content:
Mpulungu Town Council Management has appealed to the newly elected councilors to collaborate efforts and work together to develop the district.

Mpulungu Town Council Planner Wilfred Mwanza appealed to all elected office bearers to put their differences aside and work for the people in order to achieve tangible social and economic transformation of the district.

Mr Mwanza was speaking when he delivered a speech on behalf of the council Secretary Isaac Kang’ombe during the swearing in ceremony and oath of acceptance of office by councilors.

He reminded the councilors that the Mpulungu residents who elected them into office have high expectations and are eager to see them deliver and fulfil their campaign promises.

“Allow me to begin by congratulating all the Councilors on your election on 13th August, 2026 to this Council which will run up to 2031 which is a very important period for all of us to work for the people,” he explained

Mr Mwanza reminded the elected leaders that they have a huge task of ensuring that all the wards in the district are involved in the developmental agenda and that no one is left behind.

And speaking at the same function, Mpulungu District Commissioner Gehard Sikazwe urged the newly sworn in civic leaders to be accessible to communities.

Mr Sikazwe said being elected is not merely a position of honour but a call to service, responsibility and leadership.

“As you begin your term of office, remember that leadership is not about power, but about service, you will face challenges, but do not be discouraged seek advice when necessary,” Mr Sikazwe encouraged

The District Commissioner also wished the new councilors wisdom, courage and success as they take on this important responsibility.

And newly elected Mpulungu Town Council Chairperson Chalwe Simfukwe assured the people of Mpulungu of his dedication and service to all the communities.

Mr Simfukwe said as an elected leader, he understands the task of serving the people of Mpulungu and that he will ensure unity among the councilors and togetherness.

He expressed his determination to work in collaboration with all stakeholders to promote development and address the pressing issues facing the town.

“Our town’s progress depends on our ability to unite and dedicate ourselves to common objectives,” he said.

Newly elected Mpulungu Town Council Chairperson Chalwe Simfukwe, seventeen councilors and three traditional leaders took oath of office before Resident Magistrate Emmanuel Musonda as members of the Mpulungu Town Council.

World.title: Correctional Service Denies Blocking Lawyers As Treason Detainees’ Access Dispute Deepens
World.content:
A dispute over whether lawyers representing detained opposition leader Brian Mundubile and his co-accused have been denied access to their clients has widened, with the Zambia Correctional Service (ZCS) insisting no one was turned away improperly, while the accused’s legal team maintains they were barred on instructions from unnamed “powers that be.”

Lawyer Chifumu Banda, part of the defence team, said he and colleagues were shocked to find themselves blocked from seeing Mr Mundubile and running mate Makebi Zulu at Mukobeko Maximum Security Correctional Facility, roughly two hours from Lusaka. He said correctional officers told the team that clear instructions had come from above, without identifying who had issued them.

“We do not know who gave the directive, but what we have been told is that the directive has been given by the powers that be,” Banda said. He described the situation as “the worst form of injustice,” arguing that legal representation is a right, not a privilege subject to discretion.

Banda said senior lawyer Sakwiba Sikota, also part of the defence team, was separately denied access when he attempted to visit the detainees. Banda said the team would consider further options if the situation continued, without specifying what those options might involve.

ZCS head of public relations Cornelius Mwanza rejected the characterisation, saying the service has never denied lawyers access to their clients. He said all visits to correctional facilities are subject to established identity verification and security procedures that apply equally to every visitor.

“In this particular case, some of the lawyers who presented themselves for the visit did not have the required documentation and were therefore requested to return with the necessary documentation,” Mwanza said. He said lawyers who met the requirements were allowed to proceed, and that those who did not meet the documentation standard left before the standard screening process for other visitors could be completed.

Mwanza said the procedures exist to protect both inmates and legal professionals from potential misconduct or exploitation, and are not designed to be punitive.

The dispute sits inside a wider case that has drawn national attention since mid-August. Mundubile, the presidential candidate for the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP), and Zulu, his running mate, are among 18 people facing treason charges following a security operation at a Kabulonga property linked to Mundubile on August 14. Former Cabinet minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was fatally shot during that operation. Also charged are Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance spokesperson George Chisanga, retired Anglican Bishop Trevor Mwamba, Patrick Mwansa, and businessman Harry Valden Findlay, among others.

Police allege a conspiracy to overthrow the Government by unlawful means, citing weapons, ammunition and preparations for an armed insurrection. Mundubile and Zulu were formally charged at the end of August and transferred to Mukobeko along with others. Reports earlier this month indicated the accused had not yet appeared in court on the treason charge itself.

Constitutional lawyer Cephas Lumina has argued that serious allegations do not suspend constitutional protections. He pointed to Article 13, which permits arrest on reasonable suspicion but requires anyone not released to be brought before a court “without undue delay,” and Article 18, which guarantees a fair hearing, the presumption of innocence, and legal representation.

Lumina said access to counsel is a right rather than a favour, citing Section 33 of the Zambia Correctional Service Act, 2021, which requires inmates be given facilities to consult a legal adviser without undue delay and in full confidentiality. He said the Legal Aid Act, 2021 reinforces the same obligation on correctional officers.

He drew on international precedent to make his case, referencing Article 9 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, binding on Zambia, and the UN Human Rights Committee’s position that detention must be reasonable, necessary and proportionate, not simply lawful in form. He also cited Parekh v The People (1995), in which the Supreme Court held that unreasonably delayed trials entitle an accused person to what the court called “constitutional bail,” and Okello v Uganda (2012), where a Ugandan court granted bail to a treason suspect held more than 11 months without trial.

Lumina said the concern is not whether the state has the right to investigate treason, but whether continued detention without judicial oversight and confidential access to lawyers remains within constitutional bounds. He said delayed court appearances, restricted lawyer access and restricted family contact occurring together raise more serious concerns about arbitrary or incommunicado detention.

Catholic clergy Father Gladson Phiri offered a different framing of the dispute, saying the detention of Mundubile and Zulu reflects the operation of the law rather than any personal vindictiveness on the part of President Hakainde Hichilema. He urged Zambians to separate the President as an individual from the office he holds, saying the law, not Hichilema personally, is directing the process.

Phiri said the NRPUP leadership’s decision to announce it had won the August 13 election before the Electoral Commission of Zambia had completed its own declaration was a mistake that contributed to the current tensions. He called for a truth and reconciliation process involving the church and political leaders to address the underlying grievances.

Senior Chief Sandwe of the Nsenga people in Eastern Province took a different view, calling for the release of the treason detainees on the grounds that the timing of the arrests raises questions. He said if Government had prior knowledge of an alleged plot to train militias in 2023, it should have acted before the election rather than after.

“I’m not convinced that there are any treason charges here because the timing was just wrong and off,” Chief Sandwe said, while stressing his comments reflected personal opinion.

The Human Rights Commission has separately called on police and prosecutors to either charge, grant bond to, or release election-related detainees, and has raised concerns about prolonged detention and restricted access to lawyers and families. The Commission’s position stops short of commenting on guilt or innocence, focusing instead on procedural and constitutional questions.

World.title: Zambia Seals 540,000-Tonne Maize Deal With Kenya’s Baita Trading
World.content:
The Food Reserve Agency (FRA) has signed a contract with Kenya’s Baita Trading Company Limited for the export of 540,000 tonnes of white grade A non-genetically modified maize, opening a major new outlet for Zambia’s record harvest.

The agreement, signed at Cabinet Office in Lusaka, will see the maize shipped in six batches over three months, with 100,000 tonnes moving every 90 days until the full quantity is delivered.

Deputy Secretary to the Cabinet for Finance and Economic Development Siazongo Siakalenge said the deal will help Zambia earn foreign exchange while creating a reliable market for farmers’ produce. He said agricultural export earnings had already risen to more than US$1.1 billion last year, up from US$967 million in 2024, with the Kenya deal expected to push that growth further in the current year.

“The maize surplus will generate foreign exchange and contribute to stabilising the Kwacha, while increased production has ensured sufficient food for domestic consumption,” Mr Siakalenge said.

He added that securing export markets is now as important to Zambia’s agricultural ambitions as increasing production itself, particularly as the country pursues a target of raising annual maize output to 10 million tonnes.

Baita Trading director Martin Kinoti said the company is a private-sector buyer and does not represent the Kenyan government. He said the firm will now focus on implementing the agreement, which he described as a step toward meeting food requirements in the Kenyan market while strengthening agricultural trade relations between the two countries.

FRA board chairperson Suresh Desai said the agency will execute its obligations transparently and with integrity to ensure the agreement succeeds. He confirmed the contract covers the supply of up to 540,000 tonnes of Grade A white non-GMO maize, with pricing to be agreed between FRA and Baita Trading at the start of each shipment based on prevailing regional market conditions.

Mr Desai described the agreement as an important commercial opportunity for Zambia, saying it would help strengthen confidence in the quality of the country’s agricultural produce and support wider efforts to grow export markets. He said the deal is expected to move the maize to Kenya over the three-month contract period, offering an immediate outlet for part of the country’s substantial surplus while supporting farmers and the broader agricultural value chain.

The export comes on the back of a bumper harvest of more than 5.1 million tonnes, Zambia’s largest during the last farming season, which has left the country with significant maize available beyond domestic needs.

Meanwhile, the FRA in Northern Province has already paid K313 million to 9,079 farmers who supplied maize during the 2026 crop marketing season. The province has so far disbursed K312,999,899 for 902,017 by-50-kilogramme bags, with the provincial administration confirming that all funds received for farmer payments have been fully disbursed.

The Kenya agreement forms part of a broader push under the Grow Zambia Agenda to expand agricultural exports and boost farmer incomes, with Government pursuing a wider set of production targets that include raising maize output to 10 million tonnes annually by 2031.

Officials say the arrangement demonstrates the kind of private-sector-led export activity Government wants to encourage as it seeks to convert record production into sustained economic gains, both for the Treasury and for the farmers who supplied the crop.

World.title: Hichilema Presses Vedanta To Fast-Track Power Investment As Copper Push Continues
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has urged Vedanta Resources Holdings Limited to accelerate its plans to invest in power generation, tying the request directly to Government’s target of producing 10,000 megawatts of electricity under the second-term Grow Zambia Agenda.

The President made the call during a meeting with Vedanta’s Head of Strategy and Growth, Pushpender Singla, at Community House in Lusaka. Discussions covered further expansion and investment at Konkola Copper Mines (KCM), along with the company’s progress toward its copper production goals.

“We received a report on their progress and further plans to take production towards 500,000 metric tonnes of copper production, adding considerably to our three million metric tonnes target,” Mr Hichilema said. “We encouraged Vedanta to expedite their plans to also invest in power generation to support their mining operations and contribute to our 10 gigawatt target.”

Vedanta and CopperTech Metals confirmed they would back the President’s vision for a thriving and inclusive mining sector. The two firms marked the meeting by presenting the Head of State with a commemorative copper plaque, congratulating him on his re-election and inauguration.

Mr Singla said the companies remain committed to the country’s growth story. “KCM and CopperTech Metals remain committed to partners in Zambia’s growth,” he said. “We congratulate President Hichilema and pledge our full support towards realising the vision for a thriving, inclusive mining sector.”

A statement issued by KCM’s corporate affairs department said the inscription on the plaque highlighted the President’s vision for the mining sector, particularly the national target of producing three million tonnes of copper annually. It also referenced the value of jobs, community and shared prosperity that the company said underpins its partnership with Government.

The engagement forms part of a broader set of production ambitions commonly referred to as the 10-10-5-3-3-1-1-1 targets: 10 million tonnes of maize, 10,000 megawatts of electricity, five million tourists annually, three million tonnes each of copper and soya beans, one million tonnes each of wheat and sugar, and a US$1 billion beef export industry.

Government has said successful delivery of the agenda could create more than two million new jobs and raise living standards nationally. The planned expansion of KCM’s output, paired with new investment in power generation, is expected to support both the mining sector and wider efforts to grow the economy.

Under the agenda, Government is seeking to more than double the size of the national economy, targeting annual economic value beyond US$65 billion. Officials say the strategy is designed to move the country from a stabilisation phase into one focused on expansion, job creation and higher household incomes.

Economist Trevor Hambayi said the Grow Zambia Agenda has the potential to support local businesses and contribute meaningfully to economic development, but cautioned that production growth alone will not be enough. He called for a US$10 billion increase in non-traditional exports to help stabilise the exchange rate, arguing that Zambia needs to move beyond reliance on traditional exports and build sectors capable of generating foreign exchange through value addition.

Republican Progressive Party president and UPND Alliance spokesperson Leslie Chikuse said continuity of the ruling party’s programmes would give citizens confidence in the country’s economic direction. He described the Grow Zambia language as evidence of a shift from stabilisation to growth, pointing to interest rates easing from 6.3 percent in 2021 to 6.2 percent currently, alongside a more stable exchange rate and stronger GDP performance.

“These are tangible results that citizens can touch and see,” Mr Chikuse said, adding that the enactment of free education into law stood as further proof of progress delivered during the first term.

For KCM and Vedanta, the immediate task remains translating the President’s request into concrete power and copper investment. Both companies have signalled continued alignment with the national targets, though the scale of new generation capacity required, and the timeline for delivering it, has yet to be detailed publicly.

The outcome of that investment will matter well beyond the mining sector. With electricity generation identified as a precondition for nearly every other target in the Grow Zambia Agenda, the pace at which Vedanta and other mining houses move on power will shape how quickly Government can point to progress on its wider economic promises.

World.title: Stakeholders Press Hichilema For Inclusive Cabinet As Selection Drags On
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has yet to name his Cabinet more than a week after being sworn in for a second term, with civil society groups, governance advocates and disability and gender lobbies pressing him to build a team that reflects Zambia’s regional, gender and social diversity.

State House has confirmed the delay is deliberate. Chief Communications Specialist Clayson Hamasaka said the President is taking time to “meticulously construct his team,” a line that has done little to calm public speculation, with lists of possible appointees circulating daily on social media.

The pressure is coming from several directions at once. The Independent Churches of Zambia wants an all-inclusive team of “honest, hard-working and God-fearing individuals.” President David Masupa said the expanded Parliament, now 224 members strong, gives the President a wider pool of candidates than at any point since independence.

Disability groups have made the sharpest appeal. Disability Rights Watch coordinator Bruce Chooma said the President has “never had an opportunity since independence” to build a truly inclusive Cabinet, and urged him to consider appointing a person with a disability to a portfolio such as Community Development and Social Services. He also pushed for a young minister to head youth affairs, arguing the current arrangement leaves the docket without anyone close to the age group it serves.

The GEARS Initiative struck a similar note. Chairperson Lackson Lungu said the new administration’s economic approach demands ministers with the skills and experience to convert the Grow Zambia Agenda’s targets into results, rather than officials chosen on other grounds.

Gender balance has emerged as a parallel demand. The Non-Governmental Gender Organisations’ Coordinating Council wants a 50-50 Cabinet. Executive director Anne Mbewe-Anamela said equal representation would ensure the concerns of men and women are weighed equally in policy, and called for women to be placed in health, education and social protection portfolios rather than symbolic roles.

Governance advocate Ngande Mwanajiti expressed confidence the new Cabinet would maintain regional balance, pointing to the composition of the outgoing team as a guide. He said his work on the Bill 7 technical committee was aimed at building a more representative Parliament and strengthening public participation in governance more broadly.

Acton Institute for Policy Analysis Centre executive director Solomon Ngoma used the moment to revive an older argument, calling for the reintroduction of deputy ministers. He dismissed claims that the posts would strain the budget, saying his organisation’s own findings show such objections are political rather than evidence-based, and urged MPs to table a bill on the matter in the next sitting of Parliament.

Not every voice has focused on structure. Former Secretary to the Cabinet Leslie Mbula urged the President to prioritise integrity and long-serving competence over political convenience. Politician Wynter Kabimba called for a team capable of delivering on the growth and job-creation promises at the centre of the Grow Zambia Agenda, while governance analyst Teddy Mwansa said the stakes are higher this term because the job itself has changed.

“We all now know the first four years focused on fixing debt, stabilising macroeconomics and restoring international trust,” Mwansa said. “But this new phase requires ministers who can push aggressive economic growth, job creation and investment.”

That shift, from stabilisation to execution, is what most observers say will define the selection. The President has said the next Cabinet must help push production toward three million tonnes of copper, ten million tonnes of maize and 10,000 megawatts of electricity, alongside targets for tourism, soya, wheat, sugar and beef exports. Ministers will be expected to show a record of turning policy into delivery rather than managing existing programmes.

Mwanajiti said the previous administration built a team around merit, competence, a proven track record and regional balance, and argued the same approach should guide the current selection. He noted that Zambia’s diversity is a strength only if citizens can see it reflected in the people who govern them.

State House has signalled that underperformance will not be tolerated once the team is in place. Officials close to the process describe the incoming Cabinet as a performance contract rather than a reward for loyalty, with ministers expected to be replaced if they fail to deliver against the targets set for their portfolios.

For now, the country waits. With Parliament newly sworn in and the President’s own manifesto commitments already public, the composition of the Cabinet will be the clearest early signal of how the second term is meant to differ from the first.

World.title: Lusangazi civic leaders sworn-in, urged to improve service delivery
World.content:
The newly elected Lusangazi civic leaders led by the Chairperson, Geoffrey Daka, have officially assumed office after taking the Oath of Office.

The swearing-in ceremony was held at Lusangazi Civic Centre and was presided over by Resident Magistrate Misozi Banda, who administered the oath to the newly elected local government leaders.

His Royal Highness Chief Sandwe was also in attendance.

The immediate past Council Chairperson, Blackson Tembo, congratulated the newly elected Chairperson and councillors, urging them to work as a united team in addressing the developmental challenges in the district.

Mr Tembo encouraged the new Council leadership to build on the achievements of the previous administration, work closely with Council Management and staff, and remain committed to improving service delivery.

He further urged the councillors to put the interests of the people above political and personal differences.

Meanwhile, newly sworn-in Council Chairperson Geoffrey Daka described his election as a profound responsibility entrusted to him by the people of Lusangazi.

He thanked the electorate for their confidence and extended a hand of friendship to residents who may not have supported him and other councillors during the elections.

He said the conclusion of the August 13, 2026 General Election should mark the beginning of a new era of cooperation and development.

“We are now one Council, one community, and one Lusangazi,” Mr Daka said.

He pledged to lead the Council based on good governance, transparency, accountability, inclusiveness and dedicated service.

He also said the new administration would prioritise improved service delivery, including roads, water supply, sanitation, health and education infrastructure, markets, waste management and community facilities.

Mr Daka also said the Council would support initiatives aimed at creating opportunities for young people, women, farmers, entrepreneurs and vulnerable groups.

And Mr Daka called on Council Management and staff to serve residents with professionalism, integrity and dedication, while urging residents to participate actively in development programmes, protect public infrastructure and maintain clean communities.

He further pledged to strengthen collaboration between the Council and traditional leaders in promoting peace, unity, cultural values and community development.

Council Secretary Sekani Tembo described the swearing-in ceremony as a significant milestone in the democratic journey of Lusangazi District.

Mr Tembo urged the councillors to recognise their election as a responsibility to serve as voices of their respective communities.

He called for unity across political parties, wards, traditional leadership structures and communities, saying the aspirations of residents could only be realised through collective effort.

The ceremony was attended by Council Management and staff, Government representatives, political and community leaders, members of the clergy, traditional leaders, the media among other invited guests.
