Guests scheduled to brief cabinet reflect the concerns about both the trade war and Alberta separatism.

The list includes the mayors of Calgary and Red Deer, pollsters including Janet Brown — known for her insights into the Alberta political landscape — and Ian Bremmer, the founding political scientist of Eurasia Group.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who landed in Calgary Wednesday, will will also briefly address cabinet in Banff.

Missing from the list is any expert on affordability or pocketbook issues, unlike in January 2026, when Carney and his ministers heard from Food Banks Canada CEO Kirstin Beardsley.

An apparent ambivalence toward pocketbook issues might become a weakness for Carney in the long term, Coletto said.

"I think that thing that Canadians are looking for more than anything is reassurance," Coletto said. "Reassurance that their government understands the risks seized by them and is doing everything it can to mitigate them at the same time as finding ways of looking long term to how to strengthen Canada."

World.title: Canadian bank CEOs can't stop bragging about AI. Will they kill jobs?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Scotiabank CEO Scott Thomson says artificial intelligence saved his bank roughly 24,000 days' worth of work over about four and a half months. At TD Bank, CEO Raymond Chun recently said AI has reduced the time it takes to pre-process mortgages from about 15 hours to three minutes.

Canada's Big Five banks employ nearly 400,000 full-time-equivalent workers. That's more than double the number of employees in Canada's auto assembly and parts manufacturing industry. TD Bank workers alone outnumber Canada's active military force.

According to a study by Toronto Metropolitan University, 98 per cent of financial sector workers are highly exposed to AI technologies. That's far higher, they say, than the 56 per cent estimated for the Canadian workforce overall.

Last month, the Bank of Canada estimated that one‑third of jobs may "undergo substantial changes" because of AI integration, given today's capabilities. The central bank found that banking, insurance and other financial clerks are among the most exposed.

"AI is a big opportunity for us, a transformational opportunity both from an effectiveness, and an efficiency perspective," Thomson said on Wednesday at the annual Scotiabank Financials Summit in Toronto.

RBC CEO Dave McKay, who has led the bank since 2014, says AI is affecting every part of its business and that he uses it each morning to generate custom reports from RBC's internal data. (Kevin Van Paassen/Bloomberg)

His enthusiasm is shared by his C-suite peers.

"There isn't a part of our business that's not being impacted by AI," RBC CEO Dave McKay told an audience at an industry conference hosted by his bank earlier this year. At an event in June, he spoke about using AI every morning to generate custom reports based on RBC's internal data.

Last month, BMO CEO Darryl White said predictive AI modelling in his bank's insurance business can make underwriting decisions in as little as 10 seconds. The industry standard is at least 28 days, he noted.

Stock market analyst John Aiken covers the banking industry for New York-based Jefferies Financial Group. He sees top executives at Canada's Big Five — Royal Bank, TD Bank, Bank of Montreal, Scotiabank, and National Bank — brimming with excitement over the billions of dollars they've invested in AI in recent years.

What's unclear, he said, is how rank-and-file bank employees will feel the impact.

"This isn't a little pet project," Aiken told CBC News. "The funny thing is, it's the CEOs themselves that are bringing it up unprompted."

"Strangely enough, we're not seeing headcount reductions from the banks," he said. "You're presumably going to see lesser demand for lower skilled workers ... the front-line staff at the branches."

OpenAI and Anthropic logos are seen in this illustration taken June 11, 2026. (Reuters/Dado Ruvic/Illustration/File Photo)

Questions about how AI will affect some of Canada's largest private employers come amid a much broader debate over how the technology could shape humanity as a whole.

Earlier this week, an artificial intelligence researcher quit his job at Anthropic, accusing the company, and its chief rival, OpenAI, of irresponsibly "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence." On Tuesday, another Anthropic employee wrote on the social media platform X that, "we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade."

On Wednesday, federal AI Minister Evan Solomon said "there are real concerns" at the frontier of AI development

WATCH | AI Minister Evan Solomon says AI safety a top priority: Existential warnings about AI 'are not new,' minister says | Duration 5:23 AI Minister Evan Solomon said 'there are real concerns' at the frontier of AI development, when asked about an Anthropic researcher who quit the firm, citing existential safety risks. 'Our No. 1 concern always is safety, full stop,' Solomon said.

Jon Pinkus, a partner at Samfiru Tamakin LLP who specializes in employment law, sees jobs at risk throughout the white-collar world because of AI. However, he said he has yet to see a clear-cut instance of humans being replaced.

"I have real generational anxieties for the incoming workforce. Not just this generation, but for generations to come," he said.

"I think there are going to be certain positions that just don't exist, particularly more junior positions, entry-level positions," Pinkus said.

"A lot of those entry level tasks are the ones now being done by AI ... [it does] them well enough for many organizations to say, 'Why are we going to pay this person $80,000 per year?'"

Jeff Lanthier, director of media relations at RBC, told CBC News in response to questions about AI's impact on the bank's headcount that people and relationships will always be at the core of the bank's strategy.

"We see AI as an enhancement, not a replacement," Lanthier said.

The other Big Five banks did not respond to requests for comment in time for publication.

At its investor day last year, RBC announced plans to generate $700 million to $1 billion in enterprise value through AI-driven benefits by 2027. TD Bank is similarly targeting $1 billion in annual value from its artificial intelligence initiatives. Both banks have in-house AI research labs, called RBC Borealis and Layer 6, respectively.

CIBC president and CEO Harry Culham, left, greets German Vice-Chancellor and Federal Minister of Finance Lars Klingbeil before a CIBC roundtable with the German-Canadian Chamber of Industry and Commerce in Toronto, on Friday, May 8, 2026. (The Canadian Press/Sammy Kogan)

CIBC CEO sees human headcount rising

CIBC CEO Harry Culham said his bank's new AI workspace is more like a "co-worker" than a chatbot. Even so, he predicts the bank will add employees overall.

"We actually see headcount growth over the next five years," CIBC CEO Harry Culham said on his bank's Aug. 27 earnings call with stock market analysts. "We're using it all over the entire organization, and we've got thousands and thousands of people being educated."

Kiridaran Kanagaretnam, an associate dean at York University's Schulich School of Business, sees the Canadian banking industry's overall headcount drifting higher, absent a major financial crisis.

He recommends students pursue professional designations in accounting and finance to boost their value to employers.

"Everything is changing at a rapid rate," he said. "But that doesn't mean things are bleak."

World.title: TIFF's at a turning point — but how will the film festival's new focus on dealmaking affect fans?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

For years, the Toronto International Festival has prided itself as a tastemaker. Toronto was the place movie stars flocked to for the unofficial start of their Oscar campaigns.

But as major films and A-list stars increasingly look to other festivals as launchpads, TIFF is reinventing itself with a new focus on the business of buying and packaging movies.

In a tumultuous time for the industry, this transformation could help keep TIFF in the conversation, but as ticket prices rise, what does it all mean for the heart of this festival: the filmgoing public?

Here's a look at TIFF's very own movie makeover moment — plus a few choice films you may want to catch yourself.

Shifting the spotlight to dealmaking

Continuing a post-pandemic trend, many of the season's buzziest titles, including Primetime starring Robert Pattinson and You Can See Everything from Canada's own Nathan Fielder, chose Venice or Telluride over TIFF for their world premieres.

So, like the nerdy girl in a rom-com who takes off her glasses, TIFF is trying to transform itself, pivoting to embrace the dealmaking and caffeine-fuelled strategy sessions that populate many major festivals.

Launching with a $23 million boost from Ottawa, TIFF: The Market features 70 sessions and events exploring film, television and interactive content.

A sci-fi film with Russell Crowe and Priyanka Chopra, a rom-com featuring Colin Firth and Halle Berry and a new instalment of the Air Bud franchise are just a few of the projects being shopped around town.

But just like the cutthroat competition for red carpet premieres, TIFF will be facing competition from other industry players.

Diego Calva, left, and director Jordan Firstman pose at the photo call for Firstman's film Club Kid during the 79th Cannes Film Festival in May. (John Locher/The Associated Press)

First, there's the Cannes marketplace, the biggest and best known showcase that sets the tempo for the year.

Case in point, it was on La Croisette, the famous boulevard at the centre of Cannes, where the buzz began for Jordan Firstman's Club Kid, resulting in a frenzied bidding war. That film's Canadian premiere takes place at TIFF Sunday.

The Trump factor

While TIFF is trying to position itself as a fall alternative to spring's Cannes, it's also competing with the American Film Market (AFM), which takes place in November in Los Angeles .

While AFM generally caters to more mainstream films, TIFF, which has always touted international cinema, will be highlighting emerging markets in Africa and Asia as part of The Market programming.

And as U.S. President Donald Trump talks up new national incentives to reshore American film production, international buyers wary of engaging with Hollywood or even looking to avoid hassles at the border, may see TIFF as an attractive alternative.

TIFF CEO Cameron Bailey speaks at a media event for the film festival last month. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)

Tickets and tastemakers

As TIFF's star wattage continues to diminish and the festival evolves to become more business-facing, questions remain about what that means for the heart of the TIFF experience: the film fans. The ones who camp out in long lines, wait for hours to watch stars walk red carpets and scream like pirates at midnight screenings.

Director Guillermo del Toro greets fans at the premiere of his film Frankenstein at the Toronto International Film Festival last September. (Laura Proctor/The Canadian Press)

Every year TIFF rightly boasts about its track record of predicting best picture winners, touting the People's Choice Award as a barometer of Oscar worthiness.

But as ticket prices climb higher (regular screenings now begin at $30 and up), fewer members of the public who make the festival one big, beautiful focus group end up populating those screenings.

Speaking to the Toronto Star recently, TIFF CEO Cameron Bailey acknowledged that glitzy premieres with stars and filmmakers in attendance command higher ticket prices, but he also argued that they still cost less than a ticket to pro sports games in the city.

At a time when Canadians want to support the home team, that means some film fans could find themselves priced out of a seat.

Must-see movies

While the number of A-listers coming to TIFF may be shrinking, there's still a number of the upcoming fall season's most buzzworthy films making the rounds in Toronto.

WATCH | Trailer for director Danny Boyle's Ink:

Ink finds Trainspotting director Danny Boyle returning to Britain to explore the rise of The Sun tabloid newspaper, with rumoured James Bond contender Jack O'Connell as a rapacious editor in chief.

WATCH | Trailer for The Debut starring Julianne Moore:

Then there's The Debut, a love letter to community theatre written and directed by actor Jesse Eisenberg. In 2025 Eisenberg's A Real Pain helped Kieran Culkin bring home Oscar gold. Already, some are seeing a golden hue in Julianne Moore's performance as a harried housewife who abandons herself in a role.

Primetime programming

Increasingly, TIFF has embraced both the small and big screen in its programming and this year a number of TV series are showcased in the Primetime program. That includes Apple TV's Slow Horses, which is bringing its sixth season premiere to Toronto with star Gary Oldman, who will also be interviewed on stage.

WATCH | Teaser trailer for Yaga:

With shooting already underway for the second season of Heated Rivalry, another hot title is the upcoming Crave series Yaga, starring Hudson Williams as an heir to a powerful fishery and The Matrix's Carrie-Anne Moss as a university professor. Riffing on the fearsome fairy tale character Baba Yaga, the show promises a steamy mix of mischief and malevolence.

Oh Canada

It's worth remembering that, before the trade war escalated, the Canadian film industry was riding high, based on the success of films like Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie, Mile End Kicks, undertone and more.

To capitalize on the moment, there's a broad swath of Canadian titles at TIFF this year. Can't get enough of Jay Baruchel and love Canadian hosers who perform incredible feats? From FUBAR director Michael Dowse comes The Stunt Driver, which explores the true story of Canadian stuntman Ken Carter.

WATCH | Trailer for The Stunt Driver:

Music fans can check out Neil Peart: No One's Disciple, a 106 minute documentary exploring the life of the late Rush drummer with the help of Red Hot Chili Peppers drummer Chad Smith and Stewart Copeland of The Police.

If you'd like a less conventional film, Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney promises an unhinged look at the former prime minister. Director Matthew Rankin, who also helmed Universal Language, has conjured what TIFF describes as a "retro-pop fever dream," which will be premiering in the always raucous Midnight Madness category.

In Smudge the Blades, director and writer Cody Lightning, centre, also plays the coach of the Treaty 6 Blades in a movie the tells the story of an Indigenous hockey team fighting for a place in Alberta's northern league. (Liam Mitchell)

Not content to let Heated Rivalry steal all the hockey shenanigans, Smudge the Blades is a scrappy sports story about an Indigenous hockey team based in Northern Alberta.

Triple threat Cree director/writer/star Cody Lightning plays the team's beleaguered coach alongside an all-star team of Indigenous talent including Jana Schmieding and Paulina Alexis.

World.title: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrives in Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is in Canada this week for his first visit to the country in nearly a year as his country copes with an onslaught of deadly airstrikes.

Zelenskyy will be in the country from Wednesday to Friday and attend events in Calgary, Toronto and North Bay alongside his wife, Olena Zelenska, says a statement from Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Zelenskyy landed in Calgary on Wednesday night ahead of a scheduled meeting with the prime minister.

The Ukrainian leader and his wife, Olena Zelenska, were met at the Calgary airport by several officials, including Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand, before they were whisked away in a black SUV.

Carney and Zelenskyy are set to meet in the city Thursday morning, and Zelenskyy is to later address a cabinet meeting in the nearby mountain resort town of Banff, Alta.

"The visit underscores Canada's continued leadership in supporting Ukraine and reflects our unwavering commitment to a just and lasting peace," Carney said in the statement.

The visit will focus on "shared priorities" between Canada and Ukraine, including deepening defence, economic and energy co-operation, Carney's statement said.

"It will also address the human cost of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and build on the strong people-to-people ties that connect our countries."

The Ukrainian president announced that he was travelling to Canada in a social media post on Wednesday, but did not say what city he was flying into.

Zelenskyy's most recent visit to Canada was last December, where he met with Carney in Halifax before travelling to the U.S. for talks focused on ending the Russia-Ukraine war.

Carney visited Kyiv last August in his first official visit to the country, where he reiterated Canada's support for Ukraine and unveiled details of an additional $2 billion in military aid.

Flight delayed Tuesday due to drone activity

On Tuesday, a flight scheduled to carry Zelenskyy from Moldova to Norway was ​delayed when authorities closed Moldova's airspace because of a drone incursion, a government spokesperson said Wednesday.

Moldovan police said a Russian drone crashed on Tuesday in a sunflower field on the outskirts of a village in Riscani district, which caused four fires to break out but no injuries.

On Wednesday, government spokesperson Dumitru Ciorici said Moldova had closed its airspace on Tuesday afternoon to protect aircraft flying over the country at the time, delaying three departures, including Zelenskyy's.

Zelenskyy's visit comes as Kyiv copes with devastating airstrikes and as his government pleads for more air defence support. European leaders argue Russia has been widening its war.

WATCH | Russia-Ukraine war escalation: Intelligence warns Putin is preparing escalation in Ukraine | Duration 2:07 As Western intelligence warns about a planned escalation in Ukraine, Russian airstrikes have killed at least 12 people in Kyiv over six days. Meanwhile, Germany formally accused Russia of sabotage on a Ukrainian plane at the Leipzig airport.

Before travelling to Canada, Zelenskky chided the international community for not taking a tougher stance against Russia over its escalating bombardment of civilian areas of Ukraine.

"Unfortunately, there has been too little response from the international community to these strikes, which are taking people's lives practically every day," he said on social media.

"But a response is needed — Moscow must not go into the winter believing that it can get away with missile and drone terror without consequences."

Last week, Carney told reporters his message to Vladimir Putin will be straight forward if the Russian president attends this year's G20 summit in Miami.

"The message will be simple: 'Get out of Ukraine, give back all of Ukraine to Ukraine, end this war which is killing more than 30,000 of your people every single month,' and I'd leave it at that to be honest."

World.title: Fire on passenger ferry in Philippines leaves dozens missing and at least 5 dead
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A fire burned overnight on a passenger ferry off the western Philippines, leaving dozens of people missing Thursday and killing at least five.

So far, 43 people have been rescued, coast guard spokeswoman Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said. The ferry MV June Aster was afloat but listing after the fire, which started Wednesday evening, was put out. Tendrils of smoke still wafted over the charred vessel by midday.

"We are continuing search and rescue operations," she said, with a coast guard ship and high-speed response boats joined by a military vessel and other government boats, private volunteers and fishermen.

The coast guard made a radio broadcast to ships nearby to be on the lookout for passengers of the ferry. It has also coordinated with coastal villages in case some passengers drifted to the shore.

Images of the nighttime rescue efforts showed coast guard personnel tossed life jackets to survivors as the ferry burned in the background. Passengers were helped into smaller boats taking them to shallow water, and body bags were laid out at what looked like a port.

Dozens of people are still missing after the ferry MV June Aster caught fire off Palawan province, western Philippines. On Thursday, the vessel was still smouldering. (Philippine Coast Guard/The Associated Press)

The ferry had sailed from the capital Manila and was near its destination of Coron in Palawan province when the fire started around 6:45 p.m. local time on Wednesday.

Bad weather and big waves challenged rescuers. The ferry was around 7.4 kilometres off Coron's village of Turda when it sent a distress signal but strong sea currents had dragged it to a distance of 14.2 kilometres off Turda.

Cause of blaze unknown

Cayabyab said it was unclear what caused the fire, which one survivor said may have begun in the cargo hold, and the coast guard was coordinating with the shipping company and maritime authorities to get more details.

She said 134 people were on board, 117 of them passengers and 17 crew. There was no information about any foreigners onboard.

Ferries are a common transportation method in the Philippine archipelago. Sea accidents are not uncommon due to storms, badly maintained vessels, overcrowding and spotty enforcement of safety regulations, especially in remote provinces.

In 1987, the ferry Dona Paz sank after colliding with a fuel tanker in the central Philippines, killing more than 4,300 people in the world's deadliest peacetime maritime disaster.
