World.title: Ecuador: Ex-president Bucaram sentenced in corruption case
World.content:
Abdala Bucaram, Ecuador's former president, was convicted for his role in the illegal sale of COVID-19 tests and medical supplies, receiving a prison sentence of over nine years.

Abdala Bucaram, Ecuador's former president, was found guilty of corruption and sentenced on Wednesday to nine years and four months in prison for being "collaborators" in organized crime.

Bucaram's son, Jacob Bucaram, was also sentenced for the illegal sale of at least21,000 COVID-19 tests and other medical supplies during the pandemic in 2020.

The trial, which lasted six years, continued following an appeal from the attorney general's office, after a judge dismissed the charges against Bucaram and his son in 2021.

What are the details of the case?

Bucaram heard the decision remotely from a guarded clinic in Guayaquil where he was receiving medical care.

At 74 years old, he may serve his ⁠sentence ​under house ​arrest due to ​his age, in ‌accordance with Ecuadorean law.

He was arrested in 2020 following a raid on his home in Guayaquil, and was put under house arrest as he could not initially be imprisoned due to health problems.

The former president has undergone surgery for heart issues and was admitted to intensive care.

Bucaram posted a message on X stating that he had requested to be discharged from the clinic "despite being at risk of sudden death."

"I will be able to defend myself, and the country will learn horrifying things about this process," he added.

According to the investigation,COVID-19 tests were illegally transferred to Bucaram's residence, which was guarded by Quito traffic agents.

According to the public prosecutor's office, the tests and medical supplies were sold in various provinces of the country "without invoices and without paying taxes to the state."

Bucaram was removed from office in 1997 after being declared mentally unfit to rule, and had lived in exile in Panama for nearly two decades before returning to Ecuador in 2017.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

World.title: Germany 'rebuilding pillars' of national security
World.content:
Skip next section Dobrindt warns of growing threats to German security

09/10/2026 September 10, 2026 Dobrindt warns of growing threats to German security

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has defended plans to give security authorities greater investigative powers, accusing critics of putting people's safety at risk amid what he described as a heightened threat to Germany.

Speaking during a parliamentary debate on his ministry's 2027 budget, Dobrindt, of the conservative Christian Social Union, said the proposed powers were necessary to "protect our freedom."

"The threat level is high and is coming from different places," Dobrindt said.

He pointed to an explosives-laden drone discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport as evidence of the security challenges facing Germany, adding that Russia was clearly behind the incident and that it was "not an isolated event."

Dobrindt has pushed for stronger measures against drones and hybrid threats. He said under his leadership, the federal and state governments have established a new joint drone defense center, while a Joint Center for Countering Hybrid Threats (GAZ Hybrid) opened in June.

"We are rebuilding the pillars of security architecture," Dobrindt said on Thursday.

The Interior Ministry's budget is set to increase by more than €950 million ($1.1 billion) to €16.7 billion ($19.5 billion).

The Federal Criminal Police Office and Federal Police are among the agencies set to receive additional personnel.

Germany's Federal Office for Information Security, which is responsible for cybersecurity, is also due to receive more funding.

Sonja Eichwede, deputy parliamentary leader of the center-left Social Democratic Party, highlighted additional spending planned for the Federal Agency for Technical Relief, saying it was important for civil protection and disaster response.

World.title: Serbia, the conflicted EU candidate
World.content:
On paper, Belgrade has pursued EU membership for years. But accession has long been stalled. The hero's farewell given to war criminal Mladic exposed just how far Serbia has alienated itself from Europe.

The state-supported funeral of Ratko Mladic in Belgrade this week has raised a pressing question in Brussels: Can a country seek EU membership while giving a hero's farewell to a convicted war criminal? For many, the event has shown that Serbia's accession process has not merely stalled. It has largely lost its political drive.

"For too long, the EU has kept treating Serbia as a normal candidate country," Engjellushe Morina of the European Council on Foreign Relations told DW, despite Belgrade's continued backsliding on democracy and the rule of law.

Naim Leo Besiri of Serbia's Institute for European Affairs adds: "The ruling majority in Serbia has not performed anything that was promised on the reform agenda during the last five years."

Serbian armed forces stood guard at Mladic's funeral Image: Oliver Bunic/AFP

A candidate moving away from Europe

Both experts point out that Belgrade has refused to join EU sanctions against Russia. Democratic standards have deteriorated under nationalist President Aleksandar Vucic, while relations with Kosovo remain tense.

Despite having been sentenced to life imprisonment by a UN court for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, Ratko Mladic was buried in Belgrade on Monday with military honors and the participation of government representatives. President Vucic stayed away, but facilitated and defended the public mourning.

Serbia: Thousands attend 'Butcher of Bosnia' funeral To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Brussels reacted unusually strongly. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the images shocking. European Council President Antonio Costa condemned the glorification of war criminals. Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos canceled a visit to Serbia.

Has the EU been too lenient?

But both Morina and Besiri say that this is not enough. They believe Vucic has been given too much room to maneuver for too long. In their perception, he has been treated as an indispensable partner who could secure stability in the Western Balkans and keep Serbia anchored to the West, despite disregarding basic European values.

Besiri says Serbian civil society had warned Brussels for years about attacks on media freedom, the rule of law and democratic institutions. But, he adds, the EU largely turned a blind eye.

In June 2026, senior European Union and Western Balkan leaders gathered for the EU-Western Balkans Summit Image: Michailidis/Betaphoto/SIPA/picture alliance

Economic relations demonstrate the strong ties between the EU and Serbia. The bloc is Serbia's largest trading partner, investor and financial donor. Politically, however, Serbia has developed a close partnership with Moscow.

A common argument for continuing relations with Serbia is therefore based on the concern that greater pressure could push the country further towards Russia or China.

Strong economic ties, close relations with Russia

Morina accepts that isolating Serbia would be dangerous, but sees other options between accommodation and abandoning relations altogether. The EU should remain engaged with Serbian society while forcing Vucic to make clear political choices, she argues.

Besiri says Russia and China could never replace the European market. In his view, Vucic uses both countries as a threat to discourage Brussels from taking firmer action.

Both researchers see strategies behind the current approach: Vucic benefits from cooperation without implementing the necessary reforms. Brussels, meanwhile, can continue to claim that Serbia remains tied to Europe.

In 2007 already, Aleksandar Vucic decided to put on placards made like street-name signs reading 'Ratko Mladic boulevard' on a major Belgrade street Image: Oliver Bunic/dpa/picture alliance

The limits of financial pressure

The EU has not remained entirely inactive. It has started applying financial pressure. Further payments under the Growth Plan for the Western Balkans have been withheld because of concerns about judicial independence.

Besiri doubts that this will change Vucic's calculations. Broad funding cuts could hurt the population more than the political elite, he argues. Instead, he advocates targeted measures against those responsible for the country's democratic decline and the misuse of its institutions.

Thousands attended Mladic's funeral in Belgrade Image: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/picture alliance

Could the election bring change?

The early parliamentary election on October 25 could put Vucic's model to the test. After 12 years as president, he now wants to remain Serbia's dominant political figure by becoming the next prime minister.

Besiri says that the political opposition in Serbia remains fragile and that "it is extremely difficult to win democratically in undemocratic elections."

Neither expert expects one election to repair Serbia's institutions or fundamentally change its relationship with the EU.

Aleksandar Vucic did not attend the funeral himself Image: Marko Dimic/ZUMA/IMAGO

Reconciliation remains a distant prospect

Reconciliation in the region appears even more distant. According to Besiri, Serbia would first have to acknowledge its role in the wars of the 1990s and accept established facts about the crimes committed. Instead, narratives portraying Serbs exclusively as victims remain deeply embedded in Serbian politics, education and the media.

"What has been happening recently is basically the reverse of everything that has been built for so many years," Morina underlines.

Mladic's funeral did not cause this development, she adds. It simply revealed once again how far Serbia currently remains from both regional reconciliation and EU membership.

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

World.title: August hottest month ever recorded, says EU monitor
World.content:
The average global temperature in August broke the previous record set in 2023. Climate scientists say record summer heat in the northern hemisphere and warmer oceans are all part of a new normal.

Data from the European Union's Copernicus Climate Change Service released Thursday showed the average global air temperature last month measured 16.96° Celsius (62.53° F), the highest monthly global average ever recorded.

"Humans haven't seen temperatures as hot as today for, arguably, at least the last 100,000 years," Samantha Burgess from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, which oversees Copernicus, told AFP.

Copernicus data, which goes back to 1940, recorded the previous all-time monthly high only three years ago in July 2023.

Western Europe records hottest summer

Western Europe recorded its hottest summer on record this year after successive heatwaves, droughts and wildfires.

Between mid-July and mid-August, Europe saw more than 32,000 excess deaths related to heat, according to estimates from the EuroMomo monitoring platform.

Additionally, ocean temperatures also tied their record high, which extended a three-month streak of record-breaking warmth across the world's oceans.

These warm ocean temperatures come at severe cost to marine life, reefs and coastal communities.

Added to this, what is estimated to be the strongest El Nino in the modern era is set to bring unusually warm Pacific waters, raising the odds of extreme weather across the world, from floods to droughts and wildfires.

Wildfires spread beyond Europe's traditional fire zones To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Scientists point to climate change

Scientists primarily attributed the extreme heat primarily to human-caused climate change.

"The evidence is irrefutable: this is the spiraling price of humanity's fossil fuel addiction, and the global climate crisis it is fueling," United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said in response to the Copernicus report.

Stiell said "until humanity stops burning" coal, oil and gas, extreme heat would continue to break records.

The world's oceans outside of the polar regions also recorded their joint-highest sea surface temperature for any month on record Image: HPIC/dpa/picture alliance

Long-term warming currently averages at about 1.4°C higher than pre-industrial levels, just under the 1.5°C limit envisioned under the Paris Agreement.

Last week, the UN said the 1.5°C goal was no longer achievable and urged faster greenhouse gas cuts.

"It is now time to stop acting surprised that our warming planet keeps getting warmer. This is occurring exactly as forecast by scientists literally decades ago," Texas A&M University climate scientist Andrew Dessler told the Associated Press.

"The interesting question is not whether we will keep breaking heat records (we will), but whether we're going to do anything about it or just stand there while the climate train runs us over."

World.title: Trump promises Americans $5,000 if Republicans win midterms
World.content:
The US president gave a wide-ranging speech at the Republican midterm convention. He defended the war in Iran, trade wars and tariffs, and the White House ballroom. He also called Democrats evil and immigrants animals.

US President Donald Trump made a pitch to voters on Wednesday: a $5,000 (€4,300) "dividend" for every American adult if the Republican Party keeps control of both houses of Congress in the midterm elections.

"If the Republicans win ​the House of Representatives ​and ‌the United States Senate, both of them ... because of ‌our tremendous strength and success ‌economically, ​I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the ​United States of America for $5,000," Trump said at the ⁠Republican midterm ​convention on Wednesday.

"The only caveat we have is that the dividend must be spent in the United States of America," he added. "We don't want you going to Canada spending the money, we don't want you going to China or Germany."

The president did not say how he would finance the measure, nor how the government would track where citizens spend the funds. He had previously promised citizens $2,000 checks from tariff revenues that have so far not materialized.

What else did Trump talk about?

Trump made the announcement as the two-day event kicked off in Dallas, Texas.

In a wide-ranging speech, Trump talked up some of the biggest — and most divisive — aspects of his second term in office, including the crackdown on immigration, the war in Iran, tariffs and subsequent economic retaliation, the White House ballroom, and restrictions on transgender people.

The president told voters to "pretend” that he's on the ballot at the elections that will see new representatives and senators elected in November.

Trump joked about renaming a third body of water from the Strait of Hormuz to 'Trump Strait' Image: Jessica Koscielniak/REUTERS

His attempts to rename the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario after America were met with rapturous applause. Later, he riffed on renaming the Strait of Hormuz as the "Trump Strait."

Who else was at the Republican convention?

Other speakers focused less on the Trump administration's track record and instead attacked Democrats as "evil," "communists" and "socialists."

Among those who spoke on Wednesday were Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a close Trump ally who is locked in a tough Senate race against rising Democratic challenger James Talarico, who represents a younger and more progressive wing of that party.

Another Republican senator, Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania, was introduced by his Democratic counterpart, John Fetterman, in an unusual move.

Fetterman, who has increasingly broken with Democratic Party positions in recent years, introduced the Republican as his "great friend" and pledged to work with Trump to protect the state's steel industry.

Senator John Fetterman, a Democrat, made the highly unusual move of giving a video message at the Republican convention Image: Kent Nishimura/AFP

Conservative activists were also in attendance.

The Associated Press spotted Stewart Rhodes, founder of the Oath Keepers extremist group. Rhodes had been sentenced to 18 years in prison for his role in the January 6, 2021, riot at the US Capitol, but later benefited from Trump's sweeping clemency after he returned to office.

Trump also praised Erika Kirk for being in attendance on the eve of the one-year anniversary of the killing of her husband, Charlie Kirk.

Vice President JD Vance received a brief shoutout near the end of the speech.

World.title: Philippines: Several killed, dozens missing after fire on ferry
World.content:
Footage released by the Coast Guard showed the vessel engulfed in flames as rescuers brought bodies ashore in body bags. The ship's manifest listed 134 passengers and crew.

At least five people were killed and 87 are missing after a ferry caught fire in the Philippine province of Palawan, the Coast Guard said on Thursday.

The incident aboard the MV June Aster occurred on Wednesday evening about 2.2 kilometers (1.3 miles) off the shore of the municipality of Coron, where it was headed after departing from Baseco ​in Manila.

Coast Guard officials said 42 people had been rescued, including 38 passengers and four crew members.

Footage released by the Coast Guard showed the vessel engulfed in flames, and bodies placed in body bags.

Volunteer fisherfolk assisting the survivors from the ferry that caught fire off Palawan Image: Philippine Coast Guard/AFP

The ship's manifest listed 134 people onboard, including 117 passengers and 17 crew members, according to the Philippine Coast Guard.

"Based on the data we have right now on rescued (42) and the casualties, we still have 87 people who are unaccounted for," Coast Guard Captain Noemi Cayabyab said on Thursday, adding that the figures could change as search and rescue operations continued.

World.title: Finland: Google announces €13 billion AI, energy investment
World.content:
Google has announced a plan to expand AI data centers and buy massive amounts of nuclear energy. Finland's security services have warned of there are risks, but the right-wing government says the deal will bring jobs.

US tech company Google on Wednesday announced that it would be investing €13 billion ($15.1 billion) in AI infrastructure in Finland as well as penning a massive deal to buy nuclear power in the Nordic country over the next two decades.

This year, Google parent company Alphabet increased global investment to around $200 billion as it rushes to catch up in the AI race. Wednesday's announced deal is Google's biggest single investment in the EU to date.

Since repurposing a former paper mill in the coastal city of Hamina in 2009 and transforming it into a data center, Google has steadily increased its presence in the country.

The northern location offers two advantages, cold Arctic temperatures mean it needs less energy to cool energy hungry servers and the fact that Finland only has 6 million residents would seem to provide relief from the growing resistance that such projects are running up against in the US and elsewhere.

Google is not alone in looking to chilly Finland with its cheap nuclear, wind and hydroelectric energy supply to expand its business — Microsoft and TikTok parent ByteDance have also set up shop — with dozens of data centers being built in the country over the past few years.

Attracting data center investment has been a priority for Finland's right-wing Prime Minister Petteri Orpo as the nation confronts record unemployment and slow economic growth.

Why communities are fighting AI data centers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Google makes big claims about boosting Finnish GDP and creating jobs

In a statement, Google said the investment, scheduled to be doled out in 2027 and 2028, will include data centers, electrical grid improvement, and clean energy and battery projects for its chatbot, search and map services.

The company claims the investment will pump some €3.6 billion into Finland's GDP and create 37,000 jobs, with 7,000 being permanent and others coming during the construction phase.

Prime Minister Petteri Orpo echoed Google's rosy outlook for his country's economy, emphasizing that it would spur further investment while downplaying fears that Google's project could drive up energy prices and gobble up resources."This investment is historical in Finland," said Orpo. "This makes us a front-runner in digitalization and AI."

Orpo said Google is, "committed to ensuring that electricity production in Finland ⁠remains sufficient and that prices remain under ​control."

The tax-avoiding US company said the deal was, "a testament to Finland's leadership in responsibly building AI infrastructure."

"Now we are building more in Hamina, expanding that site on a remarkable level, and we are opening up data center operations in three new locations in the municipalities of Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala," said Antti Jarvinen, the company's director of operations for Finland.

Resources under pressure To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Beyond skyrocketing energy consumption, Finland's data center boom presents a potential security risk

Wednesday's deal also includes a purchase agreement for 50% of energy output from one of Finland's two nuclear power plants for the next 22 years according to plant operator Fortum, which will team up with the tech giant to explore new nuclear and renewable projects in the country.

Fortum shares jumped 15.5% on news of the deal, pushing them to their highest level in over four years and making the company the biggest winner on European stock exchanges for the day.

"We call this BYOP — bring your own power," ‌said Google President and ​Chief Investment Officer Ruth Porat, who noted, "This is Google's first nuclear energy deal outside of the United States."

Fortum said the deal would allow it to "continue operating the Loviisa Nuclear Power Plant until the end of its operating licenses in 2050," adding that without it, the plant, which currently supplies about 10% of Finland's electricity, would not have been able to continue operations past 2030.

Overall, Finland's data center boom is expected to create a massive spike in energy consumption, with network operator Fingrid forecasting a 40% jump over the coming years.

Beyond the environmental and energy concerns raised by such deals, Finland's Security and Intelligence Service (SUPO) has also issued explicit warnings that foreign-owned data centers pose potential security risks for the Nordic nation.

SUPO is concerned that municipalities may be weighing the economic potential of data centers more heavily than the security risk associated with them, noting that despite data center investments being fundamentally good for Finland there may be concerns if their owners are linked to authoritarian countries like Russia or China.

SUPO says authoritarian states may, for instance, try to use Finland to circumvent restrictions and sanctions on technology exports. For example, for advanced chips currently banned from export to China.

World.title: ¿Puede el casero obligarme a contratar un seguro del hogar que incluya responsabilidad civil por daños a terceros?
World.content:
Pregunta. ¿Es legal que en un contrato de alquiler de vivienda haya una cláusula que obligue al arrendatario a contratar y costear un seguro del hogar? Si lo es, ¿puede dicha cláusula obligar al arrendatario a asegurar el continente de la vivienda o su obligación se limitaría a asegurar el contenido?, ¿y estaría el arrendatario obligado a que su seguro del hogar incluya responsabilidad civil por daños a terceros? Pedro Milla

Respuesta. Sí, es legal que un contrato de arrendamiento incluya una cláusula que obligue al inquilino a contratar y asumir el coste de un seguro de hogar, siempre que ambas partes lo pacten de forma voluntaria al firmar el contrato.

No se trata de una obligación impuesta por la ley. La Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos (LAU) no exige al inquilino la contratación de un seguro de hogar. Esta posibilidad se fundamenta en el principio de libertad de pactos recogido en el artículo 4 de la LAU: “Respetando lo establecido en el apartado anterior, los arrendamientos de vivienda se regirán por los pactos, cláusulas y condiciones determinados por la voluntad de las partes, en el marco de lo establecido en el título II de la presente ley y, supletoriamente, por lo dispuesto en el Código Civil”. En este mismo sentido, y al amparo de lo dispuesto en el artículo 20 de la LAU y en el artículo 1255 del Código Civil, las partes pueden establecer las cláusulas y condiciones que consideren oportunas, siempre que no sean contrarias a la ley. Por tanto, si el contrato se firma incluyendo esta obligación, el inquilino deberá cumplirla.

Respecto al objeto del seguro, lo habitual es que el inquilino asegure el contenido de la vivienda, es decir, sus pertenencias, muebles, electrodomésticos y demás enseres de su propiedad. Por su parte, el continente (paredes, techos e instalaciones fijas) corresponde, en principio, al propietario como titular del inmueble. No obstante, como hemos indicado, es válido que las partes acuerden expresamente que el arrendatario contrate o asuma una póliza que cubra también el continente, o parte de este, si así se establece en el contrato.

En cuanto a la obligación de incluir una cláusula de responsabilidad civil es totalmente legal y, además, muy frecuente en la práctica. Esta cobertura protege al inquilino frente a los daños que pueda causar accidentalmente a terceros, como una fuga de agua que afecte a una vivienda colindante o un incendio originado en el inmueble arrendado. En ausencia de esta cobertura, el arrendatario deberá responder personalmente con su patrimonio de los daños y perjuicios que pudiera ocasionar.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: Por qué hay que visitar Enciña da Lastra: no parece Galicia, pero lo es
World.content:
Una encina gigante da nombre al parque natural más desconocido y sorprendente de la comunidad, de clima y paisaje mediterráneos. Es la puerta de entrada a la comarca de Valdeorras, donde se hacen excelentes mieles, vinos y aceites

Si uno se duerme yendo a Galicia por la autovía A-6 a la altura de Ponferrada (León) y el que conduce se desvía sin previo aviso por la carretera N-120 y lo despierta solo un cuarto de hora después en el mirador de Cobas (Ourense), creerá que está en el cielo, porque lo que ve es paradisíaco: un ancho río que no sospecha que es el Sil represado en el embalse de Peñarrubia, en cuya tersa superficie se refleja como sobre un espejo el sol naciente y un cañón bordado de árboles majestuosos y riscos dorados. Lo que no creerá, desde luego, es que está ya en Galicia, porque los árboles no son eucaliptos, sino encinas. Los riscos no son de granito o de pizarra —lo habitual allí—, sino de roca caliza. Y aquel alimoche común que sobrevuela este idílico panorama es tan poco gallego como una tortilla de patata con cebolla, muy hecha y sin sal.

Lo que descubre el viajero desde el mirador de Cobas no parece Galicia. Pero lo es. Es Enciña da Lastra, el parque natural más desconocido de la región, de clima mediterráneo y sustrato calizo, un paraíso de las orquídeas —hay 25 especies— y una puerta de entrada magnífica a la comarca de Valdeorras. Parque y comarca son el extremo oriente de Galicia, donde Ourense linda con León y Zamora. Tan extremo oriente es que se parece más a Castilla y León que a la propia Galicia. Al mejor amigo del hombre, los valdeorreses le dicen perro, no can. A la ventana, ventana, no fiestra. Al vino sí lo llaman viño, pero para conservarlo tienen tropecientas bodegas subterráneas, como si esto fuera la Ribera del Duero. Y lo dicho: en lugar de eucaliptos, que no hay monte en Galicia sin ellos, lo que uno encuentra al entrar en Valdeorras son majestuosas encinas, las que dan nombre al parque natural.

La guardiana de un tesoro oculto

Poco más abajo del mirador de Cobas —o de Covas, pues de las dos formas se escribe—, en la última curva que hace la carretera antes de entrar en la aldea del mismo nombre, proyecta su sombra de 25,60 metros de diámetro una encina monstruosa de 16,90 de altura y con un perímetro de 8,80 en la base de su tronco trifurcado. Es la Aciñeira de Covas o Enciño de Fontenouva, el único ejemplar de Quercus ilex reconocido y protegido por la Xunta de Galicia como árbol singular, y eso que hay 151 catalogados de otras especies. Esta encina de edad incalculable —entre 200 y 500 años— es la guardiana de la aldea, del parque natural y de la comarca. Y, según dicen, también de un tesoro oculto entre las rocas calizas donde hunde sus raíces. Allí, cuentan, lo escondieron o dejaron olvidado los mouros, seres fantásticos de la mitología gallega que habitaban bajo tierra rodeados de riquezas antes de que llegaran los humanos.

La encina centenaria que da nombre al parque de Enciña da Lastra. Andrés Campos

En Cobas se puede bajar paseando en 10 minutos a la orilla del embalse para refrescarse en las aguas del Sil y para ver somormujos lavancos, garzas reales y, en septiembre y octubre, cuando pasan camino de sus cuarteles de invierno andaluces y africanos, águilas pescadoras. O bien echarse a andar por la pista forestal que es prolongación de la calle principal y que va ganando suavemente altura, a unos 200 metros sobre la superficie del embalse, hasta Vilardesilva. Son unas tres horas de camino, siguiendo una ruta circular sencilla de 11 kilómetros.

Si somos más de ir observando la flora y la fauna que de andar por andar, con llegar hasta un antiguo horno de cal que hay a media hora del inicio ya está bien. Por el camino y al pie mismo del calero, florecen en primavera la orquídea abejera (Ophrys sphegodes) y la piramidal (Anacamptis pyramidalis), dos de las especies más llamativas de este orquidario natural, y en un escarpe calizo que hay poco antes de cruzar el arroyo de Pereda y de avistar la enorme mole troncocónica del viejo horno, arraigan plantas como la Armeria rothmaleri y la Petrocoptis grandiflora, que no lo hacen en ningún otro lugar del planeta.

El antiguo horno de cal en el parque natural Enciña da Lastra. Andrés Campos

Hay que acercarse también al centro de visitantes del parque natural, en Biobra, donde se informa con detalle de cuanto hay en él y de las rutas más curiosas, como la de Tras os Penedos —la mejor para observar mariposas— o la de As Dúas Vertentes. Recorriendo esta última, se ven en lontananza las minas romanas de Las Médulas y, en el cielo, el alimoche común, que en Galicia es un ave muy poco común, valga la redundancia. Si se viaja en un grupo de al menos ocho personas, se puede hacer las rutas acompañados por un guía del centro de visitantes sin pagar nada, solo escribiendo con antelación a su correo electrónico (servizo.conservacion.natureza.ourense@xunta.gal). Pero hay que tener en cuenta que el centro solo abre de jueves a domingo y que echa el cierre desde mediados de septiembre hasta Semana Santa. Así no es de extrañar que este sea uno de los parques naturales más desconocidos de España.

Dos pueblos ‘enxebres’: Vilardesilva y Pardollán

Además de la naturaleza inaudita de Enciña da Lastra, en el centro aconsejan visitar Vilardesilva y Pardollán, dos de los pueblos más enxebres, más auténticos, con más encanto del parque y de Valdeorras, una región donde el desarrollismo y los marmolistas han causado estragos. El feísmo apenas ha hecho mella en ellos.

Una de las calles del pueblo de Vilardesilva. Andrés Campos

En Vilardesilva abundan las casas de piedra caliza bien labrada, con galerías de madera hermosamente tallada y con buenas historias a sus espaldas. Historias como la que fue propiedad de Paco González, que emigró con sus padres a Alemania, donde fue fontanero y luego payaso —el primero titulado de Europa—, y que volvió regularmente en verano a esta aldea de su Valdeorras natal para hacer un alojamiento rural —Chao do Prao— y dar cursos de clown. Así, hasta que Paco murió en 2017 y su casa rural y su escuela se perdieron. El cercano mirador da Cruz es un buen lugar para olvidarse del triste final del sueño de verano de Paco, admirando el paisajazo —el espolón calizo de Peñarrubia aflorando de las aguas quietas del Sil como la aleta dorsal de los peces acorazados que poblaban este rincón de Galicia hace 400 millones de años, cuando era un cálido mar tropical— y oliendo a tomillo salsero, una planta tan exótica en Ourense como un clown valdeorrés en Alemania.

Pardollán, por su parte, tiene un lugar especialmente cuidado, que justifica por sí solo la visita: la céntrica plaza donde todos los vecinos —43; 10 más que Vilardesilva— beben y llenan sus regaderas en una preciosa fuente de tres caños, rodeada de macetas floridas, pinturas murales y casas con galerías azules. Este colorido rincón, más que de una aldea del interior de Galicia, diríase de un pueblo marinero de las Rías Altas.

El pueblo gallego de Pardollán. Andrés Campos

La ‘alvariza’ que surgió del fuego

En el centro de visitantes del parque también recomiendan, si se va a pasar más de un día en la zona, acercarse a conocer la empresa apícola familiar O Marquesado, en O Real. “Apicultores desde 1896”, reza un cartel en la fachada de la casa-taller, pero enseguida se da uno cuenta, viendo y oyendo a los dueños, Antonia Franco y Jens Kleinwächter, de que no llevan tanto tiempo en esto y tampoco en Valdeorras. Antonia, hija de emigrantes gallegos en Alemania­ —y prima de Paco, el clown—, volvió hace 12 años a la tierra de su padre con su marido y ambos decidieron seguir el dulce oficio del tío de ella, que iba a retirarse.

Antonia Franco en el taller de miel de O Marquesado, en O Real. Andrés Campos

El caso es que hacen lo mismo que otras cuatro generaciones de Francos —una miel con un sabor especial, gracias al microclima mediterráneo de este rincón de Ourense—, pero con una técnica y una precisión alemanas, como se ve en la limpieza y el orden del taller, de la tienda y de la sala de catas. “En Alemania”, explica Jens, “aprendimos a trabajar con la dócil abeja cárnica y aquí tuvimos que aprender de nuevo con la negra ibérica, que es mucho más nerviosa, más defensiva, más brava”. Una abeja a la que no tranquiliza y vuelve más manejable y productiva el cambio climático y tampoco los graves incendios que sufrió la comarca en 2020 y 2025. “Mi tío”, explica ahora Antonia, “producía siete toneladas al año con 150 colmenas. Nosotros, con el doble, solo cuatro”.

Para compensar, y porque no saben parar, estos emprendedores de cabeza alemana y corazón español llevan a los visitantes que lo desean a hacer de apicultores por un día en alguno de los terrenos donde tienen sus 300 colmenas. Por el camino, van parando aquí y allá para admirar los soutos, montes de castaños productivos que han sido estos últimos años eficacísimos cortafuegos. En una ladera no tan limpia, la maleza ardió como la yesca en agosto de 2025, durante el incendio más grande registrado hasta entonces en España, y entonces apareció una alvariza, una muralla circular que se usaba hace más de un siglo para defender las colmenas de los osos. “Un convenio entre la Xunta y la Fundación Reina Sofía”, informa Jens, “va a permitir recuperar en breve esta estructura patrimonial: nosotros la devolveremos a la vida, llenándola de colmenas. Ya solo queda abrir un camino para poder llegar en un 4x4 allá arriba”. Mientras tanto, Jens lleva a los apituristas al pie del monte donde reapareció la alvariza, en Oulego, y la observa de lejos con la mano en el corazón.

Jens Kleinwächter, frente a la 'alvariza' de Oulego. Andrés Campos

Beber en una cueva y comer en otra

Otra cosa que se hacía en Valdeorras desde siempre, además de miel, es vino, pero poca gente de fuera se fijaba en esta denominación de origen hasta que uno de Rafael Palacios, Sorte O Soro 2020, obtuvo 100 puntos en la guía Robert Parker Wine Advocate. Ahora todo el mundo vuelve los ojos y los paladares hacia esta comarca y alucina con sus montes llenos de vides de Godello —la uva autóctona, la más apreciada, con la que se elaboran vinos frescos, afrutados y elegantes, que se beben solos— y de cuevas. Se decía que había muchas, más de mil cuevas, y un reciente estudio de Carina Rodríguez y Cristina de la Torre, As covas de Valdeorras, ha confirmado que no es una exageración: han catalogado 1.103.

Una cueva bien conservada, que da gusto visitar, es la de Adega Melillas, una bodega familiar creada a principios de siglo por emigrantes retornados de Suiza a su pueblo natal, A Rúa. ¿Y por qué se llama Melillas? Pues porque así llamaba al abuelo de Sonia Prada —copropietaria, gerente y quien explica la saga a los enoturistas—, que hizo la mili en Melilla. Arriba se degustan y se compran los vinos —el mejor, el Lagar do Cigur Godello 2025— y abajo se entra casi a tientas en la cueva, que no es de clara roca caliza, sino de negra pizarra. Cuando los ojos se acostumbran a la oscuridad, se descubre una de las cuevas más altas de Valdeorras, con techos de más de cuatro metros, donde antiguamente el vino se conservaba bien en los veranos de clima tan poco gallego de esta comarca, igual que en una vinoteca.

Sonia Prada en la cueva de bodega Melillas, en A Rúa. Andrés Campos

Mayor aún es una cueva de Seadur, la segunda que vale la pena visitar: tan grande es, que cabe en ella un restaurante, Cova da Xabreira, con 42 comensales dando cuenta en sus mesas de las berenjenas con queso de O Cebreiro y miel de O Marquesado, el chuletón de vaca madurada Simmental y cuanto va saliendo de las brasas. Para beber, nada como el rosado Viñas de Seadur As Fontelas que elabora la misma propiedad con la autóctona y muy escasa uva brancellao. Y para elucubrar en la sobremesa: ¿cómo abrirían semejante boquete en la roca madre del monte? Porque es puro granito. No hay huellas de barrenos. Fue a pico.

Dormir a orillas del Bibei y del Sil

Después de mucho comer y elucubrar, no es mala idea dirigirse a As Ermidas, en O Bolo, para dar una cabezada en la playa fluvial del río Bibei, el principal afluente del Sil por su orilla izquierda, o un paseo por los alrededores, viendo cómo Diego de la Torre cuida los viejos olivos que se retuercen en las escarpadas márgenes, muchos de los cuales debieron de ser plantados en 1624, cuando se creó el santuario barroco de As Ermitas que hay en lo alto. Con las aceitunas que con arduos trabajos obtiene de estos y otros olivos centenarios de Valdeorras, Diego produce con cuentagotas el AOVE Terras Gigurras, que sale a 56 euros el litro y se agota en un amén. Ahora mismo hay que esperar dos meses a que los olivos y este oleicultor heroico hagan más.

Quien quiera algo más que una siesta en bañador —una con pijama—, puede volver a Seadur y alojarse en A Rectoral, la casona de 1783 donde vivía y prácticamente teletrabajaba el cura de la localidad: solo tenía que levantar la voz para decir misa en la vecina iglesia. El lugar, que tenía también algo de cueva, con sillares ciclópeos y rincones sombríos por doquier, ha sido reformado a fondo y decorado alegremente por sus propietarios, Isabel Val y Lucas Presedo, que han tenido el acierto de colgar en casi todas las habitaciones y apartamentos lienzos de la artista de A Rúa Carina Rodríguez, que evocan las máscaras y los trajes del Entroido orensano. Otro acierto: el apartamento A Lareira, con la moderna cocina y un antiguo escaño con mesa abatible integrados a modo de office dentro de la monumental campana de la vieja chimenea.

Una buena opción también para alojarse y para poner a esta ruta punto final —o aparte, porque hay que volver para seguir explorando el extremo oriente de Galicia— es el hotel rural A Pontevella, en Sobradelo. Está en un lugar difícil de creer: a orillas del Sil, junto a un puente seiscentista de 90 metros cuyos siete ojos han visto cosas tremendas —como la crecida de 2010 o como la francesada, que para detenerla se derribó su arco central en 1810—. Soraya Docampo, su propietaria, levantó con sus propias manos este hotel boutique de acabados impecables, como solo puede hacerlo alguien que antes se dedicó a la construcción. Además de buena obrera, es buena cocinera y amena anfitriona.

El puente sobre el río Sil, en Sobradelo. Andrés Campos

Mientras los huéspedes se chupan los dedos —muy ricas, las croquetas de cecina artesanal y la lubina al horno con vino Godello—, les cuenta cosas maravillosas de este pueblo que es la capital de uno de los municipios más ricos de Galicia, Carballeda de Valdeorras, el mayor productor mundial de pizarra. Las piscinas naturales de Sobradelo tienen playa de arena fina, mucha pizarra —¡claro!— y hasta hidromasaje. Mañana habrá que ir a probarlas.

World.title: Amsterdam fails to get EU backing to limit Airbnb rules
World.content:
Amsterdam mayor Femke Halsema has failed to persuade the European Commission to help crack down on people renting out their own homes to tourists.

Halsema travelled to Brussels in the spring with the mayors of other big European cities that struggle with mass tourism – like Barcelona and Paris – to lobby for tougher powers to regulate holiday rentals through sites like Airbnb.

But the EU Affordable Housing Act, presented on Wednesday, would not ban or limit holiday lets but instead establishes a standard for when an area is under “housing stress” – defined as one where house prices are at least eight times per capita disposable income and have risen over the past decade.

It then gives local authorities a legal basis to restrict commercial short-term rentals and second-home purchases in those areas.

Combating local damage

Amsterdam had asked the commission for two things, according to the Telegraaf: more powers to act against people letting out the home they live in, and for the right to intervene once an area’s liveability has been damaged by tourist rentals.

The commission seemingly dismissed both requests. The text of the act explicitly excludes a host’s primary residence from any restriction, on the grounds that renting out your own home does not take housing off the market. It also only covers measures justified by affordability and availability, not neighbourhood nuisance.

“It is questionable whether this proposal is going to help us,” Amsterdam housing alderman Zita Pels told the paper. Dirk Gotink, an MEP for the centre-right NSC, also told the Telegraaf: “we don’t need a European law to solve local problems.”

Amsterdam already restricts renting your own home through sites like Airbnb to 30 nights per year but has tried to go further in the past. In July 2020 the council banned holiday rentals outright in the red light district and part of the canal ring.

The Amsterdam district court overturned that ban in 2021, and the Council of State, the highest administrative court, upheld the ruling in 2023, saying a total ban was disproportionate and the city should first have tested less drastic measures, such as a lower night limit.

For people in the Netherlands with a second home in Spain, Portugal or France, nothing will change for now. The law would allow local authorities in stressed areas to restrict purchases of homes not used as a primary residence, but only for property bought after the measure takes effect.

The proposal must first be negotiated by the European Parliament and member states, a process likely to take a year or more.

World.title: Dutch exports to US plummet 25% as tariffs bite
World.content:
Exports from the Netherlands to the United States fell by 25% in the first half of this year, knocking the US out of the top five destinations for Dutch goods.

Dutch companies sold €13 billion worth of goods to the US between January and June, €4.3 billion less than in the same period last year, figures from national statistics office CBS show. The decline began after the Trump administration imposed a general import tariff of 15% on goods from the EU in August last year.

Almost every type of product was affected. Machinery and transport equipment, the biggest category of Dutch exports to the US, accounted for nearly half the fall. Sales of medicines and other chemical products dropped by more than 30%, and manufactured goods such as medical instruments fell by almost a quarter.

As a result, the US now takes 4% of Dutch goods exports, down from 5.5% a year earlier. Italy has overtaken it as the fifth-biggest market, with Spain also catching up. Exports to Belgium, Germany, France, Spain and Italy all rose over the same period.

Trade in the other direction has grown – imports from the US were up 19% to €27.6 billion, although most of that increase was oil and other fuels, which have become more expensive because of the conflict in the Middle East. Other kinds of imports rose by 6.7%.

The tariffs have been costly for the US as well. The country’s Supreme Court ruled in February that most of the levies Donald Trump introduced last year were illegal, and Dutch companies are now claiming back more than €1 billion in duties.

Philips has already received €186 million, and Heineken and Ahold Delhaize are expected to recover hundreds of millions between them.

In 2024, before the tariffs were introduced, the Netherlands exported more than €38 billion worth of goods to the US, nearly 6% of all its exports.

More than 3.8 million people were members of public libraries in the Netherlands in 2025, a 3% increase over the year before according to new numbers by national statistics office CBS.

The number of adult library members rose by 46,000 to nearly 1.4 million.

In particular, an increasing number of younger adults, those between the ages of 18 and 30, are joining libraries.

In total, 9% of adults are library members. That statistic is dwarfed by the number of children who are library members. Nearly two-thirds of kids, 74%, are members of a library.

The number of children joining a library has also increased in 2025. Last year saw a rise of 2.4%, or over 57,000 more kids with a library card.

The Netherlands had 802 library locations in 2025, an increase of 35 on the year before. This is due to an increase in funding from the national government, according to CBS.

The number of physical books checked out by patrons has remained stable but the number of e-book loans rose. Nearly 6 million e-books were borrowed via the online library, 3% more than in 2024, and audiobook loans rose 11% to 2.9 million.

Divers have recovered the body of a man who fell out of a boat in the IJ in Amsterdam on Wednesday.

The 47-year old went overboard near the Schellingwouderbrug, which connects Amsterdam East and Amsterdam Noord, at around 12:30PM, the regional safety board reported.

Multiple diving teams and rescue boats were dispatched as well as a helicopter equipped with a thermal camera.

After an hour of searching, the operation was scaled back as it was unlikely the man would be found alive.

Divers found his body late Wednesday evening.

It is not clear how the man ended up in the water. The police are investigating.

World.title: Trust in politics falling, more people joining protests: CBS
World.content:
Trust in politics among people in their twenties and thirties in the Netherlands has fallen sharply, according to new figures by national statistics bureau CBS, and more people of all age groups are joining political protests and demonstrations.

Among 25 to 35-year-olds those that said they had trust dropped from 50.6% to 42.4%, the steepest fall of any group. Some 55% of 18 to 25-year-olds said they had confidence in politics last year, up from 49% in 2023, making them the only age group whose trust increased.

Teenagers aged 15 to 18 remain the most trusting, at 62%, while the least trusting are 65 to 75-year-olds, at 31%. The figures come from the CBS survey on social cohesion and wellbeing, which polls people aged 15 and over every year.

Participation in protests and demonstrations rose in every age group in 2025, with 25 to 35-year-olds the most active: 9.5% said they had taken part in a protest or demonstration in the past five years, compared with 8.6% of 18 to 25-year-olds and 2.4% of the over-75s.

Students and people with a university or college degree were the most likely to have demonstrated, the CBS said.

Older people may be less trusting, but they are much more interested in politics. Some 64% of 65 to 75-year-olds said they were fairly or very interested, compared with 37% of 15 to 18-year-olds, although interest among teenagers and young adults has risen for two years in a row.

The survey was carried out during 2025, a year in which the Schoof cabinet collapsed and a general election was held in October.

Trust in politics peaked across all age groups in 2020, during the Covid pandemic, when 78% of teenagers and 71% of 18 to 25-year-olds said they had confidence in politicians. It has since fallen back to roughly where it was a decade ago.

World.title: Hidden weapons found near primary school in Overasselt
World.content:
Military police have found multiple weapons hidden near a primary school in Overassel following last week’s gun attack on a property in the Gelderland village, which resulted in the murder of one man and serious injury on two police officers.

Investigations have been ongoing since the attack, with 35 people arrested – all but two of whom are being held for murder or manslaughter – and extensive searches in the surrounding areas. It is suspected the attack was part of a feud over cocaine dealing linked with a resident of the village, who has been targetted before.

Police would not say how many weapons were found near the school or other details. In the day after the attack, dozens of men – who were seen heavily armed on CCTV footage – were caught hiding in the countryside, on the motorways and near rail stations as they fled the scene.

After the events unfolded, a video surfaced on social media of masked men holding automatic weapons and reading out a threat message to Jan G. Jr., the Overassel resident linked to the attack. They said he owed a “Belgian friend” 1,283 kilograms of “goods” and had to return it within 12 hours or they would kill his family.

They spoke in a heavy Spanish accent and said the goods had never left Spain as they were supposed to.

On Tuesday, Spanish police intercepted a shipment of exactly 1,283 kilograms of cocaine in a transport truck carrying coconuts. It is not yet clear whether the two cases are connected.

The shock of the attack on Overassel pushed justice minister David van Weel to warn that “unprecedented” violence is occurring due to international drugs smuggling, though he dismissed the idea of the Netherlands becoming a so-called “narco state”.

Reports of gunshots in nearby Nijmegen on Monday night drew in heavily armed police, who closed off several streets before determining no shots were fired. A relative of Jan G. Jr, who lives in the city, was moved for his own protection.

World.title: Five inburgering exam myths, tested against real exams
World.content:
A lot of people preparing for the inburgeringsexamen run into advice: “pick the longest answer”, “choose B if you are stuck”, “expect it to get harder as you go up a level”. Most of it is passed on in good faith. Almost none of it has ever been checked. Inburgeringscursus.nl coded 881 questions from 35 official exam sets – three years of the Staatsexamen NT2 plus the DUO practice exams.

Here are the myths that came up most often:

“Pick the answer with words you recognise from the text”

This is the most repeated piece of exam advice there is and it does not hold up against the data. We checked it on 288 reading questions. In four of them there was exactly one option that shared words with the text. The rest of the time it pointed at two or three answers at once.

The reason is simple once you see it. The most common wrong answer quotes the text accurately and then answers a different question. Both the right answer and the wrong ones borrow words from the passage, roughly 86% against 95%. A feature that shows up in nearly every option cannot tell them apart.

“Answer B is more often correct”

This one looked real. Across 176 items B came up more often than chance and it held up under statistical checking. So we tested it on all the available exams and there it landed at 31.7%. That is what guessing gets you.

Even if it had been true, it would not have helped. Answering B every time scores between 10 and 19 points across the six exams we measured. The pass mark is 24. It does not pass a single one. So when in doubt, choosing “B” is not the safe bet.

“The exam gets steadily harder from A2 to B1 to B2”

Half true. The half that is wrong matters if you are planning your study time.

A2 really is a different exam from B1. But B1 and B2 do not separate cleanly. The individual exams overlap, and the gap between them is relatively small.

There are two groups here, not three steps on a ladder. Moving from B1 to B2 is a smaller jump than the label suggests. Moving from A2 to B1 is the real one.

“The reading exam is the same task from start to finish”

Not true, and this is the most useful thing we found. It applies to the Staatsexamen NT2 at B1 and B2 level.

Above every reading text sits one line of instruction. Five of them say roughly the same thing: “Answer the question”. The last one says something different: “read the question first, then find the answer in the text”.

That line appeared on the final text of every exam we looked at, 34 items out of 34, across six exams at B1 and B2. And there the answer sits almost word for word in the text 47% of the time. Everywhere else it is 9%. The exam board is telling you to stop reading and start searching.

One warning. It is not the easy section. Half-correct answers appear twice as often there, 24% against 12%. In 13 of those 34 items the information you need sits in two separate articles. The difficulty moves from understanding to locating. Searching faster without checking is how you walk into it.

“KNM is mostly about Dutch customs and etiquette”

Not really. KNM covers eight themes across 40 questions, and they are nowhere near equal in size. Work and income runs to eight or nine questions. Institutions get seven. Together they are about 40% of the exam. Manners and education get three each.

This held across all official practice exams. It tells you where to start, not where to stop. Those two themes leave 60% elsewhere, and the pass mark is well above that.

Why we counted all this

Patterns like these are only useful if you can practise them. That is what Inburgeringscursus.nl is for: an online course for the inburgeringsexamen and the Staatsexamen NT2. The platform is built on this research so you practice exactly what the real exams ask of you.

It covers all five parts at A2, B1 and B2. It starts with theory on what each part asks, then you move on to practice questions that follow the real patterns and finally the mock exams. These mock exams are timed and marked on the official criteria. The practice never runs out either. You generate new questions yourself whenever you want them, on exactly the points you keep getting wrong. This way you can practise until you know you are ready instead of hoping you are.

World.title: Intelligence watchdogs warn new spy powers threaten rule of law
World.content:
Independent watchdogs responsible for monitoring the Netherlands’ secret service agencies are sounding the alarm about potential new powers that would allow them to surveil citizens far more easily with far less oversight.

The plans, which were set out by defence minister Yesilgöz recently, include allowing the domestic and military (AIVD and MIVD) intelligence services to track and collect data on anyone considered a threat without gaining prior permission.

This is intended to fight “obvious adversaries” she said, referring to foreign states like Russia and China and non-state attackers conducting cyber attacks on Dutch infrastructure.

But Hugo Hillenaar, chairman of the CTIVD, which checks whether the services have acted lawfully, has said the changes could threaten the democratic rule of law itself.

Currently the AIVD and MIVD must request permission to track individuals every three months. If the proposed changes go through, they will be able to designate entire organisations as enemies. This would extend to any other body seen to be collaborating with them, like universities.

“If a university collaborates with an organisation designated as an adversary, it is no longer separately assessed whether an investigation into, for example, an employee of that university is actually necessary,” Hillenaar told broadcaster NOS.

The watchdogs are also worried about what the law calls bulk datasets: large collections of data on many people, most of whom are not under investigation. The services can get hold of them by tapping an undersea internet cable, or by buying data that hackers have stolen and put up for sale.

“Think of the data from a national health screening programme, or from the Odido hack,” Hillenaar said. “That includes information about a great many people who have nothing to do with espionage or terrorism. You should not want that data to be used without limit in investigations, or shared with foreign intelligence services.”

The bill would also let the services run AI over a bulk dataset before anyone has decided whether the services’ own staff are allowed to look at it.

“The supervisors are really sounding the alarm,” said former AIVD officer and supervisor Bert Hubert. “I have never seen them so critical and I understand very well that they are concerned about human rights.”

Almost 80% of Poles say that they would want their country to come to the aid of the Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – if they were attacked by Russia. The new poll follows a controversy over comments by a senior opposition figure, former defence minister Mariusz Błaszczak, in which he refused to confirm his support for Poland fulfilling its NATO obligations by coming to the aid of the Baltic states if they were invaded. In a survey for broadcaster Radio Zet, the IBRiS agency asked: “In the event of Russian aggression, should Poland help Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia?” In response, 77.8% of those polled said that it should, while only 16.1% were opposed. Among respondents who identified as politically centrist, 92% were in favour. The figures were lower for those with left-wing (75%) or right-wing (73%) views, though in both cases a large majority still supported coming to the Baltic states’ aid. Commenting on the findings, Radio Zet wrote that “the survey shows that Poles feel responsible for the military security of their NATO allies – contrary to what some politicians have said”. That was a reference to remarks last week by Błaszczak, who is the head of the parliamentary caucus of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s largest opposition group. Between 2018 and 2023, Błaszczak served as defence minister in the former PiS-led government. In an interview with Radio Zet, Błaszczak was asked if, in the event of a Russian attack on the Baltic states, Poland should come to their aid. “Polish soldiers should defend Poland,” he responded. “We need to be strong in our alliances…We should prioritise cooperation with the United States.” The interviewer pointed out that Article 5 of the NATO treaty requires members of the alliance to come to the assistance of another member that is attacked, and again asked if Poland should help the Baltic states if such an attack occurred. “We border Russia directly, and we border a Russia that has effectively taken over Belarusian territory. So we’re also on the front line,” replied Błaszczak. “This article, of course, speaks of solidarity, but the point is that the government that governs Poland should establish the best possible relations with the United States.” With the interviewer continuing to press the question, Błaszczak simply said that “it all depends on the circumstances” and “it’s not a straightforward issue”. Błaszczak’s comments were criticised by figures from Poland’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. They accused him of calling into question the validity of Article 5, on which Poland would rely if it were attacked. “A former defence minister who undermines the sanctity of Polish security, i.e. NATO’s Article 5, is a moron,” wrote deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk. Interior minister Marcin Kiewiński said that Błaszczak had “undermined the very purpose of NATO’s existence”. In response to the criticism, Błaszczak wrote on social media that, during the PiS government’s time in power, it had significantly enhanced security ties with the Baltic states, including stationing Polish forces in Latvia and contributing Polish F-16s to NATO’s air policing mission. “NATO’s Article 5 is activated collectively, and alliance commitments are binding, but every [Polish] defence minister’s priority should be the defence of Poland and ensuring the safety of Poles,” he added. World.title: Polish school pupils second best at maths in EU
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish schoolchildren are the second best in the European Union at mathematics, the third best at reading comprehension, and the fifth best at science, according to the latest results from a major international study of pupils’ abilities. The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) is carried out every three years by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and measures the performance of 15-year-olds. The latest instalment, based on tests taken in 2025, was published on Tuesday this week. It includes results from 91 countries and territories across the world. A total of 760,000 pupils were assessed, including 7,103 in 217 Polish schools. In maths, Polish pupils obtained a mean score of 484, which was the 12th highest in the world. The top seven places were taken by Asian countries and territories. But the only other European Union country to exceed Poland’s score was Estonia (508). Poland was just behind the United Kingdom (488) and Canada (485), but ahead of the likes of Finland (469), Germany (464) and the United States (463). In reading comprehension, Poland’s mean score of 482 was 14th in the world and third best in the EU, behind Ireland (500) and Estonia (499). Polish pupils performed slightly worse, in relative terms, in science, where their mean score of 495 was 18th in the world and fifth best in the EU. A number of Polish media outlets and Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrongly reported that Poland was third best in the EU for science. In fact, it was significantly behind Estonia (527) and Finland (504) and marginally below Ireland (500) and Austria (497). Poland’s latest results continue its recent history of performing strongly in PISA. In the 2018 instalment, Polish pupils were the third best in the EU in both maths and science, and fourth best in reading. In 2022 (when PISA took place a year later than planned due to the Covid pandemic), Poland was fourth in the EU in maths and fifth in both science and reading. In 2021, a separate assessment of reading comprehension among fourth-grade pupils – called PIRLS and carried out every five years by the International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement – found Poland had the joint best result among EU countries, equal with Finland Following the announcement of the new PISA data, Polish education minister Barbara Nowacka welcomed the fact that “Poland has maintained its high ranking among European Union countries”. However, she added a note of caution, pointing to the fact that, overall, test scores have been declining, both in Poland and globally. That shows “Polish education still has a lot of work ahead of it”. Nowacka said that her ministry’s efforts to reform the school curriculum had been based on results and recommendations from previous PISA reports. World.title: Poland secures further $4bn financing from US to buy American military equipment
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has signed an agreement for a further $4 billion (14.8 billion zloty) from the United States Foreign Military Financing (FMF) programme, which provides grants and loans to fund the purchase of American military equipment. Defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz called the development a “great honour”, because FMF is “granted only to the best allies”. The agreement is not only “another important step in the modernisation of the Polish armed forces” but also “strengthens the strategic partnership between Poland and the US”. The US embassy in Warsaw likewise hailed the agreement as “reaffirming the strength of the US-Poland partnership as we work together to strengthen NATO, deter aggression, and support peace and security in Europe”. .@UnderSecT took part in the signing of a $4 billion Foreign Military Financing (FMF) loan guarantee—an important step in U.S.-Polish security cooperation. Poland’s significant investments in its defense capabilities and the U.S. defense industrial base reflect our shared… pic.twitter.com/Dz3huAp8pj — US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) September 9, 2026 Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has embarked on an unprecedented military procurement spree, with its defence budget rising to the highest relative level in NATO. Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was also the largest importer of arms in NATO. Around 44% of those purchases came from the US, including Abrams tanks, Patriot air defence batteries, and HIMARS rocket artillery. The new agreement marks the sixth time Poland has received funds through FMF, for a total of almost $20 billion. Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the latest financing would be used to “accelerate the implementation of existing contracts, including for Apache helicopters”. In 2024, Poland signed a $10 billion deal to buy 96 AH-64E Apache attack helicopters, along with a logistics and training package and a stockpile of ammunition and spare parts. It will make Poland the second-largest operator of Apaches in the world, after only the US itself. Thomas DiNanno, the US under secretary of state for arms control and international security, said that the new agreement “signifies our commitment to assistance, but also Poland’s commitment to ensuring security, building defence capabilities, and ensuring the security of NATO’s eastern flank”. “Poland is not only a trusted partner; it is not only an ally on the front line; it is a model ally of the United States,” he added, repeating recent remarks by US defence secretary Pete Hegseth. The terms of the financing have not been revealed, but Marta Postuła, vice president of Poland’s national development bank, BGK, through which the funds will be channelled, said it was “on more favourable terms than the last two [FMF] loan guarantee agreements”. This, she added, was “due to the subsidisation of a portion of the financing costs through a grant awarded for this purpose by the US government”. 💬 Obecna umowa została zawarta na korzystniejszych warunkach niż dwie poprzednie umowy z gwarancjami pożyczkowymi dzięki subsydiowaniu części kosztów finansowania w ramach grantu przyznanego w tym celu przez Rząd USA. To kolejny wyraz bardzo bliskiej, transatlantyckiej… pic.twitter.com/Ipd4cYDeFo — Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego 🇵🇱 (@BGK_pl) September 9, 2026 The issue of who Poland should buy military equipment from, and how such purchases should be funded, has become embroiled in domestic political disputes this year. President Karol Nawrocki and the right-wing opposition with which he is aligned have criticised the government for signing Poland up to the EU’s SAFE programme, which is providing €43.7 billion (188.7 billion zloty) in loans for defence and security spending. They argue that provisions requiring most of the money to be spent within Europe itself could damage Poland’s relations with the US and South Korea, who have in recent years been the main sources of military procurement. However, speaking today, Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the new loan agreement with the US shows that SAFE and FMF “do not compete with one another; they complement one another”. Amerykański sprzęt wojskowy ponownie wzmocni Wojsko Polskie i bezpieczeństwo Polaków! Właśnie zabezpieczyliśmy środki w wysokości 4 mld dolarów, czyli prawie 15 mld zł na jego zakup. Łącznie w ramach amerykańskiego programu Foreign Military Financing pozyskaliśmy już blisko 20… pic.twitter.com/hhzXcE1hoC — Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) September 9, 2026 While Nawrocki is a close ally of President Donald Trump, who endorsed him ahead of last year’s Polish presidential elections, the more liberal government, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, has at times clashed with Washington. In May this year, the sudden and unexpected cancellation of the rotational deployment of almost 4,000 US troops to Poland raised concern in Warsaw. Shortly afterwards, Trump declared that he would deploy 5,000 additional troops to Poland. However, since then, no clear details of that plan have been announced, although Poland has formally submitted a request for the US to establish a new permanent US military base on its territory. On Wednesday morning, Polish deputy defence minister Paweł Bejda told broadcaster TVP that an American delegation was in Poland this week to visit potential locations for the base and discuss the issue further. World.title: “We remember where Germany in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party can lead,” says Polish FM
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s foreign minister has expressed concern over the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party at a time when Germany is rapidly rearming – suggesting that it has echoes of the build-up to World War Two. “We want Germany, under democratic leadership and as Europe’s largest economy, to play a strong role in ensuring our common security,” Radosław Sikorski told German newspaper Handelsblatt. “But we remember all too well where a rearmed Germany in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party can lead – and that is precisely what the AfD represents,” he added. Polens Außenminister Sikorski: „Wir wollen, dass Deutschland (…) eine starke Rolle bei der Sicherung unserer gemeinsamen Sicherheit spielt. Aber wir erinnern uns nur allzu gut daran, wohin ein wiederbewaffnetes Deutschland in den Händen einer rechtsextremen, prorussischen Partei führen kann (…)“ [image or embed] — Andreas Prause (@andreas-prause.eu) 8 September 2026 at 21:05 Poland was, on 1 September 1939, invaded by Nazi Germany, marking the start of World War Two and over five years of brutal occupation. The attack was launched in cooperation with the Soviet Union, which invaded Poland from the east two weeks later. After Hitler was defeated, Germany had no major far-right party for decades. However, that has changed in recent years. In 2024, the AfD came first in the Thuringian state election, with 33% of the vote. Last Sunday, it won in Saxony-Anhalt, with 44%. The party also came second in the federal elections of 2025, with 21%, making it the main national opposition. Opinion polls now show that the AfD is the most popular party nationally, with support of around 28%, well ahead of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU), on 21%. The AfD’s growth has been watched with particular concern in Poland, a country that suffered enormously under Nazi-German occupation. Some senior AfD figures have sought to downplay the significance of the Nazi era. In 2025, when the German parliament approved plans for a memorial in Berlin to Polish victims of World War Two, the AfD was the only party not to vote in favour. The AfD’s sympathy towards and links with Russia have caused further disquiet in Poland. Last year, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said he “does not see any current threat to Germany from Russia” and that, in fact, “Poland could also be a threat to us”. This year, another senior AfD figure, Kay Gottschalk, called for Poland to pay his country €1.3 billion as reparations for its “complicity” in the sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines that used to bring Russian gas to Germany through the Baltic Sea but were damaged by explosions in 2022. Germany’s parliament has passed a motion calling on the government to establish a permanent memorial in Berlin to Polish victims of the German-Nazi occupation. The measure was supported by all parties apart from the far-right AfD https://t.co/8dk0ZSpmjJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 3, 2025 In the wake of the AfD’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk declared that “only idiots or traitors” in Poland would celebrate an AfD victory. He claimed there were some such people in Law and Justice (PiS) and Confederation (Konfederacja), the two main right-wing opposition parties. However, PiS’s reaction to AfD’s rise has been mixed. On Tuesday, PiS MP Małgorzata Golińska told Polskie Radio that it represents a “kind of browning” of politics in Germany – a reference to the brown shirts of Hitler’s SA paramilitary forces that helped bring him to power in the 1920s and 1930s. “A return to very dangerous thinking is taking place there and we must observe in which direction it will all develop,” added Golińska. “From Poland’s perspective, we should not overreact with any particular emotion, but we also cannot be naive [in thinking] that nothing is happening there.” By contrast, another PiS MP, Jarosław Sellin, told Onet Radio that PiS and the AfD “say similar things” when it comes to EU climate and migration policies. But he added that “this does not mean we have to like what the AfD says about history, relations with Poland, and Russia”. Polish PM @donaldtusk has condemned as “idiots or traitors” right-wing opposition figures who have welcomed the far-right AfD's election victory in Germany However, the response from the Polish right to the election result has so far been relatively muted https://t.co/goSWlbeGA8 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026 Responses from Confederation have likewise been mixed. The group is actually made up of two main factions, one of which, a libertarian party called New Hope (Nowa Nadzieja), is allied with the AfD in the European Parliament. New Hope’s spokesman, Wojciech Machulski, told the Fakt daily that they are “united [with AfD] in our opposition to EU migration and climate policies” but at the same time “we do not accept the anti-Polish statements”. Krzysztof Mulawa, an MP from the National Movement (RN), which makes up the other half of Confederation, told the newspaper that “several of the AfD’s demands are unacceptable from the Polish perspective”. But he said that there were areas of shared interest, such as abolishing the euro. A number of figures from PiS and Confederation have also expressed hope that the AfD’s rise at the expense of establishment parties can herald a similar development in Poland, which, like Germany, is ruled by a pro-EU coalition ranging from centre-left to centre-right. Europa się budzi, a establishment wpada w panikę. Wynik AfD pokazuje, że ludzie mają dość dyktatu Brukseli, Zielonego Ładu i niszczenia państw narodowych przez nielegalną imigrację. Polityczne trzęsienie ziemi dopiero się zaczyna. Piękna, biała Europa narodów wkrótce powróci. — Włodzimierz Skalik (@Wlodek_Skalik) September 7, 2026 One party that has been unambiguously positive in its response to AfD’s victory is the Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), a radical-right, pro-Russian group that broke away from Confederation last year and is currently polling support of around 9% “Europe is waking up, and the establishment is falling into panic,” wrote KKP’s deputy leader, Włodzimierz Skalik, on social media. “A beautiful, white Europe of nations will soon return.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers.
