World.title: Robots “protest” in Warsaw to demand regulation of AI and automation
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Around 30 robots protested outside Poland’s digital affairs ministry on Monday, calling for tougher regulation of artificial intelligence and robotisation. The human organisers say there needs to be greater public debate over the impact of new technologies on the labour market. Digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski met with the demonstrators, telling them that his department is working on regulations. However, one of the organisers said that plans currently being discussed by parliament contain insufficient protection for workers. Around 30 robots joined a protest in front of Poland’s digital affairs ministry, calling for stronger AI regulations. The demonstration was organised by campaigners to spark debate on how AI and robots could replace workers. pic.twitter.com/QEbvchb2RS — Al Jazeera English (@AJEnglish) September 7, 2026 Standing in several rows, the robots waved Polish flags and chanted slogans such as “We want regulations, we want rules, we want law” and “Don’t wait, regulate, protect jobs”. The organisers, a group called Democratism, said the event was intended to highlight the need for debate and legislation before automation has a more profound impact on employment. “Some people will benefit from new opportunities, while others may need to retrain or adapt to completely different roles,” they wrote. Society needs to discuss “who is responsible for preparing people for these changes, how workers should be protected during the transition and how reskilling should work”. Democratism appears to have been launched shortly before the protest, with the announcement about the demonstration among the first material published on its social media accounts. The initiative was launched by Delta Robots, a company that rents robots for events. However, a website they have set up to gather support for greater debate over the impact of AI and robotisation has so far only obtained signatures from 61 people. Grzegorz Kuliś of Delta Robots admitted to news website Gazeta.pl that their “campaign also has public relations value” for the company. However, he added that, “even though we’re deploying robots, we’re also humans, and we have a whole host of concerns that, if we don’t regulate this, we’ll soon find ourselves in an unprecedented situation that no human being will be able to cope with”. “We are constantly debating the impact of migrants on our society, whilst the vast majority of ‘migrants’ will arrive either via undersea cables across the Atlantic in the form of AI agents, or as humanoid robots in shipping containers from China,” he warned. Gawkowski, who went out to address the organisers, said the ministry’s objectives were aligned with the protesters’ concerns. “People come first, and that is what matters most to us,” he said, quoted by broadcaster Eska. The minister also announced plans to establish a committee on AI development and safety as well as to introduce so-called sandboxes, where companies will be able to test AI solutions before deploying them more widely, reports local news website O!Polska. Kuliś, however, told Gazeta.pl that a draft law on AI systems currently being considered by the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament, contains too little practical protection for workers affected by automation. A Polish radio station that launched a channel run almost entirely by AI – including its presenters – has decided to end the project after less than a week The head of the station admitted they were "surprised by the level of emotion" the idea had caused https://t.co/9iMlRVamSF — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 28, 2024 The rapid development of AI and robotics has sparked debate around the world on how such technologies will impact humans, including to what extent and in what ways they will replace human labour. However, a number of recent reports have found that the impact of AI on jobs has so far been smaller than many previously predicted. Analysis by the Institute of Economic Policy Research at Stanford University, published in July, found that “AI’s effects on overall employment are likely small”. A further concern has been the prospect of AI “going rogue” by starting to act without or beyond human control. Those fears were strengthened after it emerged in July this year that some of OpenAI’s AI agents had autonomously hacked Hugging Face, another AI company. The incident prompted more than 100 companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Hugging Face, to sign an open letter calling on companies and governments to step up cybersecurity efforts amid emerging threats. A recent rise in unemployment in Poland has raised concern. But that headline figure does not tell the whole story, with experts arguing that the Polish labour market is actually in good shape, writes @AlicjaPtak4 https://t.co/Pk4y7BqGrs — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 24, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland wants the European Union to deny the right to asylum for migrants who cross EU borders in organised, aggressive groups, just as Poland has itself done on its border with Belarus. “This is about depriving people who illegally cross the border in organised groups, using violence or destroying border security measures, of the right to international protection,” Maciej Duszczyk, the deputy interior minister who oversees migration policy, told broadcaster RMF. Polska zabiega o to, by Unia Europejska przyjęła jej interpretację przepisów dotyczących ochrony międzynarodowej. „Chodzi o pozbawienie prawa do ochrony międzynarodowej osób, które nielegalnie przekraczają granicę w zorganizowanych grupach, z użyciem przemocy albo niszcząc… — Fakty RMF FM (@RMF24pl) September 6, 2026 The station reports that, at a meeting of the European Council next month, Poland will propose expanding the interpretation of article 33 of the United Nations’ Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees. That section outlines the principle of “refoulement”, under which states are barred from expelling or returning refugees to places where their life or freedom would be threatened. The article includes a clause saying that the principle does not apply if “there are reasonable grounds for regarding [a refugee] as a danger to the security of the country” in which they have arrived, or if they have a criminal conviction that makes them “a danger to the community of that country”. Poland wants that clause to be applied in situations where someone applies for asylum after being part of an organised and aggressive border crossing. Since last year, Poland has itself banned asylum claims from people who illegally cross the border from Belarus. Since 2021, the Belarusian authorities have encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants, mainly from Asia and Africa, to try to irregularly – and often aggressively – enter the EU. Poland’s asylum ban, which has exceptions for certain vulnerable categories of people, was introduced as a temporary measure in March 2025 but has been repeatedly renewed since then. Warsaw now wants a similar interpretation of international refugee law to be applied across the EU Its proposals come in the wake of July’s incident in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta, where tens of thousands of migrants irregularly entered from Morocco. Soon afterwards, Poland urged the EU to adopt tougher measures, including making migrants who enter the bloc illegally ineligible for obtaining residence rights. Prime Minister Donald Tusk was also one of 22 EU leaders who signed a letter expressing “serious concern” at the situation in Ceuta and warning that the EU “cannot allow uncontrolled mass border crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration, or other hybrid threats to create the impression that illegal entry…is possible”. After last week's migration crisis in Ceuta, Poland has called for tougher EU measures, including an automatic ban on residence for anyone who enters illegally. It pointed to its own experience of dealing with "weaponised" migration from Belarus https://t.co/2VHn5ZUJx7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 5, 2026 Poland has long argued that the situation on the Belarus border is an example of how migration has been “weaponised” by Russia and its allies to sow social discord in EU countries. In response, Poland has invested billions in strengthening physical and electronic barriers along the border, has deployed thousands of additional officers there (and granted them expanded rights to use firearms), and has banned asylum claims. In 2021, Poland recorded almost 40,000 attempted illegal crossings from Belarus, and the figure remained as high as 30,000 in 2025. However, in the first half of this year, only 235 attempted crossings were recorded, which the Polish government has hailed as evidence of the success of its tough measures. However, Poland’s human rights commission recently raised concern at how long the technically “temporary” asylum ban has been in place. Some Polish courts have also ruled that Polish border guards acted unlawfully when forcing migrants back into Belarus. The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98% Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Has Karol Nawrocki’s first year as Poland’s president been a success?
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Aleks Szczerbiak Poland’s right-wing president has been largely successful at transforming his office into an assertive centre of resistance to the liberal centrist-led government, frustrating its agenda through extensive use of constitutional powers. He has emerged as the leading unifying figure on the fragmented Polish right but faces new challenges moving towards the next election. Scuppering the government’s reform agenda Last month, Polish President Karol Nawrocki marked the first anniversary of his inauguration following a surprise victory in the May-June 2025 presidential election over Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski, the candidate of the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO), Poland’s main governing party since autumn 2023, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. A relatively unknown conservative historian and head of the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), a state historical research institute, Nawrocki ran formally as an independent but was backed by the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping. The election result represented a significant upset, ushering in a period of tense “cohabitation” between the Tusk government and a hostile president. The Polish presidency is not a day-to-day governing role, and in many respects largely ceremonial, but retains important constitutional powers. Karol Nawrocki has now issued more vetoes than any other president in Polish history Three vetoes on Thursday took his total to 37 in just ten months since taking office, surpassing the 35 issued by Aleksander Kwaśniewski during his ten years as president https://t.co/xf27K8Fyn6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 12, 2026 These include a legislative veto, which the government lacks the required three-fifths parliamentary majority to overturn, and the ability to suspend a piece of legislation coming into law by referring it to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK). Given that a majority of tribunal members were appointed under previous PiS-dominated parliaments, this also functioned as a de facto veto. As a result, Nawrocki was able to severely complicate the Tusk government’s plans to push through its legislative and elite replacement programme, notably efforts to roll back PiS’s judicial reforms. This, combined with the political authority that stemmed from Nawrocki’s strong electoral mandate, meant that the government faced continued resistance for the remainder of its term of office until the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027. An assertive presidency From the outset, Nawrocki has been a much more assertive president than his predecessor Andrzej Duda, leveraging his mandate to carve out a role as an active centre of resistance to the government. Although both presidents were PiS-aligned, during cohabitation with the Tusk administration, Duda used his powers more selectively and occasionally sought common ground. Nawrocki, by contrast, interpreted his strong electoral mandate as authorising a more confrontational approach. He has surrounded himself with a strong political support base who have helped him to develop and carry forward a blaze of independent initiatives in both the domestic and foreign policy spheres. As well proposing a series of his own draft laws, Nawrocki has used the legislative veto far more frequently than Duda (who issued only 19 across two full five-year terms) or any previous post-1989 president in a comparable period. By mid-2026, he had already surpassed previous records, blocking over 40 government-sponsored laws on issues such as judicial reform, socioeconomic policy and defence financing. In foreign policy, where the president’s formal competencies are more limited, Nawrocki pursued independent initiatives that often diverged from, or complicated, the government’s line. He has, for example, prioritised close personal and strategic ties with the USA, positioning Washington as Warsaw’s primary security guarantor. He cultivated a high-profile relationship with the Trump administration that yielded commitments to ongoing US troop deployments in Poland, sometimes bypassing or challenging the Tusk government. On Ukraine, while supporting continued military and diplomatic aid, Nawrocki has adopted a more transactional and assertive approach, opposing rapid Ukrainian EU and NATO accession until bilateral issues are addressed, and taking symbolic steps such as removing a Polish state honour from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky over unresolved historical grievances. Polish President Nawrocki has announced that he will strip @ZelenskyyUa of Poland’s highest honour in response to him naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles during WWII Ukraine's foreign minister condemned Nawrocki's "reckless" decision https://t.co/CEqj4aaHYg — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 These have drawn criticisms that he is playing into Russian hands by weakening regional unity, but were clearly in line with changing Polish public attitudes towards its eastern neighbour. Uniting the fragmented right? Nawrocki has also emerged as the most important unifying figure on the increasingly fragmented Polish right. PiS, long the hegemonic force on the conservative side, has seen radical-right challengers, the free-market Confederation (Konfederacja) and ultra-nationalist Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), gaining ground. In July, PiS also suffered its biggest ever internal split, with a significant group of parliamentarians aligned with former prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki breaking away. All of this weakened PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński’s once unquestioned authority as the central broker on the Polish right; he is now one leader among several. Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of Poland's largest opposition party, PiS, has called on President @NawrockiKn to help unify the country’s various right-wing opposition forces ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections https://t.co/Q3BFSOSfTG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 10, 2026 Alone among leading right-wing politicians, Nawrocki possesses genuine crossover appeal across the fractured conservative landscape. His 2025 presidential victory showed that he could consolidate a broad right-wing coalition and attract support well beyond traditional PiS loyalists, capturing the vast majority of voters from both Confederations. Although he was the PiS candidate, Nawrocki operates as an independent authority outside of direct party control and has cultivated an image as an authoritative independent figure, which gives him greater moral and symbolic stature than any partisan leader. Nawrocki’s assertive use of his constitutional powers has further reinforced his position as a natural focal point around which the broader right can unite. Many conservatives now look to him as a potential patron or broker ahead of the 2027 election. Nawrocki can use the presidency to set a broad conservative agenda and mediate negotiations among the various right-wing groupings to secure pre- and post-election agreements. However, he has no unifying mandate and his ability to bring together the right depends ultimately on whether the various actors are willing to be led. Moreover, not only is the president expected to remain formally non-partisan and not engage too openly in day-to-day politics, Nawrocki lacks the party organisational levers needed to enforce messy backroom deals. Focus of government attacks The Tusk government knows that Nawrocki’s is now the most potent counterweight to its authority and potential unifier of the fragmented right, which is precisely why he has become the main focus of its attacks on the opposition. An essential element of this has been trying to portray Nawrocki’s more active presidency as destructive and undermining the unity of the Polish state. This forms a principal component of its broader “security” narrative, a calculated strategy to reframe political debate around the ongoing Russian threat. At a time of heightened geopolitical risk with hybrid threats against Poland, the government has portrayed presidential obstruction as undermining the country’s military readiness and ability to co-ordinate with its allies. Karol Nawrocki has sought to redefine Poland's presidency and become the figurehead of the right-wing opposition. So far, it is working, but questions remain over what his end goal is and whether these tactics will get him there, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/TNDRGGv2QT — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 22, 2025 The Tusk administration cites Nawrocki’s veto of legislation enabling Poland to access its €43.7 billion allocation from the EU’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) defence procurement initiative as an apparently perfect example of this, although the president argues that the loans saddle future generations with a huge, long-term debt and undermine Polish sovereignty. In fact, Nawrocki is fairly relaxed about the government’s attempts to portray his more active presidency as obstructive. Rather, he feels he needs to be assertive because that is precisely what those who voted for him expect: action and change, not passivity or compromise. Nawrocki’s 2025 presidential victory was based on a sharp critique of the Tusk administration and framed, and widely interpreted, as a vote of no confidence in the government’s performance. The president believes that this gives him a strong mandate to confront the ruling coalition across a wide range of issues and that the greater political risk lies in undermining the political momentum that his win created and appearing weak or inactive, rather than in the government’s counternarrative that he is a “blocking” president. A clash between the right-wing president and more liberal government over Poland's receipt of EU defence loans has sharpened polarisation and turbocharged the ruling coalition’s “Polexit” and security narratives, writes @AleksSzczerbiak https://t.co/Iu7rcJfj5e — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 2, 2026 More broadly, Nawrocki is not too concerned about what the Warsaw opinion-forming elites say about him. His approach stands in stark contrast to earlier presidents, even right-wing ones such as Duda, who, conservative critics argue, paid excessive attention to elite and liberal media criticism and received no meaningful political reward or pay-off for doing so. Instead of seeking to present himself as a “president of all Poles” in the traditional, consensus-seeking sense, Nawrocki has deliberately prioritised appealing directly to his core electoral base: Polish voters living beyond the large urban agglomerations in smaller towns, rural areas, and the provinces. By maintaining an assertive, unapologetic style that resonates with this electorate’s sense of cultural and political marginalisation, Nawrocki has sought to consolidate that support rather than diluting it in pursuit of metropolitan elite approval. Poland’s most popular politician There have obviously been plenty of missteps along the way. One clear risk has been the sheer volume and sometimes seemingly indiscriminate nature of the legislative vetoes. While this has successfully blocked key elements of the government’s agenda and reinforced Nawrocki’s image as an assertive counterweight, it has also handed the Tusk administration a ready-made narrative that the president is simply an obstructive “veto machine”. A number of Nawrocki’s more high-profile vetoes, such as the cryptocurrency regulation law, have proved highly contentious. PM @donaldtusk called a classified meeting of parliament in a bid to persuade opposition MPs to overturn the president's veto of crypto-asset regulation, which Tusk said threatens national security. However, in a subsequent vote, the veto was upheld https://t.co/Vj0Zh9wxpH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 5, 2025 Moreover, some of the other constitutional instruments that he has sought to utilise have not been particularly successful or even proved counterproductive. These include attempts to introduce his own legislation or referendum initiatives that have been stymied in parliament, as well as his original idea of holding the government to account via the so-called “Cabinet Council”, a formal meeting of the Council of Ministers chaired by the president. Nonetheless, in general, Nawrocki’s strategy appears to have delivered political dividends for him. He can, for example, point to a number of foreign policy successes, particularly in cultivating close personal and strategic ties with the USA under the Trump administration and positioning himself as a significant actor on security issues. President @NawrockiKn has recorded the highest ever level of trust (54.8%, up 8.4pp since May) of any politician in the history of regular polling by @IBRiS_PL for @onetpl Foreign minister @sikorskiradek (42.6%) was second and PM @donaldtusk (38.1%) third https://t.co/POuUFR3Khk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 26, 2026 At the same time, Nawrocki has asserted a greater degree of independence from PiS than Duda was ever able to achieve. This has been helped by the simple fact that PiS is now in opposition rather than in government, which reduces the formal and informal constraints that tied his predecessor more closely to the party. As a result, Nawrocki has emerged as Poland’s most popular politician, with consistently high approval ratings that set him apart from both the government and right-wing opposition party leaders. Challenges ahead There are clear challenges ahead for Nawrocki in the run-up to next year’s election and beyond. The first is how to respond to the argument that electing a right-wing government would concentrate excessive power in one side of the political spectrum. This is an awkward point for Nawrocki because he himself used a version of this argument during the 2025 presidential campaign, presenting his candidacy as a necessary check on the Tusk government. Opponents of the right will inevitably turn this logic against the broader conservative camp in the run-up to the 2027 election, claiming that the combination of a sympathetic president and a right-wing parliamentary majority risks the very imbalance Nawrocki once warned against. A second, related strategic challenge arises if a right-wing government does take office, and Nawrocki finds himself cohabiting with an ideologically and programmatically aligned administration rather than a hostile one. In that situation, he would still need to carve out a distinct and independent role for himself. The risk is falling into the trap that afflicted Duda during the years of PiS government: being widely perceived as little more than the government’s “notary” or a passive rubber stamp for its agenda. Maintaining personal authority, visibility, and a sense of autonomy, while avoiding conflict with an ideologically allied government, would demand a different style of presidency from the approach that has defined his first year. The very assertiveness and independence that have served him well in cohabitation with the Tusk government will prove harder to sustain if the political balance shifts after 2027. However, the response from the Polish right to the election result has so far been relatively muted. The rise of the AfD has been watched with concern by many in Poland due to the party’s attempts to downplay the significance of Germany’s Nazi history and its sympathy towards Russia. The victory continues a recent rise for the AfD, which also came first in the Thuringian state election in 2024, with 33% of the vote, and second in the federal elections of 2025, with 21%, making it the main national opposition party. The AfD’s latest result was welcomed by some figures from Poland’s right-wing and far-right opposition. “Germany is waking up,” tweeted Jacek Wilk, a former member of Poland’s parliament who is part of the radical-right Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party. World.title: Prague’s Petřín Funicular to Return to Service on September 22
World.content:
Prague’s Petřín funicular will resume passenger service on Tuesday, September 22, 2026, following a two-year reconstruction of the railway and its infrastructure, the Prague Public Transit Company (DPP) has announced.

Service will begin at 7 a.m., with the new fourth-generation cars departing from both Újezd and Petřín stations.

Trains will then run according to the regular timetable, with departures every 10 minutes until 10:15 p.m.



The reopening comes almost exactly two years after the previous funicular was taken out of service. The third-generation cars made their final journey on September 13, 2024, after prolonged heavy rainfall destabilized and eroded sections of the hillside.

New cars increase capacity

The two new cars were designed by Czech designer Anna Marešová and built by Swiss manufacturer CWA Constructions SA. The vehicles cost a combined CZK 137.7 million and were delivered to Prague in April.

Each car can carry up to 120 passengers, compared with a capacity of 100 on the previous vehicles. The design also introduces glass roofs, giving passengers a clearer view of Petřín Hill during the journey.

Air conditioning, however, will not be installed. Because of technical limitations, the cars will instead use forced-air ventilation. The decision has already drawn criticism from some Prague residents, who have questioned how comfortable the cars will be during hot summer days, particularly given their large glass roofs.

The two-year reconstruction involved more than replacing the vehicles. Workers strengthened the foundations beneath the track, installed new rails and upgraded the funicular’s traction system.

How much will the new funicular cost?

A single journey will cost CZK 100 when purchased on site. Passengers using the PID Lítačka mobile application will pay CZK 90.

Passengers with valid long-term Prague public transport passes covering one month to one year will continue to ride without paying an additional fare.

The same applies to holders of 24-hour and 72-hour passes, children under 15 and passengers aged over 65.

World.title: Prague Botanical Garden to Host Grape Harvest Festival
World.content:
The Prague Botanical Garden will host its traditional grape harvest festival at St. Clare’s Vineyard on September 12 and 13, bringing two days of wine, fresh burčák, live music and activities for visitors.

The festival, known as Vinobraní na Vinici sv. Kláry, will feature wines from producers across the Czech Republic, Moravia and other countries.

Visitors will also have the chance to taste white and red burčák made from grapes harvested this year at St. Clare’s Vineyard.



The first grapes for the festival have already been picked by hand. Workers harvested 2,700 kilograms of table grapes and the Modrý Portugal variety. The grapes are now being used to produce this year’s burčák, a young wine that is still undergoing fermentation and is traditionally associated with the Czech grape harvest season.

Alongside wines from the St. Clare’s winery, the festival will present a selection of wines from other producers from the Czech Republic, Moravia and abroad.

Two days of live music

Music will be a major part of the weekend program. Saturday’s main stage lineup includes Jordan Haj and Emma Smetana, YES BROTHERS and 20 MINUTES.

On Sunday, visitors can see the Děda Mládek Illegal Band, BRASS AVENUE, MOVEBREAKERS and OFF BEAT ORCHESTRA. A second music stage will also operate near the St. Clare’s wine shop.

The festival program includes more than music and wine. Visitors can join guided tours of the vineyard, take part in workshops and creative activities, or attend the Vínohrátky educational program. The guided tours are included in the admission price.

The event will run from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. on both September 12 and 13. Activities will take place at St. Clare’s Vineyard and in the Ornamental Garden of the Prague Botanical Garden.

Tickets bought at the venue cost CZK 280 for adults and CZK 180 for children and young people aged 3 to 17.

Online tickets purchased by September 11 are CZK 250 for adults and CZK 150 for children and young people. Children under three can enter free of charge.

World.title: September 28 Holiday in Czechia: What Will Be Open and Closed
World.content:
Czech Statehood Day falls on Monday, September 28, giving people across Czechia a three-day weekend. But anyone planning to shop should be aware that many large stores will be required to close.

The public holiday commemorates Saint Wenceslas, the patron saint of the Czech lands and one of the most important figures in Czech history. September 28 has been observed as Czech Statehood Day since 2000 and is a statutory day off.



For shoppers, however, the key issue is the country’s restrictions on retail opening hours.

Which shops will be closed on September 28

Under Czech law, shops with a sales area of more than 200 square metres must close on September 28.

This means most large supermarkets, hypermarkets and shopping centres will not be able to operate as normal.

The restriction does not apply to all businesses. Smaller shops with a sales area of up to 200 square metres can remain open, although individual owners decide whether to operate during the holiday.

Some types of businesses are also exempt from the restrictions. These include pharmacies, petrol stations and shops located at airports and major railway stations.

Restaurants, cafés and most other services are not covered by the retail law and can therefore open according to their normal schedules or the decision of their operators.

People planning to use smaller independent shops should still check opening hours in advance. Many owners choose to close during public holidays, particularly when the holiday creates a long weekend.

Why is September 28 a public holiday

Czech Statehood Day is linked to Saint Wenceslas, the medieval ruler who became the patron saint of the Czech lands.

Wenceslas was the son of Duke Vratislav I and Drahomíra. His grandmother, Ludmila, who was later canonised, played a major role in his upbringing and is traditionally credited with influencing his Christian education.

Wenceslas is believed to have been killed in Stará Boleslav on September 28, either in 929 or 935, depending on the historical source.

His death turned him into a martyr and helped establish his lasting importance in Czech religious and national traditions.

World.title: September 19: Celebrate South Africa’s Heritage Braai Day in Prague
World.content:
On Saturday, 19 September, Prague’s Rohan Beer Garden will host Heritage Braai Day, bringing the flavors and traditions of South Africa to the city.

The event is organized by Saffa Maso.



From noon, visitors can enjoy a relaxed day of grilling, music and socializing outdoors.

Heritage Day in South Africa is a public holiday celebrating the country’s cultural diversity. It has also become closely associated with the tradition of braai, or South African-style barbecuing, with friends and family gathering around the grill to share food.

In Prague, the event is open to everyone and will feature multiple grills, allowing visitors to prepare their own food. Those who prefer to leave the cooking to someone else can use the on-site grill master service, available for an additional fee.

Standard tickets include grills, coals and all braai equipment. Visitors can can buy a basic ticket or a ticket with a braai package, which includes traditional South African boerewors sausage (500g) and a portion of biltong (150g).

On-site you’ll also find original Nando’s sauces, chutney, braai spices, and more for sale.

Visitors should not bring their own drinks, as a selection of alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages will be available at the venue. Guests should bring their own plates and cutlery, although disposable options are also allowed.

World.title: Prague Unemployment Reaches 4% with 40,509 Job Seekers
World.content:
Unemployment in Prague rises to 4% at the end of August, with 40,509 people registered as job seekers at the Labour Office.

The figure was 2.1% higher than in July and 15.7% higher than a year earlier.

Despite the increase, Prague continued to record the lowest unemployment rate among Czechia’s regions. The national unemployment rate stood at 5% at the end of August.



More people registered as job seekers

A total of 5,368 people registered with the Prague Labour Office in August. That was 133 fewer than in July but 1,033 more than in August 2025.

At the end of August, Prague had 37,811 people considered reachable for employment. This category covers people aged 15 to 64 who are not temporarily unable to work and are not taking part in retraining.

The number of reachable job seekers increased by 822 compared with July and by 5,475 compared with the same month last year.

Women accounted for 55.2% of all registered job seekers, with 22,378 women listed in the Labour Office records.

More than 22,000 vacancies remain available

Employers in Prague had 22,519 registered vacancies at the end of August. That was 708 fewer positions than in July and 565 fewer than a year earlier.

There were an average of 1.8 registered job seekers for every vacancy.

Of the total number of registered vacancies, 1,676 were not marked as positions available to foreign workers. Employers could recruit workers from abroad for a further 20,843 positions.

Construction, accommodation and food services, and wholesale and retail were among the sectors with the largest number of vacancies.

World.title: AIGEL to Celebrate 10th Anniversary with Prague Concert
World.content:
On October 21, electronic duo AIGEL will perform at Futurum Music Bar in Prague as part of a special concert marking the band’s 10th anniversary.

AIGEL was formed by Tatar poet and singer Aigel Gaisina and St. Petersburg producer Ilya Baramiya. Over the past decade, the duo has developed a distinctive sound combining electronic music, trip-hop and psychedelic influences.

Get your ticket here

Their music crosses linguistic and cultural boundaries, with songs performed in Russian, Tatar, English and German.

AIGEL gained international attention with the viral tracks “Tatarin” and “Pyyala.” The latter topped streaming charts in 25 countries and reached No. 1 on the global Shazam chart.

Over 10 years, the duo has released five albums and dozens of singles. They have also received a Cannes Lion for the music video “You’re Born” and toured extensively across Europe and beyond.

Now based in Europe, AIGEL is preparing a special anniversary show in Prague, combining the duo’s electronic sound with Gaisina’s distinctive and expressive vocals.

The concert will take place on October 21 at Futurum Music Bar.

World.title: Prague to Add 51 New Trams Next Year as Network Expands
World.content:
Prague is set to receive 51 new trams next year as the city expands its tram network and begins replacing some of its oldest vehicles.

The Prague Public Transport Company (DPP) has ordered another 25 Škoda 52T trams under an existing framework agreement with Škoda Transportation.

Each tram costs CZK 82.5 million, including CZK 40 million in European subsidies. Prague has now committed to buying 71 of the new vehicles in three separate orders.



The first 20 Škoda 52T trams entered regular service in Prague last year. Another batch is being delivered this year, while the latest orders will continue into 2027.

The newest order for 25 additional trams is due to be completed by December 3 next year.

The new vehicles are needed not only because Prague is building new tram lines but also because the existing fleet needs to be renewed. Some of the oldest trams still in operation are the T3M models, while a large part of the fleet consists of reconstructed T3R.P and T3R.PV vehicles and their derivatives.

Replacing older models with a smaller number of standardised tram types should also reduce maintenance and servicing costs, according to the deputy mayor. The new trams are expected to remain in service for around 20 to 30 years, compared with approximately 15 years for buses.

The Škoda 52T is 32 metres long and 2.5 metres wide and can carry up to 243 passengers. Of these, 173 can travel standing. The tram therefore offers almost 16 percent more capacity than Prague’s Škoda 15T trams.

The maximum operating speed is 70 kilometres per hour.

The 52T was designed specifically for Prague’s tram network, including sections with narrow and sharply curved tracks. This allows the vehicles to operate on existing routes without requiring major changes to the infrastructure.

World.title: Prague Castle to Celebrate Václav Havel With Four-Month Festival
World.content:
Prague Castle will host a four-month festival celebrating the legacy of Václav Havel, with theatre, film, music, design and public debates taking place from October through January.

The Havel ALIVE festival will mark what would have been Havel’s 90th birthday and explore the continued relevance of his ideas. Most events will be free.

One of the main highlights will be the Czech premiere of The Warning, an unfinished Havel play that remained hidden for almost 40 years. The manuscript was discovered by David Dušek among the papers of writer Zdeněk Urbánek.



The production has been prepared by Jiří Havelka, artistic director of Dejvické Theatre, and will feature actors Martin Myšička and Ivan Trojan. The theatre will also present We’ll Start It Tomorrow, or Who’s the Gentleman Here at Prague Castle’s Riding Hall.

The festival will also focus on Havel’s influence on Czech design. In cooperation with Designblok, Prague Castle will present Design for Václav Havel, featuring objects connected with his presidency, including Bořek Šípek’s Olga chair, original glass pieces and Castle Guard uniforms designed by Theodor Pištěk.

For the first time, the exhibition will also show the entire presidential office, including Havel’s library. It will open during Designblok on October 7 and remain at the Riding Hall from October 21 to January 17.

Music and dance will feature prominently as well. On November 18, students and teachers from the Academy of Performing Arts in Prague will present a gala evening directed by Magdalena Švecová. Other performances will draw on Havel’s writings, his Anticodes poetry collection, his relationship with the underground music scene and the events of November 1989.

The programme will also include screenings of Citizen Havel and Leaving, a musical evening led by Pavel Klusák, and discussions about art, architecture, freedom and democracy.

Selected festival events

October 4 — Guided tours of Lány Chateau and Prague Castle focused on Havel’s presidency. Free.

October 7 — Opening of Design for Václav Havel at the Prague Castle Riding Hall.

October 8 — Pavel Klusák’s All the President’s Rockers: Václav Havel & Music. Free.

October 14 — Citizen Havel screening followed by a discussion. Free.

October 22 — Thinking Havel Live: Democracy and the Future of Europe. Free.

November 4 — Dejvické Theatre presents We’ll Start It Tomorrow, or Who’s the Gentleman Here. Tickets CZK 390–490.

November 5–6 — Czech premieres of Havel’s The Warning. Tickets CZK 390–490.

November 12 — Thinking Havel: Between the Individual and the System. Free.

November 18 — Havel: Inspiration for a New Generation, a gala evening at the Prague Castle Riding Hall from 7 p.m. Tickets CZK 250.

November 26 — Lecture on Havel’s designer and architect Bořek Šípek at the Supreme Burgrave’s Office from 5 p.m. Free.

December 3 — Thinking Havel: Politics and Spiritual Values, a debate with Alice Koubová, Milena Bartlová and Petr Kratochvíl at the Riding Hall from 6 p.m. Free.

December 8 — Literature at the Castle: Writing Havel, a lecture at the Supreme Burgrave’s Office from 5 p.m. Free.

December 15 — Screening of Leaving, followed by a discussion with Dagmar Havlová and other guests at the Supreme Burgrave’s Office from 6 p.m. Free.

January 14 — Ceremonial presentation of the Jindřich Chalupecký Award 2027 at Prague Castle.

World.title: Erasmus in Hungary ‘bleeding from multiple wounds’, student body warns
World.content:
The return of the Erasmus programme is to be welcomed, but it is not enough on its own: the scheme remains out of reach for many students for a variety of reasons, the National Conference of Student Unions (HÖOK) said on Facebook on Wednesday.

HÖOK’s position on the revived scheme

The student organisation described the reappearance of the Erasmus scholarship call as “an important and long-awaited step”. Yet it stressed that the programme offers far more than a semester abroad: it provides professional, linguistic and personal experiences that shape students’ studies and future opportunities, and strengthen Hungarian higher education in the long term.Even before the pandemic or the recent suspension of Erasmus, participation from Hungary had been exceptionally low. In the 2017–18 academic year, only 1.5 per cent of students undertook any form of study abroad, HÖOK noted according to the MTI.

Barriers to mobility

According to HÖOK, several factors are keeping participation down:

Credit recognition: A large proportion of credits earned abroad are not accepted by Hungarian universities, forcing many students to repeat a year and delaying their progress.

A large proportion of credits earned abroad are not accepted by Hungarian universities, forcing many students to repeat a year and delaying their progress. Language preparation: Students need language skills robust enough for academic and everyday life in another country. HÖOK argued that public education should lay these foundations, with teaching aimed not merely at school-leaving exams or language certificates, but at confident functioning in foreign academic and cultural settings.

Students need language skills robust enough for academic and everyday life in another country. HÖOK argued that public education should lay these foundations, with teaching aimed not merely at school-leaving exams or language certificates, but at confident functioning in foreign academic and cultural settings. Funding gaps: While the Erasmus grant is valuable, it often falls short of covering the true cost of a semester abroad. In more expensive university cities, the allowance may not even cover accommodation, and not every student can top it up from personal resources, even if working alongside their studies.“Mobility is needed in which students know their foreign credits will be recognised, and where the scholarship offers support in practice, not just on paper,” HÖOK said.

If you missed: Erasmus returns to Hungary – Hungarian university students can once again study abroad!

Government announcement and EU background

Last week, Judit Lannert, the Minister for Education and Children’s Affairs, announced that the Erasmus programme would once again be available to Hungarian students. She said all 21 universities previously affected by restrictions now hold valid Erasmus mobility applications for the 2026–27 academic year.The restrictions date to 2022, when the Council of the European Union ruled that higher education institutions placed under public-interest asset-management foundations could not conclude new Erasmus contracts, citing conflicts of interest and transparency concerns. The current government’s agreement with the EU, including commitments to reform the foundation model by 2027, paved the way for the programme’s return this autumn.

World.title: How former PM Orbán’s ex-secretary informed media about the shady businesses and was threatened with his kids
World.content:
Vilmos Vályi-Nagy, a former state secretary in Viktor Orbán’s government between 2010 and 2014 and one of investigative journalism’s most relied-upon informants over the past decade, has broken his silence in an interview with Partizan. Published on Wednesday, the wide-ranging conversation covers the former interior minister Sándor Pintér, István Tiborcz, the prime minister’s son-in-law, as well as the Microsoft procurement scandal and the long-dormant Eclipse affair.

A whistleblower steps forward

Partizán said on its YouTube channel on Wednesday evening that Vályi-Nagy, whom it described as perhaps the single most helpful source to the media in serious cases, had approached the outlet himself to tell his story on the record, face and name included, the Hungarian News Agency wrote.

Vályi-Nagy began his career at the tax and customs authority’s predecessor, the National Command of the Customs and Finance Guard (VPOP), first as IT director and later as deputy chief commander. At the National Development Ministry from 2010, initially as deputy state secretary and from 2012 as state secretary, his principal brief was to extend the VPOP’s procurement and IT practices across the entire state sector.

Ex-secretary Vilmos Vályi-Nagy, one of the most important informants of the Hungarian media about the shady businesses of the government. Source: PrtScr/Youtube

The Microsoft row

At one point, the state secretary met resistance to his drive to rationalise government IT, including from Microsoft, which the programme said was unhappy at the prospect of shrinking state orders. In 2019, OLAF, the European anti-fraud office, and the US Securities and Exchange Commission uncovered that Microsoft resellers had made huge sums through corrupt public procurement of the company’s software in dealings with the Hungarian state. Intermediary companies negotiated down the price of bulk-bought Office licences and “pocketed” the discount; Microsoft was fined in the United States, but no one was held to account in Hungary, the programme said.

Vályi-Nagy said that as early as 2011, alongside cutting licence fees, his team had been working to introduce open-source software across public administration. He alleged that János Lázár, “without our knowledge, support or approval”, reallocated billions of forints from an IT project to buy Microsoft licences. The licence package, he said, was almost twice the market rate; after his intervention the public procurement procedure was cancelled, saving the state one billion forints.

Orbán suffered a historic defeat this April. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Viktor

“You will pay a heavy price”

Valyi-Nagy said this was the first time he felt he had hurt a powerful interest. According to his account, Ferenc Vágujhelyi, then deputy head of the tax authority, told him he would “pay a heavy price”. The prime minister later affirmed that he had done the right thing, he said, but as a consequence he was given no role in the new government formed in 2014. He suspected that Humansoft, the IT company that lost out when the deal was scrapped, had manoeuvred to have him pushed out.

The accusation levelled at him was that he had taken 50 million forints in the Microsoft case. The decision, he said, was taken at a lunch with the Orbán family, and István Tiborcz, the prime minister’s son-in-law, fed information to the public. Later in the programme it emerged that he had subsequently learned from Zsuzsanna Németh, the development minister, that “István Tiborcz had lobbied Orbán”.

Ráhel Orbán, the eldest daugher of Viktor Orbán and his husband, one of the wealthiest Hungarians, István Tiborcz. Photo: Instagram/Ráhel Orbán

During his time as state secretary, numerous other state secretaries, institution heads and even ministers contacted him to complain about “unbearable” family members and oligarchs who were “bleeding the Hungarian state dry”, and who “knew exactly what was going on, but either did not dare, or were unable, or did not want to do anything about it”, he said.

The Eclipse affair and fallout

The programme also examined the Eclipse affair, in which the state spent billions developing software to record the authenticity of cars that was never delivered. Valyi-Nagy said he had come into conflict with Sándor Pintér, the interior minister, over the Eclipse case.From 2014 onwards, he said, he was under surveillance for a long period, received threats, and false data about him were recorded in the files of the Constitutional Protection Office.

Hungary releases classified government decisions from the past 16 years

Orbán and Pintér (r)

After the Eclipse affair, “dozens were fired” at VPOP who had worked on the case, and such punishments had been a recurring element of Fidesz’s personnel policy since 2010, he added.“I have seen many ministerial changes where, after the minister was fired, the state secretaries, deputies, department heads and their people were sacked to the last man … this has happened even in the last two years, in connection with the restructuring and merger of the finance ministry and the economy ministry,” he said.

World.title: Budapest house price growth slows dramatically – Why this could be good news for buyers
World.content:
The rapid rise in Budapest property prices appears to be losing steam. Annual house price growth in the capital has slowed to just 6.7%, down from 21% a year ago, while prices edged down slightly in August compared with July. Experts say the trend could make the market more favourable for buyers.

Budapest property boom loses momentum

Hungary’s housing market is showing increasingly clear signs of a slowdown, with Budapest experiencing the sharpest change. According to fresh analysis by property website ingatlan.com, annual house price growth in the capital fell to 6.7% in August, less than one-third of the 21% annual growth recorded a year earlier.

The latest monthly figures are even more striking. While property prices across Hungary rose by 0.6% between July and August, prices in Budapest fell by 0.1%. The change does not mean that Budapest homes are suddenly becoming significantly cheaper. Rather, it suggests that the rapid price increases seen over the past year have largely run their course.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

‘Sawtooth’ stagnation on the housing market

According to László Balogh, economic expert at ingatlan.com, the Hungarian housing market has entered a period of what he describes as a kind of “sawtooth stagnation”. Prices rise slightly one month, only to partially correct the following month. As a result, the overall price level is barely changing from month to month.

“The most important consequence is that annual house price growth is continuously slowing, which buyers and sellers are already beginning to feel,” Balogh said.

For buyers, this could represent a significant change after a period in which rapidly rising prices created pressure to make decisions quickly.

With prices now showing little month-to-month movement, prospective buyers may have more time to compare properties, negotiate and consider their options rather than feeling compelled to rush before prices rise further.

If you missed it: Hungary’s housing market faces a major shift as government backs social housing

Budapest still remains extremely expensive

Despite the slowdown, Budapest property prices remain high by Hungarian standards. At the beginning of September, the median price per square metre for second-hand flats and houses in the capital stood at around HUF 1.41 million, virtually unchanged from August.

There are also enormous differences between districts. The most expensive parts of Budapest remain Districts I, II, XII and V, where median prices range from approximately HUF 1.77 million to HUF 2.03 million per square metre.

At the other end of the scale, Soroksár remains the capital’s most affordable district, with a median price of around HUF 949,000 per square metre. This means that even with the slowdown, buying a home in many parts of Budapest remains a major financial commitment.

Northern and eastern Hungary still seeing double-digit growth

The slowdown is not affecting every part of the country equally. In fact, some regions are still experiencing considerably stronger annual price growth than the national average. Property prices in the Northern Great Plain rose by 15.3% year-on-year, while Northern Hungary recorded a 15.2% increase.

The pattern suggests that areas where property prices started from relatively lower levels are still catching up with more expensive parts of the country. Among county capitals, Debrecen remains the most expensive, with a median price of HUF 1.04 million per square metre for second-hand residential properties.

At the other end of the scale, Salgótarján remains the cheapest county capital, with a median price of just HUF 309,000 per square metre.

Buyers could finally get some breathing room

The slowdown could gradually improve housing affordability, according to Balogh. Two factors could work in buyers’ favour: rising incomes and a continued moderation in property price growth. After the sharp increases seen in recent years, even a period of relatively stable prices could make it easier for household incomes to catch up.

The current, more subdued pace of the housing market could also continue into 2027, Balogh believes. After around 150,000 property transactions last year, he expects approximately 130,000–140,000 transactions both this year and in 2027.

For prospective buyers, that points towards a very different housing market from the one seen during the recent price surge. Instead of racing against rapidly rising prices, buyers may increasingly find themselves in a position to take their time, and potentially negotiate better deals.

World.title: Hungary has a record number of foreign workers – now businesses want the government to ease the rules
World.content:
The number of foreign workers in Hungary reached an all-time high just before the government tightened its guest-worker rules. Now, tourism industry organisations are calling for more flexible regulations as businesses continue to struggle with labour shortages.

The number of foreign workers in Hungary surged to a record 112,300 in June, according to data cited by Portfolio, just as the new government was preparing to significantly restrict the employment of workers from outside the European Union.

The figure represents the highest number of foreign workers ever recorded in Hungary and highlights just how heavily parts of the Hungarian economy had come to rely on international labour.

The increase continued even after the April election. Foreign-worker numbers rose by around 2,000 in May and by another 1,500 in June, suggesting that companies continued bringing in workers from abroad in the final weeks before the new restrictions took effect.

Hungary tightens guest-worker rules

The government announced the tightening of the guest-worker system on 5 June, with the new rules taking effect the following day. Under the changes, citizens of several countries — including the Philippines, Georgia and Armenia — could no longer benefit from previously available fast-track arrangements for guest-worker employment.

As a result, bringing workers from outside the EU to Hungary became more complicated and, in some cases, more expensive.

However, the overall rise in foreign employment cannot necessarily be attributed solely to the traditional guest-worker system. Hungary’s immigration framework has become increasingly complex since reforms introduced in 2024. Employers can use several other residence and employment routes, including the National Card, Hungarian Card and EU Blue Card, as well as certain permits connected to investment projects.

This means that the number of foreign workers in Hungary cannot be fully understood simply by looking at the number of guest-worker permits.

In 2025, for example, authorities received 21,211 applications for residence permits for employment purposes, compared with 15,395 applications for National Cards and 15,307 for guest-worker residence permits. In other words, companies have had to navigate different legal routes to recruit workers from abroad.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Tourism businesses warn of labour shortages

The issue is particularly important for Hungary’s tourism and hospitality sector, where foreign workers have become a significant part of the labour supply. Five major tourism industry organisations have called for changes to the government’s approach, arguing that Hungary needs a more predictable and flexible labour market, Portfolio writes.

The organisations — representing inbound tourism, travel agencies, hotels, restaurants, events and tourism employers — submitted a joint package of proposals to the Hungarian Tourism Agency. Among their key demands is more flexible regulation governing workers from third countries.

They argue that employers need greater flexibility, particularly in sectors where finding enough Hungarian workers remains difficult. At the same time, they support strengthening domestic training and improving cooperation between educational institutions and tourism businesses. The proposals also include reducing administrative burdens and making employment rules more predictable so businesses can plan ahead.

If you missed it: What is the fate of foreign workers in Hungary? Serious dilemma amid labour shortage

Foreign workers could remain crucial despite restrictions

The tourism industry’s demands come as Hungary is moving in the opposite direction on guest-worker policy. The new government’s approach is to restrict the inflow of non-EU workers, while businesses are warning that they still need access to international labour.

The tension is particularly visible in hospitality, where hotels, restaurants and tourism companies often face seasonal fluctuations and difficulties recruiting sufficient staff. The industry groups have therefore called for a system that would allow employers to respond more flexibly to genuine labour-market needs while also strengthening domestic workforce development.

They are also seeking changes to taxation and employment rules, including a review of VAT regulations, the tourism development contribution and other administrative burdens. One particularly interesting proposal is the introduction of a hotel service charge, similar to the system already used in Hungary’s hospitality sector. According to the organisations, this could help improve employees’ incomes and make it easier for businesses to retain staff.

A balancing act for Hungary’s new government

The record June figure illustrates the scale of Hungary’s dependence on foreign labour: more than 112,000 foreign workers were employed in the country at the peak of the previous system. The challenge for the new government will be finding a balance between its pledge to restrict the recruitment of workers from outside the EU and the needs of employers in sectors facing labour shortages.

World.title: Buying rural property as a foreigner: The legal map all foreign buyers in Hungary should know
World.content:
For foreign buyers in Hungary, the question appears simple: can I buy this property? In the rural property market, however, the answer is rarely straightforward. It depends on precisely what the buyer intends to acquire, the buyer’s nationality and the legal structure through which the purchase is proposed. My earlier articles examined the structure of the premium Lake Balaton market and the pitfalls of zártkert property. This article completes the picture: it provides the legal map showing which rural properties a foreign buyer may acquire in Hungary, and under what conditions.

Author: Emese Széll, Private Real Estate Advisor to Premium Clients in Hungary

The first question: what is the property in legal terms?

Hungarian law does not treat all rural properties alike. The following three groups provide a useful practical starting point, but they are not separate statutory categories. In every case, the land-use category or non-agricultural (“kivett”) designation recorded on the land-registry title sheet, the property’s location status, the legal status of any building and the applicable local planning rules together determine which acquisition rules apply.

The first group comprises residential or holiday property that does not qualify as agricultural or forestry land. If the title sheet records, for example, “kivett lakóház, udvar” (non-agricultural residential house and yard), “lakás” (apartment) or another non-agricultural designation, the acquisition restrictions in the Land Transaction Act generally do not apply. Nationals of EU and EEA Member States, and persons accorded equivalent treatment under an international treaty, may generally acquire such property without authorisation. Other foreign natural persons who are subject to the authorisation requirement generally need the approval of the Government Office of the Capital City Budapest or the competent county government office. This is usually the simplest category.

The second group is zártkert property. Under the current land-registration rules, zártkert is a special type of outlying-area land unit, but the word “zártkert” does not in itself determine whether the Land Transaction Act applies. If the property is registered under an agricultural or forestry land-use category, the Act applies. If, under a municipal decree, it has been registered as land exempt from cultivation through the procedure in Section 72/E of the Land Registry Act, its treatment under the land transaction rules may be different. Its permitted use under the local building regulations (HÉSZ) and the legal status of any building must also be examined separately. This is an area in which the wording of a property  can be particularly misleading.

The third group is agricultural and forestry land as defined by the Land Transaction Act. This may include not only arable land, meadow, pasture and forest, but also vineyards, gardens and orchards, irrespective of whether the land lies inside or outside the built-up area. A Hungarian natural person, or a national of a Member State, who is not registered as a farmer may generally acquire no more than one hectare of land, subject to the statutory exceptions. A foreign natural person who is not a Member State national is generally prohibited from acquiring ownership of such land.

This might also interest you: The zártkert trap: when a rural Hungarian property is not what it seems

Foreign buyers in Hungary: EU/EEA nationals versus those requiring authorisation

Nationals of EU and EEA Member States, and persons accorded equivalent treatment under an international treaty, may generally acquire property that does not qualify as agricultural or forestry land without authorisation. Where land within the meaning of the Land Transaction Act is concerned, however, the Act’s restrictions also apply to them: a Member State national who is not registered as a farmer may generally acquire up to one hectare, subject to the statutory exceptions.

Foreign buyers who are not Member State nationals and are subject to the authorisation requirement, including UK nationals following Brexit and, as a general rule, US, Canadian, Australian and Chinese nationals, may acquire property that does not qualify as agricultural or forestry land with the approval of the competent government office. Government Decree 251/2014 (X. 2.) sets a 45-day administrative time limit for the procedure. A foreign natural person who is not a Member State national is, however, generally prohibited from acquiring ownership of land falling within the Land Transaction Act.

A corporate structure: a solution, but not in every case

In some cases, a foreign buyer can structure the purchase of rural property through a Hungarian limited liability company (korlátolt felelősségű társaság, or Kft.). A Kft. incorporated in Hungary is a domestic legal entity. When it acquires property that does not qualify as agricultural or forestry land, the authorisation rules applicable to foreign natural persons do not govern the acquisition. This is not, however, a universal loophole. A corporate structure has tax, accounting, financing, use and exit implications, and must therefore be tailored to the purpose of the transaction.

The Kft. structure also has clear limits. Under the Land Transaction Act, the acquisition of land ownership by legal entities is generally prohibited, subject only to narrow, expressly listed exceptions. A standard Kft. established to purchase real estate therefore cannot be used as a vehicle for acquiring agricultural land.

The concept of a “newcomer” (betelepülő) under Act XLVIII of 2025 is defined by reference to a natural person, so a Kft. acting as buyer is not a newcomer. Even so, the land transaction rules, pre-emption rights and local requirements applicable to the particular property must be checked in every case. A Kft. also entails continuing administration, including bookkeeping, annual accounts, tax obligations and, where the statutory conditions are met, an audit.

What foreign buyers in Hungary cannot bypass

Certain principles cannot be bypassed. If the property qualifies as land under the Land Transaction Act, the first question is whether the buyer is eligible to acquire ownership at all and, if so, what acreage limits, pre-emption rights and authority procedures apply. Farmer status is not the same as holding any one qualification, such as the Hungarian Aranykalászos gazda agricultural qualification; it is a registered legal status under the Act and its implementing rules.

A foreign natural person who is not a Member State national is generally prohibited from acquiring agricultural or forestry land. For other real property, a foreign buyer who is subject to the authorisation requirement needs government-office approval. Local identity protection rules apply only where the municipality has introduced the relevant protective measure by decree and the buyer does not fall within a statutory exemption. For zártkert property, it is also necessary to determine whether the property qualifies as land, whether the Section 72/E procedure for registration as land exempt from cultivation is available, and whether the legal status of any building is in order.

A practical guide: what should a foreign buyer do?

Classify the property. Obtain a full legal classification based on the title sheet, cadastral map data and other land-registry records, not on the . Assess the buyer. Compare the buyer’s nationality, farmer status and intended purchasing structure, whether individual or corporate, with the property’s legal classification. Check local rules. Review the local building regulations (HÉSZ), the zoning plan and municipal decrees, including any local identity protection decree. Verify the building and plan the structure. Confirm the building’s legal status under construction law, then plan any foreign acquisition authorisation, land transaction procedure or corporate structure that may be required.

The order matters, because a single point of legal classification can change the entire transaction.

The map that helps buyers navigate

Hungary’s rural property market is widely open to foreign buyers, but the legal classification of the property and the status of the buyer are decisive. Residential and holiday properties that do not qualify as agricultural or forestry land can generally be acquired, with authorisation required for certain foreign buyers, while zártkert properties require especially careful classification. Land governed by the Land Transaction Act is not closed to all foreign nationals: Member State nationals may acquire it subject to the conditions of the Act, whereas acquisition by foreign natural persons who are not Member State nationals is generally prohibited. Buyers who clarify this distinction at the outset are far less likely to build the transaction on the wrong legal structure.

Legislation cited

This article provides general market and legal information only and does not constitute individual legal advice. Before any transaction, a lawyer should review the particular legal position of both the property and the buyer. The English titles of Hungarian legislation are descriptive translations; the Hungarian-language legal text is authoritative. Legislation checked as at 3 September 2026.

World.title: Autumn is here: Summer’s final heatwave fades as Hungary braces for chilly nights
World.content:
Hungary is finally set to feel the arrival of autumn, with a significant cooling trend expected over the coming days. After temperatures soared to 30–34°C earlier this week — around 7–9°C above the seasonal average — a cold front is now sweeping across the country, bringing cooler temperatures, cloudier skies and showers.

According to HungaroMet, temperatures rose further on Wednesday ahead of the approaching cold front, reaching 30–35°C in places. The front then began moving into the country from the northwest, bringing stronger winds and stormy weather, particularly to western Hungary.

The Őrség region was already experiencing overcast skies and strong winds on Wednesday afternoon as the change in weather began to make itself felt.

Temperatures could drop below 10°C at night

The coming days will be considerably cooler. On Thursday, daytime temperatures are expected to fall to between 21 and 29°C, while scattered rain, showers and thunderstorms could occur in the evening. Night-time temperatures will also become noticeably lower, ranging from 13 to 19°C on Thursday.

The biggest change is expected over the weekend, when temperatures could fall to around 10°C or even below in some areas overnight, particularly in the northern counties. Despite the chilly nights, daytime temperatures are still expected to remain above 20°C in most places.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

A Mediterranean cyclone could briefly bring the heat back

The weather could remain unsettled, however, as a Mediterranean cyclone is expected to approach from the southwest. Its exact path remains uncertain because the system has not yet fully developed.

The cyclone could temporarily bring warmer air back into Hungary, particularly to the south-eastern parts of the country. As a result, temperatures in these areas could climb back towards 30°C on Friday, with some locations potentially exceeding that mark.

The brief warm spell would, however, come after the arrival of the cold front and is not expected to signal a return to the prolonged summer heat experienced earlier this week. For now, the message from forecasters is that Hungary’s exceptionally warm summer weather is giving way to much cooler autumn-like conditions, particularly after dark.

World.title: Hungary loses another EU Court case over frozen Russian assets and Ukraine aid
World.content:
The EU General Court has dismissed Hungary’s legal challenge against a decision to use extraordinary revenues from frozen Russian state assets to support Ukraine’s armed forces. However, the court did not rule that Hungary’s legal arguments were unfounded: it said it had no jurisdiction to review the political and strategic decision at issue.

Court rejects Hungary’s challenge

Hungary has lost another legal battle against the European Union after the EU General Court dismissed a case brought by the Hungarian government against a decision concerning military support for Ukraine, HVG reported.

The case, originally launched under Viktor Orbán’s government, centred on a decision by the committee of the European Peace Facility (EPF) to allocate extraordinary revenues generated by frozen Russian state assets to support the Ukrainian armed forces.

Importantly, the court did not dismiss Hungary’s case because it found the country’s legal arguments to be without merit. Instead, it concluded that the EU courts generally do not have jurisdiction to review the legality of political or strategic decisions adopted within the EU’s Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP) in circumstances such as this one.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

What is the European Peace Facility?

The European Peace Facility was established by the EU Council in 2021 to finance the bloc’s foreign and security policy actions. In May 2024, the Council adopted two decisions concerning extraordinary revenues generated by immobilised Russian state assets.

The first established rules for using the revenues to support Ukraine, while the second concerned the actual allocation of the funds. Hungary supported the first decision but constructively abstained from the second.

Under the EU’s system of constructive abstention, a member state can refrain from supporting a decision without blocking its adoption, while making clear that it does not consider itself bound to implement it.

On 21 June 2024, the EPF committee subsequently decided, through a written procedure, to allocate the first tranche of extraordinary revenues from the frozen Russian assets to support the Ukrainian armed forces.

The committee took the view that Hungary, having constructively abstained from the earlier decision, could not participate in the vote on the allocation. Budapest challenged this position before the EU General Court.

If you missed it: Hungary blocks Ukraine’s EU accession again: Budapest demands action on Hungarian minority rights

Hungary argued that EU rules had been breached

The Hungarian government argued that the EPF committee had acted unlawfully, including by allegedly violating the applicable voting rules. Hungary also claimed that fundamental EU principles had been breached, including the rule of law, equality between member states and the democratic functioning of the European Union.

The court, however, did not examine these arguments on their merits. The judges acknowledged that the European Peace Facility has legal personality, meaning that a challenge to a decision adopted by its committee could, in principle, fall within the General Court’s jurisdiction. The court nevertheless reached a different conclusion when considering the substance of the dispute.

Have you heard? A surprise exception for Hungary: US gives Hungarians visa priority

Why the court said it could not rule on the decision

The General Court pointed out that EU courts generally have limited jurisdiction over the CFSP. Although the EU treaties provide for certain exceptions, the court concluded that Hungary’s case did not fall within any of them. According to the ruling, the EPF committee’s decision was directly linked to political and strategic decisions taken as part of the EU’s foreign and security policy.

The contested decision determined that revenues generated by frozen Russian assets would be used to finance military equipment for Ukraine’s armed forces. It also identified the specific assistance measure for which the money would be used.

Because of this direct connection to CFSP political and strategic decisions, the General Court concluded that it was not empowered to assess whether the decision complied with EU law.

Hungary can appeal

The ruling does not necessarily mark the end of the legal dispute. Hungary can appeal the General Court’s decision to the Court of Justice of the European Union within two months and ten days of the judgment being notified.

However, any appeal would be limited to points of law, rather than allowing the entire case to be reheard on its facts. The case comes amid continued disputes between Budapest and Brussels over Hungary’s position on support for Ukraine, the use of frozen Russian assets and the EU’s response to Russia’s war against Ukraine.
