World.title: Top-Ranked Chinese Netflix Series Divides Viewers at Home
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019007/Top-Ranked Chinese Netflix Series Divides Viewers at Home
World.content:
Chinese romantic drama “The Early Spring,” an adaptation of a 2021 web novel, has become the highest-ranked Chinese series on streaming giant Netflix’s weekly non-English TV chart. However, the show has divided domestic viewers over whether it romanticizes an unhealthy power imbalance between its protagonists: a male boss and his female subordinate.

The TV series, which premiered Aug. 26 on both Netflix and Chinese streaming platform Youku, follows the workplace romance between demanding advertising agency corporate executive Luan “Luke” Nian, played by Jing Boran, and 22-year-old newcomer Shang “Flora” Zhitao, played by Sun Qian.

After a drunken encounter, the two begin a secret relationship. Over time, Shang advances in her career, while Luan’s harsh and arrogant demeanor softens.

“The Early Spring” ranked No. 2 on Netflix’s global weekly chart for non-English TV series from Aug. 24 to 30, garnering 2.4 million views. The series also made Netflix’s weekly Top 10 in 22 markets, including Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brazil, and ranked No. 1 in Thailand and Vietnam.

In China, the series recorded 547 million views and topped domestic entertainment data platform Maoyan’s weekly popularity ranking on Sept. 7.

Many domestic social media users praised the chemistry and sexual tension between the two leads — developed with the help of an intimacy coordinator, a role still relatively uncommon in Chinese television, according to the show’s producers.

Liu, a viewer in her 30s who works in the arts in Shanghai, said that the show’s appeal lies in its escapism via a “straightforward” romance.

“It’s simply: I like you, so I like you,” Liu told Sixth Tone, in reference to the show’s driving sentiment. “Physical attraction is unavoidable.” Unlike many Chinese romance dramas that typically withhold physical intimacy between their leads, she added, “The Early Spring” brings Luan and Shang together almost immediately.

Liu also praised the 24-episode TV adaptation for bringing more warmth to its relationships. She said that compared with the original work, published under the pen name Guniang Bieku on the literature platform Jinjiang, the TV series more clearly establishes Luan and Shang as two people in love rather than primarily a sexual relationship. It also fleshes out Shang’s friendships, giving her a stronger support network.

Critics, however, have questioned whether Luan exploits his workplace authority to pursue Shang, pointing to scenes where he belittles her professional abilities. For example, when he suspects she is considering another job, he describes her as “cheap” and “obedient.”

Xu Xin, a 29-year-old media professional based in Beijing, said she agreed with much of the criticism, particularly over the couple’s first sexual encounter. “Imagine this happening in real life: a young woman fresh out of college gets drunk, and her sober male supervisor takes her home and has sex with her. That’s problematic,” she told Sixth Tone. “Even if they are attracted to each other, did it have to happen that night, when she was drunk?”

“It feels like a female fantasy,” she added. “In male-oriented fantasies, the protagonist turns his life around by becoming rich or powerful. Here, the fantasy is that a woman starts invisible, works her way up and becomes ‘better’ — and then the man comes back for her.”

For her, the series also reflects how messy real relationships can be. “People aren’t always rational, nor can they always live up to their own feminist ideals.”

The power-dynamic debate has extended to the web novel the series is based on. In it, after Shang quits her job and starts her own business, she initially decides to hire only men. The TV adaptation omits this plotline, which some had previously criticized as “discriminatory.”

Two prominent female influencers — Zhan Qingyun and Pang Ying, who are known for discussing gender equality issues in China — have also faced criticism after promoting the show.

In a Sept. 6 video posted on domestic lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, the two discussed the show, arguing that a good relationship “does not require two people to be perfect from the beginning” but can involve “two imperfect people growing together.” The video was later taken down.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A still from “The Early Spring.” From Douban)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019008/One Last Night With Shanghai’s ‘Sleep No More’ Superfans
World.title: One Last Night With Shanghai’s ‘Sleep No More’ Superfans
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019008/One Last Night With Shanghai’s ‘Sleep No More’ Superfans
World.content:
SHANGHAI — On Aug. 30, Dong Minghai returned to Shanghai’s McKinnon Hotel one last time. It was his 518th visit to “Sleep No More.”

The 44-year-old machine vision quality engineer had been going roughly once a week since the production opened in 2016, enough to see nearly one in five of its 2,670 performances. “I’ve spent enough on it to buy an EV,” Dong said. “The number always shocks people.”

Over nearly a decade, the immersive production — co-produced by Shanghai Media Group and British theater company Punchdrunk — transformed a former power station into a six-story theatrical world set in 1930s Shanghai, drawing more than 750,000 visitors before its run ended. A new production of “Sleep No More” is planned for China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen in 2027.

Audience members locked away their phones, put on white masks, and roamed freely through 90 rooms as 25 characters performed simultaneous storylines inspired by Shakespeare’s “Macbeth,” the novel “Rebecca,” and the Chinese folk tale “The Legend of the White Snake.” Because scenes unfolded at the same time across the building, no one could see everything in a single visit.

Macbeth scrubbed blood from his hands in a bathtub, splashing water onto nearby spectators. At the White Snake’s wedding, paper flowers rained down over the newlyweds and audience. Elsewhere, visitors could wander through a bamboo forest smelling of damp earth, a psychiatric hospital sharp with disinfectant, or a speakeasy bar scented with whiskey.

Tang, a 38-year-old supply chain manager who asked to be identified only by her surname for privacy reasons, had attended more than 160 times since 2018. She compared repeat visits to “collecting pieces of a puzzle,” returning to see how different storylines intersected and to discover scenes she had missed.

Over time, some repeat visitors became increasingly invested in the show’s private “one-on-one” encounters. A performer could single out an audience member, lead them away from the crowd, and perform for them alone — removing their mask, sometimes clasping their hand or pulling them into an embrace. The encounters could not be reserved, and the choice was entirely the performer’s.

For fans who returned again and again, that uncertainty became part of the attraction. Being chosen could bring the thrill of feeling seen; being passed over could sting. Over hundreds of visits, those moments could begin to feel personal.

“I know how the trick works,” Tang said. “And it still works on me. But perhaps that doesn’t make the happiness any less real.”

Choose me

On Tang’s first visit, she watched an actor playing Malcolm, a prince in “Macbeth,” choose her friend for a private one-on-one scene. The actor led her through a door and closed it behind them, leaving Tang outside with no idea what was happening.

It took Tang another 20 visits to be chosen for the same encounter.

Inside, Malcolm crushed a dust-covered bird’s egg in her palm, part of a scene tied to the murder of his father, King Duncan.

“That is the final piece of the ‘Malcolm’ puzzle,” Tang said. “Only the two of you know what happened in that room at that moment. You share the same secret.”

To choose someone, a performer might turn toward a room full of masked spectators and study the crowd, ignoring people directly in front of them before reaching past others for someone farther back.

When Dong entered the same one-on-one with the same performer for a second time in 2017, the actor greeted him: “It’s you again. I’m glad you are here.”

Only later did Dong realize it was a standard line. “The line is deliberately written to create the suggestion that he recognized me,” he said.

But after enough visits, recognition could also be real. Fans said performers learned to identify regulars even behind identical white masks, picking up on their build, gait, or other physical cues.

“It’s a very clever business model,” Tang said. “It gives you the illusion that the actor favors you.”

She compared the encounters with romance-themed jubensha, live-action role-playing games where customers pay for personalized attention. “Here, everyone pays for a ticket, but the actor can still refuse you,” she said.

Fans also developed favorite performers. Different actors could give the same character markedly different personalities, Dong said.

“I’ve seen the same role played as sad and desperate, playful, or even as someone who picks on the weak,” he said. “That keeps the show feeling fresh no matter how many times I see it.”

Because casting was not announced in advance, regulars called buying tickets “gambling on the cast,” trying to work out performers’ schedules before spending around 700 yuan ($98) in hopes that a favorite would appear.

Some fans began studying performers’ apparent preferences and adjusting their own behavior accordingly. They compared who favored regulars or newcomers and who seemed drawn to particular genders, body types, or styles of dress. Some stood in particular places, wore conspicuous clothing or wigs, and kept spreadsheets tracking performers’ selections. Rival groups traded gossip about one another’s visits.

When Tang first began following a performer she liked, she would position himself at the front of the crowd and wait to be chosen. After being passed over repeatedly, she learned to “manage expectations” and step back.

One performer she liked once told her: “I didn’t pick you because I thought you’d seen the show so many times that you must have already had this interaction.”

After the final performance on Aug. 30, Tang heard a young woman crying in the bathroom after apparently being passed over during an interaction. “Why did they let go of my hand?” the woman asked her friend.

“That’s why being chosen in front of so many people feels far more intense than happiness you can simply buy,” Tang said.

For Liu, a 20-year-old university student who had seen the show 254 times since 2021, the imbalance became harder to ignore when a performer she repeatedly followed through the show stopped choosing her for interactions. On one milestone visit that she had told him was important to her, he chose a stranger instead.

“I began to realize that this model gives actors too much power,” Liu said, asking to be identified only by her surname for privacy reasons. “The relationship isn’t equal. We are the ones asking for the interaction, and the performer is the only person who can decide whether we get it. So they can hurt you very easily.”

Last dance

Liu often wondered whether she had fallen for a performer’s characters or for the performer himself. “At first, I was stubborn with myself. I told myself it was only this place that had given him that magic,” she said.

But she eventually realized she still enjoyed watching him even in roles she thought did not suit him particularly well. Over time, rejection bothered her less; she found herself paying more attention to his dancing, improvisations, and the small ways he departed from the script.

“That psychological shift was a little painful for me,” Liu said. “Was it a romantic attraction? I didn’t really dare admit it.”

She eventually stopped trying to define the feeling. “Love doesn’t have such clear divisions,” she said. “It’s difficult to say, this is romantic love, and this is admiration. You can’t really separate them.”

Outside the theater, Liu found herself “unusually shy” around him and struggled to start conversations at the stage door. “But eventually I stopped trying to guess what he thought of me,” she said. “I really appreciate what he does onstage, and I’m still happy watching him. That’s enough.”

The experience also made Liu think differently about what she wanted from relationships.

“I hope that in other relationships in the future, I’ll be a braver person,” Liu said. “If I date someone next, I hope I find someone who loves me a little more. Recently, I’ve become used to being the one who gives, and even giving without expecting anything in return.”

For Tang, meanwhile, attending “Sleep No More” on important dates became “a habit, and a kind of ritual.”

“At first, it was the unpredictability of the show that attracted me. Later, it was the opposite: its certainty,” she said. “So many uncertain things happen in the real world, and I can’t control all of them. But inside this building, I know what will happen at every point in time, with every piece of music. That’s what kept bringing me back.”

All three formed friendships through the show that lasted for years. Tang became a part-time performer in another immersive production and met the man who is now her boyfriend. Dong, meanwhile, was already planning to see “Sleep No More” in Seoul and said he would return when a new production opens in Shenzhen.

On the final night, familiar scenes began to change.

In one encounter, a witch who normally trapped a mortal in an endless cycle instead left him a letter: “You are free.” Elsewhere, performers kissed and embraced, exchanged small handmade bouquets, and arranged black sand from the set into the shape of a mask.

In the finale, when Macbeth was hanged, the audience erupted in applause. On ordinary nights, the moment was met with gasps and stunned silence.

Performers, including some who had not appeared that night, emerged around the audience. Together, they sang “A Nightingale Sang in Berkeley Square,” the song normally played as spectators left the building. Some went off-key as they cried. Audience members sobbed too.

Then the lights went out.

Tang was the last audience member to leave. As staff closed the door behind her, she thought of an adapted line from “Rebecca” that appears in one of the show’s one-on-one encounters:

“We can never go back to Manderley again, that much is certain. But sometimes, in my dreams, I do return.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header Image: Lady Macbeth washes away blood in a bathtub. From @SleepNoMore上海 on Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019002/Chinese Auto Supplier Faces Backlash for Firing 107 Recent Grads
World.title: Chinese Auto Supplier Faces Backlash for Firing 107 Recent Grads
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019002/Chinese Auto Supplier Faces Backlash for Firing 107 Recent Grads
World.content:
A Chinese auto parts maker has apologized for firing 107 recent university graduates just weeks after they began working, stating that four managers had been disciplined following public backlash.

In an apology published on its website on Sept. 7, the company, Changzhou Xingyu Automotive Lighting Systems, based in the eastern Jiangsu province, said the decision to reduce staff and reorganize positions was “incorrect.” It admitted it had caused “immense physical and psychological harm to the students” and “a serious negative impact on their families and society.”

The company also announced disciplinary measures against four managers, including withheld salaries and reassignments. It said it had dismissed its human resources director, while the head of the human resources department had been demoted and transferred. However, domestic media later reported that the company had no such human resources director at the time of the incident.

Xingyu is one of China’s major automotive lighting equipment manufacturers, producing 80 million headlights per year. It also supplies international automakers such as Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz, and BMW.

During a university campus recruitment drive earlier this year, the company signed employment agreements with 440 students set to graduate in 2026, and later hired 372.

According to its apology, however, company management decided in July to reorganize staff and reduce its workforce based on order outlook and staffing needs.

The company said that in early August, its human resources department approached 140 of the 372 new employees and informed 33 that they would be allowed to remain in their original positions. The remaining 107 signed termination agreements.

Of the 107 terminated employees, 75 held bachelor’s degrees and 32 had master’s degrees. Sixty worked in manufacturing, 39 in research and development, and eight held other roles such as quality control and project engineering.

A recent graduate who was among those terminated by the company told domestic media outlet Beijing News that they were given only two options: to “voluntarily” sign a resignation agreement for “personal reasons” or be forcibly transferred to a manufacturing line position. The graduate said they also were not offered additional compensation for the sudden termination.

The move sparked widespread backlash online, with users noting that in China, “recent graduate” status applies only in the first two years following graduation and is voided upon employment. To improve employment prospects for recent graduates, many junior positions are available only to those with “recent graduate” status, meaning such positions are no longer available to them once terminated.

On Aug. 25, local authorities said they deemed Xingyu to have used “simple and harsh” methods and failed to communicate sufficiently and effectively with employees.

In its apology, Xingyu said each of the 107 terminated workers would receive 15,000 yuan ($2,200) to ease their living costs while seeking new employment. The company added that it would offer free accommodation in its dormitories and help connect them with other employers. Those who remain unemployed by the end of November will also receive compensation equivalent to six months of their previous salary.

As of Sept. 7, 71 of the recently terminated employees had found new jobs, the company said. Local employment authorities have also organized special recruitment events and recommended positions to those affected by the cuts.

Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz, and BMW separately confirmed to domestic media that they had received details on the matter and launched their own investigations into Xingyu.

“Respecting the legitimate rights and interests of workers is a core principle that the Volkswagen Group adheres to in all its business activities,” a Volkswagen spokesperson told domestic media. “This principle also applies to the management of our supply chain system, and we require that all fundamental values and rights be fully guaranteed.”

Circulating screenshots also showed that Mercedes-Benz responded to an anonymous report regarding the incident via email, stating that Xingyu’s behavior was “inconsistent with Mercedes-Benz’s corporate principles” and that it intends to forward the report to the relevant department for further review.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018995/How a Rotten Apple Brought China’s Internet Into a Mushroom Lab
World.title: How a Rotten Apple Brought China’s Internet Into a Mushroom Lab
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018995/How a Rotten Apple Brought China’s Internet Into a Mushroom Lab
World.content:
What are the odds that two compatible spores from a wood-rotting fungus would land on the same apple, enter through its stem, germinate, meet, and eventually produce a mushroom inside the fruit?

“About the same as winning the lottery,” said Mu Liheng, a researcher at the Yunnan Wild Mushroom Protection and Development Association, in Kunming, capital of southwestern China’s Yunnan province.

In July 2024, Mu’s colleague Xu Rongju came across a photograph on the lifestyle app Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, that appeared to show exactly that: a white, fan-shaped mushroom was growing from the stem of an apple beside a woman’s kitchen sink.



Suspecting the mushroom might be worth studying, he contacted the user, a woman surnamed Deng living in the eastern Zhejiang province, and asked her to send it to him. Two days later, the rotten fruit arrived at the team’s laboratory in Kunming.

Xu’s posts about the team’s subsequent experiments helped turn the discovery into an online sensation, prompting people across China to send in mushrooms found growing on grapes, mangoes, garlic, and even used coffee capsules.

Over the next two years, the researchers drew on some of those specimens, along with strains from an existing breeding program, to develop what they called eight numbered “generations” of split-gill mushrooms.

Two varieties have emerged as particularly promising, and one could eventually reach the shelves of a major supermarket chain.

Rotten luck

The day after the apple arrived, Xu commented beneath Deng’s photograph. “This strain is very strong and has research value,” he wrote, promising to report back when the team made progress.

In one Xiaohongshu update, Xu placed photographs taken a day apart side by side. A dense white network of fungal threads, known as mycelium, had spread farther across the rotten apple. Other images showed the fungus growing rapidly in a Petri dish and thick individual threads under a microscope.

DNA sequencing identified the strain as Schizophyllum commune, commonly known as the split-gill mushroom. The team planned to isolate and purify the culture before moving on to cultivation trials.

Split-gill mushrooms normally grow on dead wood, making the inside of an apple an unusual place to find one. On Deng’s apple, no mycelium appeared in sections that remained intact. It grew most densely in tissue that had already decayed, suggesting the fungus was feeding mainly on the rotten portions.

The apple culture joined more than 1,000 split-gill strains at the team’s laboratory. The team selected about 400 for further crossbreeding.

Edible split-gill mushrooms, known in China as bai shen, can have a dry texture and mildly bitter taste. Mu, who joined the work in 2023, was looking for strains with better flavor and texture, as well as lower spore production, which could reduce respiratory risks for growers.

Some strains in the collection had previously been sent into space through a collaboration with China’s human spaceflight program, including aboard the Shenzhou-12 spacecraft in 2021. After returning to Earth, they were screened for potentially useful mutations, and promising strains were used in further breeding. The apple strain itself was not sent into space.

As Xu’s updates spread online, users gave the apple mushroom a name: “Guo Jun Wang,” or the “King of Fruit Mushrooms.” In Chinese, the name sounds like “Prince Guo,” a character in the hit Qing dynasty (1644–1911) palace drama “Empresses in the Palace.” The pun helped propel the mushroom to the top of the trending rankings on microblogging site Weibo.

Xu used the nickname in a Xiaohongshu update: “You Give Me a Rotten Apple, I’ll Give You Back the King of Fruit Mushrooms.”

“Thank you, Xiaohongshu. I really didn’t expect to find research material here,” he wrote. “Once the experiment is complete, I’ll include everyone in the acknowledgments.”

People asked what the mushroom tasted like, whether it might have an apple flavor, whether it could be grown commercially, and when they might be able to eat it.

A month after mailing the rotten apple to Kunming, Deng received mushrooms cultivated from its strain. She chopped them up, mixed them with eggs, steamed the dish, and documented the entire process online.

By then, more than a dozen people a day were tagging Xu in photographs of mushrooms they wanted him to identify. Over the following year, the researchers received specimens found growing on more than 40 different fruits, foods, and everyday objects, including persimmons, pomelos, cantaloupes, garlic, and used coffee capsules.

One of the earliest contributors was Huang Cheng, a 37-year-old medical equipment business owner in central China’s Hubei province. Days after seeing the apple mushroom online, he removed a used capsule from his coffee machine and noticed several small, white, fan-shaped mushrooms growing from it.

“Normally, I might have just taken a picture and thrown it away,” Huang said.

Instead, he remembered that Deng’s apple had been sent to a laboratory. He photographed the capsule, posted it online, tagged Xu, and asked whether it might also be useful for research.

The post drew thousands of likes. Other users began directing Xu to Huang’s photographs, and within two days, the capsules had arrived at the lab. The team later received similar coffee-capsule specimens from Shanghai and Kunming.

“We were able to see different mushrooms from all over the country, growing on different fruits and all kinds of unusual things,” Xu said. “This really went from a small laboratory to a much bigger laboratory.”

Fruit loop

In the lab, the team isolated a strain from Huang’s coffee-capsule mushroom and crossed it with one of the space-bred strains in the collection.

Their offspring was crisp, heat-resistant, and faintly apple-scented. The team classified it as the fourth generation of the “Guo Jun Wang” series and named it “Xiang Fei,” or “Fragrant Concubine,” after a legendary Qing dynasty consort said to have carried a natural fragrance.

Many of the “Guo Jun Wang” generations, including the Xiang Fei, were not descended from Deng’s apple strain. As the project expanded, researchers used the name for promising varieties they developed, drawing on samples sent in by people online as well as strains already held by the association.

Producing those varieties meant repeatedly crossing and testing hundreds of strains. Mu often worked until midnight, preparing thousands of Petri dishes and checking newly cultivated samples.

“It was too much,” he said. “We didn’t really keep count at the time. There was no set amount of time we spent on it.”

For Xu, the experiments came on top of his doctoral research. “I just thought that if we could grow it and give the internet users an answer, that would actually be something meaningful,” he said.

The first generation of Guo Jun Wang mushrooms “tasted bad and bitter,” Xu recalled. By the second half of 2025, the team had selected more than 10 promising varieties and invited dozens of mushroom enthusiasts to cook and taste them.

“Some have an average texture but look beautiful. Some grow particularly fast. Some have high levels of polysaccharides,” Xu said, referring to the complex carbohydrates that can give mushrooms immune-boosting benefits. “The one that grew on grapes has a very good, crispy texture.”

After more than a year of breeding and selection, another variety stood out in February 2026. Provisionally designated the eighth-generation Guo Jun Wang, it had an unusual growth form and produced very few spores.

The two traits were unrelated, Mu said. The low spore production resulted from a gene segment involved in spore formation failing to be expressed, while a different gene controlled the mushroom’s unusual shape.

In July, Deng received both the eighth-generation and Xiang Fei mushrooms from the laboratory, two years after sending her rotten apple to Kunming.

Small batches of the mushrooms have also been sold through Xu’s Xiaohongshu account for 19.9 yuan ($2.80) per 100 grams. Mu said split-gill varieties identified in China are edible, and that large-scale production would require routine safety checks, including tests for heavy metals and pesticide residues.

However, the number of buyers remains limited because public awareness of split-gill mushrooms in China is still relatively low, Xu said. “If someone has eaten bai shen before, they might have tried them once and thought they don’t taste very good, so won’t eat them again.”

The team has been in contact with e-commerce giant Alibaba’s supermarket chain Freshippo about potentially selling Xiang Fei, which the researchers say tastes better and stores more easily than conventional varieties.

But commercial production remains beyond their current capacity. The team lacks the funding and manpower to grow the mushrooms at scale, while questions remain over who would cultivate them, how they would be transported, and how consistent quality could be maintained. For now, the researchers grow small batches by hand; outsourcing production, they say, could make quality harder to control.

They are also studying why crossbreeding produces such pronounced differences in the split-gill mushroom’s shape, work they hope could eventually help guide the breeding of other fungi.

“We’re happy that after all the attention in 2024, the story didn’t simply disappear,” Mu said. “There have been new developments over the past two years, and at least we’ve gotten two results that we wanted.”

In the hunt for a suitable name for the eighth-generation mushroom, the researchers have turned to the internet again.

One Xiaohongshu user suggested “Popcorn,” because its unusual shape resembles popped kernels. Another proposed “Ba Xian Wang,” or “Eighth Prince” — another Qing dynasty prince and a brother of Prince Guo.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Split-gill mushrooms growing from the apple after it arrived at the laboratory, July 2024. Courtesy of Xu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018997/End of the Vine: China’s ‘Calabash Grandpa’ Cuts Down His Famous Gourds
World.title: End of the Vine: China’s ‘Calabash Grandpa’ Cuts Down His Famous Gourds
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018997/End of the Vine: China’s ‘Calabash Grandpa’ Cuts Down His Famous Gourds
World.content:
A 75-year-old man who became a sensation in China for the calabashes hanging outside his home — reminiscent of the opening scene of a classic domestic TV series — has triggered widespread debate after removing the gourds, citing exhaustion from the subsequent flood of tourists.

The man, Chen Jin’ao, went viral on Aug. 29 after a local media outlet in the eastern city of Shaoxing posted a video of the gourds on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok. The video quickly climbed the platform’s trending list, and tourists soon followed.

Chen, nicknamed “Calabash Grandpa” by tourists in reference to the character from “Calabash Brothers” — a 1986 animated series about seven brothers born from calabashes who use their superpowers to rescue their grandfather from demons — initially greeted the tourists outside his home, telling them that the gourds would bring them good luck.

In China, the calabash, or hulu, is a symbol of good fortune as its name sounds similar to the word for blessing — fulu — and represents prosperity and fertility due to its round shape and plentiful seeds.

But on Saturday, Chen cut the gourds down after his wife suffered a dizzy spell, reportedly from exhaustion caused by the volume of tourists.

The local tourism bureau told domestic media on Friday that Chen “is not an internet celebrity but an amiable and lovable Shaoxing elder … These days, we have been reflecting on the balance between viral ‘check-in’ tourism and private life. To properly guide visitors, we also ask that tourists be more considerate …”

On Sunday, a local tourism official told Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper that removal of the calabashes was Chen’s own decision. The official said Chen and his wife were exhausted by the constant visitors — some of whom even tried to enter their home — and the riverside location posed crowd safety risks.

Before Chen decided to remove the gourds, the local community tried to intervene in the surging crowds, putting up a sign on Sept. 2 that read, “Please do not shout. Grandpa is resting,” to no avail.

Despite the overwhelming fame and surging crowds, Chen and his wife, Shen Hualing, told domestic media that the virality has also had a positive emotional impact on them. “We rarely used to open the door and were basically closed off,” Shen told domestic media on Sept. 3. “People online have opened our hearts.” The elderly couple’s only daughter died 25 years ago, and they have no grandchildren.

The story has sparked 160 million views and 27,000 discussions on microblogging platform Weibo as of Tuesday, with most supporting Chen’s decision to remove the gourds and lamenting that excessive online attention had spoiled a heartwarming tale.

Now, the seven cut calabashes are neatly arranged on the second floor of Chen’s home. “I won’t grow calabashes again — this experience was enough for me,” Chen said. “Thank you all for your kindness.” He added that he would take good care of the gourds.

“The calabashes are my children.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Chen Jin’ao poses for a photo alongside the seven gourds he grew in Shaoxing, Zhejiang province, Sept. 5, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018996/When China’s Star Intellectuals Fly Too Close to the Sun
World.title: When China’s Star Intellectuals Fly Too Close to the Sun
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018996/When China’s Star Intellectuals Fly Too Close to the Sun
World.content:
In Classical Greek mythology, few things are more dangerous than hubris. In one of the most renowned examples, Icarus, fleeing the island of Crete, flew too close to the sun until the heat melted the wax on his wings, plunging him into the sea. It was a tragedy, and also a reminder of the seductive peril of overreach, especially for aspiring young people.

Recent years have seen plenty of writers, academics, and artists take Icarian falls of their own. The latest is Zhuge Yiyang, the 29-year-old political philosophy Ph.D. candidate at Boston College and founder of the wildly popular Chinese-language podcast “Monologues of a Committed Observer.” In the weeks since her August interview with director Christopher Nolan made her a global star, Zhuge, who also goes by the alias Zhong Shu, has seen her reputation in China collapse, as critics accuse her of serial plagiarism in both her writing and podcast scripts.

Zhuge has denied the allegations, but the backlash has already taken a toll on her career, with multiple public events where she was due to appear being canceled without explanation.

Prior to her viral Nolan interview, Zhuge had built an idol-like fandom among young Chinese, attracting over 970,000 subscribers to her podcast. Her fans praised her confident, assertive tone and unapologetic approach to being a young female intellectual. They were also drawn to her seemingly boundless knowledge, ranging from Greek philosophy to the modern history of the Middle East, as well as her astonishingly prolific output — in addition to her Ph.D. studies, she managed to release podcast episodes roughly every three days and publish six translated books in the span of a year, all while writing regular columns and maintaining an active presence on social media and at public events.

Zhuge is something of an extreme case, but her profile is representative of China’s new generation of public intellectuals. It’s no longer enough to be a good writer, translator, or speaker. Fans and employers alike demand all-around excellence and near-constant output. The rewards are handsome, but it’s no coincidence that all the industries Zhuge has dabbled in, including academia, media, and publishing, are struggling financially and no longer offer secure employment.

Take academia, for example. A July report on the extent of recent layoffs in British higher education — nearly 4,000 cuts in a single year, according to the Guardian — drew attention on Chinese social media, where young scholars shared their own stories of the deteriorating academic job market and the dim prospects of surviving the harsh “up or out” tenure system.

Faced with a lack of opportunities inside the ivory tower, a number of Chinese Ph.D. students in the social sciences and humanities have turned to social media. Some start podcasts or other ambitious projects; many more use their profiles to advertise tutoring and proofreading services: a side hustle to subsidize tuition fees and living costs or cushion themselves against post-graduation unemployment.

Likewise, fearing they are fighting a losing war against social media and short-form videos, news outlets are increasingly gambling on “stars” rather than subject-matter experts. Newsrooms across China now incentivize journalists to build their own “personal IP” — a euphemism for becoming online influencers.

In many cases, this means doing research, voiceover, video editing, and social media operations all by themselves or with the support of a small team. It also involves creating renshe, or “persona,” which gives the journalist a memorable public image — such as being “funny,” “knowledgeable,” or “resilient” — a strategy borrowed from the wider community of online celebrities.

For cultural workers, the distinction between being a beloved influencer or a mere expert can make a material difference. When a guest on her podcast noted that rates for Chinese translators of academic books are typically lower than 0.1 yuan ($0.015) per Chinese character, without royalties, Zhuge appeared surprised, saying that her book deal was quite different.

Indeed, publishing houses often offer more to celebrity translators with big fanbases, even if they do not deliver the finest translations. This is especially true in niche markets such as the humanities and social sciences, where the benchmark for a best-seller can be as low as 10,000 copies a year.

This influencer model ultimately shifts industry-wide crises and responsibilities onto individuals. Although intellectuals have always been entangled in market dynamics, their role as salespeople has never been more prominent than it is today. As far as industry or academia are concerned, scholars, journalists, translators, and countless others in the cultural industry who struggle financially have only themselves to blame for lacking an appealing online persona.

Many find themselves trapped in an inherently volatile situation. The race for ever more impressive public images pushes ambitious young writers, journalists, and academics to prioritize performative work, incentivizing plagiarism, polarizing content, and exaggeration of their credentials. Original work gets depreciated: doctoral research, investigative journalism, and book projects that take years of painstaking effort continue to be undervalued.

The unbalanced distribution of resources, wealth, and responsibilities eventually drains cultural institutions’ ability to attract the best talent. It also damages their most valuable asset: trust.

This is particularly frustrating for those who draw inspiration from success stories like Zhuge, including women denied the right to speak assertively under patriarchal culture; ethnic minority scholars sidelined in Western academic discourse, especially in disciplines such as Classics that have been reserved for white elites; and people eager to access knowledge that’s been paywalled by academic journals or expensive degree programs.

In Chinese fandom, an idol doesn’t fall from the sky; rather, their house collapses around them. Known as tafang, the word describes the world-ending despair fans feel when their favorite celebrity lets them down.

The recent controversies surrounding her work may not end Zhuge’s career, but they offer a useful example of what happens when intellectualism is rebuilt around the ideal of superhuman output. The cultivation of over-inflated personas has enriched a few and demoralized the rest. Addressing the challenges facing cultural institutions and workers requires sustained investment and broad-based public support. Hinging everything on individual effort, no matter how Herculean, will only speed their collapse.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018990/China Moves to Address Self-Driving Cars in National Law
World.title: China Moves to Address Self-Driving Cars in National Law
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018990/China Moves to Address Self-Driving Cars in National Law
World.content:
China has proposed adding autonomous driving to its national traffic law, marking the first time the new technology has been addressed at the national legal level.

The draft, submitted to the Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress for its first reading on Aug. 25, introduces a legal framework for when self-driving vehicles can use public roads, which party is responsible when such vehicles violate traffic rules, and how insurance liability should be handled.

China’s autonomous-driving rules have largely remained at the level of national standards, regulations, and local legislation, leading to inconsistencies when assigning responsibility in traffic accidents involving self-driving cars. The lack of a national law has also made it difficult to enforce regulations regarding self-driving cars on public roads.

In 2021, China introduced a new national standard that established a driving automation classification system, which allowed vehicles to be categorized into six levels based on their degree of automation, but did not legally address autonomous driving. Cities including Beijing and the southern tech hub Shenzhen have introduced local rules for autonomous driving, which state that autonomous driving is permitted in limited locations.

The proposed amendment is based on a basic distinction between autonomous driving vehicles and cars with driver-assistance functions.

The draft law states that autonomous vehicles can continuously perform all driving tasks without a driver. If a violation occurs when an autonomous-driving function is active, the manufacturer or importer is thus legally responsible. If the manufacturer or importer argues that a violation was unrelated to autonomous-driving functions, it would have to provide evidence to support that claim.

Driver-assistance functions, by contrast, only provide help during select maneuvers. Under the new amendment, a vehicle operating in driver-assistance mode is therefore still treated as a conventional vehicle.

Legal scholar Zheng Fei, a professor at the Institute of Evidence Law and Forensic Science at China University of Political Science and Law and a government advisor on the autonomous driving provisions, told Sixth Tone that the amendment is the first time the country has addressed responsibility in accidents involving autonomous vehicles.

Zheng said the amendment considers whether autonomous driving functions are active at the time of an accident, not just whether a vehicle has the capacity for autonomous driving. He said the distinction is intended to address problems with the country’s existing traffic law, which was written under the assumption that a human driver is always in control of a vehicle.

For consumers, Zheng said, such a distinction can also protect consumer rights and interests, allowing them to clearly judge the vehicle’s capabilities and clarify their own responsibility.

The draft amendment also addresses insurance liability for autonomous driving accidents, proposing that autonomous vehicles be subject to China’s compulsory motor vehicle traffic accident liability insurance system. It also encourages manufacturers, importers, and owners of autonomous vehicles to purchase commercial insurance.

To prevent consumers from confusing driver assistance with autonomous driving, the amendment also requires manufacturers and importers to clearly define self-driving and driver-assistance functions.

The move comes in response to previous disputes in which carmakers were accused of equating the term “intelligent driving,” or zhineng jiashi, to autonomous driving as a marketing tactic. Critics say such claims have led consumers to overtrust these systems’ capabilities, contributing to serious accidents.

However, Zheng said that the provisions do not fully address civil compensation, product liability or criminal liability. He pointed to the unresolved issue of liability during “handover” — the period when a person takes the wheel after full self-driving mode, and vice versa.

He also cautioned that autonomous driving systems can be deactivated by automakers, and could be tampered with by automakers in cases of accidents to avoid liability. Rules regarding data storage duration and anti-tampering also need clarification, he said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Vectorstock/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018966/Did AI Find Murakami’s Voice? Student’s $2 Experiment Divides China’s Literati
World.title: Did AI Find Murakami’s Voice? Student’s $2 Experiment Divides China’s Literati
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018966/Did AI Find Murakami’s Voice? Student’s $2 Experiment Divides China’s Literati
World.content:
Chinese readers of Haruki Murakami used to wait over a year for a faithful Mandarin translation of his latest book after its official release in Japanese. Not this time.

An unlicensed, high-fidelity digital version of the author’s new novel, “The Tale of KAHO,” was available to download in Chinese just hours after it went on sale in Tokyo on July 3.

There were no lengthy negotiations over rights, no translators straining to make a deadline, no pondering on how to capture Murakami’s distinct voice. Instead, it was accomplished in a relative flash for less than $2 using an AI-based tool developed by a 21-year-old university student.

“The Tale of KAHO,” a novel about a picture book illustrator who slips between dream and reality, was the first real test for Wenyi, a coding project that instructs large-language-model artificial intelligence on literary translation. Its designer, who asked to be identified by the pseudonym Ping Ming for privacy reasons, says he wanted to know whether AI could handle not only simple text but also glossary management, polishing, and rounds of spontaneous self-reviews.

What he discovered could fundamentally alter how novels are translated.

Wenyi’s unlicensed translation of the novel quickly began circulating on Chinese social media and the resale platform Xianyu, as well as the free online archive Z-Library.

Anecdotal evidence suggests readers are impressed. On China’s interest-oriented networking platform Douban, the most-liked review of the novel reads, “If this is purely AI translation, the quality is astonishing! … If AI can already do this much, what’s the point of having human translators?”

Readers might be happy, but publishing industry insiders feel AI still has a long way to go before it can replace humans — while legal experts warn that copyright holders could lose out either way.

Staying faithful

Nanshan Youlu, a part-time Japanese-to-Chinese translator who asked to use his online alias, worked with a friend on a manual translation of “The Tale of KAHO,” which they also began sharing bit by bit on the lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, or RedNote, on July 3.

Their first post received more than 2,000 likes, with many users expressing gratitude and complimenting the quality of their translation. Yet shortly after completing the final chapter, the duo wiped their version from the internet, citing that Wenyi’s translation was just too good — virtually 100% faithful to the original Japanese text.

“When human translators work on a novel, they will read the whole book first, and therefore will build their own interpretation and create their own ‘context.’ It’s basically impossible for them to achieve 100% wording fidelity,” Nanshan Youlu, a 30-something working at a tech company in Beijing, tells Sixth Tone. “They don’t translate mechanically — every sentence they translate serves the context they build.”

Wenyi works differently. Ping explains that his program started by dividing the book into chunks of fewer than 2,000 words, which it then sent one by one to the Chinese AI model DeepSeek for translation. To maintain continuity, each chunk overlapped by six paragraphs. “If you feed AI tens of thousands of words all at once, there’s a risk of AI hallucination, which can result in lots of mistakes,” he says.

The program also asked AI to extract important terms and proper nouns from the material so it can continuously update a glossary of keywords to ensure consistency. Once finished, the system reviews the entire book — again, chunk by chunk — to check for problems.

Not a single human had read the Chinese translation before Ping uploaded it to Z-Library just four hours after the official version of the novel was released in Japan. The project had cost him just 13 yuan ($1.90) in DeepSeek tokens.

However, once online, he soon began noticing mistakes. Some nouns, such as the various nicknames for the protagonist Kaho, hadn’t been extracted for the glossary and were inconsistent, while some wording was unnatural, more machine-like.

He decided to translate it again, this time refining his code to instruct the AI to be more meticulous about names, and requesting a complete polish of the text. This second version was better, he says, although it took longer.

Ping, a literature major at Nanjing Normal University in the eastern Jiangsu province, taught himself to code using the Python programming language two years ago. To train Wenyi, he used English-language literature including works by the 19th-century American writer Edgar Allan Poe and Scottish novelist Ian McEwan.

“When I was a child, I always found hackers in the movies so cool, and I wanted to have those skills,” Ping tells Sixth Tone, adding that in more recent years he has been attracted by the rapid developments in AI technology.

The idea for Wenyi partially stemmed from his passion for literature. As a fan of Murakami, Ping always wanted to read the author’s books as soon as they were released, but he can’t read Japanese. He recalls attempting to digest an unlicensed Mandarin version of Murakami’s novel “The City and Its Uncertain Walls” produced using the free DeepL online translation tool in 2023, “but it was unacceptably bad — the grammar, pronouns, proper nouns, all were a mess.” He had to wait another year for the official Chinese version, translated by the prominent literary scholar Shi Xiaowei.

Machine translation has been around a while, but conventional tools have never been considered good enough for literary works.

“Someone needs to step forward and explore how good AI translation can be,” says Ping. “If it were not me, it would be someone else. … The original AI models set the lower limit (of translation), while Wenyi sets the upper limit.”

However, not everyone is impressed. Lin Shaohua, who translated Murakami’s earlier works, including the best-sellers “Kafka on the Shore” and “Norwegian Wood,” told China Newsweek that while Wenyi’s translation was technically fluent, it had failed to capture the author’s true voice.

“AI translation has achieved ‘grammatically coherent and reads smoothly’ — but that’s all,” he’s quoted as saying. “AI is still not quite capable of conveying subtle nuances of language and stylistic nuances. … The story itself is not literature. Only its particular tone makes it literature. Literature is the art of language.”

However, over the years, Lin has faced criticism from readers over alleged mistakes in his translations that might have changed what the original author intended to convey.

Nanshan Youlu believes this is hard to avoid and sees translation as a continuation of the creative process. While some translators aim to follow an author’s style to the letter, for him, the core of the job is to convey the feelings in a text, rather than reproduce the exact wording. Sometimes, after working for hours on a draft, he will review it and find areas that aren’t exactly faithful to the source novel — though revising them might disrupt the structure and context that he’s already built.

“If you read the AI translation closely, you’ll find it’s quite fragmented when it comes to context,” he says. “There’s a certain disharmony to it, a sense that the whole thing was pieced together.”

However, for Ping, fidelity to the original is essential. “If a translation doesn’t match, I’d simply call it a mistake — that’s non-negotiable,” he says. “No matter how good your education and cultural literacy, or how beautiful and fluent your translations are, if you’re not faithful to the original, there’s nothing to talk about.”

There be pirates

Of course, without a licensing agreement, both Ping Ming and Nanshan Youlu risk accusations of copyright infringement for releasing their translations online, regardless of whether they profited financially.

Under China’s Copyright Law, using published works for personal study, research, or appreciation is considered fair use. However, this doesn’t apply if the use is seen as harmful to the copyright holder’s rights and interests — for example, negatively affecting sales of Murakami’s books in China.

“The nonprofit nature of their conduct does not constitute grounds for exemption from liability,” Zhang Jie, an attorney from Shanghai-based law firm Zhihe Partners with experience handling intellectual property (IP) disputes, tells Sixth Tone. “The law’s control over acts such as reproduction, adaptation, translation, and dissemination via information networks naturally extends to the use of AI. Whether infringement has occurred has little to do with whether a work was created by a human or with AI assistance.”

She adds that China legally protects the IP rights of overseas authors under the Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works and other international treaties.

While this initial breakthrough in AI literary translation may have skirted the law, it does demonstrate the technology’s potential legitimate use by publishing houses. However, industry insiders suggest the overwhelming preference is still for human translators, especially when handling more complex projects.

Liu Chengxu, an editor at Guangdong People’s Publishing House, says, “If the original book is straightforward to understand, I’d choose AI translation. Frankly speaking, in those cases, there isn’t much difference between the work of a seasoned human translator and that of an AI translator. But if the original is more complex, like if it’s hard sci-fi or a thought experiment, I would choose a human translator.”

Compared with the lightning speed of DeepSeek, a professional translator will need about six months to complete a 350-page book like “The Tale of KAHO.” Then come editorial reviews, proofreading, publication, and distribution, with the book finally hitting shelves after about a year. Meanwhile, translators earn 100 to 120 yuan per 1,000 characters — not a high rate, but still far more than the current cost of AI.

Despite the obvious benefits, Puzhao, an editor at the Shanghai Translation Publishing House who goes by a pen name, feels that using AI to translate fiction still isn’t a viable option. “I prefer collaborating with humans,” he says. “When it comes to literary books, we need humans to translate them in their own words.”

He cites Emily Wilson’s acclaimed 2017 version of Homer’s epic “The Odyssey” as an example that a new translation of a classical or even modern text has the power to spark widespread discussion. This, he says, demonstrates that translation is not merely a mechanical transfer of words but a way to use contemporary language to introduce stories to new audiences.

On an ethical level, Puzhao concedes that he dislikes AI translation because it “deprives humans of job opportunities,” adding that people “put so much time and effort into creating original content, only for some tech monopoly to feed it into AI training. All we can do is make some small acts of resistance. My position is non-cooperation.”

In the summer of 2023, China introduced the Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI Services, requiring tech companies to carry out training activities only with data from lawful sources and to guard against IP infringement.

Whether Ping’s experiment will fundamentally change the future of literary translation is yet to be seen — but it’s certainly got people reading into the consequences.

Editor: Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Visuals from Westend61, Shijue, and iStock/VCG, reedited by Ding Yining/Sixth Tone)

World.title: [Rappler Investigates] Refuge of the privileged accused
World.content:
You’ve probably noticed, just as we have, that there’s a common playbook being passed around by government officials facing imminent arrest or a string of legal cases. It’s finding refuge in a hospital after raising a variety of illnesses that require medical attention.

Top officials, including past presidents charged with plunder and/or graft and corruption, suddenly fell ill or developed illnesses that merited confinement. It’s not totally surprising for officials used to being accorded special attention and treatment to suddenly develop heart ailments, if not hypertension.

Researcher Lourence Marcellana reviewed the past two decades and found at least eight top officials — top, mind you, not even lower-ranking — who either sought prolonged hospital stay or temporary relief in hospitals before or during detention.

No one admitted, but many suspected, that the hospital admissions especially for the likes of former speaker Martin Romualdez — who went straight to a hospital before an arrest warrant could be served — might have been a means to delay the inevitable: imprisonment.

But assuming good faith and authentic health needs, Southern Illinois University criminology associate professor Raymund Narag pointed out in his piece: “Medical considerations… have appeared selectively available to the rich and powerful.” Whatever criteria were applied to Romualdez should likewise “apply to thousands of poor Filipinos now languishing in overcrowded jails nationwide.”

These Filipinos have been no match, too, for the likes of former presidents Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo (who had neck issues) and Joseph Estrada (knees), or even senators Jinggoy Estrada, Rodante Marcoleta, and Juan Ponce Enrile, former first lady Imelda Marcos (recently acquitted by the Supreme Court on seven counts of graft), and former public works secretary Manuel Bonoan, who all raised a garden variety of health issues.

To their credit, Bong Revilla, Jinggoy Estrada, Marcoleta, and Bonoan went to authorities first before eventually finding their way to hospitals.

These latest developments threatened to eclipse major investigations by our tech writer Gelo Gonzales, with the assistance of Lance Bustos, about this appalling, perhaps unknown-to-many forum that exploits women. I will alert you early on that this is gated content (reading the full story will require payment or membership in Rappler+) to support the journalism that we do.

This online community boasts of having 430,000 registered members who share intimate photos and videos of women, many without their consent, involving manipulation and deceit. Content is shared as if they were conquests of victimized women — mirroring repulsive behavior of the male species. Read the first part.

Part 2 discusses how abuse is rewarded financially at the expense of the victims. The forum has thrived because of challenges that face regulation and jurisdiction.

Since we published the stories, we have received emails that provide tips and more information about this exploitative forum. Gelo is in the process of compiling these reports for possible follow-up stories. If you have information to share, email us at investigative@rappler.com.

Another project we’ve been working on involves political dynasties. If you’ve been keen observers of Philippine politics, you will agree that the pattern of corruption in government is also partly enabled by the continuing domination of the same political families that just shift terms and positions among themselves.

Power remains locked within the family with little check-and-balance and ultimate accountability. It’s incredible how the same surnames surface every campaign period, leaving voters with little choice but to narrow their options of who to vote into office.

This is a running series all the way to October when we commemorate the 35th anniversary of the Local Government Code. Here’s what we have published so far, with more in the pipeline:

We continue to keep track of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte that has run for 23 days now. The latest issue on the table is the voting threshold, with Senator Erwin Tulfo seeking clarification on how many votes will be required for either a conviction or acquittal of the Vice President.

Will it be two-thirds of the 24 senators? Or will it be two-thirds of the senators who are present — just 20 at the present time because of the continuing absence of four senators: Marcoleta and Estrada, who are detained on plunder charges; Loren Legarda, who remains on extended medical leave; and Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, still a fugitive.

The impeachment court is seeking the opinion of amici curiae, friends of the court, who will likely include retired Supreme Court justices, to help them settle the question. A decision is expected by September 23. Check out the adjusted schedule of the impeachment court here.

Till Thursday after next!

– Rappler.com

Rappler Investigates is a bimonthly newsletter of our top picks delivered straight to your inbox every other Thursday. Visit rappler.com/newsletters to subscribe.

World.title: Rappler Recap: Romualdez’s health condition not an emergency case – doctor
World.content:
Admitting physician Dr. Kurt Allen Sibayan says he did not see nor examine the lawmaker because he was barred by the attending physicians from entering the room

MANILA, Philippines – Dr. Kurt Allen Sibayan, the admitting physician of former speaker Martin Romualdez, said on Thursday, September 10, that he did not see nor examine the lawmaker because he was barred by the attending physicians from entering the room.

He also said that Romualdez’s case was not an emergency.

The prosecution also noted that there’s nothing in Romualdez’s medical abstract that indicates his health condition requires confinement. The former speaker is currently facing a plunder case over P7.44-billion in alleged kickbacks.

Here’s Jairo Bolledo to recap the Sandiganbayan’s hearing on Romualdez’s request for hospital confinement. – Rappler.com

World.title: Martin Romualdez to remain in hospital until further orders from Sandiganbayan
World.content:
CONFINED. The Philippine National Police-CIDG cuffs releases a photo of former House speaker Martin Romualdez when he was served an arrest warrant in his hospital room September 7, 2026. The cops took his fingerprint and placed a detainee uniform on top of him as part of the booking process, but his mugshot was not taken yet given his condition.

MANILA, Philippines – Former House speaker Martin Romualdez, who’s facing a P7.44-billion plunder case, will remain confined in Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City “until further orders” from the anti-graft court Sandiganbayan.

“However, considering that the hearing on the said accused’s manifestation and urgent motion has not yet been terminated today and will continue tomorrow, September 11, 2026, his confinement at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center will remain until further orders from the court,” Sandiganbayan 3rd Division Clerk of Court Dennis Pulma told reporters on Thursday, September 10.

Romualdez was arrested inside his hospital room in San Juan City, but the police could not move him to the court or jail because of his medical condition. He also filed a motion with the court to remain under hospital confinement, further delaying his detention.

Play Video

The 3rd Division had set a hearing on Romualdez’s motion on Thursday morning.

There, the chamber declared that Romualdez will be detained in New Quezon City Jail in Payatas, the designated facility for flood control related cases. However, the court still needs to resolve the motion, so there’s no date yet as to when the accused will be transferred to Payatas.

“An Order of Commitment (Pending Trial) dated September 10, 2026 was issued by the court on even date for the detention/commitment of accused Ferdinand Martin G. Romualdez at the BJMP (Bureau of Jail Management and Penology)-Male Dormitory, in Payatas, Quezon City,” said Pulma.

“Meanwhile, the principal custody over the person of accused Romualdez is transferred and primarily placed under the responsibility of the BJMP Quezon City Jail-Male Dormitory, which may seek the assistance of the PNP-CIDG (Philippine National Police-Criminal Investigation and Detection Group) regarding security concerns,” he added.

During the Thursday hearing, Romualdez’s admitting physician, Dr. Kurt Allen Sibayan, revealed that the former speaker’s condition was not an “emergency case” when he was admitted to the hospital. He also said that Romualdez was immediately admitted and did not go to the emergency room.

Not only that, Sibayan said he did not see nor examine Romualdez because the attending physicians, including Romualdez’s hematologist Dr. Rosalio Torres, barred him from entering the room. He was told resident physicians cannot enter the room.

Torres explained that he ordered Romualdez’s admission because the lawmaker has a history of heart problems and complained of chest pains that day.

The Sandiganbayan 3rd Division will resume the hearing on Friday, September 11, and will bring in more Romualdez doctors for clarifications. – Rappler.com

World.title: We Belong in the Room: Filipino Youth in Global Spaces
World.content:
For many young Filipinos, international opportunities can feel out of reach. They can seem reserved for people with extensive experience, impressive credentials, or the financial means to participate. Sometimes, the biggest barrier is simply believing that we belong there.

I know that feeling.

So when I applied to the Universal Youth Leadership Summit (UYLS) 2026 in Bali, Indonesia, part of me questioned whether I was qualified enough to enter that space. I applied anyway.

From August 20 to 23, 2026, I had the opportunity to represent the Philippines as a fully funded delegate at UYLS 2026. Organized by Universal Youth Movement, the summit brought together around 50 young people from more than 20 countries under the theme “Sustainable Futures,” with discussions on leadership, green innovation, climate action, and mental wellbeing.

As my third international summit, I once again found myself in a room filled with young people from different cultures, communities, and experiences. But more than the discussions themselves, the experience reminded me of something important:

Filipino youth belong in global spaces.

Not because we need to prove that we are just as capable as young people from other countries, but because we already have perspectives, experiences, and ideas worth bringing to the table.

More Than Representation

At the summit, group discussions often challenged me to reconsider ideas I thought I already understood. A delegate would share an experience from their country, and suddenly an issue I viewed from one perspective had another dimension.

These conversations reinforced how global issues are rarely experienced equally.

Climate change may be a global problem, but its effects are shaped by geography, resources, governance, and inequality. The same can be said about education, mental wellbeing, and access to opportunities.

This is precisely why Filipino youth need to be part of these conversations.

We come from communities that have their own realities, challenges, and solutions. We understand what it means to live in a country vulnerable to climate disasters while navigating persistent inequalities. We have experiences that can enrich global conversations, not perspectives we need to leave behind before entering them.

The summit also went beyond the traditional conference setting. We participated in a beach clean-up at Jerman Beach in Kuta and attended a panel discussion on mental wellbeing at Politeknik Negeri Bali. These activities allowed us to engage with the community while learning alongside other delegates.

Even in informal conversations, cultural exchange became part of the experience. We were not simply delegates representing different countries. We were young people comparing realities, asking questions, sharing stories, and learning from one another.

Going Global, Bringing the Philippines With Us

My experience also changed how I understand the phrase “going global.”

Going global does not mean leaving the Philippines behind.

It means bringing the Philippines with us.

It means sharing our perspectives, culture, experiences, and realities with people from other countries, and returning home with lessons, connections, and ideas that can benefit our own communities.

International opportunities can sometimes become individual achievements: a certificate, a line on a resume, or a photograph taken abroad. But their value should extend beyond the individual.

When young Filipinos enter these spaces, we also expand the imagination of what other Filipino youth believe is possible for themselves.

That matters because many young people may never apply for opportunities like UYLS because they assume they cannot afford them, are not experienced enough, or simply are not the kind of person these programs are looking for.

I had those doubts, too.

But young people should not only be given opportunities because they are already confident, accomplished, or well-connected. They should also be given spaces where they can become those things.

The World Needs Filipino Youth

We are often told that young people are the leaders of tomorrow. But Filipino youth are already contributing today: organizing communities, advocating for causes, conducting research, creating art, building businesses, and engaging with issues that extend beyond our borders.

What we need is not permission to have something valuable to say.

We need more opportunities to say it.

My experience in Bali reminded me that I can enter a global space without leaving my identity at the door. I can bring my experiences, my questions, my culture, and the realities of the community I come from.

And I can return home ready to share what I have learned.

After every international opportunity, I find myself asking: What can I bring back? Who can I inspire? And how can I use what I learned to contribute to my community?

Perhaps these are questions more Filipino youth should be encouraged to ask.

Because the goal should not simply be to send Filipino youth abroad. It should be to build a generation confident enough to enter global spaces, contribute meaningfully, and return home ready to create change.

We go global not to leave the Philippines behind, but to bring the Philippines with us.
