World.title: 4 retired SC justices listed as ‘amici curiae’ for Duterte trial
World.content:
COURT SECRETARIAT. Senate President Win Gatchalian, presiding officer Chiz Escudero along with clerks of court, listen to the proceedings on Day 21 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on September 2, 2026.

The Senate impeachment court says four retired SC justices will serve as 'amici curiae' and share views on the voting threshold for Vice President Sara Duterte's trial

MANILA, Philippines – Four retired Supreme Court (SC) justices will serve as amici curiae or “friends of the court” in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte and weigh in on the 16-vote threshold for conviction.

Senate Impeachment Court spokesperson Reginald Tongol on Thursday, September 10, said the court has secured the formal participation of four retired justices as of 2 pm, with three physically appearing before the impeachment court on Wednesday, September 16.

The three are :

Retired Chief Justice Artemio V. Panganiban Retired Chief Justice Reynato S. Puno Retired Associate Justice Adolf S. Azcuna

Retired Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr., who served as presiding officer during the impeachment trial of former President Joseph Estrada in 2000, will also participate but will submit a legal memorandum instead of appearing in person.

“The Impeachment Court commends the prompt cooperation of these distinguished jurists. Securing their counsel marks a critical procedural milestone, ensuring that this trial proceeds anchored on verified constitutional bedrock,” said Tongol.

According to Tongol, the four-man panel constitutes the court’s initial list of amici curiae and additional experts may still be invited. He also said the court will not release or comment on any substantive details as regards written advisories submitted beforehand, adding that senator-judges will hold the right of first review of the documents.

“Since an amicus curiae provides expert legal doctrine, not factual evidence and the constitutional right to cross-examine applies only to fact witnesses, not scholars advising the bench, the legal panels will just sit and listen during the whole presentation,” he said.

Amici curiae panel

During the September 16 proceedings, Tongol said the three-member live panel of amici curiae will present their advisories, while Davide’s memorandum will be formally entered into the record. Only senator-judges will be allowed to ask clarificatory questions.

On September 23, the House prosecution panel and Duterte’s defense counsel will each be given exactly 15 minutes for oral arguments on the appeal. After a final round of questions from the senator-judges, the impeachment court will vote on the record, with time allotted for senator-judges to explain their votes.

“The Impeachment Court will not rush the resolution of this constitutional threshold. Doctrinal accuracy and constitutional exactitude take precedence over speed,” said Tongol.

The impeachment court raised discussions on inviting amici curiae after Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo sought clarification on the voting threshold for Duterte’s conviction or acquittal, citing the continued absence of four senators.

Four senator-judges were absent on day 23 of the trial: Loren Legarda, Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, Rodante Marcoleta and Jinggoy Estrada.

Legarda remains under extended medical leave abroad due to lung illness while Dela Rosa is in hiding in view of an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court (ICC).

Marcoleta and Estrada are detained for separate plunder charges.

Article XI, Section 3(6) of the 1987 Constitution states that the conviction of an impeachable official requires the concurrence of two-thirds of all the members of the Senate. – Rappler.com

World.title: Search expands after Palawan ferry fire kills 5 and leaves dozens missing
World.content:
FIRE. MV June Aster burns as flames and smoke rise after a fire broke out on the ferry, off the coast of Palawan, Philippines, in this screengrab taken from a handout video released on September 9, 2026.

Authorities estimate that more than 80 people remain unaccounted for, although the figures could still change

MANILA, Philippines – A large-scale search and rescue operation was underway off the western Philippine island of Palawan on Thursday, September 10, after a passenger ferry caught fire, killing five people and leaving dozens of passengers missing.

The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said multiple vessels and other assets were deployed to search for survivors, while rescue teams were using drift-modelling tools to identify areas where people may have been carried by currents.

Based on the vessel’s manifest, the number of survivors, currently at 43, and the fatalities reported so far, authorities estimated that more than 80 people remained unaccounted for, although the figures could still change.

Coast Guard spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said rescuers could not yet enter the vessel, with the search hampered by thick smoke still billowing from the ferry as well as concerns about extreme heat and the risk of explosions.

Drone footage released by the Coast Guard showed the blackened ferry surrounded by clear blue-green waters, with the vessel still generating smoke hours after the fire broke out on Wednesday night.

Cayabyab said the vessel’s manifest listed a total of 117 passengers and 17 crew members. The ferry had departed from Baseco in Manila and was bound for Coron, a popular tourist destination in Palawan known for its diving sites, beaches and island-hopping attractions.

Among the 43 people rescued were two Chilean nationals, said Aileen Ausente, spokesperson for PCG in Palawan, adding that air assets were on standby to help with rescue operations, the weather permitting.

The burned ferry had drifted farther from its original location overnight, carried by currents and winds, adding to the challenges facing rescuers, Cayabyab said.

The cause of the fire is under investigation.

Ferry travel is a common mode of transport in the Philippines, an archipelago of more than 7,600 islands, where millions of people rely on boats to travel between provinces.

The country has a patchy maritime safety record, and many previous ferry disasters have been linked to overcrowding, rough weather and lax enforcement of safety regulations. – Rappler.com

World.title: Dy dynasty dominates Isabela for decades
World.content:
SPEAKER. Isabela 6th District Representative Faustino 'Bojie' Dy III gives a speech after replacing House Speaker Martin Romualdez, at the House of Representatives on September 17, 2025.

Through strong and longstanding alliances, the Dy clan continues its dominance over Isabela politics, securing national and local posts mostly unopposed

Editor’s note: This is part of a Rappler series on Filipino families that have held political power for generations. The series traces how they built their influence, where it is strongest, and how it has endured over time. Each profile examines family ties, political networks, business interests, and roles in local and national government.

When Faustino “Bojie” Dy III assumed the speakership of the House of Representatives, the national spotlight shone on him — and on the deep political roots of his family back home.

The Dy dynasty’s rule over Isabela province began with patriarch Faustino Dy Sr. in the 1960s. He started his political career as a local councilor before becoming the mayor of Cauayan.

By 1971, the clan’s hold on the provincial capitol was established when he was elected governor for the first time. He occupied the top seat for 18 years, with a brief gap term in between, making him the longest-serving governor of Isabela to date.

The power was later passed down to his sons. Benjamin Dy served as governor from 1992 to 2001, followed by Faustino Dy Jr. from 2001 to 2004.

Another son, Faustino “Bojie” Dy III, stepped into the governorship in 2010, holding the post until reaching his term limit in 2019.

Rather than exiting the capitol, Bojie slid down to vice governor in the 2019 elections. He served until 2025 before taking over the seat of his son, Faustino “Inno” Dy V, as the representative of Isabela’s 6th District.

Currently, the Dy political dynasty simultaneously holds nine key positions across local and national fronts, according to the Congressional Policy and Budget Research Department.

The Dy Dynasty A timeline mapping the notable rotation and overlap of local government positions held by the Dy family across three decades.



Scroll or swipe right to see the dynasty’s full timeline. Tap or hover a bar for details, including family ties and each member’s years in power. Source: Comelec, public records

At the national level, Bojie Dy leads as House Speaker, anchoring a three-member family bloc in the 20th Congress that commands half of the province’s six legislative districts. Joining him are his nephews Faustino Michael Carlos “Mike” Dy III and Ian Paul Dy, representing Isabela’s 5th and 3rd District, respectively.

In the local scene, the dynasty maintains a multi-generational grip on provincial and municipal seats. In the provincial government, Bojie’s son Francis Faustino “Kiko” Dy, a former Echague mayor, serves as vice governor, while Bojie’s nephew, Manuel Faustino “King” Dy, sits on the provincial board.

Across Isabela’s towns, four other family members head key local executive and legislative offices:

Faustino “Inno” Dy V (son of Bojie, former 6th district representative) serves as mayor of Echague

Faustino “Dondon” Dy IV (son of Bojie) serves as the mayor of San Manuel

Caesar “Jaycee” Dy Jr. (nephew of Bojie) serves as the mayor of Cauayan City

Benjamin “Benjie” Dy III (nephew of Bojie) serves as the vice mayor of Cauayan City

This broad consolidation of authority was built on strategic alignments first forged by their patriarch Faustino Dy Sr., who closely aligned himself with the late dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos during and after the Martial Law years.

This historical Dy-Marcos alignment endures today, with Bojie now steering the clan’s national ties.

In the 2022 presidential elections, Bojie endorsed now-President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., helping deliver a decisive landslide victory across Isabela against the latter’s political rivals.

FAMILY. Bojie Dy and his family attend the swearing-in ceremony of his son, Echague Mayor Faustino ‘Inno’ Dy V. Photo from Inno’s FB Page

Expanding the power web

Beyond national ties, the Dys have also fortified their reign through their pacts with other local political powerhouses in their home province.

The Dy dynasty is closely tied to the Albano clan. The two families have been jointly governing Isabela for decades, maintaining continuous control and frequently rotating roles in major provincial and congressional seats.

While the Dys have kept the governorship to themselves for decades, term-limited Bojie’s transition to vice governor in 2019 allowed the Albanos to take the helm at the capitol. Since then, a Dy has yet to return to the provincial government’s top seat.

Yet far from marking a decline in influence, this strategic co-governance has only cemented the dual dominance of both families over Isabela’s political landscape.

Another political powerhouse firmly within the Dy network is the Tan clan of Santiago City.

In 2021, Bojie’s son, Inno Dy, married Alyssa Sheena Tan, who currently leads Santiago City as mayor.

Through this alliance, the Dys extended their influence in Congress through Sheena’s brother, Joseph Tan, who represents Isabela’s 4th District.

MEETING. Isabela politicians, including members of the Dy family, meet with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. Photo from Faustino Michael Carlos T. Dy III’s Facebook page.

Challenging the giant

With formidable backing from both local and national allies, challenging the Dys has proven to be a near-impossible task. Their electoral track record remains almost spotless, recording successive victories at the polls.

The Dys’ monopoly over the provincial capitol was cracked only twice in recent history, when former broadcast journalist and Ramon Magsaysay Awardee Grace Padaca snapped the clan’s long-ruling leadership in the 2004 and 2007 gubernatorial races.

Padaca’s political trajectory began in 2001 with a controversial run against Bojie Dy for Isabela’s 3rd District congressional seat. After initially trailing by 1,285 votes, Padaca contested the results before the House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal (HRET), citing alleged dagdag-bawas (vote-padding and shaving) operations in the municipality of Angadanan.

Following a lengthy process, the tribunal ultimately ruled in favor of Dy by a razor-thin margin of just 48 votes, largely after invalidating ballots simply marked as “Grace”.

Padaca redeemed herself in the 2004 elections by defeating then-incumbent governor Faustino Dy Jr., officially snapping the family’s governorship streak.

In a 2004 interview, she said that public outrage over alleged manipulation in 2001 and a growing desire to “free themselves from the claws of a dynasty” were critical factors in her victory.

She went on to secure a second term in 2007 against Benjamin Dy.

Her victories, however, proved to be a temporary pause rather than an end to the dynasty’s reign.

Padaca’s bid for a third term in 2010 was thwarted when Bojie Dy reclaimed the governorship for the family.

She mounted another challenge in 2019 by running for vice governor, initially aligning with Napoleon “Pol” Dy, who had a rift with his brother, then-governor Bojie.

But when the brothers reconciled, Pol withdrew his gubernatorial bid, leaving Padaca without a running mate. She ultimately lost the race to Bojie Dy.

Since then, the Dy clan’s grip has only tightened, developing into a multi-generational takeover of the country’s second-largest province.

In recent elections, their candidates faced virtually no opposition in key races, with Bojie, Ian Paul, and Mike sweeping congressional seats while Kiko secured the vice governorship.

Controlling the narrative

Strategic alliances are only part of the equation behind the Dys’ enduring dominance. According to a social science instructor at a local Isabela university, “dyadic clientelism” plays a central role in how voters engage with the clan.

“Iyong mga politicians, they provide ayuda, goods, and services na need ng mga tao. Dahil dito mas nagiging reliant [sila] sa concept ng patronage system sa Pilipinas,” the instructor said, referencing Julio G. Teehankee’s Patronage Democracy in the Philippines: Clans, Clients, and Competition in Local Elections.

(Politicians provide aid, goods, and services that people need. Because of this, [people] become more reliant on the concept of the patronage system in the Philippines.)

“Halimbawa na lang iyong scholarship na nakapangalan sa kanila. Tinatawag kasi itong BRO-Ed Scholarship. Branding kumbaga. (Take for instance the scholarship program carrying their name. It’s called the BRO-Ed Scholarship. It is a matter of branding.)”

“BRO-Ed” stands for Bojie-Rodito Opportunities for Education, named after House Speaker Bojie Dy and Governor Rodolfo “Rodito” Albano III, a direct reflection of their political partnership.

During the 2022 elections, The LaSallian reported that local program coordinators allegedly pressured Isabela government scholars to support the Marcos Jr.-Duterte campaign.

The Isabela Provincial Scholarship Program, said in a statement that the post was a “mere invitation” with no intention of coercing student-scholars.

With extensive political machinery and public resources at their disposal, the instructor emphasized that the Dys effectively exercise “control of the narrative” in Isabela.

“If you control the narrative, you decide what people focus on, what seems important, and what [should be] ignored,” they explained.

For JM Dela Cruz*, a political science student and an Isabela native, breaking this hold remains a monumental challenge unless an opposing force emerges with equal resources.

“They have built such popularity and reputation in the province. Hindi birong banggain ang ganyang kalaking pamilya. (It’s no joke to take on a family that huge.) It would take someone with the same great influence and machinery to match them in the elections,” Dela Cruz said.

Back in 2004, Padaca commented on the extent of the family’s influence: “Dumating na sa punto sa Isabela, kahit aso ang patakbuhin ng mga Dy ay mananalo kasi ganun sila ka-powerful.”

(It got to the point in Isabela where even if the Dys let a dog run for a government position, it would still win because they’re that powerful.)

Two decades later, that assessment continues to define the political landscape of Isabela. – Rappler.com

*Not their real names

World.title: PUP opens its Bulacan campus in Pandi
World.content:
Mayor Enrico Roque with other local officials and faculty members of the newly opened Polytechnic University of the Philippines Bulacan Campus during the inauguration of the tertiary institution in Barangay Mapulang Lupa on Monday. (Photo courtesy of the Office of Mayor Enrico Roque)

PANDI, Bulacan — The Polytechnic University of the Philippines (PUP) has opened its Bulacan campus this week, serving as the state college’s first extension facility.

The campus operates in Barangay Mapulang Lupa at Pandi town and is the first college institution to cater to residents in the municipality, said Pandi Mayor Enrico Roque during its inauguration on September 7.

He said 127 students pursuing a Bachelor of Science degrees in Tourism Management and in Business Administration, majoring in marketing management, have began regular classes.

Article continues after this 

READ: West PH Sea: China fires flares at unarmed Philippine aircraft

According to Roque, the Pandi municipal government funded the construction of the PUP Campus building and its complete facilities and will finance its operations.

“From just a dream in the past to today’s reality, we worked hard for this (on behalf of) our children and the next generation. This is the beginning of a new chapter for our beloved town. This is the legacy we bring to our people in Pandi,” the mayor said.

The PUP Pandi Campus will provide “the opportunity and easy access to quality education for all the town’s youth,” Roque told the Inquirer.

Pandi has been home to former informal settlers in Metro Manila who were relocated to various government housing settlements in many villages like Mapulang Lupa which has rapidly transformed into a suburb.

According to Roque, more courses will be offered in the coming semesters. INQ /mr

World.title: Calapan City to operate Mimaropa’s first 911 emergency hotline
World.content:
.

CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — Calapan will operate the first 911 Emergency Hotline in the Mimaropa region, bringing a faster, more coordinated response to all types of emergencies across the city.

The city government said the new emergency number, which will be officially launched on Friday, Sept. 11, shall serve as a unified, rapid-response channel for residents, guided by the principle that every second matters in times of crisis.

READ: PNP sees ‘room for improvement’ in 911 system but still cites gains

Article continues after this 

“Because every second counts, this is our swift response to any emergency situation throughout the city, in cooperation with various agencies,” Mayor Paulino Salvador Leachon said in a statement.

Leachon said the City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council, the Philippine National Police, the Bureau of Fire Protection, and the Public Safety Department will take the lead as the response group.

The initiative marks a significant upgrade in public safety and disaster response capabilities for Oriental Mindoro’s capital city. MIMAROPA is composed of the provinces of Oriental and Occidental Mindoro, Marinduque, Romblon, and Palawan. /mcm

World.title: SBMA outlines Subic port expansion, upgrades at Luzon forum
World.content:
SBMA officials pose for a photo during the Luzon Economic Corridor Investment Forum at the Grand Hyatt Manila on Thursday. From left are Seaport Department Assistant General Manager Mike Lazaro, Deputy Administrator for Operations Atty. Martin Kristoffer Roman, SBMA Director Yuri Allado, Chairman and Administrator Eduardo Jose L. Aliño, Senior Deputy Administrator for Operations Ronnie Yambao, and LEC Operating Advisor Nishant D’Souza. (Photo courtesy of SBMA)

SUBIC BAY FREEPORT — The Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority (SBMA) is advocating for the expansion and modernization of port facilities in this freeport as part of efforts to strengthen the Luzon Economic Corridor (LEC) and position the area as a major logistics and trade hub in the region.

SBMA Senior Deputy Administrator for Operations Ronnie Yambao presented the agency’s ongoing and planned port infrastructure projects during the LEC Investment Forum at the Grand Hyatt Manila on Thursday. Sept. 10.

Yambao said the projects were intended to improve port efficiency and capacity while supporting the movement of goods and attracting more investments to Subic.

Article continues after this 

“Our port infrastructure projects are designed to enhance operational efficiency, drive economic growth, and position Subic Bay as a premier logistics and trade hub in Southeast Asia,” Yambao said.

SBMA Chairman and Administrator Eduardo Jose Aliño said the agency would continue upgrading its port facilities, expanding capacity and adopting new technologies to improve cargo-handling operations.

READ: SBMA port operations revenue climbs 20% in first quarter of 2026

“We are committed to continuous modernization and innovation, supporting the Philippines’ broader goals of trade expansion and investment attraction,” Aliño said.

The push to develop Subic’s port infrastructure comes as the area assumes a larger role in the Luzon Economic Corridor, a government-backed initiative aimed at improving connectivity and linking industrial, manufacturing and logistics hubs across Luzon.

Article continues after this 

The corridor is also seen as a platform for attracting investments in strategic industries and strengthening supply chains, with the Philippines working with partner countries to develop infrastructure and economic opportunities along the corridor.

LEC, however, has also drawn concerns from local stakeholders and environmental advocates, who have raised questions about the potential impact of increased port and industrial activities on coastal communities and the environment.

Article continues after this 

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who graced the forum, underscored the importance of the LEC in developing high-technology industries, logistics, manufacturing, connectivity, and supply chains.

Subic’s strategic location and existing port facilities have long made the former US naval base a key logistics gateway in Central Luzon.

The port also serves businesses operating within the Subic Bay Freeport, which hosts manufacturing, logistics and other export-oriented industries.

In recent years, the SBMA has sought to further develop Subic as a maritime and logistics center as competition among ports and logistics hubs in the region intensifies.

The agency said the latest infrastructure initiatives were aimed at making Subic more competitive while supporting broader efforts to expand trade and investment in the Philippines.

The LEC was initially launched by the Philippines, the United States and Japan and has since expanded to include Australia, Canada, Denmark, France, Italy, South Korea, Sweden, Spain, and the United Kingdom.

World.title: Mark Villar seeks stronger mental health services amid rise in suicides
World.content:
Sen. Mark Villar —Photo from his office

MANILA, Philippines — Citing an increase in suicides in recent years, Sen. Mark A. Villar urges the government to act immediately to expand access to mental health services, strengthen prevention efforts, and provide adequate funding for mental health care.

“Our people deserve a healthcare system that treats mental health with the same urgency, respect, and dignity as physical health. The numbers are deeply concerning,” Villar said in his privilege speech in observance of Suicide Prevention Month.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, Villar cited data from the Philippine Statistics Authority showing an alarming 3,379 deaths from intentional self-harm in 2024, up from 3,133 in 2023. From January to June 2025, the Philippine National Police also logged nearly 2,000 suicide cases.

Article continues after this 

In Metro Manila alone, the National Capital Region Police Office recorded 111 cases from January to March 2026, compared with 33 during the same period last year—a 236-percent increase.

READ: DOH points to low pay for lack of psychiatrists, psychologists in PH

Shortage of professionals

Villar also raised concern over the severe shortage of mental health professionals.

A 2026 analysis cited in his speech found only 409 accredited psychiatrists nationwide, 54.52 percent of whom are concentrated in Metro Manila. This translates to just 0.38 psychiatrists for every 100,000 Filipinos, far below the WHO-recommended minimum of 10 per 100,000 cited in the speech.

“But Mr. President, how can we expect Filipinos to seek help when help itself remains difficult to access?” Villar said.

Article continues after this 

End the stigma

Villar also stressed the importance of breaking the stigma that continues to discourage Filipinos from speaking up and seeking help.

“It is high time to stop romanticizing resilience when what our people need is support. It’s not weakness to seek help. It’s not being dramatic. And most of all, it’s not something to be ashamed of,” Villar said.

Article continues after this 

He also called on families, friends, and communities to normalize conversations about mental health and provide a safe space for those experiencing difficulties.

“May we encourage, normalize, and open discussions on mental health with our friends and loved ones. Let’s end the stigma. Let’s make it a habit to check on and listen without judgment to people experiencing mental health struggles. Let’s make them feel that they’re not alone in this battle,” Villar said.

Villar emphasized that every case represents a life and a family, and that mental health services must be available regardless of a person’s location, age, or status in life.

“Self-harm and mental health-related deaths are not merely statistics. Behind every number is a person — a friend, a family member, a colleague, or a schoolmate. There are lives and stories behind every figure we present in this chamber,” Villar said.

READ: Suicide prevention begins with listening, understanding, and support

Mental health funding

With Congress now deliberating on the proposed 2027 national budget, Villar called for sufficient funding for the comprehensive implementation of existing mental health laws and the improvement of the country’s mental healthcare system.

Villar likewise highlighted some measures he filed in the previous and current Congress to strengthen prevention, early intervention, and access to support:

Student Guidance Counseling Act, which was integrated into the Comprehensive School Safety Act

One Registered Nurse in Every Barangay

Anti-Workplace Bullying Act

Youth Suicide Prevention Act, which seeks to institutionalize suicide intervention through life-planning education for the youth

“As we observe the Suicide Prevention Month, let us honor those we have lost not only with words, but with meaningful action. May their lives strengthen our resolve to act and to legislate with compassion, urgency, and purpose, in service of every Filipino,” Villar said.

“One life needlessly lost is already one too many. We must take our part in ensuring that no life would succumb to the pressures of mental health struggles,” Villar concluded.

World.title: VP Sara Duterte seeks TRO on grave threats case
World.content:
File photo of Vice President Sara Duterte (INQUIRER / GRIG C. MONTEGRANDE)

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte has asked the Supreme Court (SC) to immediately resolve her petition seeking relief for her grave threats case before a Quezon City court continues with its proceedings.

In her urgent motion dated Sept. 7, Duterte sought the urgent resolution of her application for a temporary restraining order (TRO) and/or writ of preliminary injunction as she asserted that she has immunity from suit as a sitting impeachable official.

The request for a TRO and other injunctive reliefs are included in the petition for certiorari and prohibition filed by Duterte last month.

Article continues after this 

“With the evident haste by which (Duterte’s) criminal prosecution continues to move, there is a real and present danger that the reliefs sought… the restraint of criminal prosecution of an incumbent impeachable officer–under the constitutional rule of limited procedural immunity, will be rendered moot and academic, if immediate injunctive relief is not now obtained,” read the motion released by the high court on Thursday.

The Vice President noted that Branch 98 of the Quezon City Regional Trial Court (RTC) presided by Judge Maria Angelica de Ramos, one of the respondents in her petition, already moved the case after an arrest warrant was issued on Sept. 4 and her arraignment was scheduled on Sept. 11.

“The imminent arraignment and pre-trial demonstrate that the criminal proceedings are not merely threatened but are actively and rapidly progressing, notwithstanding the serious and far-reaching jurisdictional and constitutional issues to be resolved,” Duterte added.

Aside from De Ramos, other respondents in the petition are Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida, Prosecutor General Richard Fadullon and the cybercrime division of the National Bureau of Investigation.

The latest motion by Duterte’s camp came after she posted bail last week for her provisional liberty.

Article continues after this 

Vida, in a press briefing on Thursday, maintained that Department of Justice prosecutors proceeded with filing the case against Duterte on Aug. 11 because only the President enjoys immunity from suit while in office.

Duterte is facing three counts of grave threats for her outburst in an online press conference in November 2024 wherein she said that she hired a hitman to target President Ferdinand R. Marcos, First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez if she herself gets killed. /gsg

World.title: Taguig prosecutors dismiss Sara Duterte’s perjury case vs Ramil Madriaga
World.content:
Vice President Sara Duterte. INQUIRER PHOTO / GRIG C. MONTEGRANDE

MANILA, Philippines — The Taguig City Prosecutor’s Office has dismissed the perjury complaints filed by Vice President Sara Duterte against Ramil Madriaga, her alleged former aide.

In a 19-page resolution released on Thursday, the prosecutors junked Duterte’s complaint against Madriaga due to “insufficiency of evidence.”

“While complainant has presented evidence disputing respondent’s assertions, the evidence presently on record does not establish prima facie, with reasonable certainty of conviction, that respondent knowingly and willfully made materially false statements under oath in violation of Article 183 of the Revised Penal Code,” the Taguig Prosecutor’s Office said in the decision.

Article continues after this 

READ: Sara Duterte files another perjury case vs Madriaga

“Accordingly, the Complaint must be dismissed for insufficiency of evidence,” the prosecutor added.

It was in March when Duterte filed her first perjury complaint against Madriaga after her supposed former aide submitted an affidavit to the Office of the Ombudsman claiming that he had delivered large sums of money to different people under her instructions.

The vice president denied the accusation, maintaining that she had neither personal nor professional dealings with Madriaga, and that his claim of having served as her “bagman’’ or courier for diverted confidential funds was false.

Duterte filed another perjury complaint in August consisted of approximately 1,000 pages, which “thoroughly exposes Madriaga’s malicious and deliberate falsehoods.” /mr

World.title: Spox: Sara Duterte to attend Friday arraignment for grave threats case
World.content:
File photo of Vice President Sara Duterte. INQUIRER PHOTO / GRIG C. MONTEGRANDE

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte will personally attend her arraignment on Friday morning over three counts of grave threats, her spokesperson said.

In a message on Thursday, Duterte’s spokesperson, lawyer Paolo Panelo Jr., confirmed with the Inquirer that Duterte will be arraigned at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court Branch 98 at 8:30 am on Friday, Sept. 10.

Panelo said, “as required by law,” the vice president will be physically present in her arraignment.

Article continues after this 

READ: Sara Duterte posts bail: I don’t trust the court

In the arraignment, Duterte will be formally informed of the charges against her and asked to enter a plea of guilty or not guilty.

Duterte had earlier posted P360,000 bail for the three counts of grave threats, but expressed distrust in the court, police, and even the security personnel assigned to protect her.

The vice president’s criminal case stem from remarks she made during an online press conference on Nov. 23, 2024.

There, she said she had spoken to someone about killing President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., first lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and then-Speaker Martin Romualdez if she herself were killed.

Duterte has denied the allegations. The same remarks also form part of the impeachment case against her pending before the Senate. /mr

World.title: Suicide prevention begins with listening, understanding and support
World.content:
INQUIRER GRAPHICS

MANILA, Philippines — “A thought about death does not always mean a wish to die.”

The Psychological Association of the Philippines (PAP) pointed this out Wednesday, Sept. 9, the eve of World Suicide Prevention Day, which is observed every Sept. 10 to promote awareness that suicide can be prevented.

“Suicide prevention can begin before crisis,” it said. “Sometimes, it begins by becoming more willing and more able to notice, to understand, and to talk about difficult thoughts.”

Article continues after this 

From 2024 to 2026, the International Association for Suicide Prevention (IASP) has highlighted the need to change the narrative on suicide, calling on people to “start conversations.”

The IASP said suicide is a critical public health concern with “far-reaching social, emotional and economic consequences,” with an estimated 727,000 people dying by suicide worldwide each year.

READ: Suicide cases in NCR more than double in first 3 months of 2026 — NCRPO

Based on the latest available data from the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), 3,315 Filipinos died of intentional self-harm in 2025, higher than the 3,067 deaths recorded in 2024.

Intentional self-harm killed 4,498 people in the Philippines in 2021, at the height of the Covid-19 crisis that claimed thousands of lives while bringing economic and social activities to a standstill.

Article continues after this 

The next two years saw a decline in suicide deaths, to 3,132 in 2022 and 3,133 in 2023.

From January to February this year, the PSA recorded 194 deaths.

Article continues after this 

No more silence

For the IASP, changing the narrative on suicide starts with understanding the complexity of the issue and “shifting from a culture of silence towards one of openness, empathy and support.”

“As we reach the final year of this theme, the priority is to build on three years of these conversations, to break down barriers, raise awareness and strengthen cultures of understanding and support that continue beyond 2026,” it said.

GRAPHIC: Ed Lustan/INQUIRER.net

The World Health Organization (WHO) pointed out that while suicide affects people of all ages and backgrounds in the Philippines, the latest data show that some groups bear a greater burden than others.

More than 80% of the more than 3,000 suicide deaths in 2022 were among men, while around 42% occurred among young people ages 15 to 29.

READ: 1 of 5 young Filipinos have considered suicide – UP survey

“Evidence suggests that social norms, stigma around help-seeking, and limited access to timely mental health care can make it harder for people to get the support they need,” the WHO said.

The WHO pointed out that understanding who is most affected can help shape more targeted prevention initiatives — from promoting life skills and emotional well-being among young people to strengthening community-based mental health services, early identification and access to care.

Ask, listen, stay

PAP called on everyone to make it easier for people to talk about thoughts that can be difficult to put into words.

“A thought about death does not always mean a wish to die. A wish to disappear does not always tell us what a person means. And someone thinking about suicide may not always say it directly,” it said.

“We don’t have to rush to conclusions,” it stressed. “We can become curious about what a thought means, listen without judgment, ask what we need to know, and connect someone to support when it’s needed.”

PAP said starting a conversation does not mean having all the answers.

“Sometimes, it simply means being willing to ask, listen, and stay.”
