“Suicide prevention is not one conversation, one intervention, or one person’s responsibility. It can happen in the everyday moments when someone feels seen, supported, and less alone,” it said. /dm

World.title: AFD 2026: Kazakhstan Seeks Role in Finance’s Next Digital Frontier
World.content:
ASTANA – We want to take it out of the unregulated area and make it work, because it works whether we want it or not,” National Bank Chairman Timur Suleimenov said during the plenary session Rewiring the Architecture of Finance at Astana Finance Days 2026 on Sept. 9, capturing the regulatory dilemma at the center of a financial transformation that is rapidly moving from experiment to infrastructure.

As blockchain, stablecoins, tokenization, programmable money and AI reshape how assets are created, moved and managed, Kazakhstan is betting that an early embrace of new financial technologiesm, combined with rules and institutional trust, can become a competitive advantage.

The discussion brought together Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC) Governor Renat Bekturov, Freedom Holding Corp. CEO Timur Turlov, Anchorage Digital Global Head of Stablecoin Solutions Sergio Mello and technology entrepreneur Balaji Srinivasan, who approached that transformation from different angles, but agreed that the financial system is changing not only in how services are delivered, but also in the infrastructure underpinning them.

Suleimenov identified geopolitical fragmentation and technology as two of the forces reshaping global finance, arguing that changes in trade and investment flows are already translating into changes in financial flows.

“Trade flows, the finance flows are changing fundamentally. We’re seeing division across the Atlantic. We’re seeing division on the North American continent. We’re seeing trade wars and semi-trade wars across the world. And, of course, finance has always been a part of the debate. They always went hand-in-hand,” he said.

At the same time, the emergence of blockchain and tokenized assets is challenging financial regulators to develop rules for technologies that did not exist within the traditional architecture.

“We’re still in the rule-setting phase. There is no set of rules for decentralized finance, for digital finance, crypto finance,” he said.

For Kazakhstan, however, he described that uncertainty as an opportunity to establish a regulatory framework while the global market is still taking shape.

“We have adopted a very comprehensive set of rules, not only frameworks, but rules, very hands-on with how you trade cryptocurrency, how you trade stablecoins, what you do with the real world tokenized assets and things like that,” Suleimenov said

The task, he added, is not to stop technologies that are already finding users, but to ensure they operate within a system that protects trust and financial stability.

“We want to take it out of the unregulated area and make it work, because it works whether we want it or not. It will be working, but I think it is to the greater good of all of us that it works in rightly regulated area,” he said.

AIFC as a testing ground

AIFC Governor Bekturov said Kazakhstan’s advantage lies not simply in the technologies themselves, but in the people and institutions willing to experiment with them.

“I think that the first competitive advantage of Kazakhstan is its people,” he said, pointing to regulators, entrepreneurs and younger generations that are more open to new financial models.

He also highlighted the political decision to establish the AIFC as a separate jurisdiction, noting that it has created space for Kazakhstan to test new financial products before deciding how they should be treated across the wider economy.

“You give the optionality to yourself, but also to the investors coming into the country, so they can kind of choose with which system they would like to work,” Bekturov said.

The AIFC, he added, has provided a practical environment in which regulators can observe new products, assess their risks and determine what works.

“I think in that terms, AIFC, was also helpful to the national regulators to kind of test out certain products and to see how that works, what are the risks, where we want to adapt and which part we want to regulate more or less,” he said.

That approach, Bekturov said, has helped Kazakhstan move comparatively quickly in areas including digital assets, the digital tenge, stablecoins and tokenized real-world assets.

“We are one of the leaders in the region in terms of adapting digital assets, digital tenge, stable coins in tenge and what goes beyond like tokenization of real assets,” he said.

For Turlov, the transformation is already visible from the customer and business perspective, although he cautioned that technological innovation does not necessarily change the underlying nature of a financial asset.

“Many products change their form. Very rarely they change the substance of them,” he said.

Tokenization, in his view, is often another way of representing assets that financial markets have long known how to securitize. The more meaningful change is the ability to deliver those products faster, more efficiently and across borders. Turlov said Kazakh financial companies are already competing with global firms, which makes the ability to innovate domestically increasingly important.

“We have rules, we have trust, we have money on this market. Because sometimes if it’s very easy to innovate, but it’s not much trust, not much rules, not much money, it’s also very hard to do business. But I think now here in Kazakhstan, we have this perfect balance of many different factors,” he said.

According to him, that’s why Kazakhstan can function as a testing ground for global financial technology companies.

“Kazakhstan is feeling like a great laboratory for global fintechs because if you can succeed here, so maybe you can scale out to other markets,” he added.

From digital money to digital property

Technology entrepreneur Balaji Srinivasan offered the most expansive vision of where the transformation could lead, noting that the rise of digital finance should be understood through what he called “technopolitics.”

“You can think of the cloud as almost like a new continent that has arisen above us,” he said, suggesting that the digital economy is creating a new domain through which people, businesses and assets can interact regardless of geography.

“That’s a huge opportunity for Kazakhstan because Kazakhstan is landlocked, but it’s not cloud-locked. It can access any country in the world, any person in the world through the cloud,” he said.

In his view, the next stage could involve much more than moving existing financial assets onto blockchain. Real estate, vehicles, infrastructure and other forms of capital could increasingly be represented through digital credentials and cryptographic keys.

“The fundamental innovation of Bitcoin was Internet-first registry of assets. Now, it’s a smart contract. Now, it’s code. So it actually lives in the cloud primarily,” Srinivasan said.

His proposition was that Kazakhstan could eventually position itself as a trusted physical and regulatory gateway connecting these digital assets with the real economy.

“Kazakhstan can be the registry where those things can be traded from the cloud back to the land and back to the world,” he said.

Mello took a more immediate view, saying that some of the technologies discussed are already becoming standard financial infrastructure.

“Stablecoins are a very clear example. It’s an instrument that is no longer an experiment,” he said.

According to him, the next stage is less about proving that digital finance works and more about building the regulatory and physical infrastructure to support it at scale.

“After 10 years of experimentation, the next 10 years of crypto becoming a technology standard that leads us to financial systems,” Mello said.

He compared the process to building airports, highways and railroads, saying that governments have to think ahead about the infrastructure required to support future economic activity.

“With all the rest of the world moving really fast, the pace at which innovation extends not only in financial infrastructure but also elsewhere is such that any moment of inaction today, from a regulatory policy perspective, is equivalent to a decade of inaction in the last century,” Mello said.

Digital tenge moves beyond payments

Kazakhstan’s own experience with digital currency illustrates how quickly priorities can evolve. Suleimenov said the National Bank has shifted away from viewing the digital tenge primarily as a retail payment instrument, given the range of digital payment solutions commercial banks already offer. Instead, one of the most promising uses is programmable public spending, allowing funds to be tracked and used according to the purpose for which they were allocated.

“I think the best usage for the central bank’s digital currency that we see is actually program and track the public spending,” Suleimenov said.

He said the approach can be applied to projects ranging from a kindergarten in a rural area to major industrial developments, with smart contracts helping ensure that public funds are spent as originally intended. The initiative began as a pilot in 2023 and has since been incorporated into legislation, with the government and the National Bank working to expand the areas where such mechanisms can be applied.

“It’s not just about public finances. It’s about overall government’s efficiency of running the economy, of running the social sphere, running the infrastructure to make it work with less amount of resources included,” Suleimenov said.

As financial platforms become more sophisticated, Turlov said another challenge is emerging: customers may struggle to navigate the very technology designed to make their lives easier.

“Adoption of technology sometimes is a much greater challenge than inventing some technology itself,” he said, noting that modern financial applications can combine banking, insurance, brokerage, travel and other services in a single platform.

He believes AI assistants could become an important interface between customers and increasingly complex financial infrastructure, allowing people to describe what they want in ordinary language rather than understanding the mechanics of each service.

“They just need to tell it in normal words, and that’s how I believe we can really improve the quality of life. Because sometimes products became so sophisticated that they need a very professional customer to consume them. And maybe AI Assistant will help to solve that,” Turlov said.

For Kazakhstan’s regulators, the challenge will be maintaining that openness without moving so far ahead of the market that innovation becomes detached from actual demand.

“When you’re a little front-run, you have a chance of failure or being too premature with some innovation. You are a little bit ahead because it’s still a competition, right? But yet you are not far behind because then the market is capturing this moment,” Bekturov said, describing regulation as a continuous balancing act.

That balance between innovation and trust, experimentation and regulation, the physical economy and the digital one may ultimately determine whether Kazakhstan becomes simply an early adopter of the next generation of financial technology or one of the places where that new architecture is actually built.

World.title: Rybakina Makes History as Kazakhstan’s First World No. 1
World.content:
ASTANA – Elena Rybakina has made history for Kazakhstan, becoming the first athlete from the country to rise to the top of the Women’s Tennis Association (WTA) singles rankings, a breakthrough that puts Kazakh tennis at the summit of the sport.

Rybakina secured the top position in the WTA live rankings after defeating China’s Qinwen Zheng in the quarterfinals on Sept. 9. She overtook Belarusian Aryna Sabalenka, who had previously held the top spot. The official rankings will be updated on Monday, Sept. 14.

Rybakina is the first player representing Kazakhstan, in either women’s or men’s singles, to reach the leading position in the global rankings.

Rybakina later reflected on the milestone in an Instagram post, highlighting its significance for her country.

“Anything is possible when you believe! Proud to represent Kazakhstan and make history as the country’s first world number 1,” she wrote.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev congratulated Rybakina on the achievement, praising her talent, dedication and determination.

“Reaching the top of the WTA rankings is a sporting pinnacle achieved by you through phenomenal talent, tremendous hard work and an unwavering belief in yourself,” Tokayev said in his congratulatory message.

He noted that the achievement had brought prominence to Kazakh sport and placed Rybakina’s name in the history of world tennis.

“Your journey serves as an inspiring example for thousands of young athletes in our country and millions of tennis fans around the world,” Tokayev said.

Tokayev also highlighted Rybakina’s conduct both on and off the court, noting her high standards of behavior and communication with people from different backgrounds.

He wished the tennis player continued success and urged her to maintain her champion’s mindset as she pursues new achievements.

Rybakina’s rise to the top marks a landmark moment for Kazakhstan’s tennis, giving the country its first-ever world No. 1 in singles and adding a new chapter to its sporting history.

On Sept. 11, Rybakina will face U.S. Coco Gauff in the semifinals.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan Move to Revive Caspian Passenger Ferry Service
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan are working to resume passenger ferry services across the Caspian Sea, reopening a route that connected the two countries until 2020 and could provide an additional boost to tourism and regional connectivity.

Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Azerbaijan Alim Bayel said the Kazakh side had proposed restoring passenger services on the Kuryk–Baku–Kuryk ferry route, which was suspended during the COVID-19 pandemic.

According to Bayel, around 1,500 passengers used the ferry service annually before its suspension. He expressed confidence that demand could be higher when the route resumes, as travel and tourism links between Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan have expanded in recent years. The resumption of the ferry line, he said, will give impetus to the development of passenger traffic between the two countries, strengthen tourism exchange and expand the opportunities of the Middle Corridor.

The Azerbaijani side has supported Kazakhstan’s proposal, and the transport authorities of both countries have begun working on the necessary steps to restore passenger services as soon as possible.

A specific launch date has not yet been announced.

Ferry link to complement growing air connectivity

The proposed ferry service would add a maritime connection to an already expanding network of links between Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan. Currently, 37 flights connect Baku with Astana, Almaty, Shymkent, Aktau and Atyrau, providing the main passenger connection between the two countries.

The revival of the Kuryk–Baku route would offer a different mode of travel across the Caspian, potentially creating additional opportunities for tourists and travelers interested in combining land and maritime journeys.

The route also has a broader regional significance because Kuryk is one of Kazakhstan’s key ports on the Caspian Sea and forms part of the country’s transport infrastructure supporting the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, commonly known as the Middle Corridor.

The Middle Corridor connects China and Central Asia with the South Caucasus and Europe through the Caspian Sea. While its primary role is the movement of cargo, stronger passenger connectivity can contribute to wider economic and tourism ties along the same geographic corridor.

A route returning to a changing Caspian

The planned revival comes as Kazakhstan and other Caspian countries are paying increasing attention to changes in the sea’s water level. A newly emerged island was recently reported in the Caspian Sea amid a continued decline in water levels. The development has renewed attention to the environmental and economic consequences of the Caspian’s shallowing, including potential implications for maritime transport and coastal infrastructure.

The passenger ferry proposal therefore comes at a time when the Caspian is gaining importance as a regional transport link, while its changing physical conditions are creating new challenges for maritime activity.

World.title: BlackRock at AFD 2026: AI Investors Should Stay Calm and Focus on Constraints
World.content:
ASTANA – As artificial intelligence drives a new investment boom, the best strategy may be to resist the excitement and focus instead on the bottlenecks that could constrain its growth, according to Ben Powell, managing director and chief investment strategist for Asia-Pacific at the BlackRock Investment Institute.

Speaking at the Astana Finance Days 2026 forum on Sept. 9 during a fireside chat moderated by Assel Mukazhanova, chief executive officer of Astana International Exchange (AIX), Powell said investors should “stay calm” and look for the physical constraints created by the rapid expansion of AI.

“I know it’s very exciting. But try to be more boring and focus on the constraint. Constraint is opportunity, actually. This is the philosophical approach,” Powell said.

For BlackRock, the current AI boom is not simply a story about technology companies and software. Powell said the most interesting investment opportunities are increasingly emerging from the infrastructure required to make AI possible, including power, semiconductors, memory and copper.

“We have a super boom, but we are short of copper. We are short of chip. We are short of electrician. Where we are very focused is trying to be a little bit ahead of the next constraint,” he said.

Among those constraints, power is currently the most significant opportunity, according to Powell, as the expansion of AI infrastructure drives rising demand for electricity and related infrastructure.

“Our favorite constraints at the moment is power,” he said.

Powell described AI as a major structural transformation of the global economy, noting that its significance may still be underestimated.

“We are turning sand into thinking,” he said, describing the technology as fundamentally different from conventional goods and services because intelligence can be applied across virtually every sector.

Yet for investors, he said, the task is to separate the scale of the technological transformation from the market excitement surrounding it.

The AI investment thesis was part of a broader discussion about a changing global investment environment, in which Powell said geopolitical fragmentation, higher inflation and interest rates are making markets more complex and forcing investors to become more selective.

“We expect there will be more geopolitical flashpoints. The world has become more complicated and, frankly, more dangerous,” he said.

Powell said this new environment is pushing investors toward more targeted decisions across geographies, asset classes and long-term themes, including AI.

Kazakhstan on BlackRock’s radar

Against this broader shift, Kazakhstan could have an opportunity to attract greater global institutional capital as its financial market develops, Powell said. BlackRock is watching the country’s regulatory direction, changing market infrastructure, liquidity and market breadth, he said.

“As the market becomes more liquid, we can invest more. It’s just a fact,” Powell said.

He described Kazakhstan’s potential transition to emerging market status as an important milestone, while stressing it would not mark the end of the country’s development as an investment destination.

“We are watching. When will Kazakhstan become an emerging market? It will be a great moment. We can have a celebration. It will be a great, important milestone. But don’t get confused. That is not the end of the story. The story continues forever,” he said.

Powell also said the investment environment is becoming more encouraging, using the informal term “vibes” to describe a shift that is hard to capture through quantitative indicators alone.

“It’s almost like a feel. Like the feel is getting better, and the young people, they call it the vibes. So the vibes are better. This is hard to quantify, but you can feel it,” he added.

Private markets move closer to the mainstream

The changing investment landscape is also expanding the role of private markets, according to Powell, as investors seek exposure to areas of economic growth not fully represented in public markets. Many AI companies, for example, remain privately held, meaning investors seeking exposure to the sector may increasingly need access to private markets, he said.

At the same time, governments facing balance-sheet constraints are creating greater demand for private capital to finance infrastructure and other long-term projects.

“The opportunity is going to grow because the governments are a little bit balance-sheet constrained. This is the polite way of saying they have no money, a little bit no money. So they need us,” Powell said bluntly.

Powell said private markets should increasingly be viewed as part of mainstream portfolio construction rather than as an “alternative.”

“I don’t care if we have 10% public equity, 60% public equity. I don’t care. I want a portfolio that makes sense,” he said.

Private credit is also likely to remain a structural growth area as financial systems diversify funding sources beyond banks, he said, while cautioning that investors must pay close attention to credit quality and underwriting.

Tokenization could change capital markets

Powell also sees tokenization as having the potential to fundamentally change financial markets, although the transition will take time. Tokenization could eventually allow investors to gain economic exposure to a much wider range of assets through digital instruments, he said.

“Intellectually, philosophically, I think it makes sense, and I think it will happen,” Powell said.

But realizing that potential will require regulatory frameworks and market infrastructure that can support tokenized assets. Powell said tokenized assets could become a more normal part of portfolios over the next five to 10 years as the regulatory and financial infrastructure develops. For BlackRock, the broader transformation is part of a long-term shift in how the firm approaches investment.

Powell said the company’s core philosophy remains focused on using technology to manage risk and help clients, while the tools available to investors have expanded from ETFs and public equities to private markets, infrastructure and digital assets. Technology and data, he said, will increasingly determine how asset managers operate in a more complex investment environment.

For Powell, that also means using AI himself. He said he uses an AI assistant during his morning commute to review information, process emails and prepare for the day, while BlackRock increasingly integrates AI into its operations. The underlying investment principle, however, remains surprisingly simple: as the AI boom accelerates, investors should not necessarily chase the excitement. They should look for what the boom cannot get enough of.

World.title: CPC Oil Flows Surge Despite Disruptions as Kazakhstan’s Export Routes Gain Importance, Expert Says
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan increased oil transportation through KazTransOil’s main pipeline network by 4% in the first eight months of 2026, while volumes transported into the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) system rose 39%, highlighting both stronger oil flows and the continued strategic importance of export infrastructure to the country’s resource economy.

KazTransOil transported 30.639 million tonnes of crude through its main oil pipeline system between January and August, while the company’s consolidated volume of oil transportation and petroleum-product transshipment reached 31.89 million tonnes, also up 4% year-on-year, the company reported.

The increase was recorded across several important routes, including the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC), Atasu-Alashankou, the Port of Aktau and the MunaiTas pipeline. At the same time, the distribution of those flows illustrates why Kazakhstan continues to need multiple export channels. While alternative routes are growing, the country’s largest oil volumes still depend on established pipeline infrastructure connecting its fields to foreign markets.

Growth across several routes

Kazakhstan’s domestic refining sector remained one of the largest destinations for crude transported through KazTransOil’s network. During the reporting period, 12.087 million tonnes were delivered to the country’s refineries. The Atyrau Refinery received 3.567 million tonnes, PetroKazakhstan Oil Products 3.664 million tonnes, Pavlodar Petrochemical Plant 4.316 million tonnes and Caspi Bitum 540,000 tonnes.

Export and transit routes also recorded increases. The Atyrau-Samara section of the Uzen-Atyrau-Samara pipeline transported 6.922 million tonnes, up 2% from the same period last year. A further 8.145 million tonnes passed through the TON-2 section, an increase of 5%. The Atasu-Alashankou route handled 7.602 million tonnes, up 3%. Particularly notable was the increase in Kazakhstan’s own oil exports through the route, which rose 24% to 863,000 tonnes.

The largest year-on-year increase among the major routes reported by KazTransOil was recorded in transportation into the CPC-K system. The volume reached 3.123 million tonnes, up 39%. At Aktau port, oil loaded onto tankers using KazTransOil infrastructure increased 6% to 2.384 million tonnes. Shipments toward the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline rose 12% to 1.034 million tonnes. The Kazakhstan-China pipeline system transported 13.121 million tonnes, up 2%, while oil transportation through the MunaiTas pipeline increased 10% to 4.302 million tonnes.

The figures point to a more diversified network of flows, but they do not necessarily mean that Kazakhstan has eliminated its dependence on individual corridors.

When infrastructure becomes a resource constraint

This distinction matters because the economic value of oil does not end at the wellhead. According to oil and gas analyst Abzal Narymbetov, a useful comparison comes from Qatar, where disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz have demonstrated how quickly access to a transport route can become a constraint on a resource-rich country’s ability to monetize its reserves.

The same principle, he said, applies to Kazakhstan, although the structure of the vulnerability is different. Kazakhstan has several routes for exporting crude, including CPC, the Caspian Sea and China. But the capacity of these alternatives is not currently equivalent to the volumes that can be moved through the country’s dominant export system.

This creates a strategic challenge. If the largest route experiences disruption or reduced availability, Kazakhstan cannot simply redirect all affected production elsewhere without encountering capacity, infrastructure and logistical constraints.

In other words, an alternative route is not necessarily an alternative at scale.

CPC remains central despite diversification

The latest KazTransOil figures demonstrate that Kazakhstan is already using several transportation channels. The 24% increase in the country’s own oil exports through Atasu-Alashankou and the 12% growth in shipments toward the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline indicate that eastern and trans-Caspian directions are expanding.

The increase in oil loading at Aktau also reinforces the importance of the Caspian route. But diversification should not be measured only by percentage growth. A route expanding rapidly from a relatively small base may still represent a limited share of total export capacity.

This is particularly important in the case of the CPC system, which remains a crucial outlet for Kazakhstan’s crude. In that sense, an alternative route is meaningful only when it provides real operational redundancy at scale.

Kazakhstan’s growing use of Aktau and the BTC direction is part of a broader effort to strengthen the Trans-Caspian route. Yet the Caspian itself presents another layer of infrastructure risk. Declining water levels have raised concerns about navigation, port operations and the long-term conditions for maritime transportation. Kazakhstan is therefore seeking to expand a route whose physical environment is itself changing.

This does not make the Caspian route unviable, but it underscores the need for continued investment in ports, vessels and related infrastructure, alongside adaptation to changing navigation conditions.

The weakest link determines the value of the resource

This leads to Narymbetov’s central argument.

“Reserves are not a property of the rock, but a property of the weakest link in the chain between the reservoir and the buyer,” he wrote.

For Kazakhstan, that chain extends far beyond geology. It includes foreign policy and relations with transit countries, regulation, fiscal stability, negotiations with operators, export infrastructure, tariffs, project financing and access to international markets.

It also includes the ability to attract investment into mature fields and develop new projects. Narymbetov highlighted that Kazakhstan needs a broader approach that includes predictable fiscal and contractual conditions, clear standards for reserves reporting, transparent geological data, mechanisms for financing long-term projects and planning for the eventual decommissioning of mature assets.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s First Government Meeting Puts Skilled Workers in Focus
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s first government meeting in its updated composition after the Kurultai elections focused on a topic that could determine the success of its economic transformation: whether the country will have enough skilled workers to support planned growth.

At the Sept. 8 meeting, Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov called for an accelerated pace of work at a new stage of political and economic modernization. The decision to put workforce training at the center of the government’s first meeting highlights a growing concern: Kazakhstan has jobs, but increasingly needs people with the right skills to fill them.

By 2035, the economy is expected to require 2.9 million specialists, including 1.8 million workers in skilled trades. More than half of vacancies on the electronic labor exchange are already for working professions.

Political scientist Gaziz Abishev said the problem is therefore not a shortage of jobs, but a shortage of qualified workers.

He linked demand for technical specialists to existing industrial production, new projects under the country’s reindustrialization policy, municipal infrastructure modernization and rapidly growing cities.

Abishev cited Bektenov’s warning that Kazakhstan is “forced to attract thousands of specialists from abroad so that work does not stop,” underscoring the growing gap between demand for workers and the availability of qualified specialists.

Aligning training with economic needs

The government is seeking to make vocational education more responsive to these demands.

Education Minister Zhuldyz Suleimenova said Kazakhstan’s technical and vocational education system is being transformed according to labor-market needs. Some 480 colleges train working qualifications, while 57,000 students entered such programs this year.

Training programs are also being updated for a changing economy. New professions have been added to the national classifier, while micro-qualifications and AI-related skills are being introduced.

The Science and Higher Education Ministry estimates that more than half of labor demand is for technical and vocational specialists. Regional labor-market maps have identified more than 2,000 emerging professions and transformations of existing ones, including the use of digital twins and AI in production.

Employers are also becoming more directly involved. Nearly 50,000 students at 76 universities currently participate in dual education with 6,000 enterprises. Samruk Kazyna Sovereign Wealth Fund portfolio companies train more than 10,000 students annually through dual education and internships.

The need is particularly visible in energy and industry. Expansion of Kazakhstan’s three existing oil refineries is expected to increase refining capacity from 18 million to 29.2 million tons a year, while a planned new refinery would add another 10 million tons.

Such expansion will require a substantial increase in qualified workers.

Can training make these jobs more attractive?

The government’s challenge is not only to train workers, but to persuade people to choose these professions.

Abishev said many people remain reluctant to enter industrial and technical sectors because they consider wages insufficient. But he cautioned against viewing higher wages alone as the solution.

“Simple increases in wages without productivity growth lead to lower efficiency, higher costs and, ultimately, inflation,” he wrote on his Telegram channel on Sept. 9.

At the same time, he expects competition for qualified workers to push incomes higher. Experienced professionals in technical and skilled trades will always command higher incomes, he said. A shortage of skilled workers and competition for them will drive wages higher, while those who know their profession well, keep improving and have a strong work ethic will always be valued.

This could also alter the traditional perception of working professions. As AI transforms white-collar employment, technical occupations could become among the more attractive and better-paid positions in an economy still heavily dependent on physical infrastructure and industrial production.

The bigger test

The government is now developing a digital system to forecast labor demand, update qualifications and connect training with employment.

The priority professions list has already expanded from 51 to 174, covering engineering, construction, manufacturing, biotechnology, green and nuclear energy.

The first meeting of the updated government may therefore extend beyond education policy. Kazakhstan is preparing for an economy in which growth will depend not only on investment and new projects, but on whether it has enough people with the skills to build and operate them.

The question is no longer simply whether Kazakhstan can create jobs. It is whether it can prepare enough people to fill them.

World.title: Masdar’s 1 GW Wind Plant Highlights Kazakhstan’s Race to Build More Flexible Power System
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan is moving ahead with a $1.4 billion renewable energy project with Masdar, a leading renewable energy company based in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), as the country seeks to expand wind generation while addressing electricity shortages and building a more flexible power system. The development was discussed Sept. 8 during a meeting between Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov, Masdar’s Deputy Chairman for Business and Projects Abdullah Zayed and UAE Ambassador to Kazakhstan Mohamed Saeed Mohamed Al-Ariki.

The meeting focused on the implementation of a 1-gigawatt wind power plant with an integrated energy storage system in the Zhambyl Region, as well as prospects for expanding cooperation in renewable energy.

The project, being developed within the strategic partnership between Kazakhstan and Masdar, is expected to attract approximately $1.4 billion in investment. It will include a 1,000-megawatt wind farm and a 300-megawatt battery storage system with a capacity of 600 megawatt-hours. Full commissioning is scheduled for the third quarter of 2029.

From a wind project to a test of Kazakhstan’s energy transition

The Zhambyl project comes as Kazakhstan moves toward a more complex phase of renewable-energy development. Increasing installed capacity is only one part of the transition. The country also needs storage, modern transmission networks and regulatory mechanisms capable of balancing electricity generated from weather-dependent sources.

The storage component of the Masdar project is particularly important in this context. Wind generation can fluctuate with weather conditions, while electricity demand changes throughout the day. A large-scale storage system can help absorb excess generation and make electricity available when renewable output declines or demand rises.

The Energy Ministry has identified energy storage as a strategic priority. Speaking at the Go Net Zero – Central Asia and Caspian business summit, Turar Alimzhan, director of the ministry’s Department of Renewable Energy, said legislation on energy storage systems is currently under consideration, alongside a long-term concept for the development of green energy.

“We are moving toward this goal systematically. The law on energy storage systems is already under consideration, and this is one of our strategic priorities,” he said.

Under Kazakhstan’s electricity-sector development plan through 2035, the country intends to implement at least 8.4 GW of installed renewable-energy capacity. That target means that the next challenge will increasingly be not simply generating renewable electricity, but ensuring that it can be reliably delivered to consumers.

The Masdar project has already moved beyond the planning stage

The current construction phase also marks a significant progression for the Zhambyl project. When The Astana Times spoke with Masdar Chief Operating Officer Abdulaziz Alobaidli ahead of Abu Dhabi Sustainability Week 2026, the project was still undergoing wind-resource assessment. Alobaidli explained that developing a bankable wind project requires detailed on-site measurements rather than relying only on satellite or historical data.

“We have signed the Power Purchase Agreement, and we have moved into the development phase,” he said, noting that wind projects require specific on-site work, including at least one year of ground-based measurements to establish the project’s bankability.

Since then, the project has advanced to construction. On June 29, Kazakhstan and Masdar held a capsule-laying ceremony and officially launched work at the site in the Zhambyl Region. The progression illustrates the lengthy process behind utility-scale renewable investments, from resource assessment and power-purchase agreements to financing, construction and eventual grid integration.

Masdar sees Central Asia as a core growth market

The Zhambyl project is also part of Masdar’s broader expansion across Central Asia. “In Central Asia, we remain one of the largest renewable energy investors, with Uzbekistan, Azerbaijan, and Kazakhstan as core focus markets,” Alobaidli told The Astana Times. “We also continue dialogue with other Central Asian countries, supporting energy policy development and reform to improve bankability and attract investment.”

This regional approach reflects a broader transformation underway across Central Asia, where countries face similar pressures to increase electricity generation, modernize aging infrastructure and reduce the carbon intensity of their economies.

At the Go Net Zero summit, Alimzhan said Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan were increasingly coordinating their efforts to develop a new energy model in which renewable generation, energy storage and low-carbon technologies play a central role. The discussions also focused on the development of a green energy corridor linking Central Asia, Azerbaijan and Europe. The initiative has entered a practical implementation phase and is being considered as a potential area for deeper regional energy cooperation.

The grid will determine how far renewables can go

Kazakhstan’s renewable-energy ambitions ultimately depend on infrastructure beyond the power plants themselves. Large volumes of wind and solar generation require transmission networks capable of moving electricity from resource-rich areas to major consumption centers. This is particularly relevant for southern Kazakhstan, where additional generation capacity is being developed partly to address electricity shortages.

The transition therefore requires simultaneous progress in several areas: renewable generation, storage, transmission infrastructure, digitalization and regulation. The regional dimension adds another layer. Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan already have interconnected energy interests, while the proposed Central Asia-Azerbaijan-Europe corridor could eventually create new opportunities for cross-border electricity trade.

Energy security and decarbonization are converging

For Kazakhstan, the renewable-energy transition is not only a climate-policy issue. The country needs to increase electricity supply while maintaining energy security and gradually reducing the carbon intensity of its economy. These objectives make renewable generation increasingly attractive, but they also expose the limitations of a power system designed around more predictable generation sources.

At the Sept. 8 meeting, Akkenzhenov said Kazakhstan was interested in expanding cooperation with international investors and technology partners in renewable energy.

“Partnership with Masdar contributes to the development of renewable energy and Kazakhstan’s progress toward carbon neutrality,” the minister said, adding that the project would support regional energy security, attract modern technologies and create new opportunities for energy infrastructure development.

World.title: Digital Customs Could Boost Kazakhstan’s Transit Potential, But Infrastructure Remains Key, Experts Say
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan is stepping up its partnership with the World Customs Organization (WCO) as part of a broader strategy to strengthen the country’s position as a key Eurasian transit hub. But while digital customs reforms could significantly reduce trade costs and border delays, experts say their long-term economic payoff will ultimately depend on infrastructure, regional coordination and the changing geography of global trade.

The topic came into focus during a series of high-level meetings in Astana between President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov and WCO Secretary General Ian Saunders on Sept. 8.

During the meeting, Tokayev said Kazakhstan is consistently developing a “smart border” model by introducing digital solutions to optimize customs procedures and improve freight transit across Eurasia. Saunders praised Kazakhstan’s progress in customs modernization and its growing role in developing the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), also known as the Middle Corridor.

Customs modernization becomes part of a wider logistics strategy

Beyond the diplomatic symbolism, the meetings reflect a longer-term economic objective: transforming Kazakhstan from a transit country into an internationally competitive logistics platform.

Speaking in the meeting, Bektenov emphasized that resilient transcontinental trade has become one of the key drivers of Kazakhstan’s economic development. He noted that the WCO’s 2025–2028 strategic plan, Data-Driven Customs for a Connected World, closely aligns with Kazakhstan’s own digital reform agenda.

A central element of that strategy is the rollout of KEDEN, a unified customs system integrating declarations, transit procedures and border controls, alongside the Smart Cargo platform, which combines transport services, electronic permits and cargo tracking into a single digital ecosystem.

According to official data, 14.6 million tons of transit cargo passed through Kazakhstan during the first seven months of the year. Freight volumes along the Middle Corridor reached approximately 350,000 tons, with around 24,000 vehicles using the route.

Why digital borders matter

Farkhad Kassenov, head of the A+ Analytics research center, political scientist and international relations expert, notes that cooperation with the WCO should be viewed not as an isolated initiative but as one stage of Kazakhstan’s much broader transport and logistics strategy.

“Kazakhstan has been systematically synchronizing customs procedures, tariffs and border regulations with the countries participating in the Middle Corridor. This cooperation with the WCO is one of the stages of that much larger project,” Kassenov told The Astana Times.

The Middle Corridor has gained strategic importance as trade between China and Europe increasingly seeks alternatives to traditional northern routes passing through Russia. At the same time, Kazakhstan is also positioning itself within the developing North–South corridor, despite temporary disruptions caused by conflicts affecting the Middle East and maritime trade. According to Kassenov, removing bureaucratic barriers may prove almost as valuable as building new infrastructure.

“Digitalization can increase the speed of cargo movement by roughly 30% while simultaneously reducing logistics costs. When paperwork is synchronized and businesses use a single digital window, goods spend less time waiting at borders or in dry ports,” he said.

Digital gains cannot replace physical infrastructure

Yet customs reform alone will not solve every bottleneck. Kassenov notes that the Middle Corridor still faces structural constraints that digital systems cannot eliminate, including different railway gauges between China, Kazakhstan and Europe, as well as the natural limitations of crossing the Caspian Sea.

“There are real physical barriers. Different railway gauges require cargo transfers, while navigation across the Caspian is limited during storms and seasonal ice. Digitalization improves efficiency, but it must be accompanied by major investment in transport infrastructure,” he said.

Kazakhstan has already begun expanding ports in Aktau and Kuryk, while negotiations continue with Azerbaijan, Türkiye and China on improving rail connectivity across the corridor.

A changing geopolitical map of trade

The renewed attention to Kazakhstan’s transit role is also being driven by geopolitical shifts beyond Central Asia. According to Kassenov, growing strategic competition between China and the United States has increased Beijing’s interest in secure overland trade routes.

“The Middle Corridor was once viewed as an alternative route. By the end of this decade, it may become one of the principal land connections between East and West,” he said.

That evolution creates opportunities extending beyond transit fees. Kazakhstan is seeking to develop domestic manufacturing, processing industries and exports of higher value-added products, including critical minerals and industrial goods, that can move along the same logistics network.

A customs dilemma inside the EAEU

At the same time, Kazakhstan’s customs policy faces another question that is less visible in discussions about digitalization: whether the existing distribution of import customs duties within the Eurasian Economic Union reflects the current structure of regional trade.

Aidar Kurmashev, head of the Asian Studies Department at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies, recently highlighted the issue in his Telegram channel. According to him, under the EAEU system, duties collected on imports from outside the union are distributed among the five member states according to predetermined shares. Kazakhstan’s share is 6.955%, compared with 85.065% for Russia, regardless of where the duties are actually collected.

“After 2022, trade flows changed significantly, the role of Kazakhstan in trade with China and other directions of foreign imports increased, while our share remained 6.955%,” Kurmashev wrote.

He argued that the issue raises a broader question about whether the formula still corresponds to the current structure of trade within the EAEU.

“If Kazakhstan previously benefited from the system, but now has been losing hundreds of billions of tenge for the third consecutive year, perhaps it is time to at least recalculate the economics of the existing mechanism,” Kurmashev said, highlighting that the figures refer specifically to distributed import customs duties and do not include import VAT.

Trade routes are changing faster than institutions

The EAEU perspective illustrates a broader challenge facing Kazakhstan as it tries to reposition itself within changing Eurasian trade networks. The geography of imports and transit has shifted since 2022, while Kazakhstan is simultaneously trying to deepen direct trade links with China, expand the Middle Corridor and strengthen its position as a logistics hub between Asia and Europe.

That makes customs policy increasingly relevant not only as an administrative function but as an element of economic strategy. Digitalization can make the movement of goods faster and more predictable. International standards can improve interoperability. Infrastructure investment can remove physical bottlenecks.

But the economic payoff ultimately depends on whether these elements develop together. As Kassenov put it, the Middle Corridor is moving from being an alternative route from the global lens toward becoming a potentially central Eurasian connection.

World.title: From ‘crown prince’ to prisoner: Irakli Garibashvili’s break with Georgia’s ruling party
World.content:
Irakli Garibashvili vs Georgian Dream

Georgia’s two-time former Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili is currently in prison, from where he has openly challenged the authorities he himself represented for many years.

Over the past few weeks, he has published six letters accusing the Georgian government of persecution, blackmail and attempts to destroy his political future.

Garibashvili initially said the pressure against him had been exerted on the orders of Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder and honorary chairman of the ruling Georgian Dream party. His criticism, however, later focused primarily on current Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and another influential party figure, Mamuka Mdinaradze.

The confrontation is particularly unusual for a party that for many years appeared from the outside to be an entirely monolithic political organisation.

Irakli Garibashvili is far from an ordinary former official. For almost two decades, he was one of Bidzina Ivanishvili‘s closest and most trusted associates. When Ivanishvili stepped down as prime minister in 2013, he effectively installed the then 31-year-old Garibashvili as his successor.

Now Ivanishvili’s former chosen successor is writing from prison that the very system he once served has “stabbed him in the back”.

Garibashvili’s case is therefore no longer simply a criminal case involving a former prime minister. It has exposed a conflict within Georgian Dream and raised a broader question: is a new redistribution of power beginning within the ruling party?

From prime minister’s office to prison cell

Irakli Garibashvili’s career under Bidzina Ivanishvili’s wing began long before Georgian Dream came to power in 2012.

As early as 2011, Ivanishvili referred to Garibashvili as one of his closest advisers and aides.

Following Georgian Dream’s victory in the 2012 parliamentary election, Garibashvili became interior minister. A year later, Ivanishvili stepped down as prime minister and named Garibashvili as his successor.

Garibashvili consequently served his first term as Georgia’s prime minister from 2013 to 2015. He unexpectedly left government at the end of 2015, but returned in 2019 as defence minister. In 2021, he became prime minister for a second time.

During his second premiership, Garibashvili was one of Georgian Dream’s most hardline figures. He frequently clashed with the opposition, civil society and Western critics. Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Garibashvili repeatedly echoed the government’s narrative about the threat of a “second front” being opened in Georgia and accused some Western figures of supporting the opposition.

In January 2024, he again stepped down as prime minister and was replaced by Irakli Kobakhidze. Garibashvili, meanwhile, became chairman of Georgian Dream. At the time, the party presented the change as a routine internal reshuffle.

In April 2025, Garibashvili announced that he was leaving politics altogether.

Several months later, a criminal investigation was launched against him.

How former prime minister ended up in prison

In October 2025, prosecutors charged Irakli Garibashvili with laundering a particularly large amount of illicit income.

According to investigators, the former prime minister provided false information in his asset declarations in an attempt to make illegally obtained income appear legitimate.

At the time, Garibashvili chose to remain silent and did not contest the case. On 12 January 2026, he pleaded guilty and reached a plea agreement with prosecutors. Under the deal, he was sentenced to five years in prison and fined 1m lari ($360,000). Two of his cars and $6.5m seized during a search of his home were also forfeited to the state.

After being taken into custody in the courtroom, Garibashvili was transferred directly to Penitentiary Establishment No 12 in the city of Rustavi.

Garibashvili later gave an almost sacred significance to his decision to remain silent. He now says that, at the time, he had consciously chosen not to confront the authorities.

Garibashvili and Ivanishvili: relationship spanning almost 20 years

Garibashvili worked in Ivanishvili’s circle even before Georgian Dream was founded. When Ivanishvili entered politics in 2011, Garibashvili was one of his closest associates. And, as noted above, in 2013 Ivanishvili handed him the leadership of the Georgian government.

Ivanishvili himself has often spoken about the early years of their personal relationship. In 2013, he recalled that Garibashvili had worked in the commercial department of one of his companies when Ivanishvili was buying a French-made helicopter. According to Ivanishvili, the young Garibashvili handled the negotiations with the French side so successfully that the sellers wanted to meet him in person.

In Georgian political circles, their relationship was widely seen as one between a patron and his political successor. Government opponents even described Garibashvili as Ivanishvili’s “obedient servant”, while Georgian media frequently portrayed him as a politician “groomed” by Ivanishvili and as being as close to him “as a son”.

Another episode also illustrates the hierarchical nature of their relationship.

In 2021, when Garibashvili was serving his second term as Georgia’s prime minister, a video recording of Bidzina Ivanishvili giving evidence in a Bermuda court was made public. The case concerned Ivanishvili’s legal dispute with Swiss bank Credit Suisse.

In court, Ivanishvili was asked what role Garibashvili had played in his financial affairs years earlier. Ivanishvili explained that Garibashvili had not been a financier and had mainly performed organisational tasks, such as arranging meetings, making phone calls and handling similar matters.

Asked, “So was he something like your secretary?”, Ivanishvili laughed and replied: “Call him whatever you like. Use whichever description you prefer.”

Following the release of the recording, political commentators highlighted the fact that Ivanishvili had twice appointed as the country’s prime minister a former subordinate whose earlier duties he had described in court in dismissive terms.

Ivanishvili mentioned in Garibashvili’s letter from prison

Against this backdrop, Garibashvili’s first public reference to Ivanishvili in a letter from prison, published on 17 August 2026, was particularly significant.

Garibashvili wrote that he had received an offer made on Ivanishvili’s instructions: to confess to another offence, this time a serious corruption crime. In return, he said he had been promised that the new charge would not add to his existing five-year prison sentence.

According to the former prime minister, the deal came with another condition: after his release from prison, he would not be allowed to return to politics.

Garibashvili said the authorities were seeking to ensure that he could not make a political comeback. In the same statement, he held Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream leadership personally responsible for his own safety and that of his family.

In his next letter, Garibashvili again referred to Ivanishvili, but this time in a markedly different tone.

He wrote that he had endured the authorities’ actions for many months because of his “20-year relationship with Bidzina Ivanishvili, immense love and respect for him, boundless gratitude and absolute loyalty to him“.

In subsequent letters, Garibashvili has sought gradually to shift the focus of the conflict away from Ivanishvili and towards the Kobakhidze-Mdinaradze tandem.

Some analysts believe Garibashvili is trying to avoid burning his remaining bridges with Ivanishvili and to persuade him that the real problem lies with the current prime minister and his circle.

Garibashvili, his wife Nunuka Tamazashvili and Bidzina Ivanishvili

Irakli Kobakhidze and Irakli Garibashvili

What changed after Garibashvili‘s letters

After 17 August, Garibashvili definitively broke his silence.

Several key allegations gradually emerged from his letters. He claims that the authorities deceived him, put pressure on members of his family, demanded that he confess to another corruption offence, and ultimately sought to eliminate any possibility of his return to politics.

Garibashvili also said that he had been given indications that his 75-year-old father could also be arrested.

Mamuka Mdinaradze rejected these allegations.

However, subsequent developments lent additional weight to Garibashvili’s claims.

On 24 August, prosecutors brought new charges against him.

This time, the case concerns the alleged receipt of a particularly large bribe, an offence punishable by between 11 and 15 years in prison if he is convicted.

According to prosecutors, Garibashvili received 750,000 lari ($275,735) through a scheme involving classified procurement contracts at the Defence Ministry. The investigation relies primarily on testimony from former Defence Minister Juansher Burchuladze and his alleged accomplice, Vasil Mkheidze.

Garibashvili has pleaded not guilty to the new charge.

The former prime minister says the proceedings are being used as a tool to exert political pressure on him.

Mdinaradze’s sudden departure

Meanwhile, against the backdrop of Garibashvili’s letters and his allegations against Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze, another significant development took place:

Mamuka Mdinaradze and Irakli Kobakhidze

Mamuka Mdinaradze, who for many years was one of Georgian Dream’s most influential figures and one of Kobakhidze’s closest political allies, announced that he was leaving the government and withdrawing from politics altogether.

In 2025, Mdinaradze was appointed head of the State Security Service, but remained in the post for only a short time. In July 2026, Irakli Kobakhidze announced that Mdinaradze would become regional development minister in September and was expected to play a key role in overseeing regional policy.

However, on 27 August, Mdinaradze unexpectedly announced that he was not only stepping down from his ministerial post but leaving politics altogether.

Garibashvili linked the move to his letters.

“Mamuka Mdinaradze made such serious and grave mistakes in this case that they resulted not only in his removal from office, but also in his departure from politics,” the disgraced former prime minister wrote on 2 September in his fifth letter.

Mdinaradze himself presented his departure as a personal decision.

Why Garibashvili has become a problem for Kobakhidze

Garibashvili’s letters have raised questions about how much political influence the former prime minister retains while in prison. Some analysts believe Garibashvili still has supporters within Georgian Dream and that the authorities’ sharp response to his letters is evidence of his continuing political significance.

Conflict analyst Paata Zakareishvili says Garibashvili realised that he enjoyed greater sympathy within Georgian Dream than Kobakhidze did, and that this encouraged him to continue resisting.

Kobakhidze, Zakareishvili argues, in turn discovered that “even Garibashvili sitting in prison is stronger than he is”.

One possible explanation for this assessment lies in the two men’s very different political backgrounds.

Garibashvili belongs to the first generation of the ruling party and has been part of Georgian Dream since its foundation. He was a member of Ivanishvili’s inner circle and built up strong political connections over the years, particularly in the regions.

Kobakhidze’s power, by contrast, is much more closely tied to the party apparatus and Ivanishvili’s direct backing.

Analyst Irakli Melashvili describes Garibashvili as a “symbolic figure” for supporters of the “old Georgian Dream”. In his assessment, the former prime minister was particularly close to the party’s conservative and pro-Russian electorate.

At the same time, Melashvili points to a fundamental contradiction: Garibashvili has now himself become a target of the system of which he was one of the principal architects and leaders for many years.

For that reason, his resistance cannot automatically be seen as a struggle for a democratic system.

“This is a struggle for his own survival, not for the public good,” Melashvili says.

Lazare Jorbenadze case and a new phase of confrontation

On 1 September, Garibashvili went a step further.

In another letter from prison, he demanded that the authorities provide answers about the circumstances surrounding the death of human rights activist Lazare Jorbenadze, who had publicly criticised Kobakhidze.

Garibashvili also wrote that questions remained unanswered about other cases of suicide which, he said, were linked to the period when the Kobakhidze-Mdinaradze group was in power.

Prosecutors subsequently questioned Garibashvili himself, as well as several other politicians and public figures. A prosecution service representative said Garibashvili had provided no information to substantiate claims that Jorbenadze may have been murdered.

Sixth letter: open confrontation with authorities

On 8 September, Garibashvili published his sixth letter.

He described the authorities’ response as a “ridiculous, repulsive and tragic masquerade” and said the questioning over the Jorbenadze case was an attempt to link him to the opposition United National Movement party.

Garibashvili also responded sarcastically to allegations in pro-government media that he had been acting in the interests of the “deep state” or France.

“I am lucky that I don’t know any other foreign languages, otherwise I would probably have been declared an agent of other countries as well,” he wrote.

He then addressed the authorities directly: “Stop these dirty political games against me!”

Garibashvili said he served neither the West nor the East, neither the North nor the South, and that his sole aim had been to serve Georgia.

He addressed parliament speaker Shalva Papuashvili separately: “Shalva, this is not a legal process — this is ruthless political persecution!“

The letter ends with a message the former prime minister has repeatedly made in recent weeks:

“I am not fighting anyone — you yourselves stabbed me in the back… Now I am forced to defend myself and my family against this injustice and cruelty.”

‘Criminal’, ‘traitor’, ‘agent’: how party responded to former PM

Following Garibashvili’s fifth letter, Georgian Dream’s response became particularly harsh.

A man who twice served as prime minister for the party is now being described by his former allies as a “criminal” and a “traitor”.

A politician who for years himself used harsh rhetoric against government opponents has now become a target of the same system. The language being used against him will be familiar to the government’s critics: allegations of corruption, betrayal, serving the radical opposition and acting in the interests of foreign states.

Georgian Dream representatives say Garibashvili’s narrative has become indistinguishable from that of the “radical opposition”.

MP Gia Volski suggested that the former prime minister may have been led to believe that his struggle could help advance a “revolutionary process” in the country and that he could subsequently benefit from it politically.

Another MP, Dimitri Samkharadze, described Garibashvili as a “self-confessed criminal” and a traitor.

Meanwhile, pro-government television channels, citing Azerbaijani media, circulated allegations that Garibashvili had been acting in France’s interests in Georgia.

Current Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze also responded in exceptionally harsh terms.

He described his predecessor’s letters as “ridiculous and tragic”, saying Garibashvili had “sunk to the level of a blogger for some shady little newspaper”.

Georgian Dream secretary-general and Tbilisi mayor Kakha Kaladze, meanwhile, said it was regrettable to see his former ally in such a position, but publicly expressed his full support for Kobakhidze.

Ivanishvili remains silent

The key figure in the entire confrontation has so far remained largely out of public view.

Bidzina Ivanishvili has remained silent.

This is particularly notable because both sides in the conflict ultimately derived their political weight from his backing.

Political analyst Gia Khukhashvili sees one possible scenario in which Ivanishvili himself is managing the current process, with the ultimate aim of weakening Kobakhidze’s team.

Other analysts offer a more cautious interpretation: Ivanishvili is watching the confrontation unfold and will make a decision only when it becomes clear which figure is more useful for preserving his system.

David Zurabishvili, who supports this interpretation, says Ivanishvili has no permanent allies, only permanent interests. Accordingly, neither Garibashvili nor Kobakhidze is indispensable to him.

This explanation is also consistent with Georgian Dream’s history: prime ministers have changed repeatedly during the party’s time in power, while the centre of power has consistently remained with Ivanishvili.

Kobakhidze has no intention of stepping down

Against this backdrop, speculation is already mounting in Georgia over the possible resignation of Irakli Kobakhidze himself.

He has, however, dismissed the rumours.

Kobakhidze said journalists ask him “every three months” whether he is planning to step down as prime minister, adding that he expects to be asked the same question again in another three months.

More significant, however, was his explanation of what had happened within the government after he took office.

According to Kobakhidze, he and his team needed a year and five months to address what he described as “fundamental problems” that had accumulated within the system of government, acting on Bidzina Ivanishvili’s instructions.

Kobakhidze did not directly name Garibashvili in his remarks. The chronology, however, is clear: he was referring to problems that had accumulated in the system during his namesake’s tenure as prime minister.

Is Georgian Dream’s monolith beginning to crack?

Georgian Dream formally retains almost complete control over Georgia’s political system.

It dominates parliament, is seeking to ban several opposition groups, and many opposition leaders are in prison.

Yet it is under these circumstances that a conflict has erupted not between the government and the opposition, but between current and former leaders of the ruling establishment itself.

Giorgi Melashvili, head of the Europe-Georgia Institute, describes the situation as two parallel processes: on the one hand, the circle of decision-makers is narrowing and the system is becoming increasingly centralised; on the other, the Garibashvili case has exposed cracks in Georgian Dream’s internal monolith.

In his assessment, neither the opposition nor other former Georgian Dream figures have dealt the party a blow comparable to that inflicted by Garibashvili’s letters.

Gia Khukhashvili, meanwhile, describes the developments as a confrontation between two factions “at the royal court”. In his view, Ivanishvili remains the only person with the final say.

Much about these scenarios remains speculative, but the facts themselves already present a highly unusual picture:

Former PM behind bars: A two-time former prime minister is in prison, accusing the authorities of political persecution and his former allies of trying to destroy him and his family.

A two-time former prime minister is in prison, accusing the authorities of political persecution and his former allies of trying to destroy him and his family. New criminal case: Following his first letters, he was hit with a new and significantly more serious criminal charge.

Following his first letters, he was hit with a new and significantly more serious criminal charge. Mdinaradze’s sudden departure: One of his main opponents within the ruling team, Mamuka Mdinaradze, unexpectedly left politics altogether.

One of his main opponents within the ruling team, Mamuka Mdinaradze, unexpectedly left politics altogether. Question of succession: Current Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze is already having to publicly answer questions about whether he could become the “next former” prime minister.

And Bidzina Ivanishvili, who stands at the centre of all these developments, continues to remain silent.

World.title: ‘Major cause for concern’: expert view on Armenian school students’ low level of knowledge
World.content:
Low knowledge levels among Armenian school students

School students in Armenia lag behind their peers in Georgia, Azerbaijan and Turkey in terms of their level of knowledge. The comparison focuses in particular on 15-year-old students.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) conducted its annual study as part of the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA). Experts assessed students’ knowledge of mathematics and science, as well as their ability to analyse what they read.

The study included 760,000 15-year-old students from 91 countries. The results showed that the overall state of education around the world leaves much to be desired. However, experts in Armenia are particularly concerned about the situation in their own country. The education problems have also alarmed people far beyond the field’s specialist community.

Economist Tigran Jrbashyan sees the study’s results as a major cause for concern.

“This is no longer a problem for the education ministry. It is a question of Armenia’s economic security and long-term competitiveness,” he stressed.

Jrbashyan published several posts on his Facebook page, calling on the government to take immediate action. He proposes introducing a special regime in the education sector over the coming years.

Подробнее о результатах исследования, а также комментарий экономиста Тиграна Джрбашяна.

Results for students in Armenia and leading countries

According to the study, some cities in China lead the rankings for educational achievement, followed by Japan, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan. The UK and Estonia also rank among the top 10.

Armenia’s results lag behind those of every other country in the region. Armenian school students scored below the OECD average in all areas covered by the study.

The average share of Armenian school students reaching the benchmark was

28% in science (OECD average — 74%),

28% in mathematics (OECD average — 65%),

19% in reading and the ability to analyse written text (OECD average — 67%).

Less than 1% of Armenian students achieved the highest level in mathematics, while the figure was even lower in science.

“And virtually none of the students demonstrated reading skills that would indicate an ability to understand lengthy texts, work with abstract or contradictory concepts, and distinguish facts from opinions,” Radio Azatutyun reports.

Comment

According to Tigran Jrbashyan, an economist and head of Ameriabank’s management consulting service, the PISA study assesses not so much what 15-year-olds know as their ability to apply their knowledge in practice: understanding texts, analysing information and solving problems.

“Among our 15-year-olds, 28% reach at least the minimum, Level 2 proficiency in mathematics. The figure is also 28% in science. In reading, however, only 19% reach this level. In other words, four out of five of our 15-year-olds do not even reach the basic level of functional reading literacy,” he said.

Meanwhile, according to the PISA study, 39% of teenagers in Georgia reach the basic level of reading literacy, compared with 36% in Kazakhstan and 35% in Azerbaijan.

The economist argues that no matter how much Armenia talks about its achievements in artificial intelligence and high technology, all its planned initiatives will remain unrealised projects without human capital.

“If Armenia ranks third from the bottom in problem-solving skills among 15-year-olds, our ambitions in AI and high technology cannot be limited to investment, equipment and infrastructure alone,” he explained.

Jrbashyan notes that Armenia has built, renovated and modernised schools in recent years. He considers this an unquestionable investment in the quality of education. At the same time, he says the country needs to change how it assesses the effectiveness of education policy.

In particular, he proposes assessing

how students’ reading skills and their mathematical and scientific knowledge have changed as a result of these investments;

whether the share of students who fail to reach the basic level has decreased;

whether the share of high-performing students has increased.

The analyst insists that, given the current situation, the government needs to

take immediate action to determine at which stage of the education system, and for what reasons, students lose ground;

set measurable targets for 2028 and 2031 and consistently work towards achieving them.

“The cost of inaction in the context of PISA is not simply a low ranking. It means lost economic growth and the loss of Armenia’s competitiveness for decades to come,” he stressed.

The expert believes the PISA 2025 results show that the scale of Armenia’s education problem has outgrown the pace of the government’s response. As a result, reforms carried out at the usual pace are no longer enough:

“I would propose declaring education an emergency national priority and introducing a special management regime for three to five years.”

Jrbashyan stresses that an emergency regime should mean not only faster decision-making and more resources, but also much greater accountability for results.

Moreover, he sees a need for national mobilisation on the issue. He believes education policy should not measure its success only through the next PISA study:

“We need to create a national system of regular assessment that will allow us to see every year where we are making progress and where we are not, and adjust policy accordingly.”
