World.title: Azerbaijan, China Energy International Group brainstorm renewable energy projects (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 10. Azerbaijani and China Energy International Group have discussed renewable energy projects.

This was announced in a publication by Azerbaijani Energy Minister Parviz Shahbazov on X account following the meeting with Executive President of the Group Lin Xiaodan.

"During the meeting, we discussed the completion of the study of Azerbaijan’s electricity transmission grid and the advancement of renewable energy projects in line with its findings. We also reviewed the implementation of the company’s first investment project in Azerbaijan a 160 MW solar power plant and discussed the next steps in our cooperation on offshore wind development in the Caspian Sea," the publication said.

Azerbaijan is implementing large-scale projects to increase electricity production and diversify its energy system. In particular, the development of renewable energy sources is one of the main priorities of the country’s energy strategy. Currently, major investment projects are underway in the country to build solar and wind power plants, with the participation of bp, Masdar, ACWA Power, China Gezhouba Group Overseas Investment, SOCAR Green, and other partners. As a result of these projects, Azerbaijan’s energy balance will be augmented by thousands of megawatts of new generating capacity in the coming years, which will reduce domestic demand for natural gas and increase gas exports.

According to Energy Minister Parviz Shahbazov, the implementation of these projects is expected to increase the share of renewable energy sources in Azerbaijan’s energy mix to approximately 43 percent by 2035.

The minister noted that Azerbaijan is implementing strategic projects aimed at establishing a new energy and investment platform between Central Asia and neighboring regions. According to him, one of the main initiatives is the “Central Asia–Azerbaijan Green Energy Corridor” project. “The creation of the Trans-Caspian Energy Corridor, which will connect the power grids of Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan, is an integral part of our countries’ strategic vision. This project also creates broad opportunities for the development of the Middle Corridor, which will serve as a green energy bridge between Europe, Asia, and China via the Caspian Sea,” Parviz Shahbazov emphasized.

The minister stated that the “Green Corridors Alliance” joint venture is already operating in Baku, coordinating feasibility studies funded by the Asian Development Bank and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. In addition, intensive work is underway on the Caspian-Black Sea-European green energy corridor, as well as on the Azerbaijan-Türkiye-Europe and Azerbaijan-Georgia-Türkiye-Bulgaria energy interconnections. Parviz Shahbazov stated that “green energy corridors are shaping the geo-economic map of the future” and that these initiatives will stimulate not only energy exports but also the development of digital communications, fiber-optic infrastructure, and regional economic cooperation.

As the director of the State Agency for Renewable Energy under the Ministry of Energy, Javid Abdullayev, stated in an exclusive interview with Trend, the country is playing an increasingly important role in establishing a green energy bridge between Europe and Central Asia.

“Azerbaijan is no longer just an exporter of energy resources, but also one of the initiators of regional energy links and green energy corridors. The wind and solar energy projects currently underway will strengthen the country’s energy security and significantly increase its electricity export capacity,” Javid Abdullayev emphasized.

According to him, initiatives such as harnessing the Caspian Sea’s vast wind energy potential, building new power transmission lines, and establishing the “Caspian Sea–Black Sea–Europe” green energy corridor will further strengthen Azerbaijan’s role in Europe’s energy security.

“Green energy projects will provide the country with additional export revenues, optimize the domestic energy balance, reduce natural gas consumption, and direct more gas to foreign markets,” he added.

World.title: 'We've found fresh air': Australian expert on efforts to find hydro-plant workers
World.content:
Nepali authorities have found fresh air for the first time in the tunnels filled with mud and debris in last month's floods, an Australian tunnelling expert says.

At least 11 hydropower projects were engulfed when a glacier collapsed into a river on the Nepal-China border on August 26, burying the entrances to the tunnels of the projects under debris and mud and trapping those inside.

Arnold Dix has been redeployed to Chilime in Nepal. (Supplied: ABC News)

Melbourne geologist Arnold Dix was invited to Nepal to work with rescue teams at the Chilime hydropower project in the hard-hit Rasuwa district.

"We think we've found a zone where people may have survived and that is just amazing," he said.

"This is the first time we've had fresh air, as opposed to water and mud.

"We can hear that it's hollow, we're calling out. It's not over.

" We're in miracle country. "

900 people suspected trapped in tunnels

A Chinese national was rescued by soldiers during an ongoing operation at the Trishuli-3A hydropower project. (AP: Nepal Army)

A least 1,399 people have been confirmed dead and more than 5,400 are missing in Nepal and Tibet. At least 900 of those missing are suspected to be trapped in hydropower tunnels like those Professor Dix is working on.

On Tuesday, another Australian who had been unaccounted-for was found safe. The ABC understands that the person was not in the disaster zone.

The person is the eighth Australian to be found since the floods, with 35 others still unaccounted-for.

Professor Dix said people trapped in the hydropower project tunnels have had to survive in pitch black for over two weeks, with only access to water.

"What you do is listen to your heart, you do your engineering analysis, and you go after those souls that we think could still be alive," he said.

The geologist, who also assisted rescue teams at the Trishuli 3A hydropower project, previously told the ABC people could survive in the tunnels for up to 17 days.

He said last week that some of the underground power stations likely withstood the immense pressure of the flash flooding. However, it remains unclear whether emergency systems activated in time or whether water and debris inundated them.

Rescue workers take part in a rescue operation near the tunnel of the Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project. (Nepal Prime Minister's Office/Handout via Reuters)

In recent days, search teams have rescued four people, including a Chinese national who was pulled from a tunnel on Saturday.

The others were two hydropower workers rescued from another tunnel on Friday and a Nepali woman pulled out from her buried house on Saturday.

Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah vowed there would be no let-up in the rescue operations.

"We know our responsibility and its sensitivity. We are translating the humanitarian spirit of the Nepali people into practice through the search and rescue operation," he said in a social media post late on Monday.

If you want to help support the thousands affected by the crisis, the ABC is supporting the Emergency Action Alliance member charities and their local partners. You can find more information here.

ABC/Wires

World.title: Police shooting death of Kumanjayi Walker at centre of book that won $80k
World.content:
A book about the fatal shooting of Kumanjayi Walker and the murder trial of Northern Territory police officer Zachary Rolfe is one of six winners at this year's Prime Minister's Literary Awards (PMLA).

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised this article contains the name of an Indigenous person who has died.

Journalist Kate Wild has taken out the $80,000 prize for non-fiction for her book The Red House, which explores the incident in November 2019, when Mr Walker was shot and killed by police in Yuendumu, a remote community in the Northern Territory, 300 kilometres north-west of Alice Springs.

The 19-year-old Warlpiri man was wanted by police for threatening two local police officers with an axe three days earlier.

When police came to arrest him at his grandmother's house, he stabbed then-constable Rolfe in the shoulder with a pair of medical scissors.

Mr Rolfe then fired his gun three times at Mr Walker, who died in custody an hour later.

The shooting sparked protests calling for "Justice for Walker", with more than 1,000 people marching in Alice Springs, six months before the murder of George Floyd in America kicked off a wave of Black Lives Matter protests.

"Justice for Walker" was spray-painted onto a road sign on the way to Yuendumu. (ABC News: Xavier Martin )

In March 2022, Mr Rolfe was found not guilty of Mr Walker's murder after a six-week trial in Darwin.

Three years later, in July 2025, the NT coroner released the findings of a coronial inquest into the fatal shooting. She found Mr Rolfe was "racist" and could not exclude the possibility his attitudes "were a contributing cause of Kumanjayi's death". He has been dismissed from the NT Police Force.

The PMLA judges described The Red House as "deeply compassionate … rigorous and urgently necessary to an ongoing national conversation".

"Her searing and unflinching investigation examines national difference, the depth of the colonial wound, and the awful repetition of state violence and dehumanisation that makes the confrontation at the heart of this book possible, even inevitable," the judges wrote.

Wild tells ABC Arts she feels "pretty stunned and proud" to have won the award.

" It's really affirming," she says. "It's really nice to know people care about this. "

Other PMLA winners include Rohan Howitt's The Southern Frontier, about Australia's relationship to Antarctica, which won the Australian history prize; and the fiction winner, A Piece of Red Cloth, which saw Leonie Norrington work with Yolŋu Elders, Merrkiyawuy Ganambarr-Stubbs, Djawa Burarrwanga and Djawundil Maymuru, on a book about the Indonesian fisher-traders visiting Arnhem Land.

• Jump to the full list of PMLA winners

Murky waters

Throughout The Red House, Wild reckons with the difficulty of the task she has set for herself: to write about Mr Walker's death in a nuanced way.

The Red House also won The Age newspaper's prize for non-fiction book of the year. (Supplied: Allen & Unwin)

In the book, she speaks to a former defence force chaplain who is also staying in Yuendumu, who asks why she wants to write about the shooting.

Wild writes: "Australia's collective view of history was changing and the country was changing with it, I said. How people reacted to Kumanjayi's death and Mr Rolfe's trial was one measure of how much."

The chaplain counsels: "it's not an easy path you're setting out on."

Wild replies: "One way or another I expect to be cancelled."

So far, Wild hasn't been cancelled.

"It's dangerous to write about very conflicted subjects and spaces, particularly in the world we live in at the moment," she says.

She had noticed within hours of Mr Walker's death people declaring where they stood on the issue — positions that were often diametrically opposed.

"I was so frustrated by those really predictable left-right positions they were taking without thinking," she says.

"I'm impatient with that approach to anything, but particularly to subjects which are so contested.

" What living in the Northern Territory teaches you more than anything is that nothing is left-right; nothing is Black-white. "

Wild had long conversations with both Indigenous and non-Indigenous friends about whether she — a white, middle-aged, middle-class woman — should write the book.

She soon resolved to do it, regardless of the possible backlash.

"After a lot of conversations and soul-searching, I came to the position it was part of the problem to frame this as an Aboriginal story," she says.

"It was a white police officer who shot [Mr Walker], and so the story is as much a white Australia story as it is a Black Australia story."

Wild brought her knowledge and connections, sown over six years reporting mostly on Indigenous affairs in Darwin from 2010 to 2016, to the book, but also a deep love of NT and its people.

"I didn't want [a story about the case] to be reduced to a bunch of racist white rednecks and a bunch of victim Aboriginal people," she says. "That's not the truth."

An expansive approach to time

Wild was interested in understanding how the altercation between Mr Walker and Mr Rolfe in Yuendumu reflected something broader about "where we're at as a nation in terms of race and reconciliation".

"But by the time I got to the end of it, I had an even bigger picture of history," she says.

ABC Radio National’s Top 100 Australian Books Countdown We take over Radio National on Saturday, 17 and Sunday, 18 October to count down the Top 100 Australian books as voted by you.

Former NT politician Scott McConnell alerted Wild to the parallels between the racial tensions in NT in 2019 and the 80s.

He pointed to three acts of violence: the shooting of a station owner by a group of Indigenous young people; the killing of an Indigenous man by police near Ti Tree; and the deaths of two Indigenous people after they drank from a bottle of wine deliberately laced with strychnine.

Those parallels led Wild to thinking about the "Everywhen", an Indigenous conception of time where the past, present and future are all happening simultaneously.

She found it a useful way to conceptualise how historical moments of violence between Indigenous peoples and the police seemed to repeat.

Loading YouTube content

Wild used the Everywhen as a structural device in The Red House, which allowed her to eschew a chronology, instead move fluidly between times and places.

"I learned not to look at [time] as a linear thing — this happens and that leads to this," she explains.

"What is happening now carries the ghosts of what has happened in the past."

The Everywhen also offered a unique way of looking to the future, taking away the seeming inevitability of both police violence and Indigenous disadvantage, instead engendering the possibility of change.

"Finding the Everywhen and understanding how I could use that to frame the whole story, to me, is such a hopeful way of looking at things," Wild says.

"Every single one of us has a responsibility to live in ways that make repair possible," Wild says. (Supplied: Nicholas Coghlan)

"Maybe if the non-Indigenous world can learn to look at life in this more open way, a more creative way, maybe that's where some of the answers lie.

" If we can open our view a bit more, we're going to find better answers and better relationships, rather than pointing fingers. "

Full list of winners

Australian history

The Southern Frontier by Rohan Howitt (Melbourne University Publishing)

Children's literature

Song of a Thousand Seas by Zana Fraillon (University of Queensland Press)

Fiction

A Piece of Red Cloth by Leonie Norrington, Merrkiyawuy Ganambarr-Stubbs, Djawa Burarrwanga and Djawundil Maymuru (Allen & Unwin)

Non-fiction

The Red House by Kate Wild (Allen & Unwin)

Poetry

Two Hundred Million Musketeers by Ender Başkan (Giramondo Publishing)

Young adult literature

Drift by Pip Harry (Hachette Australia)

World.title: 'No face-to-face meeting': Former One Nation candidate questions vetting process
World.content:
Warren Pickering's public reckoning with his past has raised a broader question for One Nation as it seeks to expand its political footprint: How is the party vetting candidates it puts before the electorate?

The Victorian One Nation leader this week admitted to using illicit drugs in his 20s, infidelity and losing his driver's licence three times for drink driving after allegations about his past were published by The Australian.

Mr Pickering acknowledged using speed, ecstasy and marijuana when he was younger but denied allegations from his former partner Jo Scott, herself a recovering drug addict, that he used ice.

Warren Pickering with One Nation leader Pauline Hanson as the party's candidates for the Victorian state election were announced. (AAP: Jay Kogler)

"I made mistakes," he said.

"I'll carry that regret forever."

Since his very public confession, One Nation has firmly stood behind him.

But as the party's popularity grows ahead of Victoria's election in November, the scandal has put its candidate selection and vetting procedures under scrutiny.

'I thought it was strange'

Robert Stuckey was One Nation's candidate for the Western Sydney seat of Greenway at the 2025 federal election. (ABC News: Sissy Reyes)

Robert Stuckey has first-hand experience of being recruited by One Nation.

He stood for the party in the Western Sydney seat of Greenway at the 2025 federal election.

Mr Stuckey told 7.30 his own selection involved an online interview with the party's national secretary Damian Huxham and a final phone conversation with leader Pauline Hanson.

"'We'd like you to run. We'd like to have you run for Greenway,'" he recalled being told.

" That was my selection process, so there was no face-to-face meetings. "

Mr Stuckey said he was required to complete extensive paperwork, including a police check and other documentation, but said a significant amount of it was submitted after he had already been pre-selected.

He told 7.30 he expected candidates being considered for senior positions to be interviewed in person.

Pauline Hanson said she backs Warren Pickering after his confession about taking drugs in his past. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

"I felt that it was strange that it was all done by phone, no face-to-face actual contact until we'd all been selected and there was a gathering of the candidates," he said.

Mr Stuckey said the absence of face-to-face contact made it more difficult to properly assess the person behind an application.

"You can do all of that, but do you actually check it?" he said of the paperwork candidates submit.

" If you just took that on face value without meeting the person, without talking to them and getting a feeling of what they are, how the hell do you actually make a decision? "

He said the importance of the appointment of a Victorian leader should demand significant scrutiny from the party.

"I would want to vet that person to the Nth degree and absolutely make sure that that's the person I wanted representing my party," Mr Stuckey said.

As for Mr Pickering, he said, "Is he the best candidate that they could have in Victoria?

"They're a big party now and I'm not so sure that I would think that I would have selected him on that factor."

'It was 20 years ago'

One Nation co-founder and former national director, David Oldfield. (ABC News)

One Nation co-founder David Oldfield, who created the party with Ms Hanson in 1997, has a different perspective.

He is no longer associated with the party, and said he did not know what vetting procedures One Nation currently used and could not judge the process Mr Pickering has undergone.

During his time with the party, he said candidates were expected to obtain police clearances and were subject to other background checks that could be reasonably conducted.

But he said there were limits to what any vetting process could uncover.

"To a degree you're always going to be taking a candidate somewhat on faith, and every now and again there's going to be something pop up," he told 7.30.

David Oldfield, pictured with Pauline Hanson in 1998, is no longer associated with the party. (Reuters)

He argued a candidate's past conduct should not automatically disqualify them from public life if they had not committed offences that made them unsuitable for office.

"The key point is it was 20 years ago. The key point is he's admitted it all, and the key point is, who is he today and what kind of dad is he?" Mr Oldfield said of Mr Pickering.

He said if he were still in the party and aware of Mr Pickering's past, he would still elevate the former ADF combat engineer to Victorian leader.

"If we were going to eliminate people on them being unfaithful, it could probably get rid of at least half of all of the standing members in every parliament in the country," he said.

"In this case, I don't see that any of this eliminates him."

'People throwing themselves at One Nation'

Polling shows One Nation is experiencing a surge in popularity around the country. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Mr Oldfield said One Nation faced a particular challenge as new people sought to join the growing political movement.

"The challenge that all parties face is really what is this person and who are they? Now, in a lot of parties they may have been well known for quite some time," he said.

"In One Nation's case, their challenge is a whole range of new people coming forward that they may not have known terribly well."

But Mr Stuckey said the increased interest in One Nation should make candidate selection easier, not harder.

"I think people are throwing themselves at One Nation to be selected as candidates for both state and federal in all areas," he said.

" I would hope that they would now have this massive wealth of applicants to choose from and then really be selective in their selection process. "

A One Nation spokesperson told 7.30 "all candidates, including Mr Pickering, completed the One Nation vetting process".

"His police check revealed historic drink driving offences that date back to his youth, however all financial, criminal and character references were favourable.

"One Nation's new vetting process was rolled out in 2026 and is used to assess candidates and examine branch coordinators across the country."

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: US judge rules Tate brothers as flight risk in denying jail release
World.content:
Social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate have lost their bid for release from a Miami jail as they contest extradition to Britain, where they are wanted on rape charges.

In denying bail for the Tate brothers, Miami-based US Magistrate Judge Lauren Louis said the brothers' wealth and frequent international travel made them "quintessential flight risks".

"While [the brothers] may not in fact possess what extravagant holdings they portray themselves as possessing online, the record reflects that they possess an exceptional capacity to flee the jurisdiction," Judge Louis wrote.

In a statement, the Tates' lawyers said they would "continue to defend themselves against the allegations they face and engage with the appropriate legal processes in each jurisdiction".

In court filings, their lawyers had previously said their "extraordinary public visibility" would make it impractical for them to flee, and described social media posts in which the brothers touted their wealth as "theatrical" and "grandiose".

The Tate brothers face charges across multiple jurisdictions. (Reuters: Inquam Photos/Eduard Vinatoru)

Andrew Tate, 39, and Tristan Tate, 38, were arrested in Miami on July 18 after Britain requested their extradition to face charges of rape, assault and facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation.

The Tate brothers, who have ​dual US and British citizenship, have denied any wrongdoing.

The arrests marked a new phase in the legal ‌troubles for ⁠the former kickboxers, who have built a large online following promoting their views on masculinity and wealth.

Andrew Tate has previously described himself as a misogynist.

Tate brothers claim they play characters online

Prosecutors with the Miami US Attorney's office said there was a strong presumption in favour of detention in international extradition cases.

They said the brothers could pose a danger to the public if released, citing British allegations that they strangled victims during forcible rapes.

The Tates recruited dozens of women to work for a webcam pornography business starting in 2014, and later ran online courses called "Hustler's University", prosecutors said in an August 10 court filing.

At an August 27 hearing in Miami federal court, prosecutors showed the court a video of Andrew Tate saying "slap, slap, grab, choke, shut up bitch, sex".

At the hearing, both Tate brothers testified they were playing characters online when they made crude remarks.

Ms Louis wrote on Wednesday that the nature of the allegations against the Tates indicated they posed dangers to the community.

Tate brothers arrested British prosecutors said they are seeking the extradition of the Tate brothers from the US on rape and sex trafficking charges.

The brothers have also been under investigation on charges including human trafficking since 2022 in Romania, where they were mainly based since 2017.

Romanian prosecutors officially indicted Andrew Tate on Friday on charges of trafficking minors, money laundering, sex with a minor and witness tampering.

Tristan Tate was indicted for complicity.

A Romanian lawyer for the Tates said they rejected the allegations.

British charges span seven years

The legal process ​for determining whether the Tate brothers may be extradited to Britain could take months.

​Britain has until ⁠September 16 to submit its full extradition request to the State Department, US court records show.

The impetus for the brothers' arrests in Miami was new charges brought by Britain's Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) relating to alleged offences ​involving four alleged victims between July 2010 and August 2017.

Why the Tate brothers were arrested Everything you need to know about the arrest of the Tate brothers.

They had previously faced rape and human trafficking charges in Britain related to three alleged victims, the ⁠CPS said.

A ​British judge issued a warrant for their arrests in ​2024.

They have not appeared in British court to enter a plea to those charges.

Britain is seeking to extradite the brothers to ​face both sets of charges.

REUTERS

World.title: Officer who hit man on hospital stretcher keeps job with NSW Police
World.content:
A NSW Police officer has kept his job despite being found guilty of assaulting a man who was being wheeled into hospital on a gurney by paramedics.

ABC News has obtained exclusive CCTV and body-worn camera vision of the assault, which happened at Blacktown Hospital in November 2023.

Leading Senior Constable Steven Hyde and his partner on the day, Constable Talaisai Alo, had been called to a man's Western Sydney home, where they found him unconscious after a suspected drug overdose.

An ambulance was called and paramedics managed to rouse the man before taking him to Blacktown Hospital for observation.

The incident occured at Blacktown Hospital's emergency department. (ABC News: Jak Rowland)

The man was not under arrest, but the two police officers escorted them to the hospital.

When they arrived, CCTV footage from the hospital shows the man being wheeled into the emergency department in the ambulance bay, with his legs strapped to the gurney.

He was holding a vape in one hand and a water bottle in the other when Officer Hyde approached and confiscated the vape.

The man then threw the water bottle over his shoulder, prompting Officer Hyde to react by hitting him in the side of the head.

Loading...

Officer Alo then grabs the man and restrains him, shortly before his body-worn camera begins recording audio of the incident.

The man can be heard saying, "I put water on you" before asking the officer to let go of his arm.

The officer tells the man, "I'll f***ing rip your shoulder off if you don't listen to me", before handcuffing the man behind his back.

The officer then tells the man he is being charged with assaulting police, before wheeling him into the hospital as he says, "Keep your head down, no-one deserves to look at you."

The body camera vision ends as the man is wheeled into the emergency room.

Officer claims he acted in self-defence

The man was strapped to a stretcher during the assault. (ABC News)

An ambulance officer who witnessed the incident later gave a statement to police, saying she also heard one of the police officers say to the man inside the hospital: "Why do you want to go home? No-one cares about you."

She did not specify which officer said it.

Officer Hyde was later charged with assault for hitting the man in the head.

Officer Alo has not been charged over the incident.

Officer Hyde, who had been a police officer for more than a decade, faced a local court hearing earlier this year, where he tendered a written statement claiming he acted in self-defence.

"Almost immediately after I turned, I felt something strike my right shoulder and back area … my initial belief was that [the victim] had assaulted me," his statement said. "I was very concerned that his behaviour had now escalated and he would continue his assault upon me. "To prevent this happening, I turned and struck [the victim]."

CCTV captured the incident. (ABC News)

Officer Hyde said the man "appeared to be drug-affected" and his response was based on "extensive experience dealing with people affected by drugs".

"It is my experience that many illegal drugs that are extensively used on the street result in people becoming extremely unpredictable, irrational and violent," his statement said.

"When [the victim] regained consciousness, he was immediately argumentative … he was swearing and aggressive, although not directly threatening to me."

Officer Hyde was found guilty of assault by a Local Court Judge earlier this year before he appealed the conviction and sentence in the District Court.

This week, a District Court judge again found him guilty of assault but opted not to record a conviction against him.

The judge sentenced him to a 12-month good behaviour bond.

A statement from NSW Police this week said Officer Hyde remains on the force and was "subject to management action" in June.

"The officer has also been subjected to a loss of rank, two years of restricted duties and will be required to undertake retraining under a management plan," a spokesperson said in the statement.

"Police will continue to monitor the actions of the officer and undertake regular reviews of his conduct."

World.title: No cap on gun ownership in Tasmania after Labor amendment fails
World.content:
There will not be a cap on the number of guns a person can own in Tasmania, after the lower house voted not to amend the state government's firearms reform legislation.

The amendment from the opposition lost 15-16, as debate on the government's bill continued for the third straight day.

The changes proposed by the government, including setting up the Tasmanian requirements for a national firearms register and a buyback scheme, as well as mandatory minimum jail terms for serious firearms offences, were announced in the wake of the Bondi shooting.

Caps, which were not included in the government's bill, were supported by Labor, the Greens, and independents Helen Burnet, Peter George and Kristie Johnston.

The state government, Shooters, Fishers and Farmers MP Carlo Di Falco, and independents David O'Byrne, Craig Garland and George Razay voted against them.

Professor Razay was the last MP to reveal their stance on ownership caps. All others declared their position during debate on Tuesday.

George Razay said he was not convinced the caps "equalled greater public safety, while striking a sufficient balance". (Supplied)

Professor Razay said there was merit in caps, but was wary of the impact they would have had on the agricultural community and hunters.

Under Labor's proposal, there would have been a limit of five guns, or 10 guns for primary producers and sports shooters.

It had proposed the state's police commissioner be given powers to grant exemptions to that limit.

The state government did not support the caps, having said the restrictions would target law-abiding firearms owners, rather than criminals.

The bill will continue to be debated this evening, and is expected to pass the lower house in some form.

It will then need to go through the upper house, and is likely to do so later this year.

The state government did not support the caps, saying the limits would affect firearms owners rather than criminals. (ABC News)

'Serious' debate hears strong opinions

Labor's police spokesperson Jen Butler said the issue of caps was one of the most serious she had debated during her time in parliament.

"I don't think we should be prioritising the voices of the gun lobby, or firearms dealers, above what's best for Tasmanian people," she said.

"All we are asking for is to have a reduction in the number of guns we have in our community," she said.

She was one of several members to reference the 1996 Port Arthur massacre in their contribution.

Greens police spokesperson Tabatha Badger said caps were not "the be-all and end-all", but would be "something else in the toolbox" to help improve safety.

Police Minister Felix Ellis maintained that targeting serious firearms offences was the best way to improve safety.

"It is not the number of firearms, it is the hands they are in," he said.

He also said that despite the increase in the number of firearms, the number of homicides and firearm thefts had fallen.

Mr Ellis told the house caps would not have stopped the Bondi massacre, as the shooters had just three guns between them.

Fit and proper persons test strengthened

While the bill passed its second reading late on Wednesday night, MP's have been debating each clause and potential amendments on Thursday afternoon.

Several changes were also made to the fit and proper person test, largely to address the impacts of family violence.

An amendment from independent MP Kristie Johnston passed, giving the police commissioner the power to consider if a licence applicant has a history of family violence in another state, or has displayed behaviour that was "a recognised precursor or risk factor for family violence".

That would include coercion, intimidation, damage to property or increased police attendance.

Another change will allow the commissioner to consider if a family member or partner, who is not a fit and proper person, would have access to an applicant's guns.

Ms Badger also successfully moved an amendment giving the commissioner the power to consider the likelihood of the applicant using a firearm to make threats.

Those who have been convicted of a family violence offence would also be unable to obtain a licence for 10 years, up from five in the original bill.

A bid by Mr Di Falco to create a permit system for individuals to be able to own firearms suppressors failed.

Gun ownership grandfathering to be removed

The state government had proposed reclassifying straight-pull action firearms, similar to those used by the Bondi shooters, but grandfathering the change so that current owners were not affected.

However, this grandfathering will be removed from the bill, with the support of the Greens and independents Helen Burnet, David O'Byrne and Peter George.

The government's bill also makes Australian citizenship a licence requirement; however, this change would also be grandfathered, allowing current non-Australian licence holders to keep their licences.

A bid from the opposition to remove this provision is set to fail, after not gaining enough support.

World.title: Extreme heat, fires and floods mark record hot month
World.content:
Climate data has been released confirming August 2026 as the hottest month on record after heatwaves and severe drought dominated Western Europe's warmest summer.

The recorded surface air temperature for August 2026 was 1.65°C above the estimated pre-industrial 1850-1900 average, with the period from June to August 2026 the joint-warmest on record globally, on par with 2024.

The Copernicus Climate Change Service, which authored the report with data from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), found the extreme conditions had coincided with exceptionally low river flows from the Rhine to the Danube, and had intensified wildfires across Indonesia.

Samantha Burgess, from the ECMWF, said the observations revealed "how climate change is driving extremes across both the atmosphere and the oceans".

"The impacts of these conditions are increasingly being felt by communities, economies and ecosystems across the world," Ms Burgess said.

1.5C overshoot looms A UN report warns the world is likely to overshoot warming of 1.5C as world leaders shun Australia's pre-COP talks in Fiji.

Earlier this month, a landmark report from the UN warned the world was unlikely to keep global warming below 1.8C, predicting that global temperatures would likely pass 1.5C above pre-industrial levels by 2030.

The Paris Agreement, a legally binding international treaty signed in 2016, requires countries to take action to avoid dangerous warming by keeping temperature increases well below 2C and as close to 1.5C as possible.

Scientists have repeatedly advised that keeping temperatures at or below the 1.5C target would "significantly reduce the risks and impacts of climate change".

The Copernicus report authors found that parts of North America, northern Siberia, central Asia, the Maghreb, and much of northern Australia were also drier than average in the same period.

El Niño turbocharges warming

The world's ocean temperatures also hit a record high in August, with scientists predicting the water would continue to get hotter until an El Niño weather pattern reached its peak.

Why this El Niño is different The dark, red tongue spreading in the Pacific is growing at a rate not seen in living memory. The uncertainty over what is driving it has alarmed experts.

University of Adelaide climate scientist Georgy Falster said the record was not unexpected due to the combination of ongoing global warming and the El Niño event.

"El Niño itself is changing with climate change. So, this El Niño, it's likely to be very large, possibly the biggest one on record," she said.

"And it is possible, although not guaranteed, that the strength of this El Niño is related to climate change."

Dr Falster said it was critical to mark the records as they took place.

"We as a species need to keep reminding ourselves that what is happening is unprecedented," she said.

"So, I think it is actually very important to mark every time another record topples over."

Dr Falster said she was hopeful that the extreme weather spurred governments to act.

"There is absolutely no point at which we should stop trying to reduce the effects of future climate change," she said.

"No matter when we start acting, or increasing our efforts, all of that makes the world a better place in the future."

World.title: Queensland on the brink of a credit rating downgrade
World.content:
Queensland is on the brink of a credit rating downgrade, piling further pressure onto the state's spiralling multi-billion-dollar debt and interest costs.

The ABC understands a downgrade is imminent, sparking a blame game between Canberra and the LNP state government.

AMP chief economist Shane Oliver said a knock to Queensland's AA+ rating would see the cost of maintaining its ballooning debt increase.

"That means you've got less money left over to spend on other services or alternatively you've got to raise taxes or alternatively it just leads to a bigger budget deficit," he said.

AMP chief economist Shane Oliver. (ABC News: Daniel Irvine)

"Neither of those outcomes are particularly attractive and that's where it impacts the average Queenslander because it could mean pressure for higher taxes or it could mean less in the way of government services.

" So there will be a cost to Queenslanders, unfortunately. "

Political finger pointing

Speaking in federal parliament, Federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the risk of a downgrade was "very troubling".

Federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers said he was "concerned" by the potential downgrade. (ABC News: Nick Haggarty)

"As a Queenslander, I am concerned that despite substantial and increased Commonwealth support for Queensland, the Queensland government's fiscal position has experienced a sharp deterioration," he said.

Queensland treasurer David Janetzki, who has consistently said a downgrade was likely since coming to government in 2024, would not comment on any movement in the rating.

He laid the blame for any potential downgrade at the feet of the former Labor government and impacts from the latest federal budget.

"After a decade of fiscal vandalism under the former state Labor government which left Queensland on track for a credit rating downgrade, Queenslanders are now also paying the price for Jim Chalmers' budget decisions," Mr Janetzki said in a statement.

Queensland Treasurer David Janetzki laid any potential downgrade at the feet of the former Labor government. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

"Jim Chalmers confirmed on the floor of Parliament today what we have long been saying; that Canberra's continued cost-shifting onto the states has had a material impact on state budgets."

Mr Oliver said there were arguments to make for both the state and federal governments being to blame for the potential downgrade.

"At a high level, it's a result of economic circumstances," he said.

He said while the Queensland government had been making efforts to get back to a "more sustainable" financial position, that was being threatened by a fall in stamp duty revenue due to falling property prices and fewer sales of homes.

"The falling property market, rising bond yields, the GST carve up and not enough fiscal austerity at a state level all have a role to play in this likely downgrade," he said.

Debt forecast to march past $200 billion

Total debt is forecast to exceed more than $216 billion by 2029-30, an increase of 52 per cent over the next four years.

Handing down his most recent budget in July, Mr Janetzki had expected to bring the state's books back in the black by 2029-30.

A credit rating downgrade would cast doubt on that forecast.

Interest expenses for the current financial year are expected to reach $6.83 billion, and almost $11 billion by 2029-30.

That well exceeds the entire funding envelope for infrastructure for the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games, of $7.1 billion.

Credit agency S&P would not comment on any announcement or decision.

World.title: ‘Landmark achievement’ wins $80,000 literature prize
World.content:
CultureBooksLiterature prizes ‘Landmark achievement’ wins $80,000 literature prize Melanie Kembrey September 10, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A groundbreaking collaboration drawing on Yolngu oral history has become the first co-authored book to win the $80,000 Prime Minister’s Literary Award for fiction. A Piece of Red Cloth, written by novelist Leonie Norrington and Yolngu cultural custodians Merrkiyawuy Ganambarr-Stubbs, Djawa Burarrwanga and Djawundil Maymuru, was named the fiction winner at the National Library of Australia in Canberra on Thursday night. Rohan Howitt, Kate Wild, Merrkiyawuy Ganambarr-Stubbs, Dimathaya Burarrwanga, Pip Harry, Zana Fraillon and Ender Başkan with their prize-winning books at the Prime Minister’s Literary Awards. Alex Ellinghausen Set in north-east Arnhem Land before European settlement, the novel centres on a Yolngu family confronting the arrival of Macassan fishermen from what is now Indonesia, in the late 1600s. At its heart are matriarch Batjani and her granddaughter Garritji, who is preparing for marriage when Batjani attempts to protect her from the visiting trepang fishers.



It was one of six books awarded $80,000. Kate Wild’s The Red House, which explores the fatal shooting of Kumanjayi Walker and the murder trial of Constable Zachary Rolfe, won non-fiction, while Rohan Howitt’s The Southern Frontier took out Australian history and Ender Baskan’s Two Hundred Million Musketeers won poetry. Zana Fraillon’s Song of a Thousand Seas won children’s literature, while Pip Harry’s Drift nabbed young adult literature. The fiction judging panel – made up of critics and writers Beejay Silcox, Nicholas Jose, Andre Dao and Sophie Cunningham – described A Piece of Red Cloth as “a landmark achievement in fiction”. The winners of the 2026 Prime Minister’s Literary Awards. “From its first pages, the reader is immersed in the world of the Yolngu as it was in the 1600s, a world of language, Law and Country, deep magic and petty politics, dignity and desire,” the judges said. “It is a profound work of remembrance and re-imagination, fusing oral history, novelistic technique and deep cultural knowledge.” At the heart of A Piece of Red Cloth is a collaboration between Yolngu custodians and Norrington, who grew up in the Barunga community in Arnhem Land after her family moved there in the 1960s, where her father worked as the station mechanic.



Norrington said the novel took two decades to write after her Yolngu adoptive mother, the late Clare Bush, asked her to write it so non-Indigenous Australians could see another side of Indigenous history, “not just the Captain Cook one”. The story, she said, has been passed down for generations through dance, song, poetry, storytelling and art. “I worked with the owners [the co-authors] of the story tied to my adopted mother’s Country,” Norrington said. “We first talked through the draft and then nutted out scenes. I read back the scenes and made changes – many times up to 20 people were listening and commenting because the story is owned far and wide, so lots of people have opinions about how it should be told. “The negotiations and writing all happened on Country. But the final edits were read onto recordings and then sent out via email or over the phone.” Leonie Norrington and co-writer Merrkiyawuy Ganambarr-Stubbs. Leonie Norrington The win is the latest in a run of accolades for the novel, which was also shortlisted for the Victorian Premier’s Literary Awards and The Age Book of the Year fiction award, and won the Australian Book Industry Award for social impact.



“We hope it means more people read the book and that Australia’s foundational story becomes changed to include, in a fundamental way, Australia’s first people as the Country, rather than just the people who were here first,” Norrington said. Editor's pick Literature prizes Looking for your child’s next favourite book? Start with these award winners Established in 2008, the Prime Minister’s Literary Awards are the country’s richest annual literary prize, carrying a total tax-free pool of $600,000. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the winning works demonstrated “the depth and diversity” of Australian literature. “Our stories connect us across generations, cultures and communities, and allow the world to see Australia through Australian eyes,” he said.

World.title: Farnworth can’t forget his finals heartbreak. His fab five can right those wrongs
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Farnworth can’t forget his finals heartbreak. His fab five can right those wrongs Nick Wright September 10, 2026 — 7:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The scars from his last foray in finals football may linger, but Herbie Farnworth enters the 2026 series as a changed man, and a key member of arguably the most lethal backline in the NRL. The Dolphins centre looms as his side’s X-factor in their maiden finals campaign, which begins on Saturday in New Zealand when they play a Warriors side with a parochial crowd behind them. Farnworth hasn’t featured at this point of the season since he played with the Brisbane Broncos in the heartbreaking 2023 grand final defeat at the hands of a Nathan Cleary-inspired Penrith Panthers. Dolphins’ ‘Fab Five’: (from left to right) Selwyn Cobbo, Jamayne Isaako, Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow, Herbie Farnworth, Jack Bostock. Getty While the Englishman has new ambitions in delivering silverware to Redcliffe – and holds no bittersweet feelings that Brisbane got the job done in 2025 – those memories still linger and serve as motivation.



“It’s definitely a hard one to get over, I’d be lying if I said I hadn’t thought about it a fair bit,” Farnworth revealed. “But I feel like I’ve grown a lot as a person and as a player from it. Obviously, the boys [Broncos] ended up putting it right in the end, which was good to see – it was a lot of good mates who worked really hard. “Obviously, I didn’t get a ring, so hopefully, it’s our time this year. I know how hard all those boys work, I’d been with a lot of them since the under-20s, so it was nice to see them go on and do well.” Since arriving at his former club’s nearest rival, Farnworth has gone from the best up-and-coming centre in the game to a clear standout. Despite being positioned out wide, he leads the competition for offloads (72) and tackle busts (150).



Related Article NRL 2026 A week after a fatal crash, Chester drove the same road. That was just the start of his battles He has helped his team become one of rugby league’s most attacking sides, cementing a top four place ahead of finals. “I’ve obviously got some very good players inside me in Izzy [Katoa] and Kodi [Nikorima] putting me in good spots to break those tackles and make those offloads, so the credit probably goes to those guys,” Farnworth said. Fullback Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow chimed in: “He [Farnworth] doesn’t want to get tackled even more than me, I think that’s where I get it from. “Just watching him play and how he goes about his game, he’s a special talent.”



Dolphins’ attacking style has had a ripple effect for the rest of the side, with the work of the ‘Fab Five’ – Farnworth, Tabuai-Fidow, Selwyn Cobbo, Jack Bostock and Jamayne Isaako – complementing a forward pack built on speed and skill rather than size. No team in the competition this year has run for as many metres as the Dolphins’ nearly 43,800. The backline quintet has run for more than 16,800 of them, with only the ladder-leading Panthers running for more collectively among the teams named for the first week of the finals. The more mobile and creative members of the Dolphins forward pack – Max Plath, Kurt Donoghoe and Morgan Knowles the leading examples – have expanded the side’s attack; producing faster play-the-balls and an interchange of passing to combat the increasing pace of the contest due to the six-again set restart laws. “It should be the other way around, shouldn’t it?” Dolphins forward Felise Kaufusi said with a laugh, when asked about the mountain of work his backs get through.



“We’ve got some mobile and fit forwards, and the way the game is going – and how fit and fast it is – I think you need that from your middles. Those big bodies we have in our backs, they’re like extra forwards anyway, so I think we complement each other pretty well.” Related Article NRL 2026 How an AFL great has unlocked rugby league’s next great halfback Tabuai-Fidow credits the “special bond” shared between the squad for contributing to the on-field cohesiveness. He said he had “no regrets” about his move to Redcliffe from a North Queensland Cowboys’ outfit which had just reached the 2022 preliminary finals. “It all comes down to working hard for each other. We have that special bond and that connection where the back five will do the hard yards, and the forwards will tackle for us – it’s a trade-off there where we work together and make our jobs easy,” Tabuai-Fidow told this masthead. Isaako added: “Our forward pack is not as big as most forward packs in the comp, we’re a little bit of a smaller forward pack and a bit more mobile, and that sometimes means when the ball is kicked inside our 10, 20 metres zone we have a job to take the first three of four carries to get to our kick.



“It’s something we pride ourselves on is making sure we get the ball down the other end, and having a good kick-chase. In order to do that, we need our forwards to be in that chase line, so [we need to] do as much work as we can coming out of the backfield and make it easier for them.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The government’s WFH legislation has reclaimed its central purpose: a Wedge For Her
World.content:
Analysis NationalVictoriaVictorian Parliament The government’s WFH legislation has reclaimed its central purpose: a Wedge For Her Chip Le Grand September 10, 2026 — 7:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In the end, the Labor Party has exactly what it wanted out of its promise to give people a legislated right to work from home two days a week. The laws, in all likelihood, will never come into existence. On Thursday, they were condemned to a form of legislative purgatory – an upper house select committee for inquiry. There, it will dwell in darkness until this parliament is prorogued and the bill expires along with all the other unloved, forgotten and forsaken legislation of the past four years. Ben Carroll has got everything he needed from the work from home legislation. Eddie Jim This was never really about changing the law. All along, the main game for Labor was to draw the Liberal Party into a stoush about working from home.



Remember, this, along with promising nuclear power, are the two greatest reasons the federal Liberal Party is currently in opposition. Related Article Victorian Parliament ‘Final nail in the coffin’: Parliamentary twist derails work-from-home laws It is an embarrassing outcome for the government – for perhaps a day or two. Beyond that, it is an electoral gift to Premier Ben Carroll, who despite mouthing support for people’s right to work from home since he replaced Jacinta Allan, was never enamoured with her pet policy. We should all be thankful for the Victorian opposition for being guileless enough to make all this possible.



Working from home is wildly popular, but the one thing missing from the debate was compelling evidence that it needs to be protected by law. Related Article Opinion

Work therapy I can’t get a job because I can work only from home. What can I do? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor Thanks to the depth and duration of our COVID lockdowns, Melbourne remains one of the world’s most liveable cities for workers who prefer to clock on from the comfort of their homes and elastic-waisted trousers. Employers have embraced, by necessity, WFH accommodations. When disputes arise, there is a growing body of Fair Work Commission case law to help resolve them. This is not something that should concern Victoria’s lawmakers, who 30 years ago ceded to the Commonwealth their right to regulate employment conditions. The Victorian government’s plan to somehow bolt a right to work from home onto our anti-discrimination regime always seemed too clever by half.



Had the government scrounged a couple more votes in the upper house and passed these laws, it would have faced an almost certain High Court challenge. It is difficult to imagine a greater waste of the court’s time. Instead, with the Jess Wilson-led opposition now a firm favourite among the pollsters and bookies to win the November election, WFH can reclaim its central purpose – a wedge for her. Carroll feigned disappointment at what took place in the parliament’s Legislative Council, where Jeff Bourman from the Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party – a political species on the endangered list – enlisted the help of the Coalition and some crossbench pals to delay the bill beyond this parliament’s final sitting day. Privately, he couldn’t have hoped for a better outcome. From here until November 28, he will pin on the Liberals a debacle entirely of Labor’s making.

World.title: Watch: the horrifying moment roof collapses at Curtin University worksite
World.content:
NationalWACourts Watch: the horrifying moment roof collapses at Curtin University worksite Rebecca Peppiatt September 10, 2026 — 7:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The moment a glass ceiling collapsed underneath two men, killing one of them, has been released by a Perth court after the company responsible for the roof’s construction pleaded guilty to criminal negligence. Apprentice glazier Jonathan Hartshorn, 23, was killed at Curtin University’s Bentley campus in October 2020 after falling 20 metres from a partly constructed, five-storey glass roof. Loading Workmate Rikki Issitt was also seriously injured during the same incident, on Wednesday telling Perth Magistrates Court his life had been irrevocably changed as a result. Steel fabrication company Elsdon was held responsible for the workplace incident after it was determined their staff had inadequate welding qualifications that led to poorly created steel trusses that were designed to hold the glass in place.



But it has taken six years for justice to be served, the company only pleading guilty to the charge of failing to ensure the safety or health of a person who is not an employee on Wednesday. Related Article Courts Survivor’s guilt and devastation: Court hears toll of fatal Curtin University roof collapse A second charge of failing to provide safe plant and caused death as a result was dropped and charges against the roof’s design company were also dropped earlier this year. On Thursday, Perth Magistrate Andrew Matthews released footage of the moment the roof collapsed that had been shown in court and seen by Hartshorn’s devastated mother. Susan Chappell told media outside court that watching the moment her son died was “horrible” and earlier criticised Elsdon for the length of time it took them to take responsibility for the 23-year-old’s death.



“Jonnie should be here, fulfilling his dreams, living the sweet life that he wanted,” Chappell said. “Instead his future was torn from underneath him along with mine. Now left with the wreckage.” Issitt also addressed the court and spoke about the moment he fell through the roof and thought he was going to die. “I looked up and saw the ceiling hanging above me,” he said. Issitt suffered significant injuries including breaks to both arms and legs, a fracture spine and broken pelvis.



He has been unable to work since. “The emotional consequences have been devastating,” he said, before adding that he had suffered survivors guilt following the death of Hartshorn.

World.title: ‘It’s a disaster’: How boxes of forgotten referrals led to tragedy at a Victorian hospital
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaHealthcare ‘It’s a disaster’: How boxes of forgotten referrals led to tragedy at a Victorian hospital Henrietta Cook September 10, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A cancer patient has died and another is terminal after a Victorian hospital, still reliant on paper records, failed to triage 150 critical referrals left sitting in cardboard boxes for up to 16 months. Mildura Base Public Hospital has reported the sentinel events to the state’s health watchdog, Safer Care Victoria, and is undertaking its own investigation into the lengthy and potentially fatal delays. Mildura Base Public Hospital Ben Gross The delays involve dozens of patients with cancer symptoms who need colonoscopies and other diagnostic tests, as well as patients requiring treatment for confirmed skin cancers. The situation highlights a broader issue plaguing many regional and rural hospitals, where outdated paper records and manual sorting are still used despite repeated calls from doctors’ groups for digital upgrades.



Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare Trapped and dying: Victoria’s worst hospital for emergency department waits The patient who died from cancer and another who received a terminal diagnosis were among the 150 patients caught up in the backlog, according to four hospital sources not authorised to speak publicly. It is not known whether earlier triage could have prevented the cancer patient’s death or the other cancer patient’s terminal prognosis. But a health professional who works at the hospital, who was not authorised to speak publicly, said prompt access to diagnosis and treatment would have markedly improved their quality of life. “You can’t justify having failures in the system in this day and age that might lead to someone’s death,” they said. The sources said the cardboard boxes containing the GP referrals were forgotten, so no specialist doctor was assigned the task of triaging them for the hospital’s specialist clinics.



“It’s a disaster,” said one doctor with knowledge of the situation, who also requested anonymity because they were not authorised to speak publicly. “We are already seeing bad outcomes for patients because they are not getting timely access to the care they need.” Up to 150 critical referrals were forgotten. Louie Douvis Some of the paper referrals were sent to the hospital in Victoria’s north-west in December 2024. They were not triaged until the files were discovered in April this year. In one critical case, a patient had to wait almost five months to access an initial specialist clinic appointment to discuss the removal of a melanoma detected by their GP. In another case, a patient waited 17 months to access a specialist appointment to discuss an endoscopy for suspected cancer.



If these patients had been triaged earlier, they would have been classified as category 1, which means they should have been seen at a specialist clinic within 30 days. They would then be placed on the elective surgery waiting list for treatment. Australian Medical Association Victoria president Dr Simon Judkins described the situation as “gravely concerning” and said it highlighted what could go wrong when health services relied on outdated paper-based processes. He said despite the AMA calling for IT upgrades for regional and rural hospitals for more than a decade, many still relied on “faxing bits of paper and paper referrals” while their city counterparts used electronic systems. “This is a process that relies on people collecting bits of paper and putting them in a box for someone else to look at – it’s flawed,” he said. “We won’t know the impact on patients for a long time. No one should be waiting that period of time to have their referral looked at.”



Opposition health spokeswoman Georgie Crozier said the state government had ignored repeated warnings about serious failures in the state’s health system, and patients were paying the price. “This is a disgrace,” she said. Opposition health spokeswoman Georgie Crozier. Justin McManus “Delays in diagnosis and treatment have put Victorian lives at risk. These failures cannot simply be swept under the carpet. These forgotten patients are Victorians waiting for diagnosis and treatment while their health deteriorates, and they deserve answers.” While the hospital has an IT system, it still sorts paper-based referrals from GPs into cardboard folders and boxes for each specialist clinic. There is no centralised way of tracking referrals, according to hospital insiders.



Related Article Healthcare Patients are waiting 1460 days for routine appointments. Authorities think AI can fix it Once patients visit the specialist clinic, they receive a paper slip which they have to carry to another part of the hospital to book in their elective surgery. Matthew Jukes, the interim chief executive of Mildura Base Public Hospital, said it was incredibly distressing to have to wait for medical treatment, particularly for cancer patients. “Mildura Base Public Hospital is always working to improve its service delivery and models of care, including wait times to ensure the best possible outcomes for the Mildura community,” he said. He said the hospital was unable to share specific patient details.



The hospital has now triaged the backlog of 150 critical referrals, and booked the patients into specialist clinics. A Safer Care Victoria spokeswoman said Mildura Base Public Hospital had reported these cases to the watchdog in line with its reporting obligations and also undertaken its own review of the incidents. “Safer Care Victoria’s role is to oversee and support the sentinel event reporting process. It reviews information provided by health services, provides feedback where appropriate and helps identify opportunities to improve patient safety,” she said. In Victoria, the investigation of individual sentinel events – which the watchdog describes as “adverse patient safety events that result in serious harm or death” – is the responsibility of health services.



Mildura Base Public Hospital was operated as a public hospital under a private management contract with Ramsay Health until 2020, when it was taken over by the state Labor government. In its latest annual report, the health service said it had commenced a project in its specialist clinic to transition from paper-based referrals to an electronic system. It said once this project was completed it would “result in significant efficiencies for the administration team and improved patient experience, particularly greater visibility of patients waiting for care”. It’s estimated that upgrading the system across health services in the Loddon Mallee region would cost around $70 million. An unprecedented number of patients are seeking specialist clinic care at Victorian public hospitals, as the cost-of-living crisis and soaring private doctors’ fees makes care in the private system unaffordable for many.



In response, the state government announced in May it would overhaul the state’s specialist clinics by creating regional waiting lists, shifting appointments from doctors to nurses, and using AI to flag urgent cases. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare ‘Overwhelmed by demand’: Mildura Hospital’s dire warning for Allan government It said this would provide people with quicker access to appointments, clearer communication and more care options for patients closer to home. This followed the release of a Department of Health report that found Victorians were currently waiting up to four years to access specialist care at public hospitals, with wild variability across the state. Mildura Base Public Hospital is also struggling to keep up with demand in its emergency department. Last year, this masthead revealed that hundreds of patients were languishing in the hospital’s emergency department for more than 24 hours.



In response, the board of the hospital lashed out at the state government over its lack of funding to expand bed capacity at the regional health service, and said it “can no longer meet the growing demand”. The government responded by announcing that four new sub-acute beds would open at the hospital. The latest health data shows that the median wait times for urgent first appointments at specialist clinics is 16 days. The statewide median wait time for a routine first appointment is 58 days. Mildura Base Public Hospital has 16 main specialist and outpatient clinic services, including general medicine, oncology and infectious diseases. World.title: The data on contact sport, concussion and CTE is convincing. But not conclusive
World.content:
SportConcussion crisis Opinion The data on contact sport, concussion and CTE is convincing. But not conclusive Darren Kane Sports Columnist September 10, 2026 — 7:30pm

September 10, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The International Sport Concussion Conference was held in Melbourne earlier this week, in the days preceding the first regular-season NFL game played on Australian soil. During Tuesday’s session, research figures from the Australian Sports Brain Bank were presented. Of the first 150 brains of participants in contact sport examined by the bank, 51 belonged to men who had a reported history of playing rugby league. Thirty-one of those 51 carried the pathological signature of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). Loading Rugby league players both amateur and professional; men who died in their 20s, 30s and 40s. Among them Paul Green, an NRL premiership-winning coach who died by suicide at 49, and the Manly Sea Eagles player Keith Titmuss, who was 20 when he collapsed after a training session and died of heat stroke. Rightly, those numbers can’t be ignored and are cause for concern, if not alarm. Temper your musings, however. The findings of the NSW Deputy State Coroner, handed down in 2024, were that Titmuss died of exertional heat stroke. He might have had CTE pathology at the time of his death, but it says nothing about why he died.



The finding is invoked as a marker of exposure and a portent, which isn’t an illegitimate scientific use. But it’s not a finding that he died of CTE, or that the pathology affected his function, or that it would have. He is, strictly, a case of dying with. Like the 102-year-old man who dies with prostate cancer, but not because of it. Repeated blows to the head appear to cause this CTE pathology. In brain banks replete with the brains of people who weren’t former collision and combat sport participants, the pathology is rarer. A study conducted a little over a decade ago by the Mayo Clinic detected CTE pathology in 21 of 66 former contact sport athletes and in none of 198 people who’d never participated in those activities. But those are small sample sizes. The brain of former North Queensland coach Paul Green was found to carry the signature of CTE. Getty So this isn’t the data of coincidence. The families donating these brains of their deceased loved ones aren’t hysterics. But we must be careful with what the data shows. By definition, a “concussion” is a mild traumatic brain injury caused through the violent ping-ponging of the brain inside the skull. No sport has its history and existence more intertwined with brain injury than American football.



More than a decade ago, more than 4500 former NFL players and their families sued the NFL, on the case theory that the NFL had, for decades, been aware players were being exposed to an unacceptable risk of repeated concussions and connected traumatic and degenerative brain conditions by playing gridiron within the rules set by the NFL. The plaintiffs further contended that, despite the game’s governing minds being armed with that knowledge, the NFL knowingly failed to take the necessary and appropriate steps to shield them from harm, in turn exposing the players to the possible onset of CTE manifesting in memory loss, depression, early onset dementia and a propensity to suicide. Dr Claire Shepherd examines brain tissues collected through the Sydney Brain Bank for CTE research. Dominic Lorrimer To put the quantum of plaintiffs into some semblance of context, (very) roughly 20,000 men played in the NFL between 1967 and 2014. In an unsophisticated way, that in turn illustrates that over 22 per cent of players suffered significant enough damage to qualify to join in legal proceedings. The class action was settled for a ten-figure sum and no admissions of liability, but an agreement laced with tacit recognition and responsibility which spared the players from shifting the incredibly difficult burden of proving the causal links between their professional football careers and the catastrophic afflictions with which they were left.



Risks associated with brain trauma represent an existential risk to collision and combat sports. Such matters must be treated with utmost seriousness. But care also must be taken when determining what it really means if of 150 brains analysed, the reported instances of CTE were discovered. What proportion of people might die with CTE pathology present, but not of any condition the pathology leads to? If 100,000 brains were donated and analysed post-mortem, what would the incidence of CTE pathology be in females who died when aged 70 or older, who seldom ever bought a ticket to Kogarah’s Jubilee Oval let alone played the game on the hallowed ground? Head first: Payments to NFL players have eclipsed half a billion dollars. Bob Leverone What of the recreational rugby league player who also had an unhealthy thirst0 for the Nectar of the Gods and pub fights during the “Kebab Hours” of a weekend morning? Which are the predominant causative factors for any CTE pathology identified once his brain is sliced into slivers? The conflation between identifiable and abnormal accumulation of tau protein around the blood vessels in particular parts of the brain – which is the defining pathological hallmark of CTE – is a hypothesis and inferred based on studies involving older donors over time. That pattern is consistent with progression; it is equally consistent with survivorship or with age-related tauopathy occurring alongside a static traumatic brain lesion.



Related Article Updated

Sporting rules Judge makes big call on what is a ‘combat sport’ Second, the conflation between the brain disease and the manifestation of traumatic encephalopathy syndrome, which is the clinical construct of CTE. In a 2014 study published in The Journal of the Alzheimer’s Association, a study of 336 donated brains from people exposed to repetitive head impacts from contact sports, military service, or physical violence in their lifetime concluded that while 97 per cent were clinically diagnosed with the syndrome based on exhibited symptomology, the brain pathology was only present in one-fifth of those cases. The third issue is that 31 of 51 is a proportion of donors, not of players. Families donate their loved one’s brain to research for an important and valid reason, and the reasons are not randomly distributed. A family whose father died after a decade of decline is likelier to seek an answer than one whose father died with his faculties intact. The proportion of CTE in a brain bank equals population prevalence only to the extent that a proper and statistically reliable number of brains are donated, from people from all walks of life. In a paper published in the British Medical Journal the week before last, the authors identified every former NFL player who died between 2008 and 2021, being a total of 1712 men, and determined that 338 had donated their brains. Of that cohort, 315 had a diagnosis of CTE. The remaining 1400-odd weren’t examined. Nothing here denies that repetitive head impact causes CTE pathology. The burden of persuasion on that point has shifted to those who would deny it.



Related Article Updated

Melbourne major events ‘In bed by 8pm’: Rams impose curfew before historic MCG clash What’s denied is that current evidence licenses the further steps that public discussion and litigation take for granted – that the brain lesion is the disease; that the disease is the syndrome; that the donors are the players, and that a man found with protein build-up in a specific part of his brain died because of it. Each matter is an inference, and each is under-determined. Sixty-one per cent of 51 is a number that demands further study and research. It’s not yet a number that decides an argument of existential relevance. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.
