World.title: Mum avoids prison as judge says it would be too hard on children
World.content:
An Auckland woman has been spared imprisonment for tax offending because having both parents in prison would be too hard on her children.

Faalili Vaa and his wife Belinda Heilupe Vaa were found by the court to be equally culpable but he was sentenced to 26 months behind bars while she was given home detention.

They faced representative charges of evading income tax and GST and using a document to dishonestly obtain income tax advantages and a Small Business Cashflow Scheme loan between 2015 and 2024.

Both benefited from all business profits and knew that the GST and income tax returns that were filed contained incorrect information, with sales under-stated, and the expenses inflated.

Once their tax affairs started being reviewed by Inland Revenue in 2018, they then deliberately chose not to file GST and income tax returns for their kitchen installation work.

In total, over nine years the evasion and fraud of income tax, GST and a Small Business Cashflow Scheme loan amounted to $554,998.68.

Judge Sandra Alofivae set a starting point of 44 months imprisonment for both before allowing discounts for their guilty please, remorse and autistic children.

She said it was on humanitarian grounds that she reduced Belinda Vaa's sentence and converted it to 12 months home detention, because having both parents in prison would be too hard on their children.

Alofivae said she was also concerned Faalili Vaa was still self-employed, given the charges.

World.title: Turkish delight and tax fights: Christopher Luxon and Chris Hipkins hit the campaign trail
World.content:
There was milk, Turkish delight and talk of a steak as Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and Labour leader Chris Hipkins tried to win over business owners, with less than two months to go until the election.

With Parliament on a break, the prime minister and his Labour counterpart took to the streets to campaign this week.

Donning a white overcoat, protective glasses, and a hairnet, Luxon toured the new Meadow Fresh High Value Dairy Centre on Thursday morning. The $100 million plant will produce high-protein milk products for export to Asia and has created 25 new jobs.

"It's a really awesome place, it's fantastic," he said. "I've met some incredible young people who are working here."

Speaking to media, Luxon made his case as to why businesses should vote for his party and why they should not vote for Labour.

"Labour's capital gains tax is going to smash up businesses big time.

"[On Wednesday] I was up at the Woodend Bakery. There's a baker who has actually bought his building, and when he goes to retire, he's going to be paying a Labour government a capital gains tax."

Bernard Duignan and Christopher Luxon cut the ribbon to officially open the Meadow Fresh High Value Dairy Centre in Upper Riccarton, Christchurch. Peter Meecham

Meanwhile in Auckland, Hipkins visited Dominion Road shops, joined by Labour candidates Michael Wood and former top cop Rakesh Naidoo.

First up was commercial printing store Copies Plus.

Last week Labour announced that, if elected, it would lift the tax write-off for small businesses buying equipment or tools, from $1000 to $10,000, which Hipkins was eager to share with Copies Plus owner Dave Shah.

"For a business like this, I imagine you'd be buying quite a lot of equipment that would be under the $10,000 threshold.

"That would definitely benefit me," said Shah.

Further up the road, Hipkins talked to Istanbul Halal Meat and Grocery about meat prices.

"Definitely red meat has gone up a lot in price, hasn't it? Even a kilo of mince now is $20 plus."

"That's the fatty stuff," Wood replied.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins hits the campaign trail and meets Copies Plus owner Dave Shah. Jessica Hopkins

Hipkins confirmed he only bought "cheap" mince.

The men also eyed up the store's meat selection.

"That's not a bad price on the steaks actually," Wood said. "BBQ season's about to kick off."

Then, speaking to the media, Hipkins was asked about National's criticism of Labour's capital gains tax.

"It's just desperation from National. There's no great revelation here. If you own commercial property and you sell commercial property, yes, you'll pay capital gains tax on that. But for small businesses, the goodwill, the equity you build up in your small business, that is not covered by the capital gains tax."

Michael Wood with some sweet treats. Jessica Hopkins

Wood said he was excited to be back and that his community could trust him, after he failed to disclose and sell shares in Auckland Airport in 2023.

"This has been my home for 23 years. I've served this area faithfully as the MP.

"We're in the most multicultural community in all of New Zealand, and when our community has been attacked by senior Cabinet ministers, I've spoken up for them."

Leaving Istanbul Halal Meat and Grocery, he picked up some Turkish delight.

"It's important on the campaign trail to have a little sugar hit sometimes, and this is delicious."

World.title: Decapitated dolphin washes up in Coromandel
World.content:
Decapitated dolphin washes up in the Coromandel Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

A decapitated dolphin has washed up on Pauanui beach in the Coromandel and the Conservation department wants to hear from anyone who knows what happened.

Conservation department investigation officer Hayden Loper said although the dolphin's body was decomposed, it appeared some kind of tool or implement had been used to remove its head.

Loper said marine scientists believed it was a bottle nosed dolphin, a species fully protected since 1978.

"We are asking anyone who saw what happened to this dolphin to come forward," Loper said.

"Pauanui is a small but busy settlement with a popular beach, so we're hopeful someone can provide us with information which may lead us to whoever is responsible."

World.title: Joyce vague on details, Albanese wins tennis match amid golf grant saga
World.content:
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.

Barnaby Joyce has always been a disruptor; it’s one of the reasons Pauline Hanson wanted to woo him to One Nation.

Few have had a career quite like Joyce, who was once described by Tony Abbott as Australia’s best retail politician. The man who had two turns as Nationals leader could connect with voters. He was loved and despised (in some seats) in equal measure.

His defection to One Nation was designed to bolster the party’s legitimacy. His performance as its Treasury spokesperson this week did anything but.

Joyce struggled as he was sent out to sell the party’s superannuation policy. Under the plan, renters and mortgage borrowers would be able to divert a quarter of their super contributions to their income for up to three years.

Across a series of interviews (including one he conducted from the Qantas Chairman’s Lounge) he was asked about the proposal’s inflationary impact and what this would mean for a person's foregone retirement savings.

“Interest rates keep rising,” Hanson had said as she announced the policy at a rare press conference in Parliament House. Economists told the ABC the policy, if ever adopted, would only tempt the Reserve Bank to push them higher.

Loading...

Joyce claimed the extra cash wouldn't drive up inflation because the money already sits in superannuation funds, so it's already in the economy. Economists don't share that view, with history suggesting people would most likely spend and not invest any extra money.

Joyce snapped at the ABC's Sarah Ferguson on 7.30 on Monday night for not providing questions on retirement savings losses ahead of time. He declared he was not Jesus Christ, as if that was ever in question.

He is, though, an accountant by trade (a fact he pointed out) and someone who has been on the policy sell many a time. It became clear One Nation never modelled the proposal. Joyce later claimed they didn't have the staff to do so — an argument that fails to acknowledge One Nation could've asked the Parliamentary Budget Office to help as other parties do.

Whether the policy has merit is one thing. But inflation is already running hot. Having some idea of the inflationary impact before releasing should be the bare minimum for a Treasury spokesperson.

A subplot to this is it's the second time in as many months the Coalition was reportedly gazumped by One Nation on policy (first being the tobacco excise). A similar proposal was said to have been drafted under Sussan Ley. The opposition downplayed the question of a leaker within their ranks, but it again begs the question of discipline.

The similarity between offerings from the Coalition and One Nation is something the government continues to leap on. It plays into the argument the government thinks it can win and is probably why a noticeable chunk of Labor's questions to itself in QT were about super.

Hastie v Hanson

A fight between Hanson and Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie has been brewing for a while.

The spat came to a head this week over a One Nation cartoon that called the former SAS captain a "traitor" eight times across nine minutes for testifying in Ben Roberts-Smith's failed defamation case. He was subpoenaed to do so.

"It's a slur on me. It's a slur on other veterans who have given under oath evidence to the federal court," Hastie said.

Several Liberals also condemned the cartoon. As did fellow veteran Jacqui Lambie, who echoed Hastie in calling the One Nation leader a "bloody coward".

Hastie served in Afghanistan. He's drawn the ire of One Nation and backer Gina Rinehart for giving evidence against the Victorian Cross recipient. Hanson and Rinehart say Roberts-Smith has been unfairly targeted over war crime allegations.

Andrew Hastie is taking issue with a cartoon published on Pauline Hanson's X account. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Roberts-Smith was this year charged with five counts of the war crime of murder over the alleged killings of five Afghan men between 2009 and 2012. He has not yet entered a plea but has denied the allegations.

Hastie's seat of Canning covers a large part of the state electorate of Secret Harbour, which One Nation won in a by-election last month. It's put a target on the seat as one the party thinks it can win at the next federal election.

Hastie's ruled out legal action over the video. It would be too costly of an exercise, he says, thanks to Rinehart's backing. Instead, he wants to "impose costs politically".

Hanson, and Joyce, have insisted she hasn't personally called Hastie a traitor despite the video. Earlier this week though, she did say she'd call him a "wanker".

Coalition deals it itself out

While he wouldn't agree with Hastie's description of Hanson having a "glass jaw," Opposition Leader Angus Taylor did back the call for the video to be pulled down.

It's an ironic point for him to make at the press conference where he was rallying against the government's Digital Duty of Care legislation – a bill he declared amounted to political censorship.

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

The government released draft legislation earlier this week. It's designed to force social media companies to identify and mitigate harm on their platforms. It would also force platforms to provide users with choice between an algorithmic feed and a feed simply made up of people you actually follow.

But on Thursday the Coalition effectively dealt itself out of negotiations, confirming it won't support the bill amid concerns it hands the communication minister too much power to determine what constitutes online harm.

Shadow Communications spokeswoman Sarah Henderson urged reporters to not conflate the concerns about the algorithm with the part of the bill the Coalition had problems with, ignoring the fact Matt Canavan, who was standing next to her, and others had been doing so all week.

Loading

Albanese gets tetchy

You might think with all this going it, the prime minister's week must have been smooth sailing.

After the ABC revealed the PM had an honorary membership with the Marrickville Golf Club, Albanese was under pressure over a $6m grant he promised the club for upgrades.

The $560 million Major and Local Community Infrastructure Fund was investigated by the Centre for Public Integrity and found 73 per cent of the funding went to notionally Labor-held seats.

Labor essentially spent the week insisting there was nothing to see here. The scheme was invitation only so the government could deliver its election promises. The crossbench labelled it pork-barrelling by design, calling for guidelines to be rewritten.

Loading...

Albanese turned the story into a bigger spectacle in a tetchy interview with the ABC, where he denied knowledge of the membership and took aim at the public broadcaster.

"I don't have a card. I don't go in there. I haven't been in there for years. I used to walk my dog along the path, as lots of people do because it's a community club," he said.

"The ABC should do better."

At least the prime minister can take comfort in the victory he did have in his preferred sport of tennis. Albanese defeated mortgage broker Joseph Daoud in a charity tennis match.

Daoud, a vocal critic of the government's housing tax changes, purchased the hit-out with Albanese for $16,500 in the Mid-Winter Ball's silent auction.

Despite telling reporters he'd been practising for months, Albanese had years on him and won in straight sets.

World.title: Aussie beach volleyball stars have crafty plan for success in LA
World.content:
Australian beach volleyball player Taliqua Clancy sits up excitedly, a flicker of a plan flitting across her face and dancing behind her eyes.

The three-time Olympian is sitting beside the courts at the Sandstorm Beach Volleyball Club at Nathan, in Brisbane's south, the shadow of the Queensland Sports and Athletics Centre's skeletal eastern grandstand looming up on the hill to her left.

Her newest playing partner, 21-year-old Stefie Fejes, is sitting on her right.

For a moment, conversation has turned from volleyball and the success this fledgling partnership has enjoyed since they came together in May this year, to Fejes's side project, crocheting.

Stefie Fejes (right) has only played six tournaments with Olympic silver medallist Taliqua Clancy. (Supplied: Volleyball World)

"It started in high school actually with one of my design projects," Fejes explains to ABC Sport.

"I made an eco-friendly bikini out of cotton. I'm really invested in sustainable fashion and, I guess, everything that goes with it.

"I'm really not a huge fan of fast fashion and how much waste we're producing in the world, so that's kind of where the love started.

"And then I was like, this is a great way to pass time: It's very efficient. It's productive. I can make some money. And I love doing it.

"I started doing it on the plane, do it on the bus. I would say it's like a form of meditation, for sure.

Loading Instagram content

"Everyone probably knows, but I'm quite high functioning,

"I like to move around a lot, do a lot and not a lot stops, and this is like my time where I can actually just take a breath and I make myself sit down and still be productive, but I'm actually sitting down and resting."

Clancy chips in and tells Fejes to mention one of her main projects, the crocheted ball carrier.

"On my first international event away I started realising that we have to take our [volley]ball with us everywhere, especially if we don't have a big staff and coaching team with us, and the ball takes up so much space in your bag," Fejes says.

"So I was like, OK, I'm going to create a ball carrier that I can just clip onto the outside of my bag, and everyone was obsessed with it.

"I'm still making it four years later. And sales are going great.

"I think most of the Australian tour has one, which is actually really cool, and they're supporting my journey … It's really special actually, I'm like, 'I made that,' when I see one … it's very kind and I really appreciate that everyone's getting on board with it too. I think it's really cool to connect with the community like that."

Stefie Fejes's ball pouches have become a common sight on the circuit. (Supplied: Instagram/@cheekie_handmadecrochet)

There is something in this crafting contemplation that strikes a gleeful parallel with British diver Tom Daley, whose habit of knitting in the stands during the 2021 Olympics in Tokyo sent the five-time Olympic medal winner viral at those Games and the subsequent Paris Olympics.

It has sent Tokyo silver medallist Clancy's mind working into overdrive, too.

"You need to pick an athlete that you want to gift it to," Clancy says to Fejes.

"And you've got to find them in the village.

"Snoop Dogg! He always comes out to the event. Oh my God, make him something."

Fejes laughs and agrees to cook something up. She has time to plan what to make, at least.

Snoop Dogg appears likely to be receptive to a crocheted bit of kit. (Getty Images: Joe Scarnici)

As the pair speak to ABC Sport they are each, almost absent-mindedly, turning a gold medal around in their hands, spoils from the Asian Championships in Shangluo, China, earlier this month.

Indeed, on the table to Clancy's right sits the voluminous silver trophy, with a novelty-cheque-sized banner with "QUALIFIED" emblazoned across it — the ticket to the LA28 Olympic Games.

A change to the qualification process for the LA Olympics had meant Australia has already qualified a quota spot just under two years out from the Games.

Fellow Paris Olympians Mark Nicolaidis and Izac Carracher also secured Australia a quota spot by winning the men's competition, edging out fellow countrymen Tom Hodges and Ben Hood in an epic final 21-17, 17-21, 15-12.

In Clancy's almost two-decade elite career, Olympic qualifying has never been completed this far out from a Games.

"They kind of changed the whole Olympic cycle," Clancy says.

"It was really last minute that we, and all the other countries, found out that if you win your continental champs you also secure a ticket to LA, so it was an odd one because you're kind of making a short plan within the really big, long-term plan of getting to the Games."

Taliqua Clancy, Stefie Fejes, Mark Nicolaidis and Izac Carracher have secured a quota spot for Australia at the LA Games. (Supplied: Volleyball World)

Offering crocheted gifts to US rappers isn't something that should preoccupy Fejes and Clancy's mind too much yet. Earning a quota spot does not mean that Australia will send this particular pairing to the Games; only that there is a spot there for an Australian team.

But despite only playing six tournaments together so far, the signs are looking promising that this team could make it all the way.

Prior to their Asian Championships victory — Clancy's sixth continental championship win — the pair came fifth at the World Volleyball Beach Pro Tour Elite16 event in Hamburg.

Their subsequent success in China came despite Fejes being so sick she was bedridden in the lead-up and Clancy breaking a toe. She also required treatment for a knee injury that was "a bit more severe than we anticipated" during the off-season, which limited their playing time.

Clancy noted that securing qualification so early was just "one part of the job" as far as their development as a pairing was concerned and that there was still a lot of work to do in order to improve their seeding for the Games and to work on the nuances of what they needed to do together on the court.

She has, of course, been in this position before.

Mariafe Artacho del Solar and Taliqua Clancy claimed silver in Tokyo. (AP: Petros Giannakouris)

For the past two Olympic cycles she has worked with Mariafe Artacho del Solar, a partnership that produced an Olympic silver medal, back-to-back Commonwealth Games silvers, world championship bronze and eight world tour titles.

But it is looking back to her first Games cycle where Clancy has found parallels with her new partner.

In 2016 Indigenous beach volleyballer heads to Rio alongside Louise Bawden, with whom she was partnered for five years and more than 60 tournaments.

Bawden was already a two-time Olympian in two different disciplines at that stage. Now the tables have turned and Clancy is the one with the experience in the partnership.

Taliqua Clancy (left) made her Olympic bow in Rio with Louise Bawden. (Getty Images: Paul Gilham)

"Actually it's so funny because it's kind of the complete flip," Clancy, who is now 34, says.

"I'm pretty sure me and Lou actually had pretty much the same age gap as well [Clancy was 24 during the Games and Bowden was 35 in Rio].

"So it is pretty funny. Me and Lou are very close, so I have asked a few questions. I was like, shit, OK, what do I do?

"But she's always been a great support. I still lean on her quite a lot."

Taliqua Clancy has now won six Asian Beach Volleyball Championships gold medals. (Supplied: Volleyball World)

As for Fejes, she's far from overawed from playing with a multiple global medallist.

"It's definitely not intimidating," she says.

"I've watched Taliqua's career basically my whole life and I always wanted to play with her, so it's pretty cool that this could finally happen.

"But I think the biggest thing I've learned is like coming into the space with T, the actions are 100 per cent the best. It doesn't matter how she's feeling, the consistency and the level of mastery is not something I've really experienced with the players that I've played with before.

"Maybe because of that experience, but also just the level of dedication T has shown over the past 17 years is just incredible.

"I think it was more inspiring for me than intimidating and like, yeah, this is where I want to be and I'm super excited to continue the journey."

Stefie Fejes and Taliqua Clancy are developing a strong partnership. (Supplied: Volleyball World)

That journey will have to include more trips from her home in Sydney's Northern Beaches to Brisbane, mostly for training, but also to deliver a crocheted masterclass to Clancy's nephews.

"Every time I'm with them and call them and anything, they always ask, 'Is Stefanie coming over?' 'Is she going to come crochet?'" Clancy says.

"So they're actually waiting."

Fejes seems OK with that.

"We're going to have a little crochet session together for sure. Absolutely," she says.

Perhaps they can workshop things to make for a certain US Olympic super fan while they're there, too.

World.title: At 35, there is still no end in sight for Dane Gagai
World.content:
He might be 35 and in his 16th year of NRL football, but Dane Gagai is not old.

Is he older than other players? Yes, definitely. Gagai has been around long enough that he's faced footballers involved in the Super League war.

He's the last Newcastle Knight to have played alongside Danny Buderus and when he moves to Brisbane next season he'll join Ben Hunt as the last Broncos to have played with Darren Lockyer.

Penrith legend Craig Gower, who made his first-grade debut 30 years ago, is another former teammate and Gagai is the only player in the entire league who has played in a preliminary final for the Knights courtesy of their run through the 2013 finals.

Dane Gagai is one of the NRL's longest-serving players. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Cody Hopwood, a teammate for Friday night's sudden-death semi-final against South Sydney, watched those games under a Knights blanket at his grandmother's house because he was just seven years old at the time.

Gagai is the fourth most-capped player in Knights history with 238 appearances and has already played the most first-grade games of any outside back in the history of the sport in Australia with 336 and counting.

But that doesn't mean he's old, not by a long shot, because in rugby league to be old is to be done and Gagai is far from done.

Dane Gagai will return to Brisbane next year after leaving almost 16 years ago. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

"If you call me old and I'm out on that field and I'm leaving you behind, whether it's fitness games, conditioning or in the weight room, you better back it up," Gagai said.

"I've signed another contract for next year and I don't plan on finishing up after that but whether that's the end or not, you only have a limited time in this game.

"I don't want to leave it and think, 'If only I'd put in a bit more here or there.'

"Like a lot of players say, you're a long time retired so you might as well enjoy it while you're here.

"It's that competitive side of me [that gets going] when people tell me I'm getting old. It gives me a point to prove."

Gagai has been proving that point for many years now as part of a long goodbye with no end in sight.

Dane Gagai has played some of his best football in recent years. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner)

It's a different world from the old days of "Origin Gagai", when he shrugged off indifferent club form to become a Queensland superhero.

For many years Gagai has worked hard to make the most of every moment and he still pushes himself to new limits at an age when other players are slowing down.

This year Gagai had the eighth-most tackle busts of any player in the league and was second only to Herbie Farnworth among centres.

He set a new career high for linebreaks in a season two years ago and recorded his career high for average metres per game the year before that.

Some of his best days have come when Newcastle have had little else to go on. Along with Jacob Saifiti, Gagai is one of just two players remaining at the club since its interminable one-win wooden spoon season in 2016.

Hard times like that have made him stronger.

Dane Gagai has given his all for the Knights, in good times and bad. (Getty Images: Matt King)

Case in point was last year, when the Knights again slumped to last amid a horror campaign beset by misery and blighted by attacking struggles.

On a team that couldn't attack to save itself, Gagai had the second-most tackle busts of any player in the league as he gave fine service for a hopeless cause right to the end.

This year, where the Knights have surged back into the finals despite another torrid injury toll, is both a reward and a vindication of his approach, a reminder that while winning is nice the fighting is the point.

Because of those injuries, a lot of Gagai's younger teammates have had to grow up quickly. Many of them will be making their finals debuts on Friday night and Gagai will offer advice if required, but to him most of them won't need it.

Crook elbows and big dreams propel unheralded Knights for finals Newcastle forward Francis Manuleleua might be less than two weeks off dislocating his right elbow but at the end of an interview he'll still shake your hand and shake it hard.

"I don't think I need to say much. I've been so impressed with how these young boys have stepped up," Gagai said.

"I'm sure the nerves are through the roof but nerves aren't always a bad thing. It's just about making sure you prepare well, that's what I'd say to the boys.

"Not only on the field but away from the field, be it sleep, diet, just doing everything you need to do to make sure, come Friday night, you have no doubt in your mind.

"You'll never be able to control nerves, they'll always be there. I still get them. Trust your ability, because these guys have shown what they're capable of and that doesn't change Friday night."

Sixteen years and 336 games is a long time to carry nerves around and they might be warranted this week given Gagai will be marking up on Latrell Mitchell, the apex predator of South Sydney's lethal left edge.

But Gagai learned how to turn those nerves into steel many years ago and he'll take a sense of certainty into his battle with Mitchell, where his physicality and decision-making will prove crucial to Newcastle's hopes of pulling off the upset.

"The nerves, for me, show that you care and you're worried about what could happen," Gagai said.

"But then you need to find out how to control what you can control. We know what Latrell is capable of, we know what Cody [Walker] is capable of, but I can't control what they do.

"I can only control what I do, how I go about things, what my actions are. That's one way to control those nerves, even if they'll always be there."

Dane Gagai still has plenty of mates at South Sydney. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

It'd be easy for Gagai to give into nostalgia this week of all weeks. He still has plenty of mates at South Sydney from his Rabbitoh days who he speaks with all the time. Gagai was shaking hands and slapping backs with a fair few of them at Jai Arrow's 100th NRL game last week.

He thinks Alex Johnston's record-breaking try this year was one of rugby league's best moments of the season and was proud to play a part in a few of them.

Gagai loves that he and his old teammates can fight like demons and have a laugh about it once the dust settles and the blood dries up, like he did after his memorable running battle with Cameron Munster in a match against the Storm earlier this year.

Perhaps he will swap jerseys with someone, as he has many times this year, building a collection he can one day see hanging on the walls and in which he can lose himself in memories.

But not yet. Gagai will not surrender himself to thinking of days past and the recollection of old friends and foes alike. There are still great things to come, he is sure of it.

Why Alex Johnston's record try was pure humanity After all the speculation, the fans stormed the field in the aftermath of Alex Johnston's record-breaking try and the result was an outpouring of emotion celebrating a once-in-a-lifetime achievement.

Gagai insists he has never given a single thought to retirement, or to how Friday could be his last game as a Knight, or to what awaits beyond his return to Brisbane, because to look back is to not be here and not being here is to be lost.

There is still plenty of fight in Gagai yet, especially if someone is going to call him old.

"It's that competitive side of me and I love that side, when people tell me something and I have a point to prove, not to anybody else, just to myself," Gagai said.

"Until I lose that passion, that motivation to compete and play our game, or if the body can't physically keep up, I'm not going to let anyone decide when I'm going to retire. That's my decision and my family's decision.

"I love playing rugby league, I love competing and I hate losing and I'm just glad I'm in this position where we can compete for a premiership."

World.title: Uganda pulls out of Invictus Games to avoid opposing King Charles's 'wishes'
World.content:
Uganda has withdrawn from the Invictus Games in order not to be construed as opposing King Charles's wishes, the country's defence force chief says.

The Invictus Games is an international event started by Prince Harry in 2014 for wounded, injured and sick military service people.

Muhoozi Kainerugaba says Uganda won't be participating in next year's Invictus Games for injured military veterans. (Reuters: Abubaker Lubowa)

General Muhoozi Kainerugaba, chief of Uganda's defence force and son of President Yoweri Museven, said in a post on X that Uganda would not participate in any event that did not have King Charles's approval.

"In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the Invictus Games," he said.

Back in the UK

Prince Harry and his wife Meghan Markle, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, returned to the United Kingdom in late August, six years after they moved to California amid tensions within the royal family.

In January 2020 the Duke and Duchess of Sussex announced that they would be stepping back from official royal duties.

On Tuesday, King Charles sent a letter to UK government and military officials saying that Harry and Meghan would not resume royal duties.

King clarifies Harry's status to government officials King Charles III has taken the unusual step of clarifying Prince Harry's status in a letter sent to government and military officials.

The Invictus Games have been held seven times since they were launched by Prince Harry, a military veteran, in 2014, including the 2018 edition in Sydney.

Last year the games were staged in Vancouver, Canada.

Veterans' services and mental health have become cornerstones of Harry and Meghan's philanthropy through their Archewell Foundation.

Harry's advocacy also includes visits with wounded military personnel, like last year's stop at a Ukrainian clinic that rehabilitates victims of war.

Prince Harry is a military veteran who started the Invictus Games to help former service members. (Reuters: Piroschka Van De Wouw/file photo)

Harry's British military service included two tours in Afghanistan.

He has credited his experience witnessing fellow soldiers' battlefield injuries with inspiring him to help injured veterans lead healthy lives.

Prince Harry and Meghan arrive back in UK Prince Harry and his wife Meghan arrive back in the UK with their two children, six years after they moved their lives to California amid simmering tensions within the royal family.

In a 2023 Netflix series he spoke openly about lacking the necessary emotional support upon his return from combat.

The participation of Uganda in the next games, to be held next year in Birmingham, was announced in July when Prince Harry was in London promoting the event.

In August, four members of the Ugandan boxing team reportedly failed to return home after competing in the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Ugandan sports website NBS Sport said the four athletes went missing in Scotland and had not rejoined the rest of the delegation before the team's scheduled return to Uganda.

ABC/AP

World.title: Premier says Olympic rowing concerns 'last hurrah' of 'naysayers'
World.content:
Queensland's top political brass has flown to Rockhampton to again attempt to quash any concerns around the city's accommodation capacity to host an Olympic sporting event.

The central Queensland city was last year announced as the host for rowing and canoeing for the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games but it has been subject to debate since.

On Thursday morning, amid a gathering of rowing fraternity, tourism bodies, sporting groups and local politicians, Premier David Crisafulli stood on the bank of the Fitzroy River to double down on his commitment that the state government "was not for turning" on this.

"It's about a region who deserves a fair share," he said.

"In many ways, this fight symbolises that.

"Central Queenslanders are going to prove a whole heap of people from interstate and overseas wrong because it will be world-class and it will be generational and there will be legacy."

International rowing bodies have questioned the location's suitability for competition. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

International and national rowing bodies have raised concerns over the river's suitability, most recently at last week's World Rowing congress in Amsterdam.

Mr Crisafulli labelled critics "naysayers" and said concerns raised over the past 12 months, including over the natural river course, flooding, crocodiles, infrastructure and racing conditions, had already been "debunked easily".

"Every so-called impediment that's been put up has been dismissed," he said.

"This is the last hurrah of people trying to find ways to discredit something that makes a hell of a lot of sense.

" We're not for turning on this. "

When questioned whether Rockhampton's selection was part of a strategy to shore up electorates in the region, the premier pointed to the many regions set to host events, including sailing in Townsville in the Whitsundays, equestrian in Toowoomba, football in Cairns, and archery in Maryborough.

The venue still needs approval from World Rowing. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

Accommodation concerns

This week, media outlets also reported on further concerns around a lack of accommodation in the city, citing complaints Rowing Queensland had received from parents struggling to find accommodation ahead of next weekend's Queensland Schools' Championship Regatta.

The region's peak tourism body, Capricorn Enterprise, has flagged in recent years the need for an extra 1,200 short-term accommodation rooms by 2032, for current and future demand, not including Olympic tourism requirements.

"We have lost short-term accommodation rooms to long-term rentals because of the housing shortage, [but] that's now starting to be relieved a bit because houses are coming out of the ground pretty quickly" the body's chief executive, Mary Carroll, said.

"We just don't have enough rooms. I'm desperate for more accommodation rooms in the next six years."

Tony Williams has thanked the state government for its support of Olympic rowing in the city. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie argued the Olympic event would drive investment in the accommodation sector, with planning work also underway for a 1,200-bed athlete's village.

Highlighting a shed at the rowing course, built after the Canadian Olympic team trained on the Fitzroy River ahead of the 2000 Sydney Olympics, he said the legacy would be long-lasting in terms of accommodation and housing.

"The campaign that's being run at the moment — that there's not enough accommodation — that same campaign was run months ago in Brisbane, that's why we're unlocking land," Mr Bleijie said.

Both men pointed to the city hosting Beef Australia every three years, which brought 125,000 extra people to the city.

Simon Irwin says the region is capable of hosting large-scale events. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

Beef Australia chief executive Simon Irwin said 35,000 people went through turnstiles of the event's first day.

"We do that in an environment where we have filled every possible piece of accommodation in central Queensland, almost down to Gladstone nowadays," Mr Irwin said.

He said he had been in contact with the Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority (GIICA) explaining the way the organisation handled the influx.

"The idea that we need to be able to place 25,000 people here is not new," he said.

"It happens on the first Monday in May every three years and we're more than happy to share that information and show that it can be done."

In previous years, the event has relied on residents renting out their homes for accommodation, temporary campsites near the event and even charter flights for day visits from other regional cities.

David Crisafulli says all technical assessments of the river are heading in the right direction. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

The venue still needs approval from the sport's governing body, World Rowing.

Mr Crisafulli reiterated his confidence in the river's suitability.

"The technical assessments are all heading in the right direction and that's repeatedly what we're being told," he said.

He also confirmed the results from the assessment would be made publicly available.

President of Rockhampton Fitzroy Rowing Club Sarah Black says the Olympics will bring great benefits to local rowers. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

World.title: Melbourne's NFL game is a battle of opposing jet lag strategies
World.content:
Two enormously well-resourced teams; two diametrically opposed strategies for managing one of the world's most arduous sporting road trips.

On Friday, the Los Angeles Rams will 'host' the San Francisco 49ers in the first NFL regular-season match played in Australia, at the local time of 10:35am in Melbourne.

That is 5:35pm on Thursday in Los Angeles, roughly equivalent to when a prime-time NFL fixture would kick off on the west coast of America.

Everything you need to know about NFL Melbourne The San Francisco 49ers are taking on the Los Angeles Rams at the MCG, the first NFL regular-season game to be held in Australia. Here's everything you need to know.

To prepare, the 49ers flew in a week earlier and have embarked on a series of PR appearances across the city — lauding local baristas and watching Geelong defeat Carlton in an AFL final — while the Rams arrived this morning, just 24 hours before the historic clash.

The Rams' strategy is not without precedent; last year they flew to London on the day of their game against the Jaguars and came away with a 35-7 win, returning home without needing to stay in a hotel.

The Los Angeles side will be hoping for a repeat of that result, only this time they will contend with a 16-hour flight and 17-hour time difference, and cannot avoid an overnight stay.

Both teams have opted to return as soon as possible after the game, as they prepare for week two fixtures back in the United States.

Only one strategy can prevail, with the NFL an invested onlooker.

NFL chief medical Officer Allen Sills is in Melbourne for the Rams and 49ers clash. (Getty Images: picture alliance/Maximilian Haupt)

Allen Sills, the NFL's chief medical officer, confirmed that both teams had engaged sleep experts to strategise on their approach, albeit with different outcomes.

"We don't have a league mandate [on what teams should do]," Dr Sills said.

"Frankly, it often has to do with how successful the team is. If the team did it one way and won, they'll tend to do that the next time they do it."

While the NFL is keeping a close eye on injury rates, Dr Sills said the league did not have enough data to prefer one strategy.

"We've tried to share data, but the problem is, we've had such a small number of injuries relative to the number of games that we have played [internationally], that we can't say, coming in this day versus that day is clearly different for injury.

"They're two very different approaches this year, so we're all interested in [the outcome]."

49ers using ‘gradual adjustment’ strategy

With two sets of experts advising the teams, the obvious question is: how did they come up with such different strategies?

"Each has a rationale, and either strategy is valid," said David Cunnington, an Australian-based sleep physician with over 20 years' experience in clinical practice.

The 49ers chose to acclimatise to Melbourne's time zone. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

As Dr Cunnington explained, teams can optimise performance in two ways: by syncing players' body clocks to their destination, or "keeping their body clocks in sync with their home time zone and just ducking out and playing the game in a different time zone, and then ducking back to their time zone".

The former strategy — favoured by the 49ers — requires time, a luxury most 'ordinary' travellers do not have.

"It's really going to be dependent on whether you have a spare week to acclimatise," Dr Cunnington said.

He has a 'rough and ready' rule for how many time zones you can adjust to per 24 hours.

If you are travelling west (going 'forward' in time) — such as from Los Angeles to Melbourne — you can theoretically adjust by two time zones per day.

So if Melbourne is seven time zones west of Los Angeles, you would need at least four days of adjustment time (the 49ers have allowed five).

Loading Instagram content

When choosing this strategy, Dr Cunnington advised having daily goals to incrementally adjust to the new time zone. For example, you might bring your bed and wake times forward by two hours per day.

Key to this working is adjusting your light exposure. As Dr Cunnington explained, you want to avoid exposure to light when it is your 'rest' or 'bed' time, and introduce artificial light when it is time to get up.

This is a strategy Dr Sills confirmed the NFL teams had employed.

"Our teams have engaged sleep experts to craft an individualised plan for the players starting from two weeks leading up to the game for how they should alter their sleep and light exposure," he said.

As examples, athletes may use devices like sleep masks or noise-cancelling headphones to minimise sensory input when they need to wind down or sleep, and blue light glasses to introduce light when they should be waking up.

Rams' strategy may have edge, says sleep expert

In the case of two major NFL franchises, both teams are working with significant budgets — including private jets — that allow them to control as many travel variables as possible.

Head coach Sean McVay and the LA Rams have left it as late as they could before arriving in Melbourne for their clash with the 49ers. (Getty Images: LA Times/Ronaldo Bolaños)

In the Rams' case, they have announced that players will be travelling on 'lie-flat' beds for their last-minute trip to Melbourne, alleviating one of travel's most burdensome problems: sleeping on a plane.

"People will definitely sleep better lying flat than propped upright," Dr Cunnington said, adding that this was mostly habitual.

However, it is not a foolproof strategy.

"Sleep loss is one of the challenges or cons of the Rams' strategy," he said.

"If you happen not to sleep well on the flight, you can't make that up if you're just flying in and out.

"Whereas for the 49ers, if they don't sleep well, they've got a week to acclimatise, have some naps, and make up that sleep."

Nonetheless, when pressed, Dr Cunnington said he would choose the Rams' strategy over the 49ers.

He justified this by saying it worked for the team previously, and they do not have to 're-adjust' to Los Angeles time once they return.

In addition, with the Melbourne game being played at 10:35am, they have the advantage of it being in a familiar local time slot.

"The 49ers are adjusting to Melbourne time, but when they're [back home] they wouldn't play 10am games. All their games are in the afternoon or evenings, so by acclimatising to Melbourne time, they're actually playing at a different time to what their body clocks are used to."

NFL monitoring injury risk associated with travel

Whatever the outcome, the NFL has invested significant resources into ensuring its players make it through the game unscathed.

They have employed 30 medical staff for game day, including 12 from The Alfred Hospital, to be on stand-by.

This is in part to appease the teams who make the long trek in the aim of sending the franchise international, with head of NFL International Gerrit Meier telling Reuters the players need to return "healthy" for the code to consider returning to Australia.

Dr Cunnington said there was some merit to the fear of player injury after a long-haul flight, and associated jet lag.

"There is an increased risk [of injury], but not directly," he said.

"It's not as if jet lag causes injury, but I like to think of it as a predisposition to clumsiness. Just not being quite as coordinated, and then via that mechanism, having a risk of injury."

Some — like 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan — have expressed cynicism about international travel, previously saying the San Franciscan team was "fired up" about having two international fixtures in one year.

"I think our coaches very much like routine and crave consistency of things, and international travel is always a variance," Dr Ellis said.

"What I would tell you is that we've seen players really enjoy the experience when they come over, and see the passion and energy of the fans and the enthusiasm of the countries we've been in.

"The league is always evaluating each venue, and there's so much that goes into that. Health and safety is an important part of that … we always look at injuries associated with international games, and that's an ongoing effort."

World.title: F1 debuts a new track with a corner so grand it is called Monumental
World.content:
Formula 1 debuts a new circuit to its calendar, and despite no grand prix raced yet, the Madring already boasts a corner that is poised to become an iconic scene in motorsport.

The Spanish Grand Prix has moved from Barcelona to the nation's capital, Madrid, with the brand-new Madring contracted to host the event until 2035.

Schumacher comparisons made as Antonelli continues historic F1 season Kimi Antonelli's win from 19th on the grid in Monza was epic, and the way his rivals raced with him has drawn comparisons with Ferrari legend Michael Schumacher.

The track uses a combination of public roads and private land and will at times reflect a street circuit, and other times a permanent race track.

But the defining feature of this 22-corner circuit is turn 12: La Monumental.

Turn 12 is a long, banked hairpin that promises to be unlike anything in F1 currently.

The 270-degree curve will have banking up to 13.5 degrees, not as dramatic as the 18-degrees of banking at Zandvoort, but this corner will be taken at much higher speed.

Williams driver Carlos Sainz drove around the circuit earlier this year in a Ford Mustang GT, and said he expects F1 cars to be flying around La Monumental.

"My feeling is the corner is going to be flat out the whole way, and it's going to create an overtaking opportunity into the next tight left," he said.

"The banking will allow you to maybe position the car higher up or lower down if you want to get clean air to follow.

"But if it's easy flat, then it will also be a corner where if you stay tight, you will produce quite a bit of slipstream, like you see in Zandvoort."

Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli enters this weekend with a 66-point lead in the drivers' championship over teammate George Russell, after a stunning win in Italy last Sunday despite starting 19th on the grid.

Australian Oscar Piastri is seventh in the drivers' championship, 151 points behind Antonelli, and placed fifth last Sunday at the Italian Grand Prix.

When is the Spanish Grand Prix, what time does the race begin?

This weekend's Spanish Grand Prix will be held on Sunday, September 13.

Here is when the race will begin in each state and territory.

World.title: Victoria's largest amateur football league denies 'gender bias' accusations
World.content:
Multiple Victorian Amateur Football Association (VAFA) clubs have expressed disappointment with how women's competitions are being handled this season, as players across the league say the women's competition is being treated as secondary.

The VAFA is the state's largest amateur Australian Rules football league with about 300 teams and 12,000 participants.

Last week, Fitzroy Football Club and St Mary's Salesian released public statements expressing disappointment over two separate incidents that affected their finals campaigns.

Fitzroy celebrated its final home-and-away season win, believing the victory put it into the top four and its first finals series of the premier women's division.

However, the league had declared an earlier season game between two other clubs, St Kevin's and Kew, "abandoned" due to an ineligible player, and recalculated the match ratio for the teams, putting Fitzroy outside the four.

The club said it was "bitterly disappointed" not just with how the league managed the competition, but with its communication with clubs.

"To say we are frustrated with the decision is an understatement," Fitzroy said in its statement.

"We're incredibly proud of their season and all they have achieved. The same cannot be said for the VAFA's handling of this matter, and it goes to a concern that this premier women's competition is not being as well run as it should be.

"The fact the top tier of the VAFA has only nine teams creates a situation such as this to occur. As one of the top levels of women's football in Australia, it beggars belief that an odd number of teams are in the division. Would this happen in the men's premier competition?"

Loading Instagram content

Fitzroy president David Leydon said the club took great pride in playing in the premier women's division, "a very prestigious competition" that has taken them a long time to get into.

He said making finals was a big moment for the club

"And to have that ripped away from us courtesy of an arrangement that we were unaware of until after our last game, I was heartbroken," Leydon said.

He said the abandoned game should have been communicated to all other clubs in the competition.

Earlier in division two, St Mary's Salesian won an important preliminary final but were later disqualified after a player was ruled ineligible for finals.

The St Mary's player had only played two home-and-away games instead of the required three, following a rule change that year.

VAFA changed the requirement to three games at the start of the season and updated its website. But St Mary's claim PlayHQ, the platform the VAFA runs every fixture, team list and season through, still stated the old eligibility requirement for division two women's finals as two in-season games, upon which the club relied.

St Mary's said it would never have selected an ineligible player in a final had they known.

Loading Instagram content

The player missed most of the season due to maternity leave.

The club says it was not notified of the rule change, and that the men's eligibility rule was updated on PlayHQ this year, but the women's was not.

VAFA's response

VAFA strongly refuted any "any gender bias" in applying the competition rules.

It said the club statements, and subsequent social media comments on the posts, brought the integrity of the competition into question and framed the issues as being gender-based.

"Whilst we understand the emotions that such commentary provokes, the inaccuracy of these club statements is misleading and being considered by the board for potential breaches of the VAFA's policies," the VAFA told the ABC.

It said the ineligible St Kevin's player was never a matter that would affect Fitzroy's ladder position or qualification for finals, so Fitzroy was not involved in the initial enquiries into the game result.

VAFA CEO Jason Reddick said he was in touch with Fitzroy on the Sunday of round 18, the final home-and-away round, both over the phone and in writing.

Fitzroy asked for an investigation into the matter on the Monday. The VAFA looked into it and released its findings on the Friday, the day before the finals series commenced.

In response to Fitzroy asking if something similar would happen in the men's, the league said it was not a fair question.

"This is not a gender-based issue," it said.

"The matter is about the VAFA Rules pertaining to the playing of an ineligible player. We have the example of stripping reigning Premiers Uni Blues of all their points and fining them $22k for playing ineligible players in their Premier Men's team in 2022, so there is clearly no gender bias when it comes to applying the Rules of the VAFA competition."

Regarding St Mary's statement, the league said member clubs presented and voted on any rule changes each year, so all clubs knew the finals eligibility rules at the start of the season.

It also said it sent out a reminder ahead of the finals through its portal to all clubs.

'Just looks like flat-out discriminatory'

Multiple women's players across various VAFA clubs, who wished to remain anonymous due to fear of repercussions from the league, said they were not aware of the finals eligibility rule changes this year.

One player from a premier women's side said the women's competitions were treated "1,000 per cent" like an afterthought, particularly in fixturing, scheduling and grounds.

More women are playing footy than ever before. Why are so many leaving? The women's team from Kyneton's 15-month public and bitter saga suggests it is the canary in the coal mine of a widespread issue for women's players across the country.

She gave the examples of the women's division one, two and three having their grand finals at 9:40am, 9:20am and 9:20am respectively last weekend, which she said was "just awful".

The men's competitions received their fixtures months in advance, whereas the women received theirs just weeks before their season starts, she said.

"I think if it was like at least some of the men's teams got s*** locations and times, it would be slightly more understandable, because I know that obviously the council plays a big part in that [and)]in getting access to grounds at certain times. But it just looks like flat-out discriminatory," she said.

She said the issues around player eligibility also came down to broad structural issues within women's football, where clubs were often low on volunteers and didn't receive "a whole lot of help or guidance from VAFA about how to deal with situations".

Fitzroy says it is frustrated with the league. (Supplied: Fitzroy Football Club)

"That's another issue with, and this is not VAFA's fault, but by default, women have less community support and less money, less financial support, which means that the burden often feels heavier on women's teams to make sure that they're on top of all of this admin," she said.

"It's normally someone random who has no idea how football works, who's doing the team management stuff, which is checking who the players are and if they've got their correct numbers and all of that admin that goes towards eligibility and selection and reporting and all of the flow and stuff.

"So I do think that there's also a bit of like a burden on VAFA also to make more of an active effort to communicate changes, knowing that like this is all volunteer-run clubs."

Earlier this year, the ABC reported that VAFA women's players found issues with inequitable resourcing and fixturing by the league.

'Very under-resourced'

A source who has worked in senior administrative roles across different VAFA clubs, and who wished to remain anonymous for fear of repercussions at their club, said there were many issues with how the women's competitions were run.

"Firstly … it's tough for them. I think they're very under-resourced," they said.

"They're essentially set up as a men's competition traditionally and historically, and they've added women, you know, 10 years ago. And so that's always going to come with a need for serious transition and a need for serious recalibration."

Fitzroy says the club was heartbroken to learn it didn't qualify for the finals. (Supplied: Fitzroy Football Club)

They said there wasn't a clear strategy for the women's competition, pointed to "anomalies" across the competition, highlighted "fixture mistakes", and said, "we're having administrators at the VAFA giving wrong information to clubs".

"So that's just a reflection of, well, they're not resourcing it enough, and they're not actually prioritising women's footy in their strategic goals and operations, and it's reflected in the under-resourcing, which means you have these mistakes," they said.

Leydon said after Fitzroy released its public statement, the support was overwhelming, including from other clubs in the league.

"Hopefully it turns into something positive, and we can try and fix the way the women's program is conducted and get everyone to take it a lot more seriously," he said.

Tech.title: The Trump phone just got a $250 price hike
Tech.content:
is a news editor with over a decade’s experience in journalism. He previously worked at Android Police and Tech Advisor.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Bad news if you didn’t lock in a Trump phone at launch: It now costs $749, a $250 increase on its price at launch. The T1 Phone itself hasn’t changed.

Trump Mobile didn’t announce the price increase, instead quietly changing its website overnight. This wasn’t a total surprise though, especially given the phone ships with an unexpectedly generous 512GB of storage and 12GB of RAM. When I spoke to two Trump Mobile executives earlier this year, they called the $499 launch pricing “introductory,” and a few months later, the website itself was changed to reflect that, calling it a “promotional price.” That wording is now gone.

Related I spent a year trying to figure out if the Trump phone is a scam

To my surprise, my Trump phone has received some support since it launched. There’s been exactly one software update, moving it from Android’s February 2026 security patch to the May 2026 version. It’s still running Android 15 though, which is now two years old.

While the Trump phone officially started shipping in May, almost a year after it was announced, it remains unclear just how many customers have received their phones. A report from the BBC last month found that at least some buyers still say their phones never arrived.

Tech.title: Nintendo’s latest Switch 2 update adds VRR support in TV mode
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Nintendo always promised that the Switch 2 would support variable refresh rate (VRR) when docked, but the console launched without this key feature. A new 23.0.0 firmware update now adds VRR support to the Switch 2 when it’s docked and in TV mode.

VRR adjusts a display’s refresh rate to match a game’s frame rate, smoothing out gameplay and reducing screen tearing. It will be particularly useful for games on the Switch 2 that have an unstable frame rate, and it’s a feature that the PS5 and Xbox Series S / X all support.

The latest Switch 2 firmware also includes a new toggle for handheld boost mode in quick settings, as well as an update to the Mii editor that lets you enable music for some nostalgic Wii, 3DS, or Wii U Mii creation. Nintendo has also added the ability to perform a full system transfer from one Switch 2 console to another, just in time for a Zelda-themed Switch 2 next month.

Tech.title: Xbox picks up Kojima’s Physint after PlayStation dropped it
Tech.content:
is a news editor with over a decade’s experience in journalism. He previously worked at Android Police and Tech Advisor.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Xbox will now publish Physint, an upcoming game from Metal Gear creator Hideo Kojima, after PlayStation decided to cancel it.

The unexpected swap came in a flurry of announcements from PlayStation, Xbox, Kojima Productions, and Kojima himself. Sony, which published both of Kojima Productions’ previous Death Stranding games, framed it as a “difficult decision to step away from collaborating with Kojima Productions,” but insisted their “relationship remains strong.”

Kojima put things more bluntly on his personal X account, claiming that Sony gave the studio an unexpected cancellation notice in June, and that it has spent the last three months “searching tirelessly” for a new publishing partner. He called Xbox “a partner with whom we share a common vision for the future.” It might have helped that the two companies are already working together, with Xbox lined up to publish the studio’s next game, OD.

“Creators have choices about where and how they bring their ideas to life,” said Xbox CEO Asha Sharma in a statement. “We’re honored that Kojima-san has chosen Xbox to work with Kojima Productions on Physint. His ambition to challenge conventions reflects the kind of creativity we want to support at Xbox.” Securing a title of Physint’s stature reflects the priorities Sharma laid out in a memo to Xbox staff this summer, promising a focus on “our strongest franchises and biggest new ideas.”

The Xbox announcement also notes that the relationship between the two companies will “extend beyond games,” with plans in the works across film and television, though no further details were given. Kojima Productions first announced plans for TV and film projects back in 2021, so far resulting in two upcoming Death Stranding adaptations: an animated spin-off called Mosquito and a live action adaptation from the director of Pig.

Kojima calls Physint a “genre-defining action-espionage title,” prompting hopes that it will serve as a spiritual successor to his Metal Gear series, though it’s not expected to launch until at least 2030. OD also has no release date, but should arrive sooner — the horror title was announced in 2022, and a first trailer dropped this time last year.

Tech.title: Volvo XC40 PHEV is back with a new look, better sensors, and Gemini AI
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

It’s been about three years since Volvo discontinued its plug-in hybrid XC40. The mild hybrid version remains on sale in the US and elsewhere, alongside the electric EX40. Today, Volvo announced it was bringing back the PHEV version and giving it a major facelift. When it arrives at dealerships early next year, the new XC40 will have updated exterior styling, a gut-renovated interior featuring Google’s Gemini AI assistant, enlarged infotainment screen, and a new sensor-and-software safety suite.

As a hybrid, the XC40 serves as a bridge for customers who want better gas mileage but aren’t ready for the pure EV lifestyle. Volvo itself needs that bridge, after backing down from its pledge to sell only EVs by 2030. That said, the automaker didn’t divulge any details about the powertrain, engine options, electric motor, range, or battery capacity for the XC40 — so we’ll have to wait and see whether this SUV can sufficiently compete in an increasingly cutthroat hybrid market.

On the surface, we’ve got a new take on Volvo’s signature “Thor’s Hammer” LED headlights, as well as an updated front grille, bumper, hood and front wings. Same goes for the rear: new lighting, new bumper, and an upgraded tailgate. Additionally, the XC40 is getting a trio of diamond-cut wheel options, available in 18-, 19-, and 20-inch sizes.

Previous Next











1 / 7

But the interior is where the meat of Volvo’s improvements comes through. The screen has been bumped up to a higher resolution and a larger, 11.2-inch size. It will run Volvo’s latest user interface, which the automaker designed for faster navigation with fewer taps. Google’s Gemini serves as the voice assistant, using its big AI brain to plan routes, find specific locations and detours, and manage messages. The XC40 rounds it out with an improved wireless phone charger and smart storage solutions.

What about safety? This is a Volvo after all, the automaker most committed to Safety (at least according to its well-cultivated reputation). Don’t worry, the XC40 ups the ante in that department with a new software and sensor platform that’s designed to provide real-time collision avoidance, automated emergency steering, and automatic emergency braking.

The sensor upgrade includes new front and corner radars, a new front camera, new rear corner radars, 12 new ultrasonic sensors, and new parking cameras. Cloaked in this new sensor suite, the XC40 is getting a host of new safety capabilities, including new door opening alerts that warn occupants before dooring passing cyclists, lane change assist and smoother lane following support on long drives, and an optional 3D/360-degree camera to simplify low-speed maneuvering and parking.

Previous Next





1 / 4

The ultimate goal is to build a better XC40 — one that’s safer and more capable, which hopefully translates to better sales numbers and a long, continuous shelf life for Volvo’s tiny SUV.

“By enhancing the XC40’s design, technology and safety features, we’ve created the best version of the XC40 yet,” says Akhil Krishnan, Interim Lead for the 30 and 40 Series at Volvo Cars, in a statement. “This already popular model is now set to continue being one of our best-selling cars for years to come.”

Tech.title: There aren’t AirPods with cameras yet and I hope it stays that way
Tech.content:
September Apple events are always a swirl of information and new, exciting products, and today’s was no different. Apple announced its first foldable, the iPhone Duo, alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max; active noise cancellation (ANC) is now on the cheapest AirPods model, the AirPods 5; and a Siri Recap feature comes to the Watch Series 12 and Watch Ultra 4. But missing were the AirPods Pro with cameras that have been rumored throughout the year and, according to Mark Gurman at Bloomberg, are delayed until 2027. I’m happy about that and I hope we never get them.

I have too many concerns about a company — any company — putting cameras anywhere, especially in devices like earbuds that are now so ubiquitous in our daily lives. LED lights on glasses or earbuds do little to ease people’s minds when someone is recording them. And some Meta smart glasses users have shown people will hide their recording intentions. While recording in public in the US is generally legal, it can be very creepy. And with earbuds as common as they are, someone could wear them into sensitive situations unnoticed.

Rumors say that the cameras on the potential AirPods will be low-resolution and “aren’t designed” to take images or video, but instead use what they see to inform Siri AI and Visual Intelligence. That information could be used to help with turn-by-turn directions or identify writing and objects like books. Even with a low-resolution camera, it’s still potentially always gathering information about the world (and people!) around you. That invasion of privacy is something I cannot get past.

During today’s event, Apple introduced Audio Intelligence with the Apple Watch, which sounds like a precursor to the Visual Intelligence we’re expecting on the rumored AirPods Pro 4. In its support documentation, Apple points out that audio is not stored and there’s no way to access a recording, which could be the same for video data with Visual Intelligence, and that for its Siri Recap feature, any data used to create a summary is not even accessible by Apple. Any stored data — such as a Siri Recap or a bit of text the user can save with Live Rewind — is also end-to-end encrypted. People are not identified in the Siri Recap, either. Of course, none of this is live yet, so we’ll have to wait and see how well Audio Intelligence works once it’s released.

Functionally, a camera will only gather information if it can see things. What if you have thick, long hair? Or like to wear hoodie sweatshirts? Or fancy, elaborate jewelry? The AirPods would just turn into what they should be — earbuds. It’s possible the reason the AirPods with cameras have been pushed into 2027 is to find solutions to these problems. Or maybe part of the delay is Apple separating itself from the current public climate around cameras thanks to Meta and Flock.

The one immediate benefit of the AirPods with cameras could be accessibility. They could improve situational awareness for people with visual limitations or help hard-of-hearing users read lips. They could even figure out the person you’re speaking to and focus the AirPods’ mics on them for increased intelligibility.

When you take out privacy concerns or the fact that lots of people — and companies — look for opportunities to exploit people, there’s good that can be done. But it involves a lot of trust to be put in untrustworthy hands. I’m not sure I’m ready for that. Or if I ever will be. Whether any of us are ready or not, though, it seems the cameras are coming. The introduction of Apple’s Audio Intelligence on the new Apple Watch is evidence enough that the company is going all in on using sensors to analyze the world around us.

Tech.title: The black iPhone Pro returns
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple has seen reason: It has a black model in the iPhone Pro lineup again.

Last year, Apple went bold with its colors for the iPhone 17 Pro, offering a flashy orange, a shiny silver, and a dark blue. Don’t get me wrong, they looked nice. But there was no black (or dark gray) for the first time since the start of the iPhone Pro lineup, which Apple first introduced in September 2019 with the iPhone 11 Pro and Pro Max.

I care about this because I always buy the black phone. I learned my lesson with the iPhone 6: I got it in gold to mix things up and came to regret it. I don’t need something flashy — I need a phone that blends into the background and looks decent in whatever case I throw it into. After the iPhone 6, my next phone was the iPhone 7 in the excellent matte black (I wasn’t brave enough to endure the jet black model’s potential scratches), and I’ve only ever gotten the black or gray phones since.

My black titanium iPhone 16 Pro in a black Torras case (with a mostly black homescreen) still works very well, thank you very much, and I’m not in the market for a new phone. But when I make my annual mid-September visit to the local Apple Store to look at all the new iPhones, I won’t be rushing to see the iPhone 18 Pro in burgundy, blue, or silver. I’ll be beelining for the model in black.
